track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Accumulated deliberate practice explains a minority of variance in sport performance, not the majority: 18% of variance in sports in the pooled estimate.
effect_or_estimate: Deliberate practice accounted for 18% of variance in sport performance
boxing_specific: No - cross-sport, boxing not separately reported
transfer_status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED - cross-sport meta-analytic estimate
limitations: Retrospective practice-history designs; 'deliberate practice' operationalised broadly and inconsistently across primary studies; correlational, not causal.
citation: Macnamara BN, Moreau D, Hambrick DZ. The Relationship Between Deliberate Practice and Performance in Sports: A Meta-Analysis. Perspect Psychol Sci. 2016.
ppbf_implication: SHADOW must NOT model development as hours-accumulated. Practice volume is one predictor among many; route logic needs quality, readiness, individual-difference and opportunity variables alongside volume.
verified_title: The Relationship Between Deliberate Practice and Performance in Sports: A Meta-Analysis.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Among elite-level performers specifically, accumulated deliberate practice accounted for only 1% of performance variance - practice volume does not discriminate within an already-selected elite group.
effect_or_estimate: 1% of variance in performance among elite-level performers
limitations: Range restriction in elite samples mechanically shrinks variance explained; this is a statistical artefact risk, not proof practice is unimportant at elite level. Contested by Ericsson (2016).
citation: Macnamara BN, Moreau D, Hambrick DZ. Perspect Psychol Sci. 2016.
ppbf_implication: Do not use training-hours totals as a selection or progression gate for advanced PPBF athletes. Rank athletes on demonstrated skill and assessment evidence, not logged hours.
verified_title: The Relationship Between Deliberate Practice and Performance in Sports: A Meta-Analysis.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: The claim that deliberate practice largely determines expertise is actively contested: Ericsson argues Macnamara et al. summed hours of any practice type rather than isolating structured, feedback-rich, individually-targeted practice.
effect_or_estimate: No pooled estimate - definitional dispute over what counts as deliberate practice
limitations: The dispute is definitional as much as empirical. Neither side has boxing-specific longitudinal data.
citation: Ericsson KA. Summing Up Hours of Any Type of Practice Versus Identifying Optimal Practice Activities. Perspect Psychol Sci. 2016; and Macnamara BN, Hambrick DZ, Moreau D. How Important Is Deliberate Practice? Reply to Ericsson. Perspect Psychol Sci. 2016.
ppbf_implication: SHADOW's practice-log schema must distinguish practice TYPE (coach-targeted, feedback-present, individualised vs general participation) - the two sides of this dispute cannot even be adjudicated without that field. This is a concrete data-model requirement.
verified_title: Summing Up Hours of Any Type of Practice Versus Identifying Optimal Practice Activities: Commentary on Macnamara, Moreau, & Hambrick (2016).

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: The original deliberate-practice framework specified individualised tasks with a clear performance goal and immediate informative feedback, supervised by a teacher - not merely repetition volume.
effect_or_estimate: No effect size claimed here - definitional
transfer_status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED; boxing-specific deliberate practice studies not located
limitations: Original evidence base is music, not sport; retrospective diary methods.
citation: Ericsson KA, Krampe RT, Tesch-Romer C. The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance. Psychol Rev. 1993;100:363-406.
ppbf_implication: PPBF session-quality scoring should encode the four original ingredients as separate observable fields: individualised target, explicit performance goal, feedback present, coach supervision. Maps to Module 196 Session Quality Score.
verified_title: The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: The most comprehensive pro-external-focus meta-analysis reports an external focus outperforms an internal focus for motor performance and for retention and transfer learning.
population: Mixed lab and applied motor tasks
effect_or_estimate: Hedges g = 0.264 (95% CI 0.217-0.310) performance; g = 0.583 (95% CI 0.425-0.741) retention; g = 0.584 (95% CI 0.325-0.842) transfer; age, health status and skill level did not moderate
boxing_specific: No - combat-sport studies not analysed separately
transfer_status: Transfer to boxing PARTIAL - a boxing-specific acute trial exists (see A1-008)
limitations: Superseded in part by a bias-corrected reanalysis (see A1-006). Predominantly single-session lab tasks; retention intervals typically 24h-1wk, far shorter than a boxing development cycle.
citation: Chua LK, Jimenez-Diaz J, Lewthwaite R, Kim T, Wulf G. Superiority of external attentional focus for motor performance and learning: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Psychol Bull. 2021;147:618-645.
ppbf_implication: External-focus cues are a REASONABLE DEFAULT for the PPBF cue library, but the library must not be built on the assumption that this effect is large or settled. Tag every cue with focus_type so PPBF can test it locally.
verified_title: Superiority of external attentional focus for motor performance and learning: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: A robust Bayesian reanalysis of the same external-focus data found moderate-to-strong evidence of publication bias in every analysis; after bias correction the mean effects were negligible.
population: Same underlying studies as prior meta-analyses
study_design: Robust Bayesian meta-analysis and systematic review, reanalysis of 7 prior meta-studies
sample_size: Same source data as the 7 prior meta-studies
effect_or_estimate: Bias-corrected g = 0.01 (performance), 0.15 (retention), 0.09 (transfer), 0.06 (electromyography), -0.01 (distance effect); Bayes factors favoured the null
limitations: Bias-correction models are themselves modelling assumptions and can over-correct; this is a reanalysis, not new data. Both this and A1-005 are legitimate readings of a biased literature.
citation: McKay B, Corson AE, Seedu J, De Faveri CS, Hasan H, Arnold K, et al. Reporting bias, not external focus: A robust Bayesian meta-analysis and systematic review of the external focus of attention literature. Psychol Bull. 2024;150:1347-1362.
ppbf_implication: SHADOW must NOT present 'use external cues' as validated science with a known effect size. Present it as a defensible default with contested evidence, and make the cue library A/B-testable inside PPBF.
verified_title: Reporting bias, not external focus: A robust Bayesian meta-analysis and systematic review of the external focus of attention literature.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: OPTIMAL theory proposes enhanced expectancies, autonomy support and external focus jointly improve learning by strengthening goal-action coupling.
effect_or_estimate: No pooled estimate - theoretical proposal
limitations: Two of the three OPTIMAL pillars have failed in preregistered tests (see A1-009, A1-010) and the third is bias-contested (A1-006). Treat the integrated theory as unconfirmed.
citation: Wulf G, Lewthwaite R. Optimizing performance through intrinsic motivation and attention for learning: The OPTIMAL theory of motor learning. Psychon Bull Rev. 2016;23:1382-1414.
ppbf_implication: Do not encode OPTIMAL theory as SHADOW's governing model of learning. Its components must be separately represented and separately validated.
verified_title: Optimizing performance through intrinsic motivation and attention for learning: The OPTIMAL theory of motor learning.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: In trained boxers and kickboxers, external-focus instructions produced faster and more forceful punches than internal-focus instructions in an acute single-session test.
sex: Not stated in abstract; described as trained combat athletes
effect_or_estimate: External vs internal focus: 4% faster and 5% more forceful (P<0.05); external vs control: 2% faster and 3% more forceful (P<0.05)
boxing_specific: YES - boxers and kickboxers, punch outcome measures
limitations: ACUTE PERFORMANCE, NOT LEARNING - no retention or transfer test. Small n. Punch integrator, not a live opponent. Effects are single-digit percentages.
citation: Halperin I, Chapman DW, Martin DT, Abbiss C, Wulf G. The effects of attentional focus instructions on punching velocity and impact forces among trained combat athletes. J Sports Sci. 2016;35:500-507.
verification: pubmed:PMID 27088370; crossref DOI resolved (J Sports Sci 35:500-507)
ppbf_implication: This is the strongest boxing-specific cue evidence available and it is an acute-performance finding. SHADOW may recommend external cues at the point of execution (bag/pad/bout) with an explicit 'acute performance, retention untested' label.
verified_title: The effects of attentional focus instructions on punching velocity and impact forces among trained combat athletes.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: The self-controlled practice literature shows a moderate naive benefit that does not survive bias assessment: published and unpublished findings differ significantly and the literature lacks evidential value.
effect_or_estimate: Naive random-effects g = 0.44 (95% CI 0.31-0.56); significant published/unpublished difference; authors conclude underpowered, biased, lacking evidential value
limitations: Bias-correction inference, not new trials. Does not prove autonomy support is useless - it shows the evidence cannot currently support the claim.
citation: McKay B, Yantha ZD, Hussien J, Carter MJ, Ste-Marie DM. Meta-Analytic Findings of the Self-Controlled Motor Learning Literature: Underpowered, Biased, and Lacking Evidential Value. Meta-Psychology. 2022.
verification: crossref DOI resolved (Meta-Psychology, 2022); abstract retrieved via Crossref
ppbf_implication: Athlete choice in PPBF (e.g. letting an athlete pick a drill variant) should be justified on engagement, adherence and athlete-voice grounds - which is defensible - NOT as a validated learning accelerator.
verified_title: Meta-Analytic Findings of the Self-Controlled Motor Learning Literature: Underpowered, Biased, and Lacking Evidential Value

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: A preregistered trial found autonomy-supportive instructional language raised perceived autonomy but produced no group difference in skill acquisition or retention versus controlling language.
effect_or_estimate: No group differences in motor performance at acquisition or retention; no differences in perceived competence or intrinsic motivation
limitations: Single laboratory task (cup stacking); a null on one task does not generalise to all coaching language effects, and coaching language plausibly matters for retention in the sport sense (staying in the gym).
citation: St Germain L, McKay B, Barbera L, Tandon C, Seedu J, Carrillo C, et al. Autonomy-supportive instructional language does not enhance skill acquisition compared to controlling instructional language. Psychol Res. 2024.
ppbf_implication: Separate two SHADOW outcome families: SKILL outcomes and ENGAGEMENT/RETENTION outcomes. Supportive language should be justified and measured against the second, not credited to the first.
verified_title: Autonomy-supportive instructional language does not enhance skill acquisition compared to controlling instructional language.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: The contextual interference effect is a genuine live dispute in the current literature, with two 2023-2024 meta-analyses reaching opposite headline conclusions and a published rebuttal exchange continuing into 2025.
study_design: Competing systematic reviews with meta-analysis plus commentary exchange
sample_size: See constituent rows A1-012 to A1-014
effect_or_estimate: Opposite conclusions; no single defensible pooled number for applied sport
limitations: Any product that states a single CI recommendation as settled science is misrepresenting the field as of 2026.
citation: Ammar A, et al. Educ Res Rev. 2023;39:100537; Czyz SH, et al. Sci Rep. 2024;14; Ammar A, et al. Educ Psychol Rev. 2024;36; Ammar A, et al. Educ Psychol Rev. 2025;37.
verification: crossref DOIs resolved for all four; pubmed:PMID 38987617 for Czyz 2024; web_search 2026-08-07 confirmed the published commentary exchange
ppbf_implication: SHADOW's practice-design engine must expose practice-schedule choice as a COACH DECISION with the dispute surfaced, not as an algorithmic recommendation. Maps to Module 061 Practice Design Engine.
verified_title: The Effects of Contextual Interference Learning on the Acquisition and Relatively Permanent Gains in Skilled Performance: A Critical Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-Analysis
title_consistency_check: MANUALLY REVIEWED — author-year or multi-source citation, record confirmed

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: One meta-analysis found no evidence supporting contextual interference effects in sport settings: acquisition, retention and transfer performance were unaffected by practice schedule.
effect_or_estimate: No significant schedule effect at acquisition, retention or transfer; subgroup analysis identified only constrained conditions where CI appeared
limitations: Methodology criticised in print by Czyz et al. (2024) for database selection and lack of preregistration; authors responded in 2025.
citation: Ammar A, Trabelsi K, Boujelbane MA, Boukhris O, Glenn JM, Chtourou H, Schollhorn WI. The myth of contextual interference learning benefit in sports practice: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Educ Res Rev. 2023;39:100537.
verification: crossref DOI resolved; publisher abstract confirmed via web_search 2026-08-07
ppbf_implication: Counts as direct evidence AGAINST hard-coding random practice as superior in a gym setting.
verified_title: The myth of contextual interference learning benefit in sports practice: A systematic review and meta-analysis

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: A competing meta-analysis found a medium beneficial retention effect of high contextual interference overall, but reported the benefit as almost negligible in APPLIED settings and negligible and non-significant in YOUNG participants.
population: Motor learning participants across settings and ages
study_design: Systematic review with three-level mixed model and random-effects meta-analysis
sample_size: 1,255 records; 294 full texts screened; 54 studies in meta-analysis
effect_or_estimate: High CI medium beneficial effect overall and statistically significant; effective in laboratory settings; almost negligible in applied settings; large effect in older adults, medium in adults, negligible and non-significant in young participants
limitations: Contains a sharply-worded methodological attack on the competing review, answered in print. The applied-setting and young-participant subgroup findings are the operationally relevant ones for PPBF and both point away from a benefit.
citation: Czyz SH, Wojcik AM, Solarska P, Kiper P. High contextual interference improves retention in motor learning: systematic review and meta-analysis. Sci Rep. 2024;14.
verification: pubmed:PMID 38987617 (full abstract retrieved); crossref DOI resolved
ppbf_implication: CRITICAL FOR PPBF: even the pro-CI meta-analysis reports the effect is near-zero in applied settings and near-zero in young participants - which is exactly PPBF's population and setting. Do not sell random practice to PPBF coaches as evidence-based for youth.
verified_title: High contextual interference improves retention in motor learning: systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: A multilevel meta-analysis in physical-education and sport contexts found only 20% of pooled outcomes agreed with the paradoxical CI prediction and no significant pre-to-post difference between blocked and random schedules.
study_design: Critical systematic review with multilevel meta-analysis
sample_size: 933 records screened; 36 studies included; 183 pooled outcomes
effect_or_estimate: 37 of 183 outcomes (20%) agreed with the paradoxical CI effect; delta pre-post low CI 28.9 +/- 59.5% vs high CI 27.9 +/- 52.8%, no significant difference
limitations: Very large SDs on the delta estimates indicate extreme heterogeneity; the percentages are descriptive change scores, not standardised effects.
citation: Ammar A, Trabelsi K, Boujelbane MA, Salem A, Boukhris O, Glenn JM, et al. The Effects of Contextual Interference Learning on the Acquisition and Relatively Permanent Gains in Skilled Performance: A Critical Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educ Psychol Rev. 2024;36.
verification: crossref DOI resolved; abstract retrieved via Crossref
ppbf_implication: Supports a middle path: vary practice for engagement and representativeness reasons, but do not promise a retention dividend from randomisation.
verified_title: The Effects of Contextual Interference Learning on the Acquisition and Relatively Permanent Gains in Skilled Performance: A Critical Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-Analysis

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: A gradually increasing interference schedule (blocked, then serial, then random) produced better retention than either blocked or random scheduling, and better transfer in the second experiment.
population: Novices learning golf putting and basketball passes
effect_or_estimate: Increasing schedule superior on retention (Exp 1, golf putting); superior on retention and transfer vs blocked and random (Exp 2, three basketball passes)
transfer_status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED - but the progression logic maps naturally onto boxing technical progressions
limitations: Small single-lab experiments, novices, closed skills. Not replicated at scale.
citation: Porter JM, Magill RA. Systematically increasing contextual interference is beneficial for learning sport skills. J Sports Sci. 2010;28:1277-1285.
ppbf_implication: PROPOSED PPBF DESIGN RULE: progress blocked -> serial -> random within a technical block rather than choosing one schedule. This is a reasonable, testable structure for the session builder (Module 007) - label as proposed, not validated in boxing.
verified_title: Systematically increasing contextual interference is beneficial for learning sport skills.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Serial practice and random practice produce equivalent retention and transfer, so serial is not a lower-interference midpoint on the retention outcome.
effect_or_estimate: Serial and random practice showed the same retention and transfer results
limitations: Only 9 studies; small evidence base.
citation: Lage GM, Faria LO, Ambrosio NFA, Borges AMP, Apolinario-Souza T. What Is the Level of Contextual Interference in Serial Practice? A Meta-Analytic Review. J Mot Learn Dev. 2022;10:224-242.
verification: crossref DOI resolved (J Mot Learn Dev 10:224-242); abstract retrieved via Crossref
ppbf_implication: If PPBF implements the increasing-CI progression (A1-015), the serial stage should be justified as a coaching scaffold, not as a distinct interference dose.
verified_title: What Is the Level of Contextual Interference in Serial Practice? A Meta-Analytic Review

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Differential learning has been evaluated only in an exploratory meta-analytic review with high heterogeneity; it is not established as superior to other methods.
population: Mixed motor learning and sport participants
effect_or_estimate: High overall heterogeneity reported for the acquisition phase; authors describe the analysis as exploratory and note controversy around DL theory
limitations: Small literature concentrated in a limited number of research groups; heterogeneity limits pooling; authors themselves label the analysis exploratory.
citation: Tassignon B, Verschueren J, Baeyens JP, Benjaminse A, Gokeler A, Serrien B, Clijsen R. An Exploratory Meta-Analytic Review on the Empirical Evidence of Differential Learning as an Enhanced Motor Learning Method. Front Psychol. 2021;12:533033.
ppbf_implication: Differential learning must be labelled EXPERIMENTAL in the PPBF constraint library (Module 060). It may be offered to coaches as an option to trial, with mandatory outcome capture - never as a recommended default.
verified_title: An Exploratory Meta-Analytic Review on the Empirical Evidence of Differential Learning as an Enhanced Motor Learning Method.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: The theoretical basis of differential learning is deliberate movement-pattern noise and stochastic perturbation, i.e. never repeating the same movement, which is the direct opposite of technical-model repetition coaching.
effect_or_estimate: No effect estimate
limitations: Author-advocated framework; the same author group co-authored one side of the contextual interference dispute, so independence of the DL evidence base is limited.
citation: Schollhorn WI, Hegen P, Davids K. The Nonlinear Nature of Learning - A Differential Learning Approach. Open Sports Sci J. 2012;5:100-112.
verification: crossref DOI resolved (Open Sports Sci J, 2012)
ppbf_implication: If PPBF trials DL, the boxing safety envelope must be set first: deliberate movement noise near the head, on the inside, or in sparring is a safety question, not just a pedagogy question. Route to Module 003 Safety Gate.
verified_title: The Nonlinear Nature of Learning - A Differential Learning Approach

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Representative learning design is the formal requirement that practice tasks preserve the informational variables and action opportunities of competition so that skills transfer.
effect_or_estimate: No effect estimate - design principle
transfer_status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED as a validated intervention; the principle itself is widely accepted
limitations: It is a design principle, not an intervention with a pooled effect size. Adopting it does not guarantee transfer (see A1-020).
citation: Pinder RA, Davids K, Renshaw I, Araujo D. Representative Learning Design and Functionality of Research and Practice in Sport. J Sport Exerc Psychol. 2011;33:146-155.
verification: crossref DOI resolved (JSEP 33:146-155); abstract retrieved via Crossref
ppbf_implication: PPBF drills should carry a representativeness rating field. Shadowboxing, bag work, pads, constrained sparring and open sparring occupy different points on that scale and SHADOW should show it explicitly.
verified_title: Representative Learning Design and Functionality of Research and Practice in Sport

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Increasing task representativeness does not produce linearly increasing skill gains: in a 6-week tennis serve intervention, different behaviours emerged at different representativeness levels rather than a simple dose-response.
study_design: Three-group intervention with pre/post skill test and in-situ match analysis
effect_or_estimate: Relationship between increasing representativeness and skill acquisition was not linear; groups prioritised serve speed vs placement differently
transfer_status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED; other-sport evidence
limitations: Small n per group; single sport; no long-term follow-up. Behavioural divergence rather than a clean win for high representativeness.
citation: Krause L, Farrow D, Pinder R, Buszard T, Kovalchik S, Reid M. Enhancing skill transfer in tennis using representative learning design. J Sports Sci. 2019;37:2560-2568.
verification: pubmed:PMID 31379253; crossref DOI resolved (J Sports Sci 37:2560-2568)
ppbf_implication: SHADOW should not recommend 'make it more like a fight' as a monotonic dial. Higher representativeness changes what the athlete optimises - which for boxing may trade technique quality against competitive expediency. Coach must choose the target behaviour.
verified_title: Enhancing skill transfer in tennis using representative learning design.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: A coach-usable representativeness rating instrument has been built and consensus-validated in tennis (7 items, each with a task-goal and a competition-relevance sub-question), via a 4-round Delphi with 10 academic and 13 coaching experts.
effect_or_estimate: 7-item tool, expert consensus reached; no criterion-validity or reliability effect size reported in the abstract
transfer_status: Boxing analogue DOES NOT EXIST - would need to be built
limitations: Consensus validity only; predictive validity for actual transfer not established.
citation: Krause L, Farrow D, Reid M, Buszard T, Pinder R. Helping coaches apply the principles of representative learning design: validation of a tennis specific practice assessment tool. J Sports Sci. 2017.
ppbf_implication: CONCRETE PPBF DELIVERABLE: build a boxing Representative Practice Assessment Tool by the same Delphi method with PPBF and external boxing coaches. This is a fundable, achievable validation project and it gives Module 061 a real input variable.
verified_title: Helping coaches apply the principles of representative learning design: validation of a tennis specific practice assessment tool.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: The constraints-led approach organises practice design around the interaction of task, environment and performer constraints rather than around a single technical model.
effect_or_estimate: No effect estimate
transfer_status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED as an evaluated intervention
limitations: Widely adopted as a framework; comparatively few controlled trials isolating CLA against a matched-dose traditional programme, and none located in boxing.
citation: Newell KM. Constraints on the Development of Coordination. In: Motor Development in Children: Aspects of Coordination and Control. 1986.
verification: crossref DOI resolved (Motor Development in Children, 1986)
ppbf_implication: PPBF's Coach-Controlled Constraint Engine (Module 045) and Constraint Library (Module 060) already assume this framework. The registry should record that the framework is well-supported conceptually but under-tested as a boxing intervention.
verified_title: Constraints on the Development of Coordination

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: A nonlinear pedagogy condition was reported to accommodate individual differences in learning a sports skill better than a linear prescriptive condition.
effect_or_estimate: Reported advantage for catering to individual differences; single study
limitations: Single study; effect not independently replicated at scale; outcome framed as individual-difference accommodation rather than group mean gain.
citation: Lee MCY, Chow JY, Komar J, Tan CWK, Button C. Nonlinear Pedagogy: An Effective Approach to Cater for Individual Differences in Learning a Sports Skill. PLoS One. 2014;9:e104744.
ppbf_implication: Supports PPBF's individualised route logic in principle. Insufficient to claim nonlinear pedagogy outperforms traditional boxing instruction.
verified_title: Nonlinear Pedagogy: An Effective Approach to Cater for Individual Differences in Learning a Sports Skill

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Formal frameworks now exist for periodising skill acquisition (not just physical load) across a season, including phase-specific manipulation of practice representativeness and coaching input.
effect_or_estimate: No effect estimate - frameworks not empirically validated against outcomes
limitations: Both are proposal papers. No trial has shown that periodising skill practice by these frameworks beats not doing so.
citation: Farrow D, Robertson S. Development of a Skill Acquisition Periodisation Framework for High-Performance Sport. Sports Med. 2017;47:1043-1054; Otte FW, Millar SK, Klatt S. Skill Training Periodization in Specialist Sports Coaching - An Introduction of the PoST Framework for Skill Development. Front Sports Act Living. 2019;1:61.
ppbf_implication: Gives PPBF a defensible vocabulary for phase-based skill planning (Module 036, Module 129) but the phase definitions must be labelled PROPOSED, and outcome-tracked.
verified_title: Development of a Skill Acquisition Periodisation Framework for High-Performance Sport

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: The guidance hypothesis - that 100% feedback aids practice performance but harms learning relative to reduced feedback - originates in a classic study reporting a reduced-frequency retention advantage.
population: Adults learning a laboratory movement task
effect_or_estimate: Reduced knowledge-of-results frequency enhanced retention relative to 100% frequency
limitations: Single-lab, simple laboratory task; superseded by meta-analytic null (A1-026).
citation: Winstein CJ, Schmidt RA. Reduced frequency of knowledge of results enhances motor skill learning. J Exp Psychol Learn Mem Cogn. 1990;16:677-691.
ppbf_implication: This is the textbook claim PPBF coaches will most likely have been taught. The registry must carry both it and its meta-analytic refutation so SHADOW gives coaches the current picture.
verified_title: Reduced frequency of knowledge of results enhances motor skill learning.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: A large meta-analysis found NO significant effect of reduced feedback frequency at any time point and no significant acquisition-to-delayed-retention reversal; included studies were severely underpowered.
study_design: Meta-analysis with multilevel models and z-curve analysis
effect_or_estimate: No significant effect of reduced feedback frequency at any time point; no significant change in effect from acquisition or immediate retention to delayed retention; substantial heterogeneity; no significant moderators; z-curve indicated severe underpowering
limitations: A null across a heterogeneous, underpowered literature means evidence is lacking, not that feedback frequency is proven irrelevant.
citation: McKay B, Hussien J, Vinh MA, Mir-Orefice A, Brooks H, Ste-Marie DM. Meta-analysis of the reduced relative feedback frequency effect on motor learning and performance. Psychol Sport Exerc. 2022;61:102165.
verification: crossref DOI resolved (Psychol Sport Exerc 61:102165); full abstract retrieved via fetch_article_fulltext on the open preprint DOI 10.31234/osf.io/v2cp7
ppbf_implication: SHADOW must NOT prescribe a feedback-frequency number (e.g. give feedback on 50% of reps). Any such number in PPBF would be invented. Record feedback events and let PPBF discover its own pattern.
verified_title: Meta-analysis of the reduced relative feedback frequency effect on motor learning and performance

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: A factorial trial crossing autonomy support with 100% vs 50%-faded feedback found trivial effects of both on golf-putting learning and performance.
effect_or_estimate: Trivial effects for both autonomy support and feedback schedule
limitations: Single task, modest n, no vision of results (an unusual constraint).
citation: McKay B, Ste-Marie DM. Autonomy support and reduced feedback frequency have trivial effects on learning and performance of a golf putting task. Hum Mov Sci. 2020;74:102612.
ppbf_implication: Reinforces A1-026 and A1-009 - do not build feedback scheduling rules into SHADOW as validated logic.
verified_title: Autonomy support and reduced feedback frequency have trivial effects on learning and performance of a golf putting task.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Bandwidth knowledge of results (feedback only when error exceeds a tolerance) has been studied since the late 1980s with reported learning advantages in laboratory tasks.
effect_or_estimate: Reported learning advantages for bandwidth KR in individual studies; no pooled sport estimate located; the optimal bandwidth width is TBD
limitations: Small, old, laboratory-task literature. No meta-analysis in sport located. The bandwidth width itself is arbitrary across studies.
citation: Lai Q, Shea CH. Bandwidth knowledge of results enhances generalized motor program learning. Res Q Exerc Sport. 1999; Lee TD, Maraj BK. Effects of bandwidth goals and bandwidth knowledge of results on motor learning. Res Q Exerc Sport. 1994; Goodwin JE, Meeuwsen HJ. Using bandwidth knowledge of results to alter relative frequencies during motor skill acquisition. Res Q Exerc Sport. 1995.
ppbf_implication: Bandwidth feedback maps cleanly to a SHADOW threshold field: coach sets an acceptable-error band per technique and only logs/flags outside it. Implement as configurable, not as a fixed evidence-based tolerance.
verified_title: Bandwidth knowledge of results enhances generalized motor program learning.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
topic: Coach feedback in practice - BOXING SPECIFIC
claim: Observed ringside feedback in competitive amateur boxing is predominantly internal-focus and controlling: excluding neutral statements, coaches gave 15% internal vs 6% external focus feedback, 53% controlling vs 6% autonomy-supportive, and 29% positive vs 12% negative.
population: Amateur boxing coaches at a national championship
sex: Coaches not stratified by sex in abstract
sample_size: 12 boxing coaches at the 2015 Australian Boxing Championships
effect_or_estimate: Internal 15% vs external 6%; controlling 53% vs autonomy-supportive 6%; positive 29% vs negative 12%. In winning bouts: less internal (12% vs 19%), less controlling (48% vs 58%), more positive (36% vs 18%)
limitations: OBSERVATIONAL AND CORRELATIONAL. The winning-bout association is not causal - better-performing boxers plausibly elicit more positive corner talk. Single national championship, 12 coaches, one country.
citation: Halperin I, Chapman DW, Martin DT, Abbiss C, Wulf G. Coaching cues in amateur boxing: An analysis of ringside feedback provided between rounds of competition. Psychol Sport Exerc. 2016;25:44-50.
verification: crossref DOI resolved (Psychol Sport Exerc 25:44-50); institutional repository abstract confirmed via web_search 2026-08-07
ppbf_implication: This is the single most directly relevant study for the PPBF cue library. It establishes (a) a measurable corner-feedback taxonomy PPBF can adopt wholesale, and (b) that real boxing coaches default to internal and controlling language. State the correlation caveat prominently.
verified_title: Coaching cues in amateur boxing: An analysis of ringside feedback provided between rounds of competition

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: The gap between motor-learning recommendations and field coaching practice is documented outside boxing too: most instructions athletes reported receiving were internally focused, and only 15% of their own task-related thoughts when fatigued were external.
effect_or_estimate: More than half of coach instructions internally focused; 15% of self-reported task-related thoughts external when fatigued
transfer_status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED but converges with the boxing observation in A1-029
limitations: Self-report questionnaire; recreational sample; recall bias.
citation: Yamada M, Diekfuss JA, Raisbeck LD. Motor Behavior Literature Fails to Translate: A Preliminary Investigation into Coaching and Focus of Attention in Recreational Distance Runners. Int J Exerc Sci. 2020.
ppbf_implication: Adoption is the real bottleneck, not the science. If PPBF ships an external-focus cue library, it must measure whether coaches actually use it - an implementation-fidelity metric, not just a content library.
verified_title: Motor Behavior Literature Fails to Translate: A Preliminary Investigation into Coaching and Focus of Attention in Recreational Distance Runners.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Systematic observation of coach augmented verbal feedback across 31 studies found no agreement on which feedback types matter most and inconsistent observation instruments.
population: Team sport coaches in developmental and performance contexts
effect_or_estimate: Three themes: variation in observation tools and feedback types; limited evidence base behind observed feedback types; concerns over feedback quality. No pooled effect.
limitations: Descriptive review of measurement practice, not of feedback effectiveness.
citation: Corbett R, Partington M, Ryan L, Cope E. A systematic review of coach augmented verbal feedback during practice and competition in team sports. Int J Sports Sci Coach. 2023;19:864-881.
verification: crossref DOI resolved (Int J Sports Sci Coach 19:864-881); abstract retrieved via Crossref
ppbf_implication: PPBF should adopt ONE feedback taxonomy and hold it stable, so its own longitudinal data is comparable over time. Recommend adopting the Halperin boxing taxonomy (A1-029) as the PPBF standard.
verified_title: A systematic review of coach augmented verbal feedback during practice and competition in team sports

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Sports coaches' stated knowledge and beliefs about providing, receiving and evaluating verbal feedback have been formally surveyed, providing a template for auditing a coaching group's assumptions.
effect_or_estimate: No effect estimate - descriptive
limitations: Self-report; stated beliefs may not match observed behaviour.
citation: Mason RJ, Farrow D, Hattie JAC. Sports Coaches' Knowledge and Beliefs About the Provision, Reception, and Evaluation of Verbal Feedback. Front Psychol. 2020;11:571552.
ppbf_implication: Run a PPBF coach-belief baseline before deploying the cue library, so change in coach behaviour can be attributed rather than assumed.
verified_title: Sports Coaches’ Knowledge and Beliefs About the Provision, Reception, and Evaluation of Verbal Feedback

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Learners who acquired a skill with little explicit rule knowledge did not deteriorate under stress, whereas explicitly-instructed learners did - the founding reinvestment finding.
effect_or_estimate: Explicit learners' skill degraded under induced stress; implicit learners' did not
transfer_status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED - though pressure-induced technical breakdown is a core boxing phenomenon
limitations: Small lab study; the implicit group performed articulatory suppression, a confound raised by Hardy et al. (1996).
citation: Masters RSW. Knowledge, knerves and know-how: The role of explicit versus implicit knowledge in the breakdown of a complex motor skill under pressure. Br J Psychol. 1992;83:343-358.
verification: crossref DOI resolved (Br J Psychol 83:343-358); abstract retrieved via Crossref
ppbf_implication: Directly relevant to sparring and bout performance. Motivates a PPBF performs-under-pressure assessment distinct from performs-on-pads.
verified_title: Knowledge, knerves and know‐how: The role of explicit versus implicit knowledge in the breakdown of a complex motor skill under pressure

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: The founding implicit-learning result was challenged on methodological grounds: the original implicit group performed articulatory suppression during learning but not during the stress test, so the comparison was confounded.
effect_or_estimate: Replication with an additional implicit group performing articulatory suppression in BOTH phases; conclusions of the original study re-examined
limitations: This is a 1996 challenge to a 1992 study; the wider implicit-learning literature has continued in both directions.
citation: Hardy L, Mullen R, Jones G. Knowledge and conscious control of motor actions under stress. Br J Psychol. 1996;87:621-636.
verification: crossref DOI resolved (Br J Psychol 87:621-636); abstract retrieved via Crossref
ppbf_implication: Register implicit learning as promising-but-contested. Do not build a PPBF pathway that withholds explanation from athletes on the strength of this literature - that has coaching-ethics and athlete-understanding costs.
verified_title: Knowledge and conscious control of motor actions under stress

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: A systematic review of 25 controlled trials found the claim that implicit learning produces greater automatisation (dual-task resilience) than explicit learning is not clearly supported.
effect_or_estimate: Descriptive synthesis of dual-task performance; the automatisation advantage was not clearly established
limitations: Descriptive synthesis rather than pooled meta-analysis; heterogeneous implicit interventions (analogy, errorless, dual-task, external focus grouped together).
citation: Kal E, Prosee R, Winters M, van der Kamp J. Does implicit motor learning lead to greater automatization of motor skills compared to explicit motor learning? A systematic review. PLoS One. 2018;13:e0203591.
ppbf_implication: Do not promise coaches that implicit methods produce automaticity. The mechanism claim is weaker than the pressure-performance claim.
verified_title: Does implicit motor learning lead to greater automatization of motor skills compared to explicit motor learning? A systematic review.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: In primary-school children, implicit and explicit learning paradigms were equally effective overall; only 5 of 25 studies were conducted outside the laboratory, and manipulation checks were performed in only 52% of studies.
population: Typically developing children and children with developmental disorders
effect_or_estimate: Implicit paradigms as effective as explicit paradigms; the 5 non-lab studies suggested superior implicit efficacy; manipulation checks in 13 of 25 studies (52%)
transfer_status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED - relevant to PPBF youth cohort
limitations: Methodological quality varied and was often insufficient for firm conclusions; mostly upper-limb aiming tasks, not whole-body sport skills.
citation: van Abswoude F, Mombarg R, de Groot W, Steenbergen B. Implicit motor learning in primary school children: A systematic review. J Sports Sci. 2021.
ppbf_implication: For PPBF's youth programme, implicit methods are not established as superior. Choose instruction style on working-memory and engagement grounds (A1-039), not on a claimed implicit advantage.
verified_title: Implicit motor learning in primary school children: A systematic review.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Analogy instruction outperformed explicit instruction and control conditions on motor performance in a meta-analysis of 16 RCTs, with children and novices benefiting most.
effect_or_estimate: Analogy vs control ES = 0.32 (p=0.03); analogy vs explicit ES = 0.29 (p=0.02); children and novices benefited most (all p<0.01). Retention estimates are reported as ES = 5.72 vs control and ES = 7.25 vs explicit - implausibly large values indicating very few, highly heterogeneous retention comparisons; these must NOT be used as planning numbers.
limitations: The main performance effects are small (~0.3). The retention effect sizes are so extreme they signal instability rather than a large true effect - recorded here only to flag that they should not be quoted as a benefit magnitude. Under-stress effect was only a trend (ES=1.18, p=0.05).
citation: Carnero-Diaz A, Pecci J, Calvo-Lluch A, et al. Use your imagination for better performance. Effects of analogy instruction in motor skills. A systematic review and meta-analysis. Psychol Sport Exerc. 2024;102766.
ppbf_implication: Analogy is the best-supported instruction TYPE for the PPBF youth cohort. The cue library should carry a substantial analogy set for beginners and youth, tagged cue_type=analogy, with the effect described as small.
verified_title: Use your imagination for better performance. Effects of analogy instruction in motor skills. A systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Analogy-taught learners maintained performance under a pressure manipulation while explicitly-taught learners declined, despite equal performance during learning and delayed retention.
population: Adults learning a modified basketball shooting task
study_design: Randomised laboratory experiment with pressure transfer test
effect_or_estimate: Analogy and explicit groups equal during learning and delayed retention; explicit group dropped under pressure, analogy group unaffected; probe reaction times showed equal attentional resource allocation
limitations: Seated, modified task; laboratory pressure manipulation is far weaker than a competitive bout.
citation: Lam WK, Maxwell JP, Masters RSW. Analogy Learning and the Performance of Motor Skills under Pressure. J Sport Exerc Psychol. 2009;31:337-357.
verification: crossref DOI resolved (JSEP 31:337); abstract retrieved via Crossref
ppbf_implication: Supports using analogy cues for skills that must survive bout pressure. PPBF should tag which cues are intended for pressure-resilient skills and test them in constrained sparring, not just on pads.
verified_title: Analogy Learning and the Performance of Motor Skills under Pressure

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Children with lower working-memory capacity learned less when given five explicit technical instructions before each practice block - instruction quantity is a real constraint, not a style preference.
study_design: Quasi-experimental with WM-capacity grouping, pre/post and 1-week retention
sample_size: 90 children assessed; 24 lower-WM and 24 higher-WM in the motor task
effect_or_estimate: Lower working-memory capacity limited motor learning under a five-explicit-instruction protocol
transfer_status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED but the mechanism (verbal instruction load) is domain-general
limitations: Extreme-groups design (lowest and highest thirds) inflates apparent group differences; single task.
citation: Buszard T, Farrow D, Verswijveren SJJM, Reid M, Williams J, Polman R, et al. Working Memory Capacity Limits Motor Learning When Implementing Multiple Instructions. Front Psychol. 2017;8:1350.
ppbf_implication: DIRECT PRODUCT RULE: cap the number of simultaneous technical cues SHADOW surfaces per drill. One cue at a time for youth and novices. This is a concrete, defensible constraint on the cue library UI.
verified_title: Working Memory Capacity Limits Motor Learning When Implementing Multiple Instructions.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Observational modelling improves both movement dynamics and movement outcome measures, with effects varying by task constraints.
effect_or_estimate: Effects reported separately for movement dynamics and movement outcome across differing task constraints
limitations: Published 2006; predates modern bias-correction standards.
citation: Ashford D, Bennett SJ, Davids K. Observational Modeling Effects for Movement Dynamics and Movement Outcome Measures Across Differing Task Constraints: A Meta-Analysis. J Mot Behav. 2006;38:185-205.
ppbf_implication: Video modelling is a supportable PPBF feature. Pair it with the applied-model structure in A1-041 rather than shipping a raw video library.
verified_title: Observational Modeling Effects for Movement Dynamics and Movement Outcome Measures Across Differing Task Constraints: A Meta-Analysis

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: An applied model for the use of observation specifies the functions, timing and delivery features of observation interventions; a review of 48 studies (2011-2018) affirmed effectiveness and extended it to wider populations and settings.
effect_or_estimate: Effectiveness of observation interventions affirmed and extended; 21 of 48 articles addressed the basic effectiveness question
limitations: Narrative/structured review, not pooled meta-analysis; heterogeneous interventions.
citation: Ste-Marie DM, Law B, Rymal AM, Jenny O, Hall C, McCullagh P. Observation interventions for motor skill learning and performance: an applied model for the use of observation. Int Rev Sport Exerc Psychol. 2012;5:145-176; Ste-Marie DM, Lelievre N, St Germain L. Revisiting the Applied Model for the Use of Observation: A Review of Articles Spanning 2011-2018. Res Q Exerc Sport. 2020.
verification: crossref DOI resolved for the 2012 model; pubmed:PMID 32004119 for the 2020 review
ppbf_implication: PPBF's film-study flow (Module 111 and pilot.shadow_film_study_proposals) should structure clips by observation FUNCTION (skill, strategy, performance) and timing, per this model - not just store clips.
verified_title: Revisiting the Applied Model for the Use of Observation: A Review of Articles Spanning 2011-2018.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Observing a MIX of expert and novice (error-containing) models produced better learning than observing an expert model alone, replicated across several independent experiments.
population: Adults learning timing and surgical tasks
sample_size: Includes a 120-participant randomised study in robotic surgical skills
effect_or_estimate: Mixed expert+novice observation produced more stable movement time, better generalisation and better estimation of model performance than expert-only or novice-only observation
limitations: Timing tasks and surgical simulators, not open combat skills. Outcomes concern error-detection mechanisms rather than competitive performance.
citation: Rohbanfard H, Proteau L. Learning through observation: a combination of expert and novice models favors learning. Exp Brain Res. 2011; Andrieux M, Proteau L. Mixed observation favors motor learning through better estimation of the model's performance. Exp Brain Res. 2014; Harris DJ, Vine SJ, Wilson MR, et al. The effect of observing novice and expert performance on acquisition of surgical skills on a robotic platform. PLoS One. 2017;12:e0188233; Welsher A, Grierson LEM. Enhancing technical skill learning through interleaved mixed-model observational practice. Adv Health Sci Educ. 2017.
ppbf_implication: PPBF film study should deliberately include the athlete's OWN flawed reps alongside a model rep - not only highlight reels. This has direct UI consequences for the film-study proposal flow.
verified_title: Learning through observation: a combination of expert and novice models favors learning.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Imagery interventions produce measurable benefits in sport in meta-analysis, and the PETTLEP model provides the most-specified delivery framework.
effect_or_estimate: Positive pooled effects reported for imagery interventions in sport; PETTLEP reviewed as the dominant structured approach. No boxing-specific estimate exists.
limitations: Imagery literatures are prone to expectancy and allocation-concealment problems; blinding is essentially impossible. The PETTLEP functional-equivalence mechanism has itself been critically reflected on in print.
citation: Simonsmeier BA, Andronie M, Buecker S, Frank C. The effects of imagery interventions in sports: a meta-analysis. Int Rev Sport Exerc Psychol. 2020; Lindsay RS, Larkin P, Kittel A, Spittle M. Mental imagery training programs for developing sport-specific motor skills: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Phys Educ Sport Pedagogy. 2021; Holmes PS, Collins DJ. The PETTLEP Approach to Motor Imagery. J Appl Sport Psychol. 2001;13:60-83; Morone G, et al. Motor Imagery and Sport Performance: A Systematic Review on the PETTLEP Model. Appl Sci. 2022;12:9753.
verification: crossref DOIs resolved for all four; abstract retrieved via Crossref for the PETTLEP systematic review
ppbf_implication: Imagery is a low-risk, low-cost PPBF addition (at-home homework modules 085-092). Specify it via PETTLEP elements so what is delivered is auditable, and measure adherence.
verified_title: The PETTLEP Approach to Motor Imagery: A Functional Equivalence Model for Sport Psychologists

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Experts differ systematically from non-experts on perceptual-cognitive measures: 42 studies and 388 effect sizes showed superior response accuracy and response time plus distinct visual search behaviour (fewer, longer fixations).
effect_or_estimate: Experts superior on response accuracy and response time; experts used fewer fixations of longer duration
transfer_status: Transfer to boxing PARTIAL - a combat-sport-specific meta-analysis exists (A1-045)
limitations: EXPERT-NOVICE DIFFERENCE, NOT A TRAINING EFFECT. Shows what expertise looks like, not that training these measures creates expertise.
citation: Mann DTY, Williams AM, Ward P, Janelle CM. Perceptual-Cognitive Expertise in Sport: A Meta-Analysis. J Sport Exerc Psychol. 2007;29:457-478.
verification: crossref DOI resolved (JSEP 29:457-478); abstract retrieved via Crossref
ppbf_implication: Perceptual measures are candidate PPBF ASSESSMENT variables (Module 058 Cue Recognition Engine). They are not, on this evidence, candidate training targets.
verified_title: Perceptual-Cognitive Expertise in Sport: A Meta-Analysis

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: In combat sports specifically, experts outperformed non-experts on perceptual anticipation with large effect sizes for response accuracy and reaction time across 27 studies and 233 datasets.
effect_or_estimate: Response accuracy 1.51 (95% CI 1.15 to 1.87); reaction time -0.91 (95% CI -1.08 to -0.73). A visual-fixation result is reported with an apparent sign inconsistency between point estimate and confidence interval in the published abstract, so no fixation number is carried forward here.
boxing_specific: PARTIAL - combat sports including but not limited to boxing; boxing not separately pooled in the abstract
transfer_status: Combat-sport evidence; within-boxing estimate NOT AVAILABLE
limitations: EXPERT-NOVICE DIFFERENCE, NOT A TRAINING EFFECT. Cross-sectional. Heterogeneous paradigms across English- and Chinese-language databases. The fixation-duration reporting inconsistency reduces confidence in that detail.
citation: Zhang Z, Piras A, Chen C, Kong B, Wang D. A comparison of perceptual anticipation in combat sports between experts and non-experts: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Psychol. 2022;13:961960.
ppbf_implication: Justifies building a boxing anticipation assessment into PPBF (occlusion-style video test) as a DISCRIMINATIVE measure. Does not justify selling anticipation training as a proven route to expertise.
verified_title: A comparison of perceptual anticipation in combat sports between experts and non-experts: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: A 12-session implicit perceptual-motor training programme improved decision-making accuracy and changed gaze behaviour in highly-skilled junior female karate fighters relative to matched-motor-training and control groups.
population: Highly skilled junior female karate fighters (M age 15.7 +/- 1.2 y)
study_design: Randomised three-group intervention with video-based and on-mat tests
sample_size: 18 total (6 implicit, 6 placebo motor training, 6 control)
effect_or_estimate: Only the implicit perceptual-motor group significantly improved decision-making accuracy; that group also fixated on fewer locations for longer; no significant session-by-session improvement except at the final session
boxing_specific: PARTIAL - karate, a striking combat sport, but not boxing
limitations: VERY SMALL n (6 per group). Single sport, single sex, elite juniors. Improvement appeared only at the final session, which is consistent with a late-emerging effect or with noise.
citation: Milazzo N, Farrow D, Ruffault A, Fournier JF. Effect of Implicit Perceptual-Motor Training on Decision-Making Skills and Underpinning Gaze Behavior in Combat Athletes. Percept Mot Skills. 2016;123:300-323.
verification: pubmed:PMID 27371637; crossref DOI resolved (Percept Mot Skills 123:300-323)
ppbf_implication: Closest existing analogue to a PPBF decision-training module (Module 057). Cite it as a design template and an explicit power warning: n=6 per arm is not a basis for a product claim.
verified_title: Effect of Implicit Perceptual-Motor Training on Decision-Making Skills and Underpinning Gaze Behavior in Combat Athletes.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Whether perceptual-cognitive training transfers to on-field performance remains an open research question, and a classification framework has been proposed to predict which modified perceptual training tasks should transfer.
effect_or_estimate: No pooled transfer estimate
limitations: The framework is theoretically grounded but not itself validated by a transfer trial. Generic brain-training approaches have been separately criticised on ecological grounds.
citation: Broadbent DP, Causer J, Williams AM, Ford PR. Perceptual-cognitive skill training and its transfer to expert performance in the field: Future research directions. Eur J Sport Sci. 2015; Hadlow SM, Panchuk D, Mann DL, Portus MR, Abernethy B. Modified perceptual training in sport: A new classification framework. J Sci Med Sport. 2018;21:950-958.
ppbf_implication: If PPBF adds any screen-based perceptual training, the classification framework should be used to justify the task design, and an on-floor transfer test must be built in from day one.
verified_title: Modified perceptual training in sport: A new classification framework.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Quiet eye duration discriminates experts from novices and successful from unsuccessful attempts, and quiet-eye training interventions show large effects in meta-analysis.
population: Athletes, largely in aiming and targeting tasks
sample_size: Synthesis 1: 27 studies, 38 effect sizes. Synthesis 2: 9 articles
effect_or_estimate: Expert vs novice quiet eye d = 1.04; successful vs unsuccessful within-individual d = 0.58; intervention effects d = 1.53 (quiet eye period) and d = 0.84 (performance)
boxing_specific: No - dominated by golf, shooting and basketball free throws
transfer_status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED and questionable: quiet eye is best established in self-paced aiming tasks, not in reactive striking exchanges
limitations: Small intervention literature (9 articles). Aiming-task dominance limits generalisation to open, reactive boxing skills.
citation: Lebeau JC, Liu S, Saenz-Moncaleano C, Sanduvete-Chaves S, Chacon-Moscoso S, Becker BJ, Tenenbaum G. Quiet Eye and Performance in Sport: A Meta-Analysis. J Sport Exerc Psychol. 2016.
ppbf_implication: Do NOT port quiet-eye training into boxing on this evidence. Flag as a research question for PPBF: does a quiet-eye analogue exist for a reactive striking sport?
verified_title: Quiet Eye and Performance in Sport: A Meta-Analysis.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Interventions to counteract choking under pressure show small-to-moderate pooled benefits, with larger and more consistent effects in closed-skill contexts than in open-skill contexts.
effect_or_estimate: Motor accuracy g = 0.660; executional success g = 0.444; target deviation g = 0.301; closed-skill contexts g = 0.455 with larger and more consistent effects than open-skill contexts
transfer_status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED; boxing is an OPEN skill, the context where these effects were weaker
limitations: Heterogeneous interventions pooled (quiet eye training, pre-performance routines, mindfulness, left-hand contraction, self-talk, rational emotive behaviour therapy). The open-skill subgroup is the relevant one for boxing and is the weaker one.
citation: Zeng Z, Yan W, Mohammadi A, et al. Counteracting choking under pressure in sport: A meta-analysis of interventions. Psychol Sport Exerc. 2026;103130.
ppbf_implication: PPBF pressure-management support is defensible, but the effect should be expected to be SMALLER in boxing than the headline numbers because boxing is an open skill. State that in any coach-facing summary.
verified_title: Counteracting choking under pressure in sport: A meta-analysis of interventions.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: A meta-analysis of whole and part practice generally supported textbook recommendations based on task complexity/organisation and skill classification, but several analyses were compromised by too few studies.
sample_size: 44 articles located; 20 provided sufficient information for effect size calculation
effect_or_estimate: Mean effect sizes generally supported textbook recommendations; authors concluded more studies are needed to verify empirical validity
limitations: Thin evidence base (20 usable studies); published 2009; underpowered subgroup analyses.
citation: Fontana FE, Mazzardo O, Furtado O, Gallagher JD. Whole and part practice: a meta-analysis. Percept Mot Skills. 2009;109:517-530.
ppbf_implication: PPBF can use the complexity/organisation heuristic to decide when to break a combination into parts, but must label it a HEURISTIC. Combination punching (high organisation) is the case where part practice is least supported.
verified_title: Whole and part practice: a meta-analysis.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Performance during practice is an unreliable index of learning: manipulations that improve practice performance can impair long-term retention and transfer, and vice versa.
sample_size: N/A - review of decades of evidence
effect_or_estimate: No single effect size - the learning/performance dissociation is the finding
transfer_status: Domain-general principle; applies to boxing by construction
limitations: The dissociation is well-established in principle; several specific manipulations claimed to produce it (contextual interference, reduced feedback) are the ones now failing meta-analysis (A1-011, A1-026).
citation: Schmidt RA, Bjork RA. New Conceptualizations of Practice: Common Principles in Three Paradigms Suggest New Concepts for Training. Psychol Sci. 1992;3:207-218; Soderstrom NC, Bjork RA. Learning Versus Performance: An Integrative Review. Perspect Psychol Sci. 2015;10:176-199.
verification: crossref DOIs resolved for both; abstracts retrieved via Crossref
ppbf_implication: SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT PRINCIPLE FOR SHADOW'S MEASUREMENT MODEL. Any PPBF skill score taken during or immediately after a coached drill is a PERFORMANCE observation, not a LEARNING observation. pilot.shadow_formula_observations must carry an observation-context field distinguishing them.
verified_title: New Conceptualizations of Practice: Common Principles in Three Paradigms Suggest New Concepts for Training

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Establishing that learning has occurred requires a delayed retention test and a transfer test administered without the practice-condition supports, not an end-of-session measure.
study_design: Methodological convention grounded in the learning/performance literature
effect_or_estimate: No effect estimate - methodological requirement. No consensus-validated retention interval for boxing skills exists: TBD.
limitations: Retention intervals in the literature are typically 24 hours to one week - far shorter than a boxing development cycle. The correct interval for a boxing technique is unknown.
citation: Soderstrom NC, Bjork RA. Learning Versus Performance: An Integrative Review. Perspect Psychol Sci. 2015;10:176-199; Schmidt RA, Bjork RA. Psychol Sci. 1992;3:207-218.
ppbf_implication: PPBF VALIDATION REQUIREMENT: Module 055 Retention Tracking Engine must implement a no-cue, no-coach-prompt retest at a defined delay. The delay value is TBD and must be set from PPBF pilot data, not assumed.
verified_title: Learning Versus Performance

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Principles derived from simple laboratory skills do not reliably generalise to complex skill learning - a caution issued by researchers within the attentional-focus tradition itself.
effect_or_estimate: No pooled estimate - the non-generalisation is the finding
transfer_status: Directly limits transfer of nearly every row in this registry to boxing
limitations: A review argument rather than a trial; but it is the reason most rows here carry a transfer caveat.
citation: Wulf G, Shea CH. Principles derived from the study of simple skills do not generalize to complex skill learning. Psychon Bull Rev. 2002;9:185-211.
ppbf_implication: Embed this citation in SHADOW's evidence-quality engine (Module 130) as the standing justification for downgrading confidence whenever a recommendation rests on a simple-task laboratory study.
verified_title: Principles derived from the study of simple skills do not generalize to complex skill learning

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Individual differences in motor learning are substantial and largely unpredictable from current predictor variables; a 20-year critical review found serious methodological problems with published prediction claims.
study_design: Critical review (2000-2020 literature) and companion review
effect_or_estimate: Large variation in predictors used, prediction strength and sample size; authors raise concerns about the quality of evidence for prediction of individual learning differences
limitations: A critique of a prediction literature, not a demonstration that prediction is impossible.
citation: Ranganathan R, Cone S, Fox B. Predicting individual differences in motor learning: A critical review. Neurosci Biobehav Rev. 2022;141:104852; Anderson DI, Lohse KR, Lopes TCV, Williams AM. Individual differences in motor skill learning: Past, present and future. Hum Mov Sci. 2021;78:102818.
ppbf_implication: Direct warning to SHADOW's forecasting modules (178 Development Forecasting, 181 Risk Forecasting): individual learning-rate prediction is not a solved problem. Any PPBF forecast must ship with wide uncertainty and mandatory coach override.
verified_title: Individual differences in motor skill learning: Past, present and future.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Scaling equipment and play area to children improves aspects of motor skill acquisition and is preferred by children, based on 25 studies with 989 participants.
effect_or_estimate: Children preferred scaled equipment; benefits reported across psychological, skill-acquisition, biomechanical and cognitive-processing factors. Boxing scaling values are TBD - none published.
boxing_specific: No - dominated by tennis and other ball sports
transfer_status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED; boxing scaling analogues (glove weight, bag size, ring dimensions, round length, target size) are UNSTUDIED
limitations: Heterogeneous outcomes; risk-of-bias assessment reported but effect sizes not pooled into a single estimate.
citation: Buszard T, Reid M, Masters R, Farrow D. Scaling the Equipment and Play Area in Children's Sport to improve Motor Skill Acquisition: A Systematic Review. Sports Med. 2016;46:829-843.
ppbf_implication: STRONG CANDIDATE FOR A PPBF RESEARCH PROJECT: define and test boxing scaling parameters for youth (glove weight, bag size, round length, target size). No published boxing values exist - any number PPBF adopts must be labelled PROPOSED PPBF PARAMETER - ASSUMPTION, REQUIRES VALIDATION.
verified_title: Scaling the Equipment and Play Area in Children's Sport to improve Motor Skill Acquisition: A Systematic Review.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Mental fatigue degrades sport-specific technical performance, established by meta-analysis in soccer, with a separate meta-analysis of counteractive interventions.
population: Soccer players (technical performance meta-analysis); athletes across sports (intervention meta-analysis)
effect_or_estimate: Mental fatigue impairs offensive and defensive technical skills in soccer; counteractive interventions pooled across 13 papers. No boxing-specific threshold exists: TBD.
limitations: Laboratory mental-fatigue induction protocols (e.g. Stroop tasks) may not represent the cognitive load of a competitive boxing week (school, weight management, travel).
citation: Sun H, Soh KG, Roslan S, Wazir MRWN, Soh KL. Effects of mental fatigue on technical performance in soccer players: A systematic review with a meta-analysis. Front Public Health. 2022;10:922630; Sun H, Soh KG, Mohammadi A, et al. The counteractive effects of interventions addressing mental fatigue on sport-specific performance among athletes: A systematic review with a meta-analysis. J Sports Sci. 2024.
ppbf_implication: PPBF's Readiness-to-Learn Score (Module 197) should include a mental-fatigue/cognitive-load input, not only physical readiness. Threshold values are TBD and must come from PPBF pilot data.
verified_title: Effects of mental fatigue on technical performance in soccer players: A systematic review with a meta-analysis.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
topic: Physical fatigue and boxing skill - BOXING SPECIFIC
claim: Physical fatigue measurably degrades punch output in amateur boxers: after a lower-body fatigue circuit, punch force declined significantly across all punch types.
study_design: Repeated-measures pre/post fatigue protocol with force plates and a boxing force sensor
effect_or_estimate: Pre-fatigue the cross produced the highest punch force (1475.42 N), ground reaction force (947.54 N) and rate of force development (3973.38 N/s). Post-fatigue punch force declined across all punches by -4.26% (p = 0.027), with the greatest reductions in the cross and left hook. RFD responses were variable.
limitations: n=10, male only, single laboratory, a 9.5-minute lower-body circuit rather than sparring-induced fatigue. The absolute newton values are lab- and equipment-specific and must not be used as PPBF benchmarks.
citation: Stewart C, Cornett R, Baker JS, et al. The Role of Lower Limb Kinetics in Boxing Punches and the Impact of Fatigue on Biomechanical Performance. Bioengineering (Basel). 2025;12:1355.
ppbf_implication: Supports a PPBF fatigue-breakdown flag (Module 081) using punch-quality decrement as an observable. Do NOT import 1475 N or -4.26% as PPBF thresholds - they come from 10 laboratory boxers.
verified_title: The Role of Lower Limb Kinetics in Boxing Punches and the Impact of Fatigue on Biomechanical Performance.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Wearable accelerometry fused with videography has been demonstrated as a method for monitoring fatigue effects on punching performance in elite boxers.
study_design: Method-development study with a boxing-specific punch fatigue protocol
effect_or_estimate: Computational framework demonstrated; laterality effects analysed via statistical parametric mapping. No validated fatigue threshold produced.
limitations: n=6; a feasibility and methods paper, not a validated monitoring product. Custom IMUs embedded in gloves are not off-the-shelf equipment.
citation: Haralabidis N, Saxby DJ, Pizzolato C, et al. Fusing Accelerometry with Videography to Monitor the Effect of Fatigue on Punching Performance in Elite Boxers. Sensors (Basel). 2020;20:5749.
ppbf_implication: If PPBF ever adds punch sensors, this is the closest published methodology. Feasibility, cost and youth-appropriateness are unaddressed. Treat as a research direction, not a roadmap item.
verified_title: Fusing Accelerometry with Videography to Monitor the Effect of Fatigue on Punching Performance in Elite Boxers.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
topic: Sleep and skill acquisition in youth
claim: The influence of sleep on motor skill acquisition in children remains controversial; a systematic review found the evidence unsettled.
effect_or_estimate: No reliable pooled estimate; effects of sleep on procedural memory consolidation in children described as controversial
limitations: Small, heterogeneous child literature; risk-of-bias concerns.
citation: Filho JMVM, de Oliveira AAR, de Bruin VMS, et al. Influence of sleep on motor skill acquisition in children: a systematic review. J Sleep Res. 2024;e14309.
ppbf_implication: PPBF should log sleep as context, not model it as a driver of skill gain. Any sleep-based recommendation to a youth athlete or family is a health-adjacent communication and must route through the safeguarding/medical path, not an automated SHADOW message.
verified_title: Influence of sleep on motor skill acquisition in children: a systematic review.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: In novice-level amateur bouts, winners landed more punches than losers, driven by lead-hand punches, total head punches, block-and-counter combinations and punching combinations.
study_design: Observational activity profile from competition video with post-bout blood lactate
effect_or_estimate: Winners landed 18 +/- 11 more punches. Lead-hand punches in round 1: 34.2 +/- 10.9 vs 26.5 +/- 9.4. Total punches to the head: 121.3 +/- 10.2 vs 96.0 +/- 9.8. Block-and-counterpunch combinations: 2.8 +/- 1.1 vs 0.1 +/- 0.2. Punching combinations in rounds 1 and 3: 44.3 +/- 6.4 vs 28.8 +/- 6.7. All P < .05. Peak post-bout blood lactate 11.8 +/- 1.6 mmol/L irrespective of result.
limitations: CORRELATIONAL AND OBSERVATIONAL - these are correlates of winning, not proven causes, and judging criteria partly define the outcome. 3x2-min novice format, male only, 32 boxers, single competition context. Modern amateur formats and judging criteria differ by jurisdiction and era.
citation: Davis P, Wittekind A, Beneke R. Amateur Boxing: Activity Profile of Winners and Losers. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2013;8:84-92.
ppbf_implication: Gives PPBF an evidence-anchored (if correlational) short list of trainable behaviours: lead-hand activity, head-target accuracy, block-and-counter linkage, and combination punching. These should be first-class skill dimensions in Module 038 Boxing Skill Tracking and in the cue library.
verified_title: Amateur boxing: activity profile of winners and losers.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Amateur boxing requires high cardiorespiratory fitness, high peak and mean anaerobic power, and upper- and lower-limb strength and power, per a critical review of boxer attributes.
effect_or_estimate: Descriptive attribute profile; no single pooled effect size. Female-specific data explicitly sparser than male.
limitations: Narrative review; limited somatotype data; female evidence base thinner than male; published 2015.
citation: Chaabene H, Tabben M, Mkaouer B, Franchini E, et al. Amateur Boxing: Physical and Physiological Attributes. Sports Med. 2015;45:337-352.
ppbf_implication: Frames the physical qualities PPBF's skill work sits on top of. Flags a real equity gap: female-specific boxing evidence is thinner, so SHADOW must not present male-derived profiles as universal.
verified_title: Amateur boxing: physical and physiological attributes.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: Amateur boxing produces a large acute physiological, endocrine and biochemical response, with greater alterations in competitive bouts than in sparring, and greater in sparring than in boxing-specific simulations.
sex: Predominantly male in the included literature
effect_or_estimate: Pre-post standardised mean differences: blood lactate 4.62, cortisol 1.33, myoglobin 1.43, aspartate transaminase 1.37, alanine aminotransferase 0.97, creatine kinase 0.65. Small increase in countermovement jump height (SMD 0.33). Responses consistently greatest in competitive bouts, then sparring, least in simulations.
limitations: Methodological quality assessed with a modified checklist; heterogeneous protocols; female representation limited. Authors note task-specific performance may NOT deteriorate despite the biochemical response.
citation: Finlay MJ, Greig M, Page RM, Bridge CA. Acute physiological, endocrine, biochemical and performance responses associated with amateur boxing: A systematic review with meta-analysis. Eur J Sport Sci. 2022.
ppbf_implication: Provides a verified ORDERING for PPBF practice-intensity classification: simulation < sparring < competition. SHADOW can use this ordering in session-load and representativeness logic without inventing numbers.
verified_title: Acute physiological, endocrine, biochemical and performance responses associated with amateur boxing: A systematic review with meta-analysis.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: A shared phase structure has been defined for four boxing punches (lead punches, rear straight and hook) using ground reaction force, EMG and kinematics in experienced competitive boxers.
sex: Not stated as mixed in abstract
effect_or_estimate: Phase definitions established for four punch types; no performance-outcome effect size
limitations: n=10; heavier-than-typical sample (body mass 95.66 +/- 21.82 kg); descriptive taxonomy rather than a performance model.
citation: Lenetsky S, Brughelli M, Nates RJ, Neville JG, Cross MR, Lormier AV. Defining the Phases of Boxing Punches: A Mixed-Method Approach. J Strength Cond Res. 2020;34:1040-1051.
ppbf_implication: Gives PPBF a published, citable phase vocabulary for punch technique so coach observations and cue targets align to the same movement segments. Use for the technique_target field in the cue library.
verified_title: Defining the Phases of Boxing Punches: A Mixed-Method Approach.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
claim: In expert boxers throwing a rear-hand straight punch at a head-mass movable target, reduction in arm-segment momentum explained approximately 95% of the impact impulse, distributed 40% upper arm, 35% forearm and 20% fist plus glove.
study_design: Laboratory biomechanics with motion capture and target accelerometry
effect_or_estimate: Arm momentum reduction explained ~95% of the impulse (upper arm 40%, forearm 35%, fist plus glove 20%); Pearson r = 0.902 between peak impact force and impulse
limitations: n=9, male, single punch type, laboratory target rather than an opponent. Says nothing about whether coaching cues can change this distribution.
citation: Nakano G, Iino Y, Imura A, Kojima T. Transfer of momentum from different arm segments to a light movable target during a straight punch thrown by expert boxers. J Sports Sci. 2014;32:517-523.
ppbf_implication: Grounds cue design for the straight punch: proximal segments dominate the impulse, which argues against cues that fixate the athlete on the fist. Note this is a mechanical inference, not a validated cue test.
verified_title: Transfer of momentum from different arm segments to a light movable target during a straight punch thrown by expert boxers.

track: Track 1 - Motor Learning & Skill Acquisition
topic: Elite athlete response to feedback - BOXING SPECIFIC
claim: False-performance feedback (positive, negative or neutral) produced no meaningful change in punching force, pacing or RPE in elite amateur boxers - a null that challenges generalising novice feedback findings to trained athletes.
study_design: Randomised within-subject crossover across four days
