ppbf_implication: Correlation is not a training rationale. Do NOT let SHADOW recommend commercial vision training on the basis of these associations; log as a research backlog item.
verified_title: Relationship between visual ability assessment and punch performance in competition in male amateur boxers.

track: A2-technical-curriculum
claim: Mental fatigue induced by a 45-minute Stroop paradigm impaired temporal perceptual prediction of attack and defence action recognition in both expert and novice boxers, tested at occlusion points of -80 ms, -40 ms and action onset.
study_design: Mixed-design experimental study with induced mental fatigue
effect_or_estimate: Effects of mental fatigue on RT and accuracy across technique types and occlusion windows
limitations: Laboratory Stroop-induced fatigue rather than training- or school-induced fatigue; video-based recognition task
citation: 'Mental Fatigue Impairs Temporal Perceptual Prediction: A Study on Boxing Performance Across Skill Levels', Sports
ppbf_implication: Justifies capturing a mental-state/mental-fatigue context field on every technical assessment. A youth athlete assessed after a school exam day is not being assessed on skill alone.
verified_title: Mental Fatigue Impairs Temporal Perceptual Prediction: A Study on Boxing Performance Across Skill Levels.

track: A2-technical-curriculum
topic: boxing technical skill acquisition and retention in novices
claim: A short-term structured boxing programme in novice female university students produced significant improvements in stance, straight punches, hooks and uppercuts from baseline to four weeks, assessed under both static and dynamic conditions with a two-month follow-up retention assessment.
study_design: Pre/post/follow-up intervention study with a customised scoring system
effect_or_estimate: Significant improvement in all technical skills at 4 weeks (T2 vs T1); two-month follow-up (T3) conducted
limitations: Custom scoring system with no reported reliability or validity evidence; no control group in the abstract; single cohort
citation: 'Short-Term Effects of a Structured Boxing Program on Technical Skill Acquisition in Novice Female Students', Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology
ppbf_implication: The closest existing analogue to what PPBF is building, and it illustrates the field's core weakness: a customised technical scoring system used without published reliability. PPBF must not repeat that. Also a rare study with a genuine delayed retention timepoint — copy that design.
verified_title: Short-Term Effects of a Structured Boxing Program on Technical Skill Acquisition in Novice Female Students.

track: A2-technical-curriculum
claim: Pad-based and bag-based boxing-specific training protocols elicit different physical responses in elite amateur boxers across heart rate, oxygen consumption, blood lactate and RPE during matched 3x3-minute protocols.
study_design: Within-subject comparison of two training modalities
effect_or_estimate: Differences in HR, VO2, blood lactate and RPE between pad and bag routines
limitations: n=14; physiological outcomes only, not skill or learning outcomes
citation: 'Physical Response to Pad- and Bag-Based Boxing-Specific Training Modalities', Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
ppbf_implication: Pads and bags are not interchangeable in the session model. Note the evidence here is physiological; their relative value for SKILL LEARNING is an evidence gap PPBF could fill.
verified_title: Physical Response to Pad- and Bag-Based Boxing-Specific Training Modalities.

track: A2-technical-curriculum
claim: The hand is the most frequently injured body location in elite amateur boxing: five-year prospective surveillance of the Great Britain squad found more injuries affected the hand than any other body location.
population: Great Britain elite amateur boxing squad
effect_or_estimate: Hand was the most frequently injured location
limitations: Single national squad; elite training volumes; medically diagnosed injuries only
citation: 'Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study of medically diagnosed injury incidence and outcome', British Journal of Sports Medicine
ppbf_implication: DIRECT CURRICULUM CONSEQUENCE: fist formation, wrist alignment and hand-wrapping competency must be a HARD PREREQUISITE gate before any full-power bag work, not a footnote. This is the strongest evidence-based prerequisite in the entire Track 2 graph.
verified_title: Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study of medically diagnosed injury incidence and outcome.

track: A2-technical-curriculum
claim: Pooled competition injury incidence in amateur boxing was estimated at 54.7 (95% CI 33.8-88.4) injuries per 1000 athlete-exposures in a meta-analysis of 17 prospective cohort studies, with separate per-minute and training-hour estimates modelled.
population: Amateur boxers in competition and training
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies
effect_or_estimate: Competition IIR 54.7 per 1000 athlete-exposures (95% CI 33.8-88.4)
limitations: Wide confidence interval; heterogeneous injury definitions across included studies despite IOC consensus guidance
citation: 'Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis', Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
ppbf_implication: Baseline for PPBF's own surveillance. PPBF must record exposure (athlete-exposures and training hours), not just injury counts, or its rates will be uninterpretable.
verified_title: Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: A2-technical-curriculum
claim: The IOC consensus statement provides the standard for recording and reporting epidemiological data on injury and illness in sport, including a STROBE checklist extension, to make injury data comparable across studies.
population: Sport injury and illness surveillance generally
effect_or_estimate: Standardised definitions, methodology and reporting checklist
limitations: A methodological standard, not a boxing finding
citation: 'International Olympic Committee consensus statement: methods for recording and reporting of epidemiological data on injury and illness in sport 2020', British Journal of Sports Medicine
ppbf_implication: PPBF should adopt IOC 2020 definitions verbatim for any injury field in the schema so its data can later be compared with published rates rather than being locally idiosyncratic.
verified_title: International Olympic Committee consensus statement: methods for recording and reporting of epidemiological data on injury and illness in sport 2020 (including STROBE Extension for Sport Injury and Illness Surveillance (STROBE-SIIS)).

track: A2-technical-curriculum
claim: The Association of Ringside Physicians position statement holds that headguards are highly effective at reducing facial lacerations in amateur boxers and appropriate for avoiding auricular injury, but should not be relied upon to reduce concussion or other traumatic brain injury risk.
study_design: Position statement of a professional physician body
effect_or_estimate: Effective for lacerations and auricular injury; not established for concussion reduction
limitations: Position statement synthesising limited evidence; a related Current Opinion argues insufficient evidence supports headguard BANS, so the policy debate remains live
citation: 'Headguard use in combat sports: position statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians', The Physician and Sportsmedicine
ppbf_implication: SHADOW must never present headgear as concussion protection in any coach, athlete or parent-facing text. Equipment gating logic should state the actual protective claim (lacerations, ears) and nothing more.
verified_title: Headguard use in combat sports: position statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians.

track: A2-technical-curriculum
claim: Laboratory punch-machine and drop testing show headguards alter head impact dynamics but with performance varying by test condition: peak contact forces of 1.9-5.9 kN were recorded across impact speeds of 4.1-8.3 m/s, with differences between an AIBA-approved headguard and a bare headform depending on impact location.
population: Instrumented Hybrid III headform and ISO rigid headform
effect_or_estimate: Peak contact forces 1.9-5.9 kN; performance varied by test condition and location
limitations: Laboratory headforms are not human heads; linear impactor and drop tests do not reproduce rotational injury mechanisms of real punches
citation: 'Boxing headguard performance in punch machine tests' and 'The impact performance of headguards for combat sports', British Journal of Sports Medicine
ppbf_implication: Reinforces A2-073: bench performance under linear impact does not license a concussion-protection claim to parents.
verified_title: Boxing headguard performance in punch machine tests.

track: A2-technical-curriculum
claim: The evidence base for the IBA/AIBA headguard ban is contested: a Current Opinion argues headguards are effective against cuts and lacerations and that there is insufficient evidence supporting headguard bans, while a systematic review of head trauma in boxing assessed headguard efficiency alongside concussion ratios.
study_design: Current Opinion article plus systematic reviews
effect_or_estimate: Insufficient evidence characterised as supporting the ban; effectiveness against cuts affirmed
limitations: Policy debate with governing-body and scientific positions not aligned; jurisdictional variation
citation: 'The Case for Protective Headguards in Amateur Boxing and Implications for International Policy on Headguard Bans' (Sports Medicine - Open) and 'A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Investigating Head Trauma in Boxing' (Clin J Sport Med)
ppbf_implication: PPBF's equipment policy must follow the applicable governing body and jurisdiction (USA Boxing for US amateur competition), and SHADOW must never present one nation's or one body's rule as universal.
verified_title: The Case for Protective Headguards in Amateur Boxing and Implications for International Policy on Headguard Bans.

track: A2-technical-curriculum
claim: Head impacts occur routinely in boxing sparring at measurable rates: an average of 27.63 +/- 17.87 impacts above a 9.6 g threshold per boxer were recorded across two 2-minute sparring rounds in collegiate boxers, with average peak linear acceleration 23.48 +/- 15.20 g.
study_design: Instrumented headgear measurement with pre/post neurocognitive testing
effect_or_estimate: 27.63±17.87 impacts >9.6 g per boxer in two 2-min rounds; peak linear acceleration 23.48±15.20 g; peak rotational 1761.40±1064.34 rad/s^2
limitations: Instrumented headgear sensors have known accuracy limitations (see A2-077); single short sparring exposure; 'small but measurable' neurocognitive changes reported
citation: 'Quantifying head impacts and neurocognitive performance in collegiate boxers', Journal of Sports Sciences
ppbf_implication: Head-impact exposure is the reason the curriculum's sparring ladder exists. Every rung that can be taught without head contact should be, and the gating layer must make that the default.
verified_title: Quantifying head impacts and neurocognitive performance in collegiate boxers.

track: A2-technical-curriculum
claim: Wearable head-impact sensors substantially over- or under-count events in boxing: against 5,168 video-verified events across 115 sparring rounds, an instrumented mouthguard recorded 695 events while a skin patch recorded 1,579 and a headgear patch 1,690; a companion study found a large proportion of kinematic traces were of questionable or low quality.
study_design: Video-referenced sensor validation with sensitivity, specificity and PPV
effect_or_estimate: Event counts 695 / 1,579 / 1,690 against 5,168 video-verified contacts; trace quality categorised as high, questionable or low
limitations: Seven boxers; specific sensor models and firmware; video identification of contacts is itself imperfect
citation: 'Capturing Head Impacts in Boxing: A Video-Based Comparison of Three Wearable Sensors' and 'Quality Issues in Kinematic Traces from Three Head Impact Sensors in Boxing', Annals of Biomedical Engineering
ppbf_implication: HARD PRODUCT RULE: SHADOW must not ingest wearable head-impact counts as a safety signal or exposure metric. A device disagreeing with video by a factor of two cannot underwrite a gating decision. Coach-observed and video-verified contact counts are the only defensible input.
verified_title: Capturing Head Impacts in Boxing: A Video-Based Comparison of Three Wearable Sensors.

track: A2-technical-curriculum
claim: The acute dose-response relationship between head impact exposure and concussion remains unresolved; an exploratory cohort in seven competitive boxers tracked SCAT5 symptom-scale changes before, immediately after and 48 h after sparring against instrumented-mouthguard impact data.
effect_or_estimate: Exploratory; the authors state the acute dose-response relationship remains elusive
limitations: n=7; exploratory; sensor limitations per A2-077
citation: 'Exploring the link between acute symptom changes and repetitive head impacts in boxing sparring', Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
ppbf_implication: There is NO validated sparring-volume threshold. Any PPBF sparring dose limit is a PROPOSED PPBF PARAMETER requiring validation, and the decision owner is a qualified coach plus medical oversight, never SHADOW.
verified_title: Exploring the link between acute symptom changes and repetitive head impacts in boxing sparring.

track: A2-technical-curriculum
claim: Concussion recognition, management and return-to-play decisions are governed by the 6th International Consensus Statement on Concussion in Sport (Amsterdam 2022), with paediatric-specific recommendations issued separately; SCAT tools show best diagnostic discrimination within the first 72 hours and subacute evaluation beyond 72 hours requires a multimodal assessment.
study_design: International consensus statement informed by 10 systematic reviews
effect_or_estimate: SCAT best diagnostic discrimination within 72 h post-injury; multimodal tool required subacutely
limitations: Consensus statements reflect expert synthesis and are periodically superseded
citation: 'Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport-Amsterdam, October 2022' (BJSM) and 'Pediatric Sport-Related Concussion: Recommendations From the Amsterdam Consensus Statement 2023' (Pediatrics)
ppbf_implication: HARD BOUNDARY: SHADOW performs NO concussion assessment, no symptom interpretation and no RTP decision. It routes to a qualified healthcare professional and records that a human decision is pending. Decision owner: licensed medical provider; PPBF role: escalate and document.
verified_title: Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport-Amsterdam, October 2022.

track: A2-technical-curriculum
claim: A systematic review of observational studies concluded on the risk of chronic traumatic brain injury from amateur boxing across 36 papers with extractable data, and a subsequent systematic review examined later-in-life health risks associated with sport-related concussion and repetitive head impacts.
population: Amateur boxers; athletes with RHI exposure across sports
effect_or_estimate: Chronic traumatic brain injury defined by clinical neurological examination, psychometric testing, neuroimaging and EEG abnormality
limitations: Observational study designs with substantial methodological heterogeneity and selection bias; causal inference is limited
citation: 'Amateur boxing and risk of chronic traumatic brain injury: systematic review of observational studies' (BMJ) and 'Examining later-in-life health risks associated with sport-related concussion and repetitive head impacts: a systematic review' (BJSM)
ppbf_implication: The ethical basis for PPBF's no-contact-first curriculum design and for maximising the proportion of technical development achievable without head contact. This is a programme-design consequence, not a medical claim.

track: A2-technical-curriculum

verified_title: Biological maturation of youth athletes: assessment and implications.

track: A2-technical-curriculum
claim: A left-hander advantage in interactive combat-type sports is documented in fencing and is generally attributed to a frequency-dependent (negative frequency-dependent) mechanism — rarity giving left-handers more practice against right-handers than the reverse — with alternative innate-ability explanations also proposed but less well supported.
population: Fencers and elite interactive individual sport athletes
study_design: Historical/analytical review plus large archival distribution study over 10 years (2007-2016)
effect_or_estimate: Frequency-dependent explanation supported by both historical fencing-master consensus and modern laterality research; handedness examined alongside relative age effects
boxing_specific: NO - fencing and mixed interactive sports; no boxing-specific test retrieved
limitations: No boxing-specific southpaw advantage study was retrieved. Transferring the fencing finding to boxing is inference. Frequency-dependence predicts the advantage shrinks with exposure, which is itself testable
citation: 'In fencing, what gives left-handers the edge? Views from the present and the distant past' (Laterality) and 'Handedness and Relative Age in International Elite Interactive Individual Sports Revisited' (Front Sports Act Living)
ppbf_implication: The frequency-dependence account has a direct curriculum consequence: deliberately schedule orthodox-vs-southpaw exposure so orthodox athletes are not systematically under-practised against southpaws. Flag as transfer from fencing.
verified_title: In fencing, what gives left-handers the edge? Views from the present and the distant past.

track: A2-technical-curriculum

effect_or_estimate: Significant device-measured accuracy differences at posttest and retention; no handgrip differences
limitations: Fencing, not boxing; bilateral practice; single study

ppbf_implication: Includes a four-week retention test — exactly the design PPBF needs for its own retention variants. Cite as method template, not as boxing evidence.
verified_title: Effectiveness and Durability of Transfer Training in Fencing.

track: A2-technical-curriculum

sample_size: 120 participants across 8 groups in the CI/errorless experiment
effect_or_estimate: Combined effects of random/blocked practice with errorless/errorful conditions examined at retention
limitations: Errorless learning and high contextual interference pull in partly opposite directions, so their combination is not settled; the meta-analysis was identified at protocol/publication stage in this search
citation: 'A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of errorless motor learning on movement outcomes' (Front Psychol) and 'An Examination of the Contextual Interference Effect and the Errorless Learning Model during Motor Learning' (J Motor Behav)
ppbf_implication: Directly relevant to PPBF's adaptive and beginner lanes, where early success matters for retention in the programme (not just skill retention). Reconcile with the CI finding: errorless-first for the introduction phase, high CI for consolidation, is a coherent but UNTESTED sequencing hypothesis.
verified_title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of errorless motor learning on movement outcomes: a lifespan and impairment perspective.

track: A2-technical-curriculum
topic: acquisition-retention dissociation is the central measurement risk
claim: Multiple independent lines of evidence show that within-practice performance and durable learning dissociate: high contextual interference depresses acquisition while improving retention and transfer; self-controlled feedback shows no acquisition advantage but retention and transfer benefits; and augmented kinematic feedback produced no group differences during acquisition with differences emerging only at delayed retention tests.
population: Motor learners across laboratory and sport settings
study_design: Convergence of three meta-analyses and one RCT with delayed retention testing
sample_size: 54 studies (CI retention); 34 studies (CI transfer); 29 studies (self-controlled); 40 participants (shooting RCT)
effect_or_estimate: Consistent direction across independent literatures: acquisition performance is a biased estimator of learning
limitations: Boxing-specific confirmation is absent; the principle is imported
source_type: convergence of systematic reviews and RCT
citation: Scientific Reports PMID 38987617; Frontiers in Psychology PMID 39205981; Behavioral Sciences PMID 41009321; Journal of Sports Sciences PMID 14620030
ppbf_implication: THE governing principle of the A2 deliverable. Every rubric carries a retention_test_variant and a transfer_test_variant because a score taken inside the teaching drill measures acquisition, and acquisition is a biased proxy for learning. SHADOW must not mark a skill 'achieved' on same-session evidence.
verified_title: High contextual interference improves retention in motor learning: systematic review and meta-analysis.

effect_or_estimate: High-quality traces: 53% mouthguard, 20% skin patch, 26% headgear patch
limitations: Device-specific; quality criteria are the authors' own.
citation: Quality Issues in Kinematic Traces from Three Head Impact Sensors in Boxing: Prevalence, Effects, and Implications for Exposure Assessment. Ann Biomed Eng 2024.
verification: pubmed:PMID 39625630 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1007/s10439-024-03647-1

verified_title: Quality Issues in Kinematic Traces from Three Head Impact Sensors in Boxing: Prevalence, Effects, and Implications for Exposure Assessment.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
topic: Cumulative sparring exposure and neurological function
claim: In 237 professional boxers competing in Maryland between 2003 and 2008, higher scores on a Cumulative Sparring Index were associated with poorer performance on both a cognitive test (Symbol Digit Modalities Test) and a balance test (Sharpened Romberg Test), with a threshold effect noted whereby those reporting index values above about 150 experienced a decline in cognition.
study_design: cross-sectional association study using self-reported exposure
effect_or_estimate: Threshold effect at Cumulative Sparring Index above approximately 150
transfer_status: direct - PROFESSIONAL boxers; does NOT transfer to youth or novice amateur
limitations: CROSS-SECTIONAL AND ASSOCIATIONAL - does not establish causation. Exposure was self-reported. The index is a composite; the '150' threshold is specific to that index and is not a rounds-per-week number.
citation: Sparring and neurological function in professional boxers. Front Public Health 2014.
verification: pubmed:PMID 25101253 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.3389/fpubh.2014.00069
ppbf_implication: Supports monitoring CUMULATIVE sparring exposure, not weekly counts alone. Does NOT license PPBF to publish a safe dose. The threshold value must never be quoted as a PPBF limit.
verified_title: Sparring and neurological function in professional boxers.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: In 42 volunteer professional boxers, neuropsychological test performance was not associated with age, boxing record, career length or history of knockout or technical knockout, but the amount of sparring was inversely associated with performance on several tests, with impairments in attention, concentration and memory.
study_design: cross-sectional volunteer cohort with neuropsychological testing
effect_or_estimate: Inverse association between sparring amount and several neuropsychological test scores
limitations: n=42, volunteer sample, cross-sectional, 1996. Self-reported exposure. No causal claim possible.
citation: Sparring and cognitive function in professional boxers. Phys Sportsmed 1996.
verification: pubmed:PMID 20086991 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.3810/psm.1996.05.1358
ppbf_implication: A second, independent associational signal pointing the same direction as A3-037. Two associational studies are still not a dose-response finding.
verified_title: Sparring and cognitive function in professional boxers.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
topic: Sparring and brain volumes - competing evidence
claim: In 94 active professional mixed martial arts fighters, a higher number of weekly sparring rounds during typical training was significantly associated with LARGER left (beta 13.5 microlitres per round, 95% CI 2.26-24.8) and right (14.9 microlitres per round, 95% CI 3.64-26.2) caudate volumes, and was not significantly associated with thalamus, putamen, hippocampus or amygdala volumes.
study_design: cross-sectional multivariable regression within a brain health study
effect_or_estimate: Caudate volume: +13.5 uL/round left, +14.9 uL/round right
transfer_status: OTHER COMBAT SPORT - MMA, not boxing
limitations: Cross-sectional; larger volume is not automatically better; motor-skill training is a plausible competing explanation the authors raise; MMA sparring differs from boxing sparring.
citation: Sparring and the Brain: The Associations between Sparring and Regional Brain Volumes in Professional Mixed Martial Arts Fighters. Sports Med 2023.
verification: pubmed:PMID 36972014 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1007/s40279-023-01838-9
ppbf_implication: PPBF must present the sparring literature as genuinely mixed. A brief that only cites the harm-direction studies would be selective reporting.
verified_title: Sparring and the Brain: The Associations between Sparring and Regional Brain Volumes in Professional Mixed Martial Arts Fighters.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: In ten non-professional male boxers, circulating cell-free mitochondrial DNA levels increased after each of three weekly sparring matches, with reduced DNA integrity after each match, particularly in the naked (unprotected) form.
effect_or_estimate: Increase after each of three weekly sparring matches; cumulative increase in one plasma fraction across weeks
limitations: n=10, male, no control condition. The clinical significance of circulating mitochondrial DNA for long-term brain health is NOT established.
citation: Increase of circulating cell free mitochondrial DNA in amateur boxers after sparring matches. J Sci Med Sport 2025.
verification: pubmed:PMID 39934060 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1016/j.jsams.2025.01.011
ppbf_implication: A measurable acute biological response to sparring exists. Do not over-interpret: this is a biomarker signal, not a demonstrated harm.
verified_title: Increase of circulating cell free mitochondrial DNA in amateur boxers after sparring matches.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: In 14 amateur boxers undergoing lumbar puncture 7-10 days after a bout and again after three months of rest, neurofilament light protein (845 +/- 1140 vs 208 +/- 108 ng/L) and total tau (449 +/- 176 vs 306 +/- 78 ng/L) were increased after the bout relative to after rest.
population: amateur boxers (11 men, 3 women) and 10 non-athletic male controls
effect_or_estimate: NFL 845 vs 208 ng/L (p=.008); total tau 449 vs 306 ng/L (p=.006)
limitations: n=14; markers of neuronal and axonal injury elevated 7-10 days post-bout with resolution after rest - the long-term significance of transient elevation is not established.
citation: Neurochemical aftermath of amateur boxing. Arch Neurol 2006.
verification: pubmed:PMID 16966505 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1001/archneur.63.9.1277
ppbf_implication: Supports the principle that rest after competition is biologically warranted, and supports the regulated post-stoppage restriction periods.
verified_title: Neurochemical aftermath of amateur boxing.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 prospective cohort studies in amateur boxing produced pooled competition injury incidence estimates of 54.7 per 1,000 athlete-exposures (95% CI 33.8-88.4) and 6.8 per 1,000 minutes of exposure (95% CI 4.2-10.9), and a training injury incidence of 1.3 per 1,000 hours (95% CI 0.2-7.0); the most commonly injured regions were head and neck in competition (median 72%, range 46-100%) and upper limb in training (median 49%, range from 40%).
study_design: systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohorts
effect_or_estimate: Competition 54.7/1000 AE and 6.8/1000 min; training 1.3/1000 h; head/neck 72% of competition injuries
limitations: Wide confidence intervals, especially for training injuries (0.2-7.0), indicating substantial heterogeneity. Population-level rates cannot be converted into an individual's risk or a safe bout number.
citation: Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sci Med Sport 2022.
verification: pubmed:PMID 36195527 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1016/j.jsams.2022.09.165
ppbf_implication: Two design consequences: head and neck dominate competition injury (exposure control), upper limb dominates training injury (hand/wrist conditioning is not optional in the warm-up).
verified_title: Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 21st-century boxing epidemiology studies (14 studies) produced pooled injury incidence rates of 223.9 per 1,000 boxers (95% CI 157.5-290.4), 233.3 per 1,000 competition exposures (95% CI 161.3-305.2) and 13.0 per 1,000 minutes of competition (95% CI 8.9-17.1).
population: boxers across organised boxing activities worldwide
effect_or_estimate: 223.9/1000 boxers; 233.3/1000 competition exposures; 13.0/1000 competition minutes
limitations: Most included studies were of moderate quality (11 of 14); estimates differ substantially from A3-042 because of different denominators and inclusion criteria - the two syntheses are not directly comparable.
citation: Incidence Rates and Pathology Types of Boxing-Specific Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Epidemiology Studies in the 21st Century. Orthop J Sports Med 2023.
verification: pubmed:PMID 37025124 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1177/23259671221127669
ppbf_implication: Cite alongside A3-042 and show both. Presenting one injury rate as THE rate would misrepresent the literature.
verified_title: Incidence Rates and Pathology Types of Boxing-Specific Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Epidemiology Studies in the 21st Century.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: A prospective study of injuries in competitive boxing was published in the International Journal of Sports Medicine in 2014.
sex: not established from the retrieved record
age_range: not established from the retrieved record
sample_size: not established from the retrieved record

ppbf_implication: Add to the reading list for PPBF's injury-surveillance design. Do not cite any statistic from it until read.
verified_title: Injuries in competitive boxing. A prospective study.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: A 2025 mixed-methods study examined whether it is feasible to implement an injury surveillance system for amateur boxing events in Australia.
sample_size: not established from the retrieved record
effect_or_estimate: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE - detailed findings not retrieved; existence and topic verified
limitations: Included as a directly relevant methods precedent for PPBF's own surveillance design; findings not extracted.
citation: Is it feasible to implement an injury surveillance system for amateur boxing events in Australia? A mixed methods study. J Sci Med Sport 2025.
verification: pubmed:PMID 41421883 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1016/j.jsams.2025.12.007
ppbf_implication: Read before designing PPBF injury surveillance - it is the closest published precedent to what PPBF needs.
verified_title: Is it feasible to implement an injury surveillance system for amateur boxing events in Australia? A mixed methods study.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of head trauma in boxing (35 of 84 articles included) reported that boxers have a significantly elevated risk of sustaining a concussion compared with other combat sports, and that among the boxers analysed 147 of 631 (23.3%) had cavum septum pellucidum and 125 of 411 (30.4%) presented with some form of brain atrophy.
sample_size: 35 included articles; 631 and 411 boxers for the imaging findings
effect_or_estimate: Cavum septum pellucidum 23.3%; brain atrophy 30.4%
limitations: Pooling heterogeneous imaging studies with varying definitions and eras; selection into imaging studies may not be representative; no comparable non-boxing control prevalence is given in the abstract.
citation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Investigating Head Trauma in Boxing. Clin J Sport Med 2023.
verification: pubmed:PMID 37862081 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1097/JSM.0000000000001195
ppbf_implication: PPBF must present head-trauma risk honestly in guardian and athlete informed consent. Not a SHADOW output; a governance and disclosure requirement.
verified_title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Investigating Head Trauma in Boxing.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
topic: Amateur boxing and chronic brain injury - the counterweight
claim: A systematic review of observational studies on chronic traumatic brain injury in amateur boxing found the quality of evidence was generally poor, and that the best-quality studies - cohort designs and those using psychometric tests - yielded the most negative results, with only four of 17 (24%) better-quality studies finding any indication of chronic traumatic brain injury.
study_design: systematic review of observational studies (MOOSE protocol)
sample_size: 36 papers with extractable data from 93 evaluated
effect_or_estimate: 4 of 17 (24%) better-quality studies found any indication of chronic traumatic brain injury
limitations: Published 2007 - predates much modern imaging and biomarker work. Poor underlying evidence quality means absence of a finding is not strong evidence of absence.
citation: Amateur boxing and risk of chronic traumatic brain injury: systematic review of observational studies. BMJ 2007.
verification: pubmed:PMID 17916811 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1136/bmj.39342.690220.55
ppbf_implication: CRITICAL FOR HONEST COMMUNICATION: the amateur-boxing chronic-injury literature is weaker and more equivocal than the professional literature. PPBF must not import professional-boxing risk estimates into an amateur or youth context.
verified_title: Amateur boxing and risk of chronic traumatic brain injury: systematic review of observational studies.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
topic: Amateur boxing and later cognitive impairment
claim: In the Caerphilly Prospective Study of 1,123 men aged 45-59 at baseline followed for 35 years, a self-report of having boxed 'seriously' when younger was associated with a two-fold increase in cognitive impairment (odds ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.18-4.38), rising to 2.78 (95% CI 1.37-5.65) for amnestic impairment, and with an advancement in dementia onset of 4.8 years (95% CI 0.9-8.8).
population: men in a representative population cohort
effect_or_estimate: Cognitive impairment OR 2.27 (1.18-4.38); amnestic OR 2.78 (1.37-5.65); onset advanced 4.8 y (0.9-8.8)
transfer_status: direct - male amateur; historical exposure era
limitations: Exposure was self-reported at a single examination with no dose measure; 'boxed seriously' is undefined; confounding by era, occupation and other exposures is plausible; wide confidence intervals.
citation: Amateur Boxing and Dementia: Cognitive Impairment Within the 35-Year Caerphilly Cohort Study. Clin J Sport Med 2021.
verification: pubmed:PMID 35470341 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1097/JSM.0000000000000976
ppbf_implication: Sits in direct tension with A3-046. Both must be presented. This is the strongest single argument for PPBF minimising unnecessary head contact even in amateur and recreational settings.
verified_title: Amateur Boxing and Dementia: Cognitive Impairment Within the 35-Year Caerphilly Cohort Study.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
topic: Later-in-life health after concussion and repetitive head impacts
claim: A systematic review informing the Amsterdam consensus examined later-in-life health risks associated with sport-related concussion or exposure to repetitive head impacts, including ten studies of former amateur athletes and 18 of former professional athletes; depression was examined in five studies of former amateurs with none identifying an increased risk, and nine studies examining suicidality or suicide as manner of death found no association with increased risk.
population: former amateur and professional athletes across sports
study_design: systematic review of case-control and cohort studies
effect_or_estimate: No increased depression or suicidality risk identified in former amateur athletes in the included studies; some professional-vs-general-population associations reported for dementia and ALS
transfer_status: OTHER SPORTS - multi-sport review, boxing is not the focus
limitations: No post-mortem neuropathology or neuroimaging studies met inclusion criteria. Absence of an identified association in a limited set of studies is not evidence of safety.
citation: Examining later-in-life health risks associated with sport-related concussion and repetitive head impacts: a systematic review of case-control and cohort studies. Br J Sports Med 2023.
verification: pubmed:PMID 37316187 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2023-106890
ppbf_implication: Use to keep PPBF's risk communication calibrated: the amateur-level later-life picture is less alarming than public discourse assumes, and less reassuring than the absence of findings suggests.
verified_title: Examining later-in-life health risks associated with sport-related concussion and repetitive head impacts: a systematic review of case-control and cohort studies.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: The 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport (Amsterdam, October 2022) produced a consensus statement supported by ten systematic reviews, together with revised tools including the Concussion Recognition Tool 6, Sport Concussion Assessment Tool 6 and Child SCAT6, and a new Sport Concussion Office Assessment Tool 6.
study_design: international consensus statement informed by systematic reviews
effect_or_estimate: Consensus process outputs: CRT6, SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, Child SCOAT6
transfer_status: general sport consensus applied to boxing
limitations: Consensus, not a trial. Boxing is a sport where head impact is intentional, which differs from the sports that dominate the evidence base.
citation: Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport-Amsterdam, October 2022. Br J Sports Med 2023.
verification: pubmed:PMID 37316210 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2023-106898
ppbf_implication: PPBF should adopt the current consensus tools rather than invent its own. Recognition and removal is a coach responsibility; assessment and clearance are clinician responsibilities. SHADOW does neither.
verified_title: Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport-Amsterdam, October 2022.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: A systematic review of factors relevant to advising athletes about retirement or discontinuation from contact or collision sport after sport-related concussion screened 4,355 articles and included 93, and found that NONE of the included articles directly examined retirement or discontinuation.
population: athletes in contact and collision sports
effect_or_estimate: Zero included studies directly examined retirement or discontinuation
limitations: The finding is the absence of evidence, which is itself important.
citation: When should an athlete retire or discontinue participating in contact or collision sports following sport-related concussion? A systematic review. Br J Sports Med 2023.
verification: pubmed:PMID 37316181 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2023-106815
ppbf_implication: Retirement advice has no evidence base. SHADOW must never generate a retirement recommendation. This is a clinician-and-athlete conversation with acknowledged uncertainty.
verified_title: When should an athlete retire or discontinue participating in contact or collision sports following sport-related concussion? A systematic review.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: The American Academy of Pediatrics policy statement, developed with the Canadian Paediatric Society, states that because the sport of boxing encourages and rewards deliberate blows to the head and face and participants are at risk of head, face and neck injuries including chronic and even fatal neurological injuries, both organisations oppose boxing as a sport for children and adolescents and recommend that physicians vigorously oppose youth boxing and encourage alternative sports.
population: children and adolescents under 19 in North America
effect_or_estimate: Categorical position: opposition to youth boxing
limitations: A policy position weighing risk against acknowledged benefits (exercise, self-discipline, self-confidence), not a new empirical finding. Published 2011.
citation: Policy statement—Boxing participation by children and adolescents. Pediatrics 2011.
verification: pubmed:PMID 21873697 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1542/peds.2011-1165
ppbf_implication: MUST be disclosed to guardians at intake. A youth boxing programme that does not surface the paediatric position is not operating with informed consent. Governance decision for Jason and the board.
verified_title: Policy statement—Boxing participation by children and adolescents.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: The Canadian Paediatric Society issued a joint statement with the American Academy of Pediatrics on boxing participation by children and adolescents.
effect_or_estimate: Joint position corroborating A3-051
limitations: Position statement; 2012.
citation: Boxing participation by children and adolescents: A joint statement with the American Academy of Pediatrics. Paediatr Child Health 2012.
verification: pubmed:PMID 23277756 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1093/pch/17.1.39
ppbf_implication: Confirms the paediatric position is cross-national, not a single-body view.
verified_title: Boxing participation by children and adolescents: A joint statement with the American Academy of Pediatrics.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
topic: Headguards - what they do and do not do
claim: The Association of Ringside Physicians position statement holds that headguards are highly effective at reducing facial lacerations in studies of amateur boxers and are appropriate especially in sparring prior to competition where avoidance of laceration and blood-borne pathogen exposure matters, but that headguards should NOT be relied upon to reduce the risk of concussion or other traumatic brain injury, since they have not been shown to prevent these injuries in combat sports and human studies on their effect on concussive injury are lacking.
effect_or_estimate: Effective for lacerations and auricular injury; NOT demonstrated for concussion prevention
limitations: Position statement. The statement notes biomechanical studies suggest reduced linear and rotational cranial acceleration, but also raises behavioural risk compensation when wearing headguards.
citation: Headguard use in combat sports: position statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians. Phys Sportsmed 2023.
verification: pubmed:PMID 37559553 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1080/00913847.2023.2242415
ppbf_implication: PPBF must never present headgear as concussion protection to athletes or guardians. Headgear is laceration and ear protection with an unproven brain-injury effect.
verified_title: Headguard use in combat sports: position statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: A systematic literature review of protective headgear and head injury prevention in Olympic boxing (39 articles) concluded that headguards protect well against lacerations and skull fractures, while less is known about their protective effects against concussion and other traumatic brain injuries.
effect_or_estimate: Protective for lacerations and skull fractures; uncertain for concussion
limitations: Heterogeneous article types including grey literature; the underlying evidence on concussion is what is missing, not the review.
citation: Concussions, cuts and cracked bones: A systematic literature review on protective headgear and head injury prevention in Olympic boxing. Eur J Sport Sci 2021.
verification: pubmed:PMID 33607924 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1080/17461391.2021.1872711
ppbf_implication: Corroborates A3-054 from an independent review.
verified_title: Concussions, cuts and cracked bones: A systematic literature review on protective headgear and head injury prevention in Olympic boxing.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: A cross-sectional observational study comparing World Series of Boxing (without head guards) to other AIBA competitions (with head guards), and comparing the 2009 and 2011 world championships (with head guards) to 2013 (without), found that the number of stoppages due to head blows was significantly decreased without head guards, alongside a notable increase in cuts.
study_design: prospective cross-sectional observational, data recorded by ringside physicians
sample_size: stoppages per 10,000 rounds across the compared competitions
effect_or_estimate: Significantly fewer stoppages due to head blows without head guards; increase in cuts
limitations: CONTESTED. Stoppages are a proxy for acute brain injury, not a measure of it. Behaviour, refereeing and boxer style all changed simultaneously. A published response letter exists (PMID 27740948; DOI 10.1097/JSM.0000000000000401, Clin J Sport Med 2018) and a 2025 Sports Med Open opinion argues the evidence does not support headguard bans.
citation: Use of Head Guards in AIBA Boxing Tournaments-A Cross-Sectional Observational Study. Clin J Sport Med 2017.
verification: pubmed:PMID 27116592 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1097/JSM.0000000000000322; response letter also verified pubmed:PMID 27740948 (DOI 10.1097/JSM.0000000000000401), 2026-08-07
ppbf_implication: Do not present headguard removal as settled science in either direction. This is the clearest example in the file of a CONTESTED PRACTICE claim.
verified_title: Use of Head Guards in AIBA Boxing Tournaments-A Cross-Sectional Observational Study.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: A 2025 current-opinion article argues that headguards are effective in protecting against cuts and lacerations, that there is insufficient evidence supporting headguard bans, and that a gap exists in collaboration and communication between the IBA and smaller representative bodies.
effect_or_estimate: Position: insufficient evidence supports headguard bans
limitations: Opinion piece, not a systematic review. Represents one side of an active policy dispute.
citation: The Case for Protective Headguards in Amateur Boxing and Implications for International Policy on Headguard Bans. Sports Med Open 2025.
verification: pubmed:PMID 40377858 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1186/s40798-025-00871-4
ppbf_implication: Cite alongside A3-056 so the dispute is visible. PPBF follows the applicable rulebook; it does not take a side.
verified_title: The Case for Protective Headguards in Amateur Boxing and Implications for International Policy on Headguard Bans.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: A review of 29,357 Olympic-style boxing bouts from 1952 to 2011 examined how rule changes altered verdict rates, reporting an increase in referee-stopped-contest-injury rate (0.72% to 2.42%) after the introduction of the standing-count rule, and changes in RSC-Head rates associated with subsequent rule modifications.
effect_or_estimate: RSC-Injury 0.72% to 2.42% after the standing-count rule (p<0.03)
limitations: Retrospective; verdict coding changed over the period; era confounds are substantial; rule changes did not occur in isolation.
citation: Amateur boxing in the last 59 years. Impact of rules changes on the type of verdicts recorded and implications on boxers' health. Br J Sports Med 2013.
verification: pubmed:PMID 23314931 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2012-091771
ppbf_implication: Historical evidence that rule changes shift injury-relevant outcomes in measurable ways - supports treating rule sets as a variable in PPBF's data model, not a constant.
verified_title: Amateur boxing in the last 59 years. Impact of rules changes on the type of verdicts recorded and implications on boxers' health.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: The Association of Ringside Physicians identifies criteria for combat sports athletes at significantly increased risk of injury and mortality: age younger than 13 or older than 35; three consecutive losses, particularly by KO/TKO (professional) or referee-stops-contest (amateur); inactivity exceeding one year (professional); no prior wins; significant mismatches in record, experience, age or physical conditioning; history of concussion, lack of full recovery and clearance from the most recent concussion, or other significant neurological injury; severe pre-bout hypertension (systolic above 160 or diastolic above 100 mmHg in adults, or stage 2 hypertension in paediatric athletes); and any medical condition identified at licensing or pre-bout examination that compromises defensive abilities.
age_range: all, with explicit under-13 and over-35 markers
study_design: professional body position statement with graded levels of evidence per criterion (LOE II-V)
effect_or_estimate: Eight named risk criteria; most graded LOE V (expert opinion), concussion history graded LOE II, three-consecutive-losses LOE III
limitations: MOST CRITERIA ARE LEVEL V EVIDENCE, i.e. expert opinion. The authors label the levels honestly and PPBF should too.
citation: Identifying High-Risk Combat Sport Athletes: Position Statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians. Clin J Sport Med 2025.
verification: pubmed:PMID 41413937 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1097/JSM.0000000000001403
ppbf_implication: The single most directly implementable safety artefact found in this track. Encode as coach-facing FLAGS with the LOE shown, never as an automated block or clearance.
verified_title: Identifying High-Risk Combat Sport Athletes: Position Statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: The Association of Ringside Physicians defines Older Fighters as combat sports athletes older than 35 and states that age-related changes to the neurological, cardiopulmonary, endocrinological, thermoregulatory, osmoregulatory and musculoskeletal systems increase injury risk and may prolong recovery, warranting special considerations for competition, licensure, pre-fight clearance, in-fight supervision, post-fight examination and retirement counselling, including more comprehensive neurological evaluation and neuroimaging, careful cardiac assessment, and individualised post-injury clearance.
effect_or_estimate: Age threshold 35 for enhanced medical consideration
limitations: Position statement based on general age-related physiology rather than combat-sport-specific trials.
citation: Care of The Older Fighter: Position Statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians. Phys Sportsmed 2024.
verification: pubmed:PMID 38708547 (metadata + abstract retrieved via PubMed MCP, 2026-08-07); DOI 10.1080/00913847.2024.2344227
ppbf_implication: Directly drives the S11 Masters stage design: enhanced medical clearance is a hard gate, recovery is the planning variable, and clearance is individualised by a clinician.
verified_title: Care of The Older Fighter: Position Statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians.

track: Track 3 - Level/stage structures, regulatory pathway, session and annual/camp templates
claim: A systematic review informing the Amsterdam consensus examined prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors for sport-related concussions and head impacts.
