verified_title: Athlete Burnout and the Risk of Dropout Among Young Elite Handball Players

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: AMSSM position statement addresses overuse injuries and burnout in youth sport, recommending diversification and monitoring of training volume and psychological signs.
effect_or_estimate: Consensus recommendations
transfer_status: Youth sport generally; boxing not separately specified
limitations: Consensus, not trial evidence; jurisdiction-neutral
citation: DiFiori JP, Benjamin HJ, Brenner JS, et al. Overuse injuries and burnout in youth sports: a position statement from the American Medical Society for Sports Medicine. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2014.
ppbf_implication: Anchors PPBF youth load policy; medical interpretation stays with qualified clinicians.
verified_title: Overuse injuries and burnout in youth sports: a position statement from the American Medical Society for Sports Medicine

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: IOC consensus statement on mental health in elite athletes sets out recognition, screening and management principles and stresses that non-clinicians must not diagnose.
effect_or_estimate: Consensus recommendations
transfer_status: ELITE — explicit caution against extending to youth community sport without adaptation
limitations: Elite focus; youth community applicability limited
citation: Reardon CL, Hainline B, Aron CM, et al. Mental health in elite athletes: International Olympic Committee consensus statement (2019). British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2019.
ppbf_implication: Definitive basis for the SHADOW prohibition on psychological scoring as clinical judgement.
verified_title: Mental health in elite athletes: International Olympic Committee consensus statement (2019)

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: The IOC Sport Mental Health Assessment Tool 1 (SMHAT-1) and Recognition Tool 1 were developed for use with elite athletes as a triage-to-clinician pathway.
effect_or_estimate: Tool structure and intended use defined; not validated for children
transfer_status: ELITE, 16+ — NOT validated for younger youth community participants
limitations: Age floor; requires clinician follow-up; not a diagnostic instrument
citation: Gouttebarge V, Bindra A, Blauwet C, et al. International Olympic Committee (IOC) Sport Mental Health Assessment Tool 1 (SMHAT-1) and Sport Mental Health Recognition Tool 1 (SMHRT-1). British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2021.
ppbf_implication: PPBF should NOT deploy SMHAT-1 to under-16s; if used at all it requires a named clinician receiving results.
verified_title: International Olympic Committee (IOC) Sport Mental Health Assessment Tool 1 (SMHAT-1) and Sport Mental Health Recognition Tool 1 (SMHRT-1): towards better support of athletes’ mental health

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Systematic review and meta-analysis reports substantial occurrence of mental health symptoms and disorders among current and former elite athletes.
effect_or_estimate: Prevalence estimates reported with wide heterogeneity
transfer_status: ELITE adult; do not apply rates to PPBF youth
limitations: Heterogeneous instruments; self-report; elite samples
citation: Gouttebarge V, Castaldelli-Maia JM, Gorczynski P, et al. Occurrence of mental health symptoms and disorders in current and former elite athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2019.
ppbf_implication: Do not quote elite prevalence figures in PPBF grant or parent materials as if they describe PPBF athletes.
verified_title: Occurrence of mental health symptoms and disorders in current and former elite athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Systematic review of interventions to raise mental health awareness in sport reports feasibility and some knowledge gains, with limited evidence on behaviour change or athlete outcomes.
effect_or_estimate: Knowledge/awareness gains; downstream outcomes under-evidenced
limitations: Weak outcome measurement; short follow-up
citation: Breslin G, Shannon S, Haughey T, Donnelly P, Leavey G. A systematic review of interventions to increase awareness of mental health and well-being in athletes, coaches and officials. Systematic Reviews, 2017.
ppbf_implication: Coach mental-health-literacy training is defensible for referral quality; do not claim it improves athlete mental health.
verified_title: A systematic review of interventions to increase awareness of mental health and well-being in athletes, coaches and officials

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Systematic review and meta-analysis found psychological readiness (including fear of reinjury) is associated with returning to sport after ACL reconstruction.
effect_or_estimate: Positive psychological responses associated with higher return rates
transfer_status: ORTHOPAEDIC/KNEE population — transfer to boxing head-impact or post-knockout fear is NOT established
limitations: Knee-injury specific; cannot be applied to concussion or knockout return
citation: Ardern CL, Taylor NF, Feller JA, Webster KE. A systematic review of the psychological factors associated with returning to sport following injury. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2013/2014.
ppbf_implication: Establishes that psychological readiness is a distinct, measurable dimension — but PPBF has NO validated post-knockout equivalent.
verified_title: The impact of psychological readiness to return to sport and recreational activities after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction
title_consistency_check: MANUALLY REVIEWED — author-year or multi-source citation, record confirmed

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: The ACL-RSI scale was developed and preliminarily validated to measure the psychological impact of returning to sport after ACL reconstruction.
effect_or_estimate: Preliminary validity reported
transfer_status: Knee-specific; NOT a general fear instrument
limitations: Injury-site specific; not transferable to combat-sport fear without new validation
citation: Webster KE, Feller JA, Lambros C. Development and preliminary validation of a scale to measure the psychological impact of returning to sport following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction surgery. Physical Therapy in Sport, 2008.
ppbf_implication: Template for how a PPBF post-layoff readiness item set would have to be built and validated — it does not exist yet.
verified_title: Development and preliminary validation of a scale to measure the psychological impact of returning to sport following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction surgery

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: The TSK-11 is a shortened Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia with reported psychometric support in pain populations.
effect_or_estimate: Reliability and validity reported for the short form
transfer_status: CLINICAL PAIN population — not a sport-fear or combat-fear instrument
limitations: Pain-population validation; adult; not youth-validated
citation: Woby SR, Roach NK, Urmston M, Watson PJ. Psychometric properties of the TSK-11: A shortened version of the Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia. Pain, 2005.
ppbf_implication: Frequently misapplied in gyms; PPBF should not use it for boxers without clinical governance.
verified_title: Psychometric properties of the TSK-11: A shortened version of the Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: No adequate peer-reviewed evidence base was located quantifying psychological sequelae of knockout or heavy defeat in boxing, or specifying safe psychological return criteria.
effect_or_estimate: No estimate available
boxing_specific: Yes — this is a boxing-specific gap
transfer_status: Not applicable; the gap is boxing-specific
limitations: Searches across PubMed, OpenAlex and Crossref did not surface a controlled or systematically reviewed body of work on this question
citation: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE — no qualifying source located
verification: pubmed + openalex + crossref searches 2026-08-07 returned no qualifying evidence
ppbf_implication: SHADOW must NOT generate return-after-knockout psychological guidance. Medical clearance is a physician decision; psychological readiness is a coach + qualified practitioner conversation.

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Systematic review of martial arts and combat sports training effects on anger and aggression reports mixed findings, with results varying by style, instructional approach, participant age and study design.
population: Martial arts and combat sport participants
effect_or_estimate: MIXED — no single direction supported
boxing_specific: Partly — includes combat sports; boxing not separately isolated
limitations: Heterogeneous designs and measures; many non-randomised; instructional context often unreported
citation: Lafuente JC, Zubiaur M, Gutiérrez-García C. Effects of martial arts and combat sports training on anger and aggression: A systematic review. Aggression and Violent Behavior, 2021.
ppbf_implication: PPBF must NOT market boxing as aggression-reducing. The honest claim is: outcome depends on how it is taught.
verified_title: Effects of martial arts and combat sports training on anger and aggression: A systematic review

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
topic: Aggression — power sports and antisocial involvement
claim: A longitudinal study of preadolescent and adolescent boys found participation in power sports was associated with increased antisocial involvement over time.
effect_or_estimate: Increase in antisocial involvement associated with power-sport participation
boxing_specific: Partly — 'power sports' category includes boxing/wrestling/weightlifting; boxing not isolated
limitations: Single national context; selection effects possible; category aggregates several sports
citation: Endresen IM, Olweus D. Participation in power sports and antisocial involvement in preadolescent and adolescent boys. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 2005.
ppbf_implication: This is the strongest counter-evidence to the PPBF thesis and MUST be represented in the evidence registry, not omitted.
verified_title: Participation in power sports and antisocial involvement in preadolescent and adolescent boys

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Early studies reported that traditional martial arts training (with explicit philosophical/ethical instruction) was associated with lower aggressiveness, whereas modern/sport-only training was not.
effect_or_estimate: Direction reported but designs are weak and dated
limitations: Dated; small samples; non-random assignment; self-selection strongly plausible; not replicated to modern standards
citation: Nosanchuk TA. The Way of the Warrior: The Effects of Traditional Martial Arts Training on Aggressiveness. Human Relations, 1981; Nosanchuk TA, MacNeil MLC. Aggressive Behavior, 1989.
ppbf_implication: Supports the DESIGN hypothesis (explicit ethical instruction matters) but is too weak to be a PPBF evidence base on its own.
verified_title: The Way of the Warrior: The Effects of Traditional Martial Arts Training on Aggressiveness

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Meta-analytic review of sports participation and juvenile delinquency found no simple protective effect; associations depend on sport type and context.
effect_or_estimate: No overall protective effect established; moderators matter
limitations: Heterogeneous delinquency measures; observational designs
citation: Spruit A, van Vugt E, van der Put C, van der Stouwe T, Stams GJ. Sports Participation and Juvenile Delinquency: A Meta-Analytic Review. Journal of Youth and Adolescence, 2016.
ppbf_implication: Directly refutes 'boxing keeps kids out of trouble' as an evidence claim. PPBF grant language must be corrected accordingly.
verified_title: Sports Participation and Juvenile Delinquency: A Meta-Analytic Review

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: The Prosocial and Antisocial Behavior in Sport Scale and the Moral Disengagement in Sport Scale provide validated measures of in-sport moral behaviour.
effect_or_estimate: Factor structures supported
limitations: Measures behaviour inside sport — cannot evidence transfer outside the gym
citation: Kavussanu M, Boardley ID. The Prosocial and Antisocial Behavior in Sport Scale. Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology, 2009; Boardley ID, Kavussanu M. Moral Disengagement in Sport Scale.
ppbf_implication: Usable for PPBF gym-behaviour metrics — but explicitly NOT usable as evidence of life-skill transfer.
verified_title: The Prosocial and Antisocial Behavior in Sport Scale

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: The CART-Q operationalises the coach–athlete relationship via closeness, commitment and complementarity (with co-orientation as the '+1'), with initial validation support.
effect_or_estimate: Multidimensional structure supported
limitations: Self-report; later work has debated factor structure
citation: Jowett S, Ntoumanis N. The Coach-Athlete Relationship Questionnaire (CART-Q): development and initial validation. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, 2004.
ppbf_implication: Gives PPBF a defensible relationship construct; a boxing gym's corner relationship is a plausible but unvalidated application.
verified_title: The Coach–Athlete Relationship Questionnaire (CART‐Q): development and initial validation

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Research links leadership and relationship quality with psychological safety, and psychological safety with quality coach–athlete relationships.
effect_or_estimate: Associations reported; causal direction not established
limitations: Cross-sectional; construct imported from organisational psychology
citation: Jowett S, do Nascimento-Júnior JRA, Zhao C, Gosai J. Creating the conditions for psychological safety and its impact on quality coach-athlete relationships. Psychology of Sport and Exercise, 2023.
ppbf_implication: Psychological safety is the mechanism by which a boxer will report pain, fear or a disclosure — instrument it at gym level.
verified_title: Creating the conditions for psychological safety and its impact on quality coach-athlete relationships

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: A pilot test of transformational leadership training for youth sport coaches reported effects on athletes' developmental experiences.
effect_or_estimate: Pilot-level effects reported
limitations: Pilot; small sample; short follow-up
citation: Vella SA, Oades LG, Crowe TP. A Pilot Test of Transformational Leadership Training for Sports Coaches. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching, 2013.
ppbf_implication: Coach-development lane in PPBF should copy this evaluation design rather than assume the outcome.
verified_title: A Pilot Test of Transformational Leadership Training for Sports Coaches: Impact on the Developmental Experiences of Adolescent Athletes

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: IOC consensus statement on harassment and abuse in sport defines forms of non-accidental violence and sets prevention and response obligations for sport organisations.
effect_or_estimate: Consensus obligations, not effect estimates
limitations: Consensus; implementation varies by jurisdiction and governing body
citation: Mountjoy M, Brackenridge C, Arrington M, et al. International Olympic Committee consensus statement: harassment and abuse (non-accidental violence) in sport. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2016.
ppbf_implication: Primary authority for PPBF safeguarding policy; SHADOW never triages, only routes and preserves.
verified_title: International Olympic Committee consensus statement: harassment and abuse (non-accidental violence) in sport

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer

citation: Tuakli-Wosornu YA, Burrows K, Fasting K, Hartill M, et al. IOC consensus statement: interpersonal violence and safeguarding in sport. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2024.
ppbf_implication: Current authority; PPBF safeguarding policy should be dated against this and reviewed on update.
verified_title: IOC consensus statement: interpersonal violence and safeguarding in sport

effect_or_estimate: Framework recommendations
limitations: Framework; implementation evidence limited

ppbf_implication: Directly applicable to PPBF's youth lane; use as the checklist source for Module 003 / 194.
verified_title: Safeguarding the child athlete in sport: a review, a framework and recommendations for the IOC youth athlete development model

transfer_status: EUROPEAN — US community-gym rates are not established by this study

ppbf_implication: Establishes that safeguarding is a base-rate problem, not an exceptional one. Do not quote European rates as PPBF's rates.
verified_title: Prevalence of interpersonal violence against children in sport in six European countries

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer

verified_title: Psychological, Physical, and Sexual Violence Against Children in Australian Community Sport: Frequency, Perpetrator, and Victim Characteristics

claim: Research on children's experience of disclosing interpersonal violence in community sport documents barriers to telling adults and inadequate adult responses.

verified_title: Telling adults about it: children’s experience of disclosing interpersonal violence in community sport

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer

ppbf_implication: PPBF should measure safeguarding culture (reporting rate, response latency), not just policy existence.
verified_title: Safeguarding culture: towards a new approach to preventing child maltreatment in sport

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Work on trauma-informed approaches in sport coaching is emerging; it is largely conceptual and practice-oriented rather than an evaluated intervention literature.

verified_title: Implementing trauma-informed approaches to coaches’ workplaces in sport to enhance their safety and wellbeing: A critical commentary

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: A definition and model of life-skills transfer specifies transfer as the application of a skill learned in sport to a different life domain, with individual, contextual and mechanism-level components.

verified_title: Definition and model of life skills transfer

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Positive youth development outcomes are conceptualised on an implicit–explicit continuum: implicit approaches rely on the sport environment alone, explicit approaches deliberately teach, label and discuss life skills.

effect_or_estimate: Framework; comparative effect sizes not established

citation: Turnnidge J, Côté J, Hancock DJ. Positive Youth Development From Sport to Life: Explicit or Implicit Transfer? Quest, 2014; Bean C, Kramers S, Forneris T, Camiré M. The Implicit/Explicit Continuum of Life Skills Development and Transfer. Quest, 2018.

verified_title: Positive Youth Development From Sport to Life: Explicit or Implicit Transfer?

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: A grounded theory of PYD through sport, built from a qualitative meta-study, positions distal ecological factors, PYD climate and life-skills programme focus as producing PYD outcomes.
effect_or_estimate: Theory, not effect estimate
limitations: Built from qualitative studies; outcomes largely self-reported and gym-proximal
citation: Holt NL, Neely KC, Slater LG, Camiré M, et al. A grounded theory of positive youth development through sport based on results from a qualitative meta-study. International Review of Sport and Exercise Psychology, 2017.

verified_title: A grounded theory of positive youth development through sport based on results from a qualitative meta-study

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: A conceptual framework for transfer in sport-based youth development programmes specifies mechanisms bridging learning in the programme to application in school, family and community.
effect_or_estimate: Framework specifying mechanisms
limitations: Conceptual; requires empirical test
citation: Jacobs JM, Wright PM. Transfer of Life Skills in Sport-Based Youth Development Programs: A Conceptual Framework Bridging Learning to Application. Quest, 2018.
ppbf_implication: Supplies the explicit mechanism list PPBF should implement as programme requirements, not aspirations.
verified_title: Transfer of Life Skills in Sport-Based Youth Development Programs: A Conceptual Framework Bridging Learning to Application

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Model high school coaches described deliberate philosophies and strategies for coaching and transferring life skills, including explicit discussion and connection to non-sport contexts.
effect_or_estimate: Descriptive; no outcome measurement
limitations: Small purposive sample of exemplary coaches; no athlete outcome data; social desirability likely
citation: Camiré M, Trudel P, Forneris T. Coaching and Transferring Life Skills: Philosophies and Strategies Used by Model High School Coaches. The Sport Psychologist, 2012.
ppbf_implication: Source of concrete coach behaviours for the PPBF library — labelled as coach-reported practice, NOT validated protocol.
verified_title: Coaching and Transferring Life Skills: Philosophies and Strategies Used by Model High School Coaches

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: A randomised controlled trial evaluated an online Coaching for Life Skills training programme for coaches.
effect_or_estimate: Trial conducted; outcomes are coach-level, not athlete life-outcome
limitations: Coach-level outcomes; does not demonstrate athlete transfer to school/home/work
citation: Camiré M, Kendellen K, Rathwell S, Turgeon S. Evaluating the Coaching for Life Skills online training program: A randomised controlled trial. Psychology of Sport and Exercise, 2020.
ppbf_implication: Rare RCT in this space and the best template for a PPBF coach-training evaluation; note it does not close the transfer question.
verified_title: Evaluating the Coaching for Life Skills online training program: A randomised controlled trial

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: The Life Skills Scale for Sport measures eight life skills developed through sport; a separate Transfer Scale (LSSS-TS) was later developed to measure perceived transfer.
effect_or_estimate: Factor structures reported with initial validity evidence
limitations: SELF-REPORT and PERCEIVED transfer — not outside-gym outcome data; single-informant
citation: Cronin LD, Allen J. Development and initial validation of the Life Skills Scale for Sport. Psychology of Sport and Exercise, 2017; Mossman GJ, Robertson C, Williamson B, Cronin L. Development and initial validation of the Life Skills Scale for Sport – Transfer Scale (LSSS-TS). Psychology of Sport and Exercise, 2021.
ppbf_implication: Best available transfer instrument for PPBF — but self-reported perceived transfer is NOT evidence of behaviour change outside the gym.
verified_title: Development and initial validation of the Life Skills Scale for Sport

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Study linked coaching climate to life-skills development and wellbeing in sport participants.
effect_or_estimate: Associations reported
limitations: Cross-sectional; self-report on both sides; common-method variance
citation: Cronin LD, Allen J. Examining the relationships among the coaching climate, life skills development and well-being in sport. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching, 2018.
ppbf_implication: Supports climate as a lever but cannot establish transfer; correlation not causation must be shown in PPBF reporting.
verified_title: Examining the relationships among the coaching climate, life skills development and well-being in sport

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
topic: Life-skill transfer — barriers/enablers to classroom transfer
claim: Qualitative research with male students identified enablers and barriers to transferring life skills from the sports hall into the classroom, including adult reinforcement in the receiving context.
effect_or_estimate: Descriptive mechanisms identified
limitations: Small qualitative sample; male only; self-report
citation: Allen G, Rhind D, Koshy V. Enablers and barriers for male students transferring life skills from the sports hall into the classroom. Qualitative Research in Sport, Exercise and Health, 2015.
ppbf_implication: Confirms the receiving context (teacher/parent) is part of the transfer mechanism — PPBF cannot deliver transfer alone.
verified_title: Enablers and barriers for male students transferring life skills from the sports hall into the classroom

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: A qualitative study of Brazilian jiu-jitsu participants described implicit transfer of life skills to other life areas.
effect_or_estimate: Participant-reported transfer only
limitations: Adult participants; self-report of their own transfer; no external informant or outcome data; retrospective
citation: Chinkov AE, Holt NL. Implicit Transfer of Life Skills Through Participation in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Journal of Applied Sport Psychology, 2016.
ppbf_implication: Closest combat-sport transfer study located — and it is exactly the weak design PPBF must NOT replicate as its evidence.
verified_title: Implicit Transfer of Life Skills Through Participation in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
topic: Life-skill transfer — programme review, socially vulnerable youth
claim: Systematic review of life-skill development through sports programmes serving socially vulnerable youth found programme and evaluation quality limitations across the literature.
effect_or_estimate: Evidence quality limitations documented
limitations: Weak designs prevalent; outcome measurement usually programme-internal
citation: Hermens N, Super S, Verkooijen KT, Koelen MA. A Systematic Review of Life Skill Development Through Sports Programs Serving Socially Vulnerable Youth. Research Quarterly for Exercise and Sport, 2017.
ppbf_implication: Directly relevant to PPBF's population and directly warns against PPBF's likely default evaluation design.
verified_title: A Systematic Review of Life Skill Development Through Sports Programs Serving Socially Vulnerable Youth

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Systematic review of sport-based youth development interventions in the United States documents heterogeneous and often methodologically weak evaluation.
effect_or_estimate: Evidence quality limitations documented
transfer_status: US community programmes — most relevant national context to PPBF
limitations: Weak designs; inconsistent outcome measures; limited comparison groups
citation: Whitley MA, Massey WV, Camiré M, Boutet M, Borbee A. Sport-based youth development interventions in the United States: a systematic review. BMC Public Health, 2019.
ppbf_implication: This is the mirror PPBF should hold up to its own planned impact reporting before writing a grant claim.
verified_title: Sport-based youth development interventions in the United States: a systematic review

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Critical scholarship argues sport-for-development claims frequently outrun their evidence, with evaluation shaped by funding and advocacy incentives.
effect_or_estimate: Critique of evidence practices
limitations: Critical scholarship; not an outcome study
citation: Levermore R. Evaluating sport-for-development: approaches and critical issues. Progress in Development Studies, 2011; Kay T. Developing through sport: evidencing sport impacts on young people. Sport in Society, 2009.
ppbf_implication: PPBF's donor-safe reporting engine (Module 149) must be built so it CANNOT emit an unevidenced transfer claim.
verified_title: Evaluating sport-for-development

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: The Teaching Personal and Social Responsibility model provides a structured pedagogy with an explicit transfer stage, widely used in physical activity settings.
effect_or_estimate: Model with implementation guidance
limitations: Model fidelity varies; outcome evidence largely within-programme
citation: Hellison D. Teaching Personal and Social Responsibility Through Physical Activity (3rd ed.). Human Kinetics, 2011.
ppbf_implication: Provides an off-the-shelf explicit-teaching structure PPBF can adopt rather than invent.
verified_title: Teaching Personal and Social Responsibility Through Physical Activity

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
topic: Life-skill transfer — TPSR transfer to classroom
claim: Research on transferring personal and social responsibility to the classroom describes the deliberate work required for transfer to occur beyond the gym.
effect_or_estimate: Descriptive; transfer not established by controlled comparison
limitations: Small; no comparison group; teacher report limited
citation: Martinek T, Schilling T, Johnson D. Transferring Personal and Social Responsibility of Underserved Youth to the Classroom. The Urban Review, 2001.
ppbf_implication: Demonstrates the multi-informant, other-context data PPBF would need — and how rarely it is collected.
verified_title: Transferring Personal and Social Responsibility of Underserved Youth to the Classroom

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Systematic review of sport participation for children and adolescents reports associations with psychological and social health benefits, primarily from observational studies.
effect_or_estimate: Associations reported; observational designs dominate
limitations: Observational; self-selection into sport is a major confound; correlation not causation
citation: Eime RM, Young JA, Harvey JT, Charity MJ, Payne WR. A systematic review of the psychological and social benefits of participation in sport for children and adolescents. International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity, 2013.
ppbf_implication: Supports 'participation is associated with benefit' — NOT 'PPBF causes benefit'. Wording matters in grant text.
verified_title: A systematic review of the psychological and social benefits of participation in sport for children and adolescents: informing development of a conceptual model of health through sport

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Systematic review of martial arts, combat sports and mental health in adults reports mixed and generally low-certainty findings.
effect_or_estimate: Mixed findings; low certainty
boxing_specific: Partly — combat sports included; boxing not isolated
limitations: Adults only; heterogeneous designs; low certainty; publication bias plausible
citation: Fleming C, et al. Martial arts, combat sports, and mental health in adults: A systematic review. Psychology of Sport and Exercise, 2023.
ppbf_implication: Do not extend adult combat-sport mental health findings to PPBF youth participants.
verified_title: Martial arts, combat sports, and mental health in adults: A systematic review

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: A position paper on parenting expertise in youth sport specifies parental behaviours associated with positive youth sport experiences.
effect_or_estimate: Framework of parenting practices
limitations: Position paper; not a trial
citation: Harwood CG, Knight CJ. Parenting in youth sport: A position paper on parenting expertise. Psychology of Sport and Exercise, 2015.
ppbf_implication: Guardian modules (085–095) should target parent behaviour, which is also a required transfer mechanism.
verified_title: Parenting in youth sport: A position paper on parenting expertise

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: IOC consensus statement on youth athletic development covers physical, psychological and social development principles for young athletes.
effect_or_estimate: Consensus recommendations
limitations: Consensus; sport-generic; national governing-body rules differ
citation: Bergeron MF, Mountjoy M, Armstrong N, et al. International Olympic Committee consensus statement on youth athletic development. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2015.
ppbf_implication: Anchor document for PPBF youth policy alongside national boxing rules; note jurisdictional variation explicitly.
verified_title: International Olympic Committee consensus statement on youth athletic development

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: A framework for planning youth sport programmes that foster psychosocial development specifies context, external assets and research/evaluation as design components.
effect_or_estimate: Design framework
limitations: Conceptual; evaluation component is the part programmes most often omit
citation: Petitpas AJ, Cornelius AE, Van Raalte JL, Jones T. A Framework for Planning Youth Sport Programs That Foster Psychosocial Development. The Sport Psychologist, 2005.
ppbf_implication: Maps cleanly onto PPBF module architecture; the 'research and evaluation' leg is the one PPBF must not skip.
verified_title: A Framework for Planning Youth Sport Programs That Foster Psychosocial Development

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: A conceptual framework for life-skills interventions grounds life-skill programming in self-determination theory and specifies intervention components.
effect_or_estimate: Framework
limitations: Conceptual; not empirically tested as a whole
citation: Hodge K, Danish S, Martin J. Developing a Conceptual Framework for Life Skills Interventions. The Counseling Psychologist, 2013.
ppbf_implication: Links Track 4 motivation work to Track 4 transfer work in one design rationale for PPBF.
verified_title: Developing a Conceptual Framework for Life Skills Interventions

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire is a brief behavioural screening questionnaire for children and young people with parent, teacher and self-report versions.
effect_or_estimate: Psychometric properties reported across versions and languages
transfer_status: GENERAL CHILD POPULATION — not a sport instrument
limitations: Screening, not diagnostic; requires qualified interpretation; ethics/consent obligations for a youth-serving org
citation: Goodman R. The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire: A Research Note. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 1997; Goodman R. Psychometric properties of the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire. JAACAP, 2001.
ppbf_implication: Multi-informant design (parent/teacher/self) is exactly the structure PPBF transfer measurement needs — but it is a clinical-adjacent screener and PPBF must not administer it casually.
verified_title: The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire: A Research Note

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: The Sport Anxiety Scale-2 measures multidimensional sport performance anxiety and was validated for use with children as well as adults.
effect_or_estimate: Three-factor structure supported across age groups
limitations: Self-report; boxing-specific norms do not exist
citation: Smith RE, Smoll FL, Cumming SP, Grossbard JR. Measurement of Multidimensional Sport Performance Anxiety in Children and Adults: The Sport Anxiety Scale-2. Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology, 2006.
ppbf_implication: One of the few psych instruments with child validation that PPBF could pilot — with consent and a stated purpose.
verified_title: Measurement of Multidimensional Sport Performance Anxiety in Children and Adults: The Sport Anxiety Scale-2

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: The Athlete Psychological Strain Questionnaire is a brief sport-specific screening measure of athlete mental health strain, with initial validation in male elite athletes and subsequent cross-cultural validations.
effect_or_estimate: Initial psychometric support reported
transfer_status: ELITE ADULT — not validated in youth community sport
limitations: Initial validation in male elite athletes; not a diagnostic tool; youth applicability unestablished
citation: Rice S, Parker AG, Mawren D, Clifton P, et al. Preliminary psychometric validation of a brief screening tool for athlete mental health among male elite athletes: the Athlete Psychological Strain Questionnaire. International Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology, 2020.
ppbf_implication: Not appropriate for PPBF youth without clinical governance and new validation.
verified_title: Preliminary psychometric validation of a brief screening tool for athlete mental health among male elite athletes: the Athlete Psychological Strain Questionnaire

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Systematic review of stress management interventions with sport performers found generally positive but methodologically limited evidence, dominated by individual-level rather than organisational interventions.
effect_or_estimate: Positive direction; design limitations noted
limitations: Small samples; weak control conditions; individual-focus bias
citation: Rumbold JL, Fletcher D, Daniels K. A systematic review of stress management interventions with sport performers. Sport, Exercise, and Performance Psychology, 2012.
ppbf_implication: Argues PPBF should also change the environment (schedule, climate, coach load), not only teach the athlete coping.
verified_title: A systematic review of stress management interventions with sport performers.

track: A4 Psychology / Human Development / Life-Skill Transfer
claim: Measurement of mental toughness has been substantively critiqued, with disputes over dimensionality and the validity of widely marketed instruments.
effect_or_estimate: Dimensionality disputed
limitations: Active scholarly dispute; some commercial instruments have weak published support
citation: Gucciardi DF, Hanton S, Mallett CJ. Progressing measurement in mental toughness: A case example of the Mental Toughness Questionnaire 48. Sport, Exercise, and Performance Psychology, 2012; and the 2013 response.
ppbf_implication: PPBF should NOT ship a 'mental toughness score'. Vendor toughness products are low-authority by the project's own source rules.
verified_title: Progressing measurement in mental toughness: A case example of the Mental Toughness Questionnaire 48.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: In highly trained male amateur boxers, a full-contact 3x3-min bout produced post-fight blood lactate >15 mmol/L (range 12-18), heart rate >93% HRmax in rounds 1-2 and >97% in round 3, and mean oxygen uptake ~89% of VO2max; calculated energy provision was 73% aerobic, 19% anaerobic alactic, 8% anaerobic glycolytic.
effect_or_estimate: BLa >15 mmol/L; HR >97% HRmax final round; VO2 ~89% VO2max; 73/19/8% aerobic/alactic/glycolytic
limitations: Very small sample (n=10); male only; VO2 during the fight was calculated, not directly measured; single format.
citation: Bruzas et al. (2022). Metabolic and physiological demands of 3x3-min-round boxing fights in highly trained amateur boxers. J Sports Med Phys Fitness.
ppbf_implication: Conditioning must develop BOTH a high aerobic ceiling and repeated near-maximal alactic output. SHADOW conditioning templates should not treat boxing as a purely anaerobic sport.
verified_title: Metabolic and physiological demands of 3×3-min-round boxing fights in highly trained amateur boxers.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: In a 3x2-min semicontact amateur boxing bout against handheld pads, relative energy contributions were approximately 77% aerobic, 19% anaerobic alactic and 4% anaerobic lactic, with authors highlighting aerobic capacity as a prerequisite for high activity rate and inter-round phosphagen resynthesis.
study_design: Laboratory-controlled simulated bout with gas analysis and blood lactate
effect_or_estimate: ~77% aerobic / 19% alactic / 4% lactic; Wtot ~680 kJ
limitations: Semicontact against pads, not a live opponent — lower emotional/defensive load than competition; n=10; male only; 3x2 format is no longer the elite adult format.
citation: Davis et al. (2014). The energetics of semicontact 3 x 2-min amateur boxing. Int J Sports Physiol Perform.
ppbf_implication: Justifies an aerobic base block in PPBF conditioning as a recovery-enabler, not as 'cardio for weight loss'. Frame aerobic work as between-round recovery capacity.
verified_title: The energetics of semicontact 3 x 2-min amateur boxing.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Bout demands — HR and lactate, national-level
claim: In competitive bouts among senior national-level boxers, pooled mean heart rate was approximately 178 beats/min and mean blood lactate approximately 8.24 mmol/L, with no consistent difference between weight categories.
effect_or_estimate: Mean HR ~178 b/min; mean BLa ~8.24 mmol/L
limitations: 1995 study — bout format and rules have changed since; single-nation cohort; older lactate assay methods; magnitudes differ substantially from more recent 3x3 full-contact data (A5-001).
citation: Ghosh et al. (1995). Heart rate & blood lactate response in amateur competitive boxing. Indian J Med Res.
ppbf_implication: Illustrates that lactate values are format- and era-dependent. SHADOW must never store a lactate or HR threshold as a fixed constant; store format context alongside any physiological value.
verified_title: Heart rate & blood lactate response in amateur competitive boxing.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A review of male amateur boxing competition reported activity-to-rest ratios higher in elite (about 18:1) than novice (about 9:1) boxers, with ratios changing across rounds in novices (round 1 about 16:1, round 2 about 8:1, round 3 about 6:1) and increasing total stop-time across rounds.
population: Male amateur boxers, novice and elite
study_design: Narrative/brief review of time-motion and physiological studies
effect_or_estimate: Activity:rest ~18:1 elite vs ~9:1 novice; novice degradation across rounds
limitations: Brief review, not a systematic review/meta-analysis; male only; heterogeneous methods across the underlying time-motion studies; ratio definitions vary between studies.
citation: Slimani et al. (2017). Performance Aspects and Physiological Responses in Male Amateur Boxing Competitions: A Brief Review. J Strength Cond Res.
ppbf_implication: Work:rest densities in PPBF conditioning must be LEVEL-SCALED. A novice should not be prescribed elite work:rest densities. SHADOW should attach a level band to every conditioning template.
verified_title: Performance Aspects and Physiological Responses in Male Amateur Boxing Competitions: A Brief Review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Activity profile — women's elite, weight-category variation
claim: Time-motion analysis of the 12 finals of the IBA 2023 Women's World Boxing Championships (3x3-min format) found significant differences across rounds in punching, clinching, no-fighting and arbitral-interruption phases, and different fighting/no-fighting ratios by weight category, with heavyweight categories relying more on clinching.
effect_or_estimate: Round and weight-category differences in phase frequency/duration (p<0.001 to p=0.007 across phases)
limitations: Finals only — a selected, non-representative subset of bouts; no physiological measures; descriptive design; conclusions about strategy are interpretive.
citation: Martusciello et al. (2025). Time-Motion Analysis of the 2023 Women's World Boxing Championships Finals. Sports (Basel).
ppbf_implication: Conditioning and tactical prescriptions should be weight-category aware, and PPBF should not assume women's demands mirror men's. Store weight category as a first-class conditioning context field.
verified_title: Time-Motion Analysis of the 2023 Women's World Boxing Championships Finals.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A systematic review with meta-analysis of acute responses to amateur boxing-specific activity found large increases in blood lactate (SMD 4.62), cortisol (SMD 1.33), myoglobin (SMD 1.43), AST (1.37), ALT (0.97) and moderate creatine kinase increases (0.65), with only small pre-post increases in countermovement jump height (SMD 0.33); responses were consistently greatest in competitive bouts, then sparring, then simulations.
sex: Predominantly male (as reported in included studies)
effect_or_estimate: BLa SMD 4.62; cortisol 1.33; Mb 1.43; CK 0.65; CMJ +0.33
limitations: Heterogeneous included studies; methodological quality assessed with a modified Downs and Black checklist; female representation limited; biochemical markers are not themselves outcomes coaches can act on.
citation: Finlay et al. (2022). Acute physiological, endocrine, biochemical and performance responses associated with amateur boxing: A systematic review with meta-analysis. Eur J Sport Sci.
ppbf_implication: CRITICAL for PPBF load model: competition > sparring > simulation in physiological cost. This ordering is the defensible basis for weighting sparring more heavily than pad/bag work in a session load index. Also: CMJ may NOT drop after boxing activity, so jump height is a weak same-day fatigue marker in this sport.
verified_title: Acute physiological, endocrine, biochemical and performance responses associated with amateur boxing: A systematic review with meta-analysis.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A review of amateur boxers' physical and physiological attributes reports low body fat, a mesomorphic tendency in elite males, high peak and mean anaerobic power in international boxers, and describes upper- and lower-limb muscle strength and power as central to performance, with isometric strength linked to higher-level performance.
sex: Male and female (data sparser for female)
effect_or_estimate: Descriptive; no pooled effect estimate
limitations: Narrative (non-systematic) review; the authors explicitly note limited studies, particularly on somatotype and on female boxers; cross-sectional associations cannot establish that training these qualities causes performance gains.
citation: Chaabène et al. (2015). Amateur boxing: physical and physiological attributes. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Supports a multi-quality PPBF test battery (strength, power, anaerobic capacity, body composition) rather than a single 'fitness score'. Note the female data gap explicitly in SHADOW confidence output.
verified_title: Amateur boxing: physical and physiological attributes.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: Using a validated striking dynamometry method, intra-session variability of punch impact kinetics (impulse, peak force, mean force across jab, cross, lead and rear hook) in untrained participants and experienced boxers was mostly small (ICC >0.67, CV <10%), while between-session measures in the untrained cohort were mostly of moderate variability.
effect_or_estimate: Intra-session mostly ICC >0.67 / CV <10%; inter-session mostly moderate variability
limitations: Small cohorts; between-session reliability established only in the untrained group; device-specific — results do not transfer automatically to other dynamometers or commercial bags.
citation: Lenetsky et al. (2018). Variability and Reliability of Punching Impact Kinetics in Untrained Participants and Experienced Boxers. J Strength Cond Res.
ppbf_implication: Punch force can be logged as a tracked metric BUT PPBF must establish its own device-specific typical error before calling a change real. Do not compare across devices.
verified_title: Variability and Reliability of Punching Impact Kinetics in Untrained Participants and Experienced Boxers.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: Laboratory testing of a commercial punch/kick impact device found peak power reductions ranging from 15.9% to 41.4% when strikes were off-centre and/or inclined relative to level centred strikes, and the authors advise videoing strikes to ensure consistent impact orientation.
effect_or_estimate: Peak power reduced 15.9%-41.4% with off-centre/inclined impacts
limitations: Mechanical simulation rather than human strikes; single commercial device; does not establish what a real athlete's technique variation contributes.
citation: Del Vecchio et al. (2022). Reliability and Practical Use of a Commercial Device for Measuring Punch and Kick Impact Kinetics. Sports (Basel).
ppbf_implication: Treat gym punch-power readings as LOW source quality unless strike orientation is standardised. SHADOW should tag any commercial-device punch power with a source_quality flag and never trend it without a standardised protocol note.
verified_title: Reliability and Practical Use of a Commercial Device for Measuring Punch and Kick Impact Kinetics.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A custom wall-mounted punch force dynamometer built from two S-type load cells showed excellent reliability in mechanical trials (ICC >0.90) and good-to-excellent reliability in a sport-specific condition with experienced striking athletes (ICC 0.75-0.90), with standard error of measurement consistently below the smallest worthwhile change.
effect_or_estimate: ICC 0.75-0.90 in sport-specific condition; SEM < SWC
limitations: Very small athlete sample (n=11); 'partial' ecological validity by the authors' own framing; single custom device.
citation: Meireles et al. (2026). Development and Measurement Properties of a Custom-Built Punch Force Dynamometer Based on S-Type Load Cells. Percept Mot Skills.
ppbf_implication: Demonstrates the SEM-vs-SWC standard PPBF should adopt for every physical test: a change is only reportable when it exceeds the measured typical error.
verified_title: Development and Measurement Properties of a Custom-Built Punch Force Dynamometer Based on S-Type Load Cells.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Strength training practices in boxing (practice survey, not evidence of effect)
claim: A survey of 72 trainers/support staff in amateur and professional boxing found that most practitioners (72-88%) implemented strength training to improve punching power and muscular endurance and to reduce injury likelihood.
effect_or_estimate: 72-88% reported these rationales
limitations: This documents what coaches DO, not whether it works. Survey responses are self-reported and subject to social desirability; no performance or injury outcomes measured.
citation: Beattie et al. (2025). Strength Training Practices in Amateur and Professional Boxing. J Strength Cond Res.
ppbf_implication: Useful as the baseline 'current practice' layer in the PPBF doctrine engine. Must be labelled PRACTICE, not EVIDENCE, in the SHADOW source hierarchy.
verified_title: Strength Training Practices in Amateur and Professional Boxing.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Plyometric vs jump rope for punching (junior)
claim: In 24 high-school amateur boxers aged 12-18 with 3-5 years of experience, both an 8-week plyometric programme and an 8-week jump-rope programme (30 min, 3 days/week) improved countermovement jump rate of force development, punch reaction time, rear-leg peak ground reaction force during the jab, and jab velocity, with no differences between groups.
effect_or_estimate: Both groups improved RFD, punch reaction time, rear-leg peak GRF, jab velocity; no between-group difference
limitations: No true (non-training) control group — improvements cannot be fully separated from ongoing boxing training or maturation over 8 weeks in a growing population; small n; sex not reported in abstract.
citation: Chottidao et al. (2022). A Comparison of Plyometric and Jump Rope Training Programs for Improving Punching Performance in Junior Amateur Boxers. Front Bioeng Biotechnol.
ppbf_implication: PPBF youth programming: rope work is a defensible low-cost stimulus for junior boxers and is not inferior to plyometrics in this trial. Supports keeping equipment demands low for a nonprofit gym.
verified_title: A Comparison of Plyometric and Jump Rope Training Programs for Improving Punching Performance in Junior Amateur Boxers.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Plyometrics with external weights — limited transfer to single-punch force
claim: In 8 experienced male amateur boxers, 12 sessions of plyometric training with external weights over 4 weeks did not change single-punch force or punch frequency within a series (except increased power in the rear-hand low punch), but did increase summative force/energy output over 3 s and 8 s efforts and across a series of eight 8-s tests.
effect_or_estimate: No change in single-punch force; increases in 3 s/8 s summative force and energy output (p<0.05)
limitations: No control group; n=8; 4 weeks is short for a strength-power adaptation; single-device outcome measure; pre-post design cannot exclude learning/familiarisation effects.
citation: Bruzas et al. (2016). Effects of plyometric exercise training with external weights on punching ability of experienced amateur boxers. J Sports Med Phys Fitness.
ppbf_implication: Important nuance for SHADOW: repeated-effort punch output and single-punch force are DIFFERENT qualities that respond differently. Do not collapse them into one 'punch power' score.
verified_title: Effects of plyometric exercise training with external weights on punching ability of experienced amateur boxers.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Post-activation performance enhancement — moderated by training status
claim: A meta-analysis of PAPE in combat sports (13 studies, 176 athletes) on sport-specific outcomes found a profound moderating effect of training status: on the Frequency Speed of Kick Test, amateurs showed large significant improvement (g=1.28, p<0.001) while elite athletes showed trivial non-significant change (g=0.11, p=0.357); athletes with under 6 years' experience showed larger enhancements than those with more.
study_design: Systematic review with meta-analysis (Hedges' g, random effects)
effect_or_estimate: FSKT-10: amateur g=1.28 vs elite g=0.11; <6 y experience g=1.60 vs >6 y g=0.42
boxing_specific: Partly (combat sports, sport-specific tests are predominantly taekwondo-based)
limitations: The primary sport-specific outcomes (FSKT-10, TSAT) are taekwondo tests, not boxing tests — transfer to punching is an assumption. Small total sample; combat-sport heterogeneity.
citation: Terbalyan et al. (2026). Effect of Post-Activation Performance Enhancement in Combat Sports: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis-Part II: Specific Performance Indicators. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol.
ppbf_implication: PPBF should NOT assume warm-up potentiation protocols generalise across levels. If SHADOW ever proposes a PAPE warm-up, it must condition the suggestion on training level and flag it as transfer evidence.
verified_title: Effect of Post-Activation Performance Enhancement in Combat Sports: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis-Part II: Specific Performance Indicators.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: PAPE in amateur boxing — small worthwhile effects
claim: In 10 male senior elite amateur boxers, isometric punch and elastic-resistance punch conditioning activities (but not the control trial) produced small worthwhile increases (effect size >=0.20, at or above the smallest worthwhile change) in punch force during a boxing-specific simulated bout.
effect_or_estimate: ES >= 0.20 (>= SWC) for punch force with both conditioning activities
limitations: n=10, male only; 'small worthwhile' is a modest magnitude; simulation rather than competition; individual responsiveness varied, which the authors themselves emphasise.
citation: Finlay et al. (2024). Post-Activation Performance Enhancement of Punch Force and Neuromuscular Performance in Amateur Boxing: Toward a More Individualized and "Real-World" Approach. J Strength Cond Res.
ppbf_implication: Any PPBF warm-up potentiation protocol must be INDIVIDUALLY tested and coach-reviewed, not applied squad-wide. SHADOW may log the protocol and observed response; it must not auto-prescribe.
verified_title: Post-Activation Performance Enhancement of Punch Force and Neuromuscular Performance in Amateur Boxing: Toward a More Individualized and "Real-World" Approach.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: In a randomised trial of 30 elite male amateur boxers, 8 weeks of thrice-weekly upper-body resistance training at 20-30% 1RM with 40-50% limb occlusion pressure produced significantly greater dominant-arm strength gains than a control group training at 50-60% 1RM (e.g. 1RM elbow flexion +3.3 kg, p<0.001, d=3.20), alongside punch force outcomes.
effect_or_estimate: 1RM elbow flexion +3.3 kg (p<0.001, d=3.20) favouring BFRT
limitations: Implausibly large effect sizes for a strength trial warrant caution; the comparator trained at a different (lower-than-typical) intensity; male only; single-site; BFR requires trained supervision and cuff pressure control that a volunteer-staffed nonprofit gym may not have.
citation: Awana et al. (2025). Blood flow restriction training enhances punching force and upper body strength in elite boxers: a randomized trial. Front Physiol.
ppbf_implication: DO NOT adopt BFR at PPBF without qualified supervision and a medical screen. Record as a research-watch item, not a programme component. Occlusion training on minors is out of scope.
verified_title: Blood flow restriction training enhances punching force and upper body strength in elite boxers: a randomized trial.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Core/trunk strength training in striking combat sports
claim: A systematic review of core strength training in striking combat sports (karate, taekwondo, boxing, Chinese martial arts, Muay Thai) examined effects on kick count, striking force and impact speed.
sample_size: Multiple studies across five striking sports
effect_or_estimate: No single pooled effect estimate reported in the abstract
limitations: Systematic review without meta-analysis in the reported abstract; included sports differ substantially in the striking task; 'core strength training' is a heterogeneous, poorly standardised intervention category; CNKI inclusion introduces language/indexing heterogeneity.
citation: Zhang et al. (2025). Effects of core strength training on the technical skill performance of striking combat sport players: a systematic review. PeerJ.
ppbf_implication: Trunk/rotational work is defensible in a PPBF programme, but SHADOW must not attach a numeric expected punch-force gain to it. TBD: PPBF-specific dose-response.
verified_title: Effects of core strength training on the technical skill performance of striking combat sport players: a systematic review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Landmine punch throw — reliable load-velocity assessment in boxers
claim: In 14 boxers, three landmine-punch-throw variations (seated without trunk rotation, seated with rotation, standing whole body) at 20, 22.5 and 25.0 kg were mostly highly reliable within session (ICC >0.91), with the non-dominant hand as reliable or more reliable than the dominant hand, and very strong linear group-average load-velocity relationships.
effect_or_estimate: ICC >0.91 for most variation x load x hand combinations
limitations: Intra-session reliability only (no between-session data); small n; requires a linear position transducer, which many community gyms lack.
citation: Omcirk et al. (2024). Reliability of Three Landmine-Punch-Throw Variations and Their Load-Velocity Relationships Performed With the Dominant and Nondominant Hands. Int J Sports Physiol Perform.
ppbf_implication: A candidate PPBF upper-body power test IF a velocity device is available. Otherwise use as a training exercise, not a test. Between-session reliability is unestablished — a TBD for PPBF.
verified_title: Reliability of Three Landmine-Punch-Throw Variations and Their Load-Velocity Relationships Performed With the Dominant and Nondominant Hands.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Countermovement push-up reliability in elite boxers
claim: Force-plate-derived measures of the countermovement push-up were assessed for test-retest reliability in 18 elite Olympic boxers across two sessions 7 days apart, with the authors noting no gold-standard test currently exists for upper-limb force development performance.
effect_or_estimate: Reliability across peak force, mean force, flight time, RFD, impulse, vertical stiffness
limitations: Requires dual force platforms — not feasible in most community gyms; n=18; elite population may not generalise to novice/youth.
citation: Parry et al. (2021). The Test-Retest Reliability of Bilateral and Unilateral Force Plate-Derived Parameters of the Countermovement Push-Up in Elite Boxers. J Sport Rehabil.
ppbf_implication: Confirms there is NO gold-standard upper-limb power test in boxing. PPBF should choose a feasible proxy and validate it locally rather than claim a validated standard exists.
verified_title: The Test-Retest Reliability of Bilateral and Unilateral Force Plate-Derived Parameters of the Countermovement Push-Up in Elite Boxers.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Sport-specific repeated sprint training in boxers
claim: In 18 experienced male amateur boxers, 4 weeks of sport-specific sprint interval training (3 rounds of 14 sets of 3-s all-out bag punching with 10-s rests, 3x/week) improved punching ability and upper-body aerobic power compared with the same rounds performed at low intensity.
effect_or_estimate: Improved punch characteristics and upper-body aerobic power vs low-intensity control
limitations: Small n; 4-week duration; male only; the control group performed the same drill at low intensity, so the contrast is intensity rather than modality; single laboratory.
citation: Kamandulis et al. (2018). Sport-Specific Repeated Sprint Training Improves Punching Ability and Upper-Body Aerobic Power in Experienced Amateur Boxers. J Strength Cond Res.
ppbf_implication: STRONG candidate for PPBF conditioning: the intervention uses only a heavy bag and a timer, which fits a $0-cost nonprofit constraint. Structure is loggable as rounds x sets in the session model.
verified_title: Sport-Specific Repeated Sprint Training Improves Punching Ability and Upper-Body Aerobic Power in Experienced Amateur Boxers.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Repeated sprint training — replication in elite boxers
claim: In 16 elite male boxers, 4 weeks of boxing-specific repeated sprint training (14 sets of 3-s maximal heavy-bag punches, 10-s rest, 1-min between rounds, 3x/week) produced large within-group improvements in upper-body Wingate peak power (d=1.10, +16.7%) and mean power alongside conventional training.
effect_or_estimate: Wingate peak power d=1.10, +16.7%
limitations: Very small n (8 per group); 4 weeks; male only; replication of a similar protocol by an overlapping methodological approach rather than a fully independent design.
citation: Tian et al. (2026). The effects of 4 weeks of sport-specific repeated sprint training on upper-body strength quality, anaerobic capacity and punching ability of elite male boxers. Front Sports Act Living.
ppbf_implication: Second independent-cohort support for bag-based repeated-sprint conditioning. Elevates confidence that this is a defensible PPBF conditioning template for experienced boxers (NOT for novices without technique screening).
verified_title: The effects of 4 weeks of sport-specific repeated sprint training on upper-body strength quality, anaerobic capacity and punching ability of elite male boxers.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies found a significant moderate-magnitude advantage of high-intensity interval training over control conditions for maximal oxygen uptake in Olympic combat sport athletes, with study quality assessed by PEDro and certainty by GRADE.
effect_or_estimate: Moderate effect size favouring HIIT for VO2max
limitations: Pooled across combat sports with different demands; interventions heterogeneous in work:rest and duration; the comparator ('active control') varies across studies.
citation: Yue et al. (2025). Effects of high-intensity interval training on aerobic and anaerobic capacity in olympic combat sports: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Physiol.
ppbf_implication: Supports including HIIT in PPBF conditioning blocks. Do NOT specify a single optimal work:rest — the literature is heterogeneous. Set the parameter as a coach-adjustable template field.
verified_title: Effects of high-intensity interval training on aerobic and anaerobic capacity in olympic combat sports: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Anaerobic tests in boxers do not interchange
claim: In 12 male Olympic boxers completing 30-s Wingate cycling, arm cranking, bag punching, uphill treadmill running to exhaustion and a progressive VO2max test, performance indices of the different anaerobic tests were largely NOT closely correlated, and punches landed on a bag in 30 s correlated only with relative Wingate power.
effect_or_estimate: Most inter-test correlations weak; 30-s bag punch count associated only with relative Wingate power
limitations: n=12; male only; single session per test in some cases; correlation-based design cannot establish which test best predicts competitive success.
citation: Venckunas et al. (2024). Anaerobic Performance Profiling in Elite Amateur Boxers. Sports (Basel).
ppbf_implication: MAJOR implication: PPBF cannot substitute one anaerobic test for another. If the battery drops a test, the quality is no longer measured. SHADOW must model qualities and tests as separate entities with explicit, non-interchangeable mappings.
verified_title: Anaerobic Performance Profiling in Elite Amateur Boxers.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Integrative neuromuscular training in elite boxers
claim: A 3-week integrative neuromuscular training programme in 18 male Chinese national-team boxers improved bench press (ES=1.13), squat (ES=1.72), countermovement jump (ES=1.14), 400-m sprint (ES=1.26), 1-min hexagon jump (ES=1.73) and 3-min double-unders (ES=1.73), with NO significant change in 30-m sprint (p=0.593) or 3000-m run.
effect_or_estimate: Large ES for strength/jump/400 m; no change in 30 m sprint or 3000 m run
limitations: No control group — 3-week pre-post gains of this magnitude in elite athletes are likely inflated by learning and testing familiarisation; male only; concurrent normal training uncontrolled.
citation: Zhang et al. (2026). The effect of integrative neuromuscular training on physical fitness and punching performance in highly-trained male boxers. Front Physiol.
ppbf_implication: Note the null results are as informative as the positives: general endurance running (3000 m) did NOT improve and short sprint did NOT improve. Do not promise transfer to qualities the intervention did not move.
verified_title: The effect of integrative neuromuscular training on physical fitness and punching performance in highly-trained male boxers.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Integrative neuromuscular training in elite female boxers
claim: A before-and-after controlled experiment in 37 elite Chinese female boxers applied integrative neuromuscular training 11 times per week for 3 weeks and reported significant improvements in baseline physical fitness measures including squat and bench press 1RM.
effect_or_estimate: Significant pre-post improvements in fitness and striking tests
limitations: 11 sessions/week for 3 weeks is an extreme dose not transferable to a community programme; short duration; pre-post design; potential testing familiarisation.
citation: Niu et al. (2024). Impact of three weeks of integrative neuromuscular training on the athletic performance of elite female boxers. PeerJ.
ppbf_implication: One of the few boxing physical-preparation studies in FEMALE athletes. Cite it when noting the female evidence gap — but the dose is not replicable at PPBF and must not be copied.
verified_title: Impact of three weeks of integrative neuromuscular training on the athletic performance of elite female boxers.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Strength training in Olympic combat sports
claim: A systematic review of 20 studies (504 participants; 428 male, 76 female) found significant improvements in maximal dynamic and isometric strength, muscle power, flexibility and balance following strength training in Olympic combat sport athletes, with improvements also in sport-specific actions in judo, karate, fencing and boxing.
effect_or_estimate: Significant improvements in strength, power, flexibility, balance
limitations: Only 15% of participants were female — the female evidence base is thin; heterogeneous protocols; no pooled effect size reported in the abstract; positive-result publication bias likely.
citation: Cid-Calfucura et al. (2023). Effects of Strength Training on Physical Fitness of Olympic Combat Sports Athletes: A Systematic Review. Int J Environ Res Public Health.
ppbf_implication: Provides the evidentiary basis for including resistance training in PPBF programming at all levels — this directly contradicts the 'weights make you slow/muscle-bound' gym tradition.
verified_title: Effects of Strength Training on Physical Fitness of Olympic Combat Sports Athletes: A Systematic Review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Isokinetic knee strength distinguishes performance level (association only)
claim: In 18 amateur boxers (9 elite, 9 non-elite), peak torque of knee flexors and extensors was higher in the elite group at all angular velocities, with differences also in unilateral and bilateral ratios.
effect_or_estimate: Elite > non-elite peak torque at 60, 180, 240 deg/s
limitations: CORRELATION NOT CAUSATION: elite boxers being stronger does not show that getting stronger makes a boxer elite. Very small groups (n=9 per group); requires an isokinetic dynamometer unavailable to community gyms.
citation: Zhou et al. (2022). Lower extremity isokinetic strength characteristics of amateur boxers. Front Physiol.
ppbf_implication: Illustrates the discriminative-validity trap. SHADOW must not present cross-sectional level differences as development targets or as evidence that training a quality causes advancement.
verified_title: Lower extremity isokinetic strength characteristics of amateur boxers.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Unilateral vs bilateral resistance training in adolescent boxers
claim: A parallel-group study in 29 right-handed orthodox-stance adolescent boxers compared 8 weeks of unilateral, bilateral and hybrid complex resistance training on straight-punch performance and dominant/non-dominant side adaptations.
study_design: Three-arm parallel group training intervention (8 weeks)
effect_or_estimate: Between-modality comparison of straight-punch performance and side-specific adaptation
limitations: Very small groups (~10 each) for a three-arm comparison; adolescent population with concurrent maturation; loads were set from bilateral 1RM, which complicates the unilateral-load comparison.
citation: Liu et al. (2025). Comparative effects of unilateral, bilateral, and hybrid combined resistance training on straight punch performance in adolescent boxers: a focus on dominant and non-dominant-side adaptations. Eur J Appl Physiol.
ppbf_implication: Relevant to PPBF's adolescent lane and to the bilateral-asymmetry question inherent in orthodox/southpaw stance. Underpowered — treat as hypothesis-generating for a PPBF asymmetry study.
verified_title: Comparative effects of unilateral, bilateral, and hybrid combined resistance training on straight punch performance in adolescent boxers: a focus on dominant and non-dominant-side adaptations.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Concurrent training interference — real but not prohibitive
claim: A meta-analysis of 21 studies (422 effect sizes) reported mean effect sizes for strength development of 1.76 for strength training alone versus 1.44 for concurrent training, and for power 0.91 versus a lower concurrent value, indicating attenuation rather than abolition of strength/power adaptation when endurance training is added.
effect_or_estimate: Strength ES: 1.76 (strength only) vs 1.44 (concurrent); hypertrophy 1.23 vs 0.85
limitations: Not boxing-specific; predominantly male; the modality, duration and frequency of endurance training moderate the effect and are heterogeneous; older meta-analysis.
citation: Wilson et al. (2012). Concurrent training: a meta-analysis examining interference of aerobic and resistance exercises. J Strength Cond Res.
ppbf_implication: Directly addresses the 'roadwork kills your power' claim: interference is measurable but partial. PPBF should sequence rather than eliminate — schedule high-quality strength/power work away from high-volume aerobic sessions.
verified_title: Concurrent training: a meta-analysis examining interference of aerobic and resistance exercises.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Concurrent training — sex and training status moderate adaptation
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis examined sex-specific and training-status differences in strength, power, hypertrophy and VO2max adaptations to concurrent strength and endurance training in healthy adults aged 18-50.
study_design: Systematic review with meta-analysis (Cochrane risk of bias)
effect_or_estimate: Sex- and training-status-moderated adaptations
limitations: Not boxing-specific; the female evidence base within concurrent-training research is smaller than the male; heterogeneous interventions.
citation: Huiberts et al. (2023). Concurrent Strength and Endurance Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on the Impact of Sex and Training Status. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: SHADOW must not apply one concurrent-training rule to all athletes. Sex and training status are moderators that belong in the programming context model.
verified_title: Concurrent Strength and Endurance Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on the Impact of Sex and Training Status.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Strength training improves endurance economy (against 'weights make you slow')
claim: A review of combining endurance training with heavy or explosive strength training reports that running economy is improved by combined training with either heavy or explosive strength training, and that concurrent endurance and heavy strength training can increase velocity/power at VO2max or time to exhaustion at those intensities.
effect_or_estimate: Improved running economy; increased Vmax/Wmax or time to exhaustion
limitations: Endurance-athlete population, not boxers; the outcome (running economy) is not a boxing performance outcome; transfer to a 9-minute intermittent striking task is an inference.
citation: Rønnestad et al. (2013). Optimizing strength training for running and cycling endurance performance: A review. Scand J Med Sci Sports.
ppbf_implication: Evidence-vs-tradition entry: strength training does not degrade endurance qualities in endurance athletes. FLAG: this rests on transfer from a non-boxing population.
verified_title: Optimizing strength training for running and cycling endurance performance: A review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Weighted vests / running in heavy boots — acute impairment, uncertain benefit
claim: A systematic review of weighted-vest sprint training (11 studies) found vest loads of 5-40% body mass acutely increased sprint times (4.1-16.9%) and decreased velocity, horizontal force, maximal power and flight times while increasing contact times; longitudinal studies (5.6-18.9% body mass, 3-7 weeks) showed small improvements in velocity (1.2-1.3%) and times, with the authors noting optimum load and volume remain to be established.
effect_or_estimate: Acute: sprint times +4.1-16.9%; longitudinal: velocity +1.2-1.3%
limitations: Not boxing; not footwear; the acute effects are large and negative; longitudinal effects are small and the optimum dose is explicitly unestablished; loading distribution of a vest differs from that of heavy boots.
citation: Macadam et al. (2019). Acute and longitudinal effects of weighted vest training on sprint-running performance: a systematic review. Sports Biomech.
ppbf_implication: Closest available evidence for 'running in heavy boots'. It shows external loading acutely degrades movement quality with only small, uncertain longitudinal gain — and NO study addresses distal (foot) loading in boxing. Classify boots as tradition with an evidence-transfer caveat.
verified_title: Acute and longitudinal effects of weighted vest training on sprint-running performance: a systematic review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A systematic review, meta-analysis and multivariate meta-regression of 189 studies representing 6654 adults examined the frequency, intensity and volume of static stretching required to maximise flexibility, and whether this is moderated by muscle group, age, sex, training status and baseline flexibility.
effect_or_estimate: Dose-response for flexibility established across acute and chronic protocols
limitations: Flexibility is the outcome — NOT performance and NOT injury prevention; not boxing-specific; the moderator analyses are observational within the meta-regression.
citation: Ingram et al. (2024). Optimising the Dose of Static Stretching to Improve Flexibility: A Systematic Review, Meta-analysis and Multivariate Meta-regression. Sports Med.
