ppbf_implication: PPBF may prescribe static stretching to increase range of motion with a good evidence base, but must NOT claim it prevents injury or improves punching. Separate the mobility goal from the performance goal in the app.
verified_title: Optimising the Dose of Static Stretching to Improve Flexibility: A Systematic Review, Meta-analysis and Multivariate Meta-regression.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Cold-water immersion — soreness yes, adaptation caution
claim: A systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression (28 studies) found cold-water immersion superior to other recovery methods for recovery from muscle soreness and similar to other methods for recovery of muscular power and flexibility in physically active populations.
study_design: Systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression
effect_or_estimate: CWI superior for soreness; similar to other methods for power and flexibility recovery
limitations: Not boxing-specific; the outcomes are short-term recovery markers, not competitive performance; long-term interference with strength adaptation was not the focus; predominantly male.
citation: Moore et al. (2022). Effects of Cold-Water Immersion Compared with Other Recovery Modalities on Athletic Performance Following Acute Strenuous Exercise in Physically Active Participants: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Meta-Regression. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: If PPBF offers cold exposure it should be framed as soreness management around competition, not as a routine training adjunct. Ice baths for minors require guardian consent and supervision — route to the safety lane.
verified_title: Effects of Cold-Water Immersion Compared with Other Recovery Modalities on Athletic Performance Following Acute Strenuous Exercise in Physically Active Participants: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Meta-Regression.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A separate systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression compared cold-water immersion with passive recovery on athletic performance, perceptual measures and creatine kinase after a single bout of strenuous exercise, dividing studies into eccentric-exercise and high-intensity-exercise subgroups.
study_design: Systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression
effect_or_estimate: Subgroup-dependent effects on performance, perception and CK
limitations: Not boxing; heterogeneous protocols (temperature, duration, immersion depth); single-bout designs cannot address chronic adaptation.
citation: Moore et al. (2022). Impact of Cold-Water Immersion Compared with Passive Recovery Following a Single Bout of Strenuous Exercise on Athletic Performance in Physically Active Participants: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis and Meta-regression. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Second source confirming cold-water immersion evidence is context-dependent. SHADOW should present recovery modalities with their evidence class visible, not as a checklist.
verified_title: Impact of Cold-Water Immersion Compared with Passive Recovery Following a Single Bout of Strenuous Exercise on Athletic Performance in Physically Active Participants: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis and Meta-regression.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A review located 36 studies examining the validity and reliability of the session-RPE method using the modified CR-10, and reported that these studies confirmed the validity, good reliability and internal consistency of session-RPE across several sports.
effect_or_estimate: Validity and reliability confirmed across sports; influencing factors identified
boxing_specific: No (multi-sport, includes combat sports elsewhere in the literature)
limitations: A review rather than a meta-analysis; session-RPE is influenced by factors including exercise mode, intensity distribution and individual characteristics, which the review itself flags; correlations with objective load vary by modality.
citation: Haddad et al. (2017). Session-RPE Method for Training Load Monitoring: Validity, Ecological Usefulness, and Influencing Factors. Front Neurosci.
ppbf_implication: FOUNDATION of the PPBF internal load model: sRPE x duration is the defensible primary internal load metric. It is cheap, requires no hardware, and fits a nonprofit budget.
verified_title: Session-RPE Method for Training Load Monitoring: Validity, Ecological Usefulness, and Influencing Factors.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Athlete-reported sRPE more valid than coach rating
claim: A study comparing player and coach ratings concluded that player session-RPE is a more valid tool than coaches' ratings for monitoring internal training load.
effect_or_estimate: Player sRPE outperformed coach rating
limitations: Single study in a team-sport context; boxing has a different coach-athlete observation relationship (one-on-one padwork gives coaches better visibility than a team field session).
citation: Lupo et al. (2019). Player Session Rating of Perceived Exertion: A More Valid Tool Than Coaches' Ratings to Monitor Internal Training Load in Elite Youth Female Basketball. Int J Sports Physiol Perform.
ppbf_implication: PPBF should collect sRPE FROM THE ATHLETE, not have the coach estimate it. This is a concrete app requirement: an athlete-entered RPE field, with coach observation stored separately as a different data type.
verified_title: Player Session Rating of Perceived Exertion: A More Valid Tool Than Coaches' Ratings to Monitor Internal Training Load in Elite Youth Female Basketball.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: Session rating of perceived exertion has been validated for quantifying internal training load in adolescent athletes, with a separate study also supporting the validity of retrospective session-RPE in youth athletes.
effect_or_estimate: Acceptable validity for internal load quantification in youth
limitations: Youth comprehension of RPE scales varies with age and cognitive development; scale choice and anchoring instructions matter; rating timing affects the value; not boxing-specific.
citation: Mann et al. (2019). The Validation of Session Rating of Perceived Exertion for Quantifying Internal Training Load in Adolescent Distance Runners. Int J Sports Physiol Perform.
ppbf_implication: PPBF may use sRPE with adolescents but must standardise the scale, anchoring script and collection timing (consistent post-session delay). Youngest bands may need a pictorial scale.
verified_title: The Validation of Session Rating of Perceived Exertion for Quantifying Internal Training Load in Adolescent Distance Runners.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: sRPE validation in combat sports specifically
claim: Session-RPE has been validated for quantifying training load in karate athletes and used to quantify the load of different youth taekwondo training sessions.
effect_or_estimate: Acceptable validity/reliability in combat-sport sessions
limitations: Karate and taekwondo differ from boxing in session structure and contact; small samples; no boxing-specific sRPE validation study was located in this search.
citation: Tabben et al. (2015). Validity and reliability of the session-RPE method for quantifying training load in karate athletes. J Sports Med Phys Fitness.
ppbf_implication: Closest combat-sport validation available. GAP: no boxing-specific sRPE validation was found — this is a concrete PPBF validation study opportunity.
verified_title: Validity and reliability of the session-RPE method for quantifying training load in karate athletes.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Subjective measures outperform common objective markers
claim: A systematic review of 56 original studies reporting concurrent subjective and objective measures of athlete well-being found that subjective and objective measures generally did NOT correlate, and that subjective measures reflected acute and chronic training loads with superior sensitivity and consistency than objective measures.
effect_or_estimate: Subjective measures superior in sensitivity and consistency to objective measures
limitations: Not boxing-specific; 'superior' refers to sensitivity to load, not to predicting injury or performance; subjective measures are vulnerable to reporting bias, especially where athletes fear being withheld from sparring or selection.
citation: Saw et al. (2015). Monitoring the athlete training response: subjective self-reported measures trump commonly used objective measures: a systematic review. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Strongly supports a low-cost PPBF wellness questionnaire as a primary monitoring tool over expensive objective kit. BUT the app must protect against athletes gaming reports to secure sparring — see governance section of the load model.
verified_title: Monitoring the athlete training response: subjective self-reported measures trump commonly used objective measures: a systematic review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: An international consensus statement arising from the 2016 Doha conference on monitoring athlete training loads set out a shared conceptual framework for internal and external load monitoring for coaches, sport-science and sport-medicine staff.
effect_or_estimate: Framework, not an effect estimate
limitations: Consensus statements reflect expert agreement rather than pooled data; the field has moved on since 2017, particularly regarding ACWR criticism; not boxing-specific.
citation: Bourdon et al. (2017). Monitoring Athlete Training Loads: Consensus Statement. Int J Sports Physiol Perform.
ppbf_implication: Adopt the internal/external load distinction as the PPBF data-model backbone: external = what was done (rounds, sets, minutes, punches counted); internal = how it was experienced (sRPE, wellness).
verified_title: Monitoring Athlete Training Loads: Consensus Statement.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Monitoring training load to understand fatigue
claim: A review of methods for monitoring training load to understand fatigue in athletes surveyed the available internal and external load monitoring tools and their interpretation.
effect_or_estimate: Descriptive synthesis
limitations: Narrative review; tool availability and validity have both changed since publication; not boxing-specific.
citation: Halson (2014). Monitoring training load to understand fatigue in athletes. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Background reference for the PPBF monitoring rationale. Not a source of thresholds.
verified_title: Monitoring training load to understand fatigue in athletes.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: In 25 experienced athletes, illnesses and minor injuries were related to indices of training load, monotony (daily mean divided by standard deviation) and strain (load multiplied by monotony), with a high percentage of illnesses accounted for when individuals exceeded INDIVIDUALLY identifiable training thresholds, mostly related to strain.
effect_or_estimate: Illness incidence related to individually identified strain thresholds
limitations: Small n; observational; the thresholds were INDIVIDUAL, not population thresholds — a critical caveat routinely lost in secondary citation; illness is self- or coach-reported; 1998 study.
citation: Foster (1998). Monitoring training in athletes with reference to overtraining syndrome. Med Sci Sports Exerc.
ppbf_implication: PPBF may compute monotony and strain as DESCRIPTIVE trend variables. It must NOT apply a population monotony/strain cut-off: the original evidence is explicitly individual-threshold based. Any PPBF threshold is an ASSUMPTION requiring local validation.
verified_title: Monitoring training in athletes with reference to overtraining syndrome.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Monotony/strain vary seasonally and by context
claim: Studies tracking training load, monotony and strain across seasons in team-sport athletes have described variations across the competitive year and examined dose-response relationships with aerobic fitness.
effect_or_estimate: Seasonal variation in monotony and strain described
limitations: Observational; team-sport calendars differ fundamentally from boxing's bout-driven calendar; no causal claim supported.
citation: Clemente et al. (2019). Variations of training load, monotony, and strain and dose-response relationships with maximal aerobic speed, maximal oxygen uptake, and isokinetic strength in professional soccer players. PLoS One.
ppbf_implication: PPBF should baseline its OWN monotony distribution across a season before interpreting any value as high or low.
verified_title: Variations of training load, monotony, and strain and dose-response relationships with maximal aerobic speed, maximal oxygen uptake, and isokinetic strength in professional soccer players.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: ACWR — mathematical coupling produces spurious correlation
claim: An analysis published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine argued that mathematical coupling inherent in the conventional acute-to-chronic workload ratio calculation causes spurious correlation, because the acute load appears in both the numerator and the denominator of the chronic load.
effect_or_estimate: Demonstration of spurious correlation arising from coupling
limitations: A methodological argument rather than an empirical outcome study; the practical magnitude of the resulting bias is itself debated (see A5-046).
citation: Lolli et al. (2017). Mathematical coupling causes spurious correlation within the conventional acute-to-chronic workload ratio calculations. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: PPBF MUST NOT ship a coupled ACWR as a risk indicator. If any ratio is displayed at all it must be uncoupled and labelled CONTESTED, with no threshold-based action attached.
verified_title: Mathematical coupling causes spurious correlation within the conventional acute-to-chronic workload ratio calculations.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: ACWR — coupling effect size disputed in real data
claim: Using training and competition workload data from international-level basketball and weightlifting athletes before Olympic qualifying tournaments, a commentary found that although some differences existed between coupled and uncoupled chronic load and ACWR data, the effect sizes of those differences were almost all trivial (g=0.04-0.21), with ACWR-to-uncoupled-ACWR correlations of r=0.88-0.99.
study_design: Case-study commentary using real monitoring data
effect_or_estimate: Coupled vs uncoupled differences g=0.04-0.21; r=0.88-0.99
limitations: A case study from two sports, not a general proof; being numerically similar does not resolve the underlying inferential problem the coupling critique raises; the debate remains unresolved.
citation: Coyne et al. (2019). Does Mathematical Coupling Matter to the Acute to Chronic Workload Ratio? A Case Study From Elite Sport. Int J Sports Physiol Perform.
ppbf_implication: Present BOTH sides in the PPBF evidence ledger. The existence of an active methodological dispute is itself the reason SHADOW must not automate any ACWR-driven decision.
verified_title: Does Mathematical Coupling Matter to the Acute to Chronic Workload Ratio? A Case Study From Elite Sport.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: ACWR — systematic reviews report methodological heterogeneity, not a validated threshold
claim: Systematic reviews of the acute:chronic workload ratio and injury risk report substantial heterogeneity between studies in the variables studied (e.g. total distance vs high-speed running), the ratio cut-offs analysed (1.50-1.80 vs >=1.50), and the reference groups used (0.80-1.20 vs <=0.85), leading to caution about utilising ACWR for external load.
effect_or_estimate: High between-study variability in variables, ratios and reference groups
limitations: Study quality scores were modest (48.2-64.3%); no boxing or combat-sport data; the heterogeneity means no single threshold is supportable.
citation: Maupin et al. (2020). The Relationship Between Acute: Chronic Workload Ratios and Injury Risk in Sports: A Systematic Review. Open Access J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: DEFINITIVE for PPBF: there is NO validated ACWR threshold to hand the product. Any number in a PPBF UI would be invented. Do not ship a 'danger zone'.
verified_title: The Relationship Between Acute: Chronic Workload Ratios and Injury Risk in Sports: A Systematic Review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: ACWR — team-sport review population is male, adult, professional
claim: A systematic review of 20 studies comprising 2375 injuries from 1234 athletes examining the ACWR and time-loss injury risk in adult elite team sports reported that all participants were male, with a mean age of 24 years.
study_design: Systematic review (modified Downs and Black appraisal)
effect_or_estimate: Population characteristic: 100% male, mean age 24
transfer_status: Other-sport transfer (male adult team sport only)
limitations: The entire evidence base underpinning ACWR in this review is male, adult and professional team sport. There is no female, no youth and no combat-sport evidence in it.
citation: Andrade et al. (2020). Is the Acute: Chronic Workload Ratio (ACWR) Associated with Risk of Time-Loss Injury in Professional Team Sports? A Systematic Review of Methodology, Variables and Injury Risk in Practical Situations. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: This single fact disqualifies ACWR for a PPBF population that includes youth, women, novices and adaptive athletes. State it explicitly in the app's methods note if ACWR is ever discussed.
verified_title: Is the Acute: Chronic Workload Ratio (ACWR) Associated with Risk of Time-Loss Injury in Professional Team Sports? A Systematic Review of Methodology, Variables and Injury Risk in Practical Situations.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: ACWR — a separate review reports supportive association
claim: A systematic review of 22 articles (median Newcastle-Ottawa Scale score 8, range 5-9) examining the association between injury occurrence and the ACWR, using rolling-average and exponentially weighted moving-average models, reported findings supporting an association between the ACWR and injury in team sports.
effect_or_estimate: Reported association supported; best application method not resolved
limitations: Reports association, NOT causation; even this supportive review did not resolve which calculation method should be used; observational designs throughout; the coupling critique (A5-045) applies to the underlying studies.
citation: Griffin et al. (2020). The Association Between the Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio and Injury and its Application in Team Sports: A Systematic Review. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: CONTESTED PRACTICE: reviews disagree. PPBF's position must be to log the inputs (acute and chronic load) and let a qualified human interpret, rather than to compute a ratio verdict.
verified_title: The Association Between the Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio and Injury and its Application in Team Sports: A Systematic Review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: ACWR research is methodologically inconsistent even within one sport
claim: A systematic review of methodological variation in ACWR research in elite male football players found twelve eligible articles, judged all studies to be of poor quality, and documented heterogeneity in workload measures, running-intensity zone thresholds, exposure type, data collection timing, ratio windows (1:2, 1:3, 1:4 weeks) and statistical analysis.
effect_or_estimate: All studies rated poor quality; extensive methodological heterogeneity
limitations: Single-sport (football) review; 'poor quality' is the reviewers' own overall appraisal; does not itself test the ACWR-injury relationship.
citation: Wang et al. (2020). A systematic review on methodological variation in acute:chronic workload research in elite male football players. Sci Med Footb.
ppbf_implication: Closes the case for PPBF: even within one well-resourced sport the ACWR literature is of poor quality and non-comparable. ACWR is CONTESTED PRACTICE and must be labelled as such wherever it appears.
verified_title: A systematic review on methodological variation in acute:chronic workload research in elite male football players.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: An influential British Journal of Sports Medicine paper framed a training-injury prevention paradox, arguing that appropriately high chronic training loads may be protective and that rapid load spikes are the risk, popularising load-ratio thinking in applied sport.
effect_or_estimate: Conceptual framing
limitations: This is a conceptual/position paper, not primary evidence; it has been extensively criticised in the subsequent methodological literature (A5-045, A5-047, A5-050); widely cited in ways that overstate its evidentiary weight.
citation: Gabbett (2016). The training-injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder?. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Include in the PPBF ledger explicitly as a HIGH-CITATION, CONTESTED source so that SHADOW's source-reliability engine does not treat citation count as authority.
verified_title: The training-injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder?

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: IOC consensus on load and injury risk
claim: The International Olympic Committee convened an expert group and published a consensus statement on load in sport and risk of injury, providing guidelines for the prescription of training and competition load and for the monitoring of training, competition and psychological load, athlete well-being and injury.
effect_or_estimate: Guidelines, not effect estimates
limitations: Consensus reflects expert judgement; published 2016 and predates much of the ACWR methodological critique; the guidance is general rather than sport-specific.
citation: Soligard et al. (2016). How much is too much? (Part 1) International Olympic Committee consensus statement on load in sport and risk of injury. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Authoritative anchor for the PPBF load-monitoring policy. Cite for the PRINCIPLE (monitor load, well-being and injury together) not for any numeric threshold.
verified_title: How much is too much? (Part 1) International Olympic Committee consensus statement on load in sport and risk of injury.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: IOC consensus on load and illness
claim: A companion IOC consensus statement addressed the relationship between load — including rapid changes in training and competition load, calendar congestion, psychological load and travel — and the risk of illness and overtraining, with practical guidelines for load management.
effect_or_estimate: Guidelines, not effect estimates
limitations: Consensus-level evidence; 2016 publication; general rather than boxing-specific; the authors themselves identified urgent research priorities, indicating the evidence base was incomplete.
citation: Schwellnus et al. (2016). How much is too much? (Part 2) International Olympic Committee consensus statement on load in sport and risk of illness. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Supports logging illness alongside injury in the PPBF model. Illness is an under-collected but cheap and informative monitoring signal.
verified_title: How much is too much? (Part 2) International Olympic Committee consensus statement on load in sport and risk of illness.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Overtraining syndrome — diagnosis is exclusionary and belongs to clinicians
claim: The joint European College of Sport Science / American College of Sports Medicine consensus statement distinguishes functional overreaching, non-functional overreaching and overtraining syndrome, notes that the distinction between non-functional overreaching and overtraining syndrome is very difficult and depends on clinical outcome and exclusion diagnosis, and states there is no scientific evidence to confirm or refute the suggestion that overtraining-syndrome symptoms are more severe.
effect_or_estimate: No validated diagnostic marker; exclusion diagnosis required
limitations: Consensus level; explicitly acknowledges the absence of a validated diagnostic marker; the boundary between overreaching and overtraining syndrome is not measurable by any field tool.
citation: Meeusen et al. (2013). Prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of the overtraining syndrome: joint consensus statement of the European College of Sport Science and the American College of Sports Medicine. Med Sci Sports Exerc.
ppbf_implication: HARD BOUNDARY: SHADOW must NEVER output 'overtrained' or 'overtraining syndrome'. That is an exclusion diagnosis requiring a physician. SHADOW may only surface descriptive patterns (e.g. 'load rising while wellness declines for N sessions') and route to a qualified human.
verified_title: Prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of the overtraining syndrome: joint consensus statement of the European College of Sport Science and the American College of Sports Medicine.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A narrative review and 2021 expert consensus reported that elite athletes are particularly susceptible to sleep inadequacies characterised by habitual short sleep (under 7 hours/night) and poor sleep quality, that performance is reduced by a night or more without sleep while the effect of partial sleep restriction over 1-3 nights remains unclear, and that habitually sleeping under 7 hours/night increases susceptibility to respiratory infection in the wider population.
sex: Male and female (authors note a lack of females in the literature)
effect_or_estimate: Habitual short sleep <7 h/night; respiratory infection susceptibility (general population evidence)
transfer_status: Cross-sport consensus; infection evidence transferred from general population
limitations: The authors explicitly note inadequate experimental control, a lack of female participants and questions about sleep-assessment tool validity in the athlete sleep literature; the infection link is transferred from non-athlete populations.
citation: Walsh et al. (2020). Sleep and the athlete: narrative review and 2021 expert consensus recommendations. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Sleep is a high-yield, zero-cost PPBF monitoring target. Collect self-reported sleep duration and quality. Do NOT set a PPBF-specific sleep threshold beyond flagging habitual short sleep for coach conversation.
verified_title: Sleep and the athlete: narrative review and 2021 expert consensus recommendations.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Acute sleep loss impairs physical performance
claim: A systematic and meta-analytical review of 227 outcome measures classified performance tasks into anaerobic power, speed/power endurance, high-intensity interval exercise, strength, endurance, strength-endurance and skill categories, comparing normal sleep (over 6 h in any 24 h) with sleep loss (6 h or less), and examined sleep-loss protocol, time of day and upper- versus lower-body strength as moderators.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis with meta-regression
effect_or_estimate: Impairments varied by exercise category and by time of day
limitations: Laboratory sleep-restriction protocols do not replicate real athlete sleep patterns; predominantly male; effects differ by task type, so a single 'sleep loss harms performance' statement oversimplifies.
citation: Craven et al. (2022). Effects of Acute Sleep Loss on Physical Performance: A Systematic and Meta-Analytical Review. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Supports flagging acute sleep loss before high-skill or high-contact sessions. PPBF coaching translation: consider reducing sparring intensity after reported poor sleep — as a coach decision, not an automated gate.
verified_title: Effects of Acute Sleep Loss on Physical Performance: A Systematic and Meta-Analytical Review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Sleep extension improved performance in one small athlete trial
claim: In 11 male collegiate basketball players, a 5-7 week sleep extension period targeting a minimum 10 hours in bed increased objective nightly sleep by 110.9 minutes and produced faster timed sprints and improved shooting accuracy compared with baseline.
effect_or_estimate: Sleep +110.9 ± 79.7 min; faster sprint; improved shooting accuracy
limitations: n=11, male, single sport, no control group over a long study period during which normal training progression could account for gains; 10 h in bed is not achievable for most working or school-attending athletes.
citation: Mah et al. (2011). The effects of sleep extension on the athletic performance of collegiate basketball players. Sleep.
ppbf_implication: Frequently over-cited. PPBF may encourage sleep opportunity but MUST NOT promise a performance gain from a specific sleep duration. Do not put a sleep-hours target in the app as if validated.
verified_title: The effects of sleep extension on the athletic performance of collegiate basketball players.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Short sleep associated with injury in adolescent athletes
claim: In a survey of 112 adolescent athletes (mean age 15 y) with retrospective injury-record review, multivariate analysis found hours of sleep per night and school grade to be the best independent predictors of injury, with athletes sleeping under 8 hours per night 1.7 times (95% CI 1.0-3.0, p=0.04) more likely to have had an injury.
study_design: Cross-sectional survey with retrospective record review
effect_or_estimate: OR 1.7 (95% CI 1.0-3.0) for <8 h sleep
limitations: CORRELATION NOT CAUSATION — cross-sectional with retrospective injury recall; the confidence interval's lower bound touches 1.0, so the association is marginal; self-reported sleep; single school.
citation: Milewski et al. (2014). Chronic lack of sleep is associated with increased sports injuries in adolescent athletes. J Pediatr Orthop.
ppbf_implication: Cite carefully. PPBF may raise sleep as a modifiable factor with adolescents and guardians, but must not tell a family that short sleep caused an injury.
verified_title: Chronic lack of sleep is associated with increased sports injuries in adolescent athletes.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A review of sleep in teenage athletes (13-19 y) concluded that few studies exist on the effects of disordered sleep in this population and noted a paucity of evidence-based recommendations to promote sleep quantity and quality in athletes of this age.
effect_or_estimate: No pooled estimate; explicit evidence paucity
limitations: The review itself is level 4; it documents an evidence gap rather than filling it.
citation: Coel et al. (2022). Sleep and the Young Athlete. Sports Health.
ppbf_implication: Honest position for PPBF's guardian-facing material: sleep matters, the youth-specific evidence base is thin, and PPBF should not present numeric sleep prescriptions to families as established science.
verified_title: Sleep and the Young Athlete.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A systematic review of 25 intervention studies published 2011-2021 examined sleep hygiene, naps and other sleep interventions in athletes, requiring at least one objective performance or recovery outcome.
effect_or_estimate: Heterogeneous interventions and outcomes
limitations: Heterogeneous interventions prevent pooling; short intervention durations; adherence rarely reported; not boxing-specific.
citation: Cunha et al. (2023). The Impact of Sleep Interventions on Athletic Performance: A Systematic Review. Sports Med Open.
ppbf_implication: Sleep hygiene education is a low-risk, low-cost PPBF intervention worth piloting with a defined outcome, but the expected effect size is not established.
verified_title: The Impact of Sleep Interventions on Athletic Performance: A Systematic Review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Travel fatigue and jet lag consensus
claim: A review and consensus statement by 26 researchers and clinicians on travel fatigue and jet lag in athletes concluded that evidence on optimal assessment and management is lacking, which restricted the strength of the recommendations possible, and provided fundamental principles and travel toolboxes for pre-flight, in-flight and post-flight strategies.
effect_or_estimate: Principles only; the panel explicitly noted weak evidence
limitations: The consensus panel states directly that the lack of evidence restricts recommendation strength; no combat-sport-specific data.
citation: Janse van Rensburg et al. (2021). Managing Travel Fatigue and Jet Lag in Athletes: A Review and Consensus Statement. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: For PPBF, travel is mostly regional (short trips). Log travel as a context flag on session and competition records rather than applying an unvalidated jet-lag adjustment.
verified_title: Managing Travel Fatigue and Jet Lag in Athletes: A Review and Consensus Statement.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A meta-analysis of 27 studies in competitive athletes found the optimal strategy to be a taper of 2 weeks' duration (overall effect 0.59 ± 0.33, p<0.001) achieved by decreasing training volume while examining intensity, frequency, taper pattern and duration as independent variables.
effect_or_estimate: Overall taper effect 0.59 ± 0.33 (p<0.001); 2-week duration optimal
limitations: The underlying studies are predominantly endurance sports, NOT intermittent combat sports; predominantly male; 2007 publication; a 2-week taper conflicts with the frequent, short-notice matchmaking common in amateur boxing.
citation: Bosquet et al. (2007). Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis. Med Sci Sports Exerc.
ppbf_implication: PPBF should implement a taper TEMPLATE (reduce volume, maintain intensity) and NOT a fixed 2-week rule, because amateur boxing bout notice is often shorter. Flag as transfer from endurance sport.
verified_title: Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Taper in team sports — neuromuscular and metabolic outcomes
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies in team-sport athletes found limited evidence of a moderate taper-induced improvement in repeated sprint ability (SMD 0.41, 95% CI 0.26-0.55, I2=0%) and moderate evidence of moderate increases in maximal power (SMD 0.44, 95% CI 0.32-0.56, I2=15%), change-of-direction speed (SMD 0.38, 95% CI 0.15-0.60, I2=28%) and maximal oxygen uptake.
effect_or_estimate: RSA SMD 0.41; max power SMD 0.44; COD SMD 0.38
transfer_status: Other-sport transfer (team sports, intermittent — closer to boxing than endurance)
limitations: Team sports, not combat sports; predominantly male; only 14 studies; the authors themselves describe the RSA evidence as limited.
citation: Vachon et al. (2020). Effects of tapering on neuromuscular and metabolic fitness in team sports: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Sport Sci.
ppbf_implication: Better transfer anchor than the endurance taper literature because the sports are intermittent. Supports maintaining power qualities through a PPBF fight-week taper.
verified_title: Effects of tapering on neuromuscular and metabolic fitness in team sports: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Taper in endurance athletes — volume reduction range
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies in endurance athletes found significant improvements in time-trial performance (SMD -0.45) and time to exhaustion (SMD 1.28) but no improvement in maximal oxygen consumption or movement economy, with subgroup analysis showing that reducing training volume by 41-60% while maintaining intensity and frequency, over durations of up to 7 days, 8-14 days or 15-21 days, significantly improved time-trial performance.
effect_or_estimate: TT SMD -0.45; TTE SMD 1.28; volume reduction 41-60% effective
limitations: Endurance sport outcomes (time trial, time to exhaustion) are not boxing performance; the 41-60% volume reduction figure comes from endurance protocols and has NOT been tested in boxing.
citation: Wang et al. (2023). Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PLoS One.
ppbf_implication: The 41-60% volume reduction is the only published range with meta-analytic support, but transferring it to boxing is an ASSUMPTION. If PPBF uses it, label it: PROPOSED PPBF PARAMETER — ASSUMPTION, REQUIRES VALIDATION.
verified_title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 prospective cohort studies produced pooled amateur boxing competition injury incidence estimates of 54.7 per 1000 athlete-exposures (95% CI 33.8-88.4) and 6.8 per 1000 minutes of exposure (95% CI 4.2-10.9), and a training injury incidence of 1.3 per 1000 hours (95% CI 0.2-7.0); the most commonly injured region was the head and neck in competition (median 72%) and the upper limb in training (median 49%).
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohorts
limitations: Confidence intervals are very wide, especially for training (0.2-7.0), reflecting between-study heterogeneity in injury definitions and exposure recording; female data sparse; underlying studies span decades and rule eras.
citation: Alevras et al. (2022). Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sci Med Sport.
ppbf_implication: PRIMARY reference incidence for the PPBF injury model. Note that competition is where head/neck injury concentrates and training is where upper-limb injury concentrates — different prevention targets for different contexts.
verified_title: Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 epidemiology studies published 2000-2021 calculated a pooled overall injury incidence rate of 223.9 per 1000 boxers (95% CI 157.5-290.4) and 13.0 per 1000 minutes (95% CI 8.9-17.1), with professional boxing showing a higher rate than the pooled figure.
effect_or_estimate: 223.9/1000 boxers (157.5-290.4); 13.0/1000 min (8.9-17.1); professional rate higher
limitations: Only moderate study quality in most included studies; incidence denominators (per 1000 boxers vs per 1000 minutes) are not interchangeable and are frequently confused in secondary citation; heterogeneous injury definitions.
citation: Mao et al. (2023). Incidence Rates and Pathology Types of Boxing-Specific Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Epidemiology Studies in the 21st Century. Orthop J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Establishes that professional injury rates exceed amateur. Supports PPBF treating the professional lane as a distinct risk context requiring different documentation.
verified_title: Incidence Rates and Pathology Types of Boxing-Specific Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Epidemiology Studies in the 21st Century.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Elite amateur boxing — hand injury dominates
claim: Five-year prospective surveillance of the Great Britain amateur boxing squad (66 boxers, 2005-2009) with injuries recorded by the team doctor and physiotherapist found the hand was the most-injured location overall, in training and in competition; the total competition injury rate was 828 per 1000 hours, hand injury rate in competition was 302 per 1000 hours, more injuries occurred in training than competition, and the incidence of concussion was comparatively low.
effect_or_estimate: Total competition 828/1000 h; hand 302/1000 h; concussion comparatively low
limitations: Single national squad — an elite, well-medically-supported population that may under-represent community-gym risk; medically diagnosed injuries only, so self-managed injuries are missed; per-1000-hour competition rates look alarming but competition hours are very small denominators.
citation: Loosemore et al. (2015). Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study of medically diagnosed injury incidence and outcome. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: MOST ACTIONABLE injury finding for PPBF: hands and wrists are the dominant injury target, and MORE injuries occur in training than competition. Prioritise hand/wrist protection, wrapping quality and bag-work technique in the prevention lane.
verified_title: Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study of medically diagnosed injury incidence and outcome.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Hand and wrist injury detail in elite boxing
claim: Longitudinal prospective surveillance of the Great Britain boxing squad from 2005 to 2012 found finger carpometacarpal instability and metacarpophalangeal joint extensor hood/capsule sprain ('boxer's knuckle') significantly more common than other diagnoses; the competition hand/wrist injury rate was 347 per 1000 hours while the estimated training rate was under 0.5 per 1000 hours, with a similar absolute number of injuries occurring in training and competition despite far greater training hours.
effect_or_estimate: Competition hand/wrist 347/1000 h; training <0.5/1000 h; similar absolute counts
limitations: Single elite squad; estimated (not directly measured) training exposure hours; specialist diagnosis may not be available in a community setting.
citation: Loosemore et al. (2016). Hand and Wrist Injuries in Elite Boxing: A Longitudinal Prospective Study (2005-2012) of the Great Britain Olympic Boxing Squad. Hand (N Y).
ppbf_implication: Concrete PPBF prevention target: boxer's knuckle and CMC instability. Build a hand/wrist symptom flag into the observation intake, routed to a clinician — never self-diagnosed by the app.
verified_title: Hand and Wrist Injuries in Elite Boxing: A Longitudinal Prospective Study (2005-2012) of the Great Britain Olympic Boxing Squad.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A one-year prospective cohort of 33 amateur and 14 professional boxers in Victoria, Australia found 21 injuries, most to the head region (71%) with concussion the most common individual injury (33%), and an overall injury rate of 2.0 injuries per 1000 hours of boxing, with the authors concluding that boxing's acute injury rates were comparable to and often lower than other contact and non-contact sports given the high training exposure.
effect_or_estimate: 2.0 injuries/1000 h overall; 71% head region; 33% of injuries were concussion
limitations: Very small cohort (21 injuries total) producing a wide underlying uncertainty; the 'comparable to other sports' conclusion applies to ACUTE injury rate per hour only and says nothing about cumulative head-impact exposure; single Australian state.
citation: Zazryn et al. (2006). A prospective cohort study of injury in amateur and professional boxing. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Important nuance: per-hour acute injury rate is not the main safety concern in boxing — cumulative head impact is. PPBF messaging to guardians must not use the low per-hour rate to imply overall low risk.
verified_title: A prospective cohort study of injury in amateur and professional boxing.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Professional boxing injury rate and risk factors
claim: A retrospective cohort of 545 professional boxers across 907 fights over 8.5 years recorded 214 injuries, corresponding to 23.6 injuries per 100 professional fights, with the majority being lacerations to the head and face, and with increasing age and increasing number of fights both significant predictors of injury.
sex: Predominantly male (gender examined as a variable)
effect_or_estimate: 23.6 injuries per 100 fights; age and bout count predicted injury
limitations: Retrospective, based on a commission fight-statistics database with possible incomplete data entry (the authors note this); physician-reported bout injuries only, so training injuries are absent; single jurisdiction (Victoria, Australia) — rules and reporting differ elsewhere.
citation: Zazryn et al. (2009). Injury rates and risk factors in competitive professional boxing. Clin J Sport Med.
ppbf_implication: Supports PPBF tracking cumulative career bout count as a persistent athlete-record field. Age and accumulated bouts are administrative facts SHADOW can surface — the medical implication remains a physician's call.
verified_title: Injury rates and risk factors in competitive professional boxing.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A prospective cohort using IOC injury surveillance across Beijing 2008, London 2012 and Rio 2016 (7712 athlete exposures) found an overall competition injury incidence of 7.8 per 1000 minutes (95% CI 7.0-8.7), with boxing at 9.2 (95% CI 7.6-10.9) significantly higher than wrestling at 4.8 (3.6-6.2); the proportion of injuries causing more than 7 days' absence was LOWER in boxing (21.0%) than wrestling (39.6%), judo (35.9%) or taekwondo (32.5%); there was no difference in injury risk by sex, weight category or tournament round, but losing athletes had a rate ratio of 3.59 (95% CI 2.68-4.79) versus their winning opponents.
study_design: Prospective cohort using standardised IOC surveillance
effect_or_estimate: Boxing 9.2/1000 min; no sex difference; losers RR 3.59 (2.68-4.79)
limitations: Competition injuries only — training injuries not captured; Olympic-level athletes; the loser/winner rate ratio is associational and confounded by the fact that being outclassed both causes injury and causes losing.
citation: Lystad et al. (2020). Injury incidence, severity and profile in Olympic combat sports: a comparative analysis of 7712 athlete exposures from three consecutive Olympic Games. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Two PPBF-relevant facts: (1) no sex difference in competition injury risk at this level, and (2) boxing injuries are frequent but comparatively LESS time-loss severe than other combat sports. Use both to counter over- and under-statement of risk to guardians.
verified_title: Injury incidence, severity and profile in Olympic combat sports: a comparative analysis of 7712 athlete exposures from three consecutive Olympic Games.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A systematic review of prospective epidemiological research in Olympic combat sport (9 studies, most at moderate risk of bias) provided level 1/2b evidence that the most frequently injured areas in boxing were the head/face (45.8%), wrist (12.0%) and lower back (7.8%), and noted that heterogeneity in injury severity classification and inconsistency in exposure measures prevented direct cross-sport comparison of severity or incidence.
effect_or_estimate: Boxing: head/face 45.8%, wrist 12.0%, lower back 7.8%
limitations: Most included studies had moderate risk of bias; the authors state that heterogeneous definitions prevented cross-sport comparison; body-region proportions are not incidence rates.
citation: Bromley et al. (2017). A systematic review of prospective epidemiological research into injury and illness in Olympic combat sport. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Adds LOWER BACK to the PPBF prevention target list alongside hand/wrist and head/face — a region often ignored in boxing conditioning.
verified_title: A systematic review of prospective epidemiological research into injury and illness in Olympic combat sport.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: Injury surveillance at the 4th Elite Women's National Boxing Championship in India (235 female boxers) recorded an injury rate of 43.98 per 1000 athlete bouts (95% CI 33.71-54.07) and 293.21 per 1000 athlete hours of competition (95% CI 225.94-360.47), with head, face and neck the most commonly injured sites, mostly bruises/contusions followed by cuts and epistaxis, and NO concussions reported.
limitations: Zero reported concussions in a striking tournament almost certainly reflects under-detection or a reporting threshold rather than true absence — treat the null concussion count with strong scepticism; single tournament; single nation; the authors' conclusion that women are less injury-prone than men is not supported by this design.
citation: Dande et al. (2021). Injury surveillance during elite women's national boxing championship in India. Med J Armed Forces India.
ppbf_implication: Illustrates why PPBF must define concussion RECOGNITION and reporting procedure explicitly. An absence of recorded concussions in a log is evidence about the log, not about the athletes.
verified_title: Injury surveillance during elite women's national boxing championship in India.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A prospective study of injuries in competitive boxing documented injury patterns across training and competition contexts.
effect_or_estimate: Descriptive injury profile
limitations: Limited detail available from the abstract; single cohort; adds to but does not change the pooled estimates in A5-065.
citation: Siewe et al. (2014). Injuries in competitive boxing. A prospective study. Int J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Supporting reference for the PPBF training-injury context. Pooled estimates (A5-065) should take precedence.
verified_title: Injuries in competitive boxing. A prospective study.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: Multiple ophthalmology reports and reviews have documented ocular complications of boxing including retinal and other eye injuries in boxers.
effect_or_estimate: Descriptive prevalence of ocular pathology
limitations: Older clinical literature; case-series designs without denominators; screening practice and glove/rules eras have changed; prevalence figures from these series should not be applied to current amateur populations.
citation: Bianco et al. (2005). Ocular complications of boxing. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Supports PPBF requiring documented eye examination as part of medical clearance where the governing body requires it. SHADOW surfaces whether the document EXISTS; it never interprets an eye exam.
verified_title: Ocular complications of boxing.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A retrospective analysis of Australian news media reports 1832-2020 identified 163 boxing-related fatalities (122 professional, 40 amateur), of which traumatic brain injury was the most common cause (n=121, 74.2%) followed by cardiac arrest (11, 6.7%); the fatality rate declined precipitously from the 1930s to the 1980s, with eleven deaths since regulatory legislation began in the mid-1970s and no discernible further reduction after that legislation.
effect_or_estimate: 74.2% traumatic brain injury; 6.7% cardiac arrest; steep pre-legislation decline
limitations: News media reports are an incomplete and biased ascertainment source with no denominator, so no rate can be computed; single country; the finding that decline preceded legislation is descriptive, not causal.
citation: Alevras et al. (2021). Boxing-related fatalities in Australia: A retrospective analysis of news media reports. J Sci Med Sport.
ppbf_implication: Establishes that catastrophic outcomes in boxing are real but rare and dominated by traumatic brain injury. Grounds honest, non-alarmist guardian communication. Death is a governing-body and medical matter, never a SHADOW computation.
verified_title: Boxing-related fatalities in Australia: A retrospective analysis of news media reports.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Neuroimaging in professional combat sports — consensus
claim: The Association of Ringside Physicians issued a consensus statement on neuroimaging in professional combat sports, noting that deaths in the ring are usually the result of an acute catastrophic neurological event such as acute subdural haematoma, and that although neuroimaging is included in licensing in some jurisdictions, required imaging specifics and frequency vary with no consensus guidelines.
effect_or_estimate: Explicit statement that imaging requirements vary by jurisdiction with no consensus
limitations: Consensus level; addresses professional combat sports and does not automatically apply to amateur or community programmes; jurisdictional variation is explicitly acknowledged.
citation: Sethi et al. (2022). Neuroimaging in professional combat sports: consensus statement from the association of ringside physicians. Phys Sportsmed.
ppbf_implication: JURISDICTION IS A DATA FIELD. PPBF must store which sanctioning body and jurisdiction applies to each athlete, because imaging and clearance requirements differ. SHADOW surfaces the requirement and whether documentation is on file; it never determines clearance.
verified_title: Neuroimaging in professional combat sports: consensus statement from the association of ringside physicians.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Head impact exposure in boxing and MMA — instrumented mouthguard
claim: A cross-sectional study using custom-fit instrumented mouthguards in 23 boxing and MMA athletes (4 women) collected data from 53 amateur training sessions and 6 competitions with video verification of true-positive impacts, characterising peak linear and peak angular acceleration by sport, activity type, sex and impact location.
study_design: Cross-sectional instrumented-mouthguard study with video verification
sample_size: 23 athletes; 896+ impacts across 53 training sessions and 6 competitions
effect_or_estimate: Impact counts and accelerations characterised by sport/activity/sex
limitations: Only 4 female participants, so sex comparisons are underpowered; sensor accuracy issues affect this class of measurement (see A5-081); training sessions vastly outnumbered competitions.
citation: Jansen et al. (2021). Characterizing Head Impact Exposure in Men and Women During Boxing and Mixed Martial Arts. Orthop J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Confirms training/sparring is where the bulk of head-impact exposure accrues by count. Directly justifies the PPBF proxy model: count SPARRING rounds, not just bouts.
verified_title: Characterizing Head Impact Exposure in Men and Women During Boxing and Mixed Martial Arts.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Head kinematics in introductory boxing instruction
claim: Instrumented mouthguards worn by 22 male US Military Academy cadets during a compulsory introductory boxing course recorded 809 video-verified impacts across 205 analysed player-bouts, averaging 3.9 impacts per player-bout, with mean peak linear acceleration 16.5 ± 7.1 g (maximum 70.8 g) and a right-skewed distribution in which 640 of 809 events (79.1%) fell between 10 and 20 g, and mean peak angular acceleration 1.52 ± 0.96 krad/s2 (maximum 8.85 krad/s2).
effect_or_estimate: 3.9 impacts per player-bout; mean PLA 16.5 ± 7.1 g; 79.1% between 10-20 g; max 70.8 g
limitations: Male only; military cadets in a compulsory course are not volunteer community boxers; a single course; sensor quality issues apply (A5-081); impacts per bout will differ with sparring intensity and rules.
citation: Fetchko et al. (2023). Measurement of Head Kinematics Using Instrumented Mouthguards During Introductory Boxing Courses in U.S. Military Academy Cadets. Mil Med.
ppbf_implication: The most directly relevant head-impact data for a BEGINNER boxing programme like PPBF's entry lane. Note most impacts are low magnitude — but the count accumulates. This supports counting exposure rather than only reacting to visible events.
verified_title: Measurement of Head Kinematics Using Instrumented Mouthguards During Introductory Boxing Courses in U.S. Military Academy Cadets.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Acute symptoms after sparring do not track exposure straightforwardly
claim: In an exploratory observational cohort of 7 competitive boxers monitored with instrumented mouthguards and SCAT5 symptom scales before, immediately after and 48 hours after sparring, group analyses showed no difference in symptom scores pre versus post sparring (median change in total symptom severity score -1, p=0.85), symptoms were significantly LOWER at 48 hours than pre-sparring (p=0.02), and 4 of 16 sessions (25%) from three participants showed a symptom-severity increase greater than 5, with no strong relationship found between exposure metrics and symptom change.
effect_or_estimate: No group-level pre/post symptom change; 25% of sessions showed individual increase >5; no strong exposure-symptom relationship
limitations: Only 7 participants and 16 sessions — exploratory by the authors' own framing; symptom scales are subjective and may be under-reported by athletes wanting to keep sparring; the null result is as likely to reflect insufficient power as a true absence of relationship.
citation: Le Flao et al. (2026). Exploring the link between acute symptom changes and repetitive head impacts in boxing sparring. J Sci Med Sport.
ppbf_implication: CRITICAL for PPBF: symptom checklists after sparring have low signal at the group level but flagged individual sessions. Symptom reporting must be treated as a routing trigger to a qualified human, NEVER as a computed clearance or all-clear.
verified_title: Exploring the link between acute symptom changes and repetitive head impacts in boxing sparring.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Head-impact sensor data quality is a major limitation
claim: Comparing instrumented mouthguards, skin patches and headgear patches across 442 boxing sparring events each, predefined quality criteria were met in only 53%, 20% and 26% of events respectively; high-quality recordings were less frequent for impacts near the sensor (30% vs 61% for the mouthguard) and showed LOWER peak kinematics than low-quality recordings (p<0.001), and even among carefully selected simultaneous high-quality recordings there was little to no association between sensors.
effect_or_estimate: Mouthguard 53%, skin patch 20%, headgear patch 26% high-quality; little to no inter-sensor agreement
limitations: Single study; the quality criteria are the authors' own predefined objective criteria; does not address whether any sensor is 'correct' in absolute terms.
citation: Le Flao et al. (2024). Quality Issues in Kinematic Traces from Three Head Impact Sensors in Boxing: Prevalence, Effects, and Implications for Exposure Assessment. Ann Biomed Eng.
ppbf_implication: DECISIVE for the PPBF monitoring architecture: even instrumented sensors produce largely low-quality, non-agreeing data in boxing. This REMOVES the argument that PPBF is disadvantaged by using proxies. Proxies (counted rounds, intensity category, coach-observed impacts) are honest and cheap; sensors would be expensive and still unreliable.
verified_title: Quality Issues in Kinematic Traces from Three Head Impact Sensors in Boxing: Prevalence, Effects, and Implications for Exposure Assessment.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Head trauma in boxing — pooled neurological findings
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 35 included articles reported that boxers have a significantly elevated risk of sustaining a concussion compared with other combat sports (risk ratio 0.253 vs 0.065, p<0.001); among 631 amateur and professional boxers analysed, 147 (23.30%) had cavum septum pellucidum, and 125 of 411 (30.41%) presented with some form of brain atrophy.
effect_or_estimate: Concussion RR 0.253 vs 0.065 other combat sports; CSP 23.30%; brain atrophy 30.41%
limitations: The imaging findings pool studies across eras, exposure levels and imaging methods; cavum septum pellucidum occurs in non-boxers too, so a prevalence figure without a matched control group cannot establish attribution; heavily weighted toward professional and historically high-exposure boxers; publication bias likely toward positive imaging findings.
citation: Donnelly et al. (2023). A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Investigating Head Trauma in Boxing. Clin J Sport Med.
ppbf_implication: Report to guardians as: structural imaging abnormalities are found in a substantial minority of studied boxers, chiefly professionals with high cumulative exposure, and the amateur/community picture is far less established. Do not extrapolate professional imaging prevalence to youth non-contact or light-contact programmes.
verified_title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Investigating Head Trauma in Boxing.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: CTE neuropathology — established as a distinct pathology
claim: A consensus paper on neuropathological diagnostic criteria describes chronic traumatic encephalopathy pathology as unique, characterised by a pathognomonic lesion of perivascular neuronal phosphorylated tau accumulation with variable astrocytic aggregates at the depths of cortical sulci and a distinctive molecular structural configuration of p-tau fibrils unlike ageing, Alzheimer's disease or other tauopathies; CTE has been reported in boxers among many other contact-sport participants, and can currently be definitively diagnosed ONLY by postmortem neuropathological examination, with the corresponding clinical condition termed traumatic encephalopathy syndrome.
effect_or_estimate: Pathognomonic perivascular p-tau lesion at sulcal depths; postmortem diagnosis only
transfer_status: Boxing included; much of the case series is American football
limitations: Postmortem case series are subject to profound ascertainment bias — brains are donated because of symptoms — so prevalence cannot be estimated from them; the pathology-to-symptom relationship is not established; no in-life diagnosis exists.
citation: McKee et al. (2023). Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE): criteria for neuropathological diagnosis and relationship to repetitive head impacts. Acta Neuropathol.
ppbf_implication: PPBF position: the PATHOLOGY is established; the RISK MAGNITUDE for a given athlete and the dose-response are not. SHADOW must never estimate an individual's CTE risk. This is a physician and researcher domain.
verified_title: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE): criteria for neuropathological diagnosis and relationship to repetitive head impacts.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A published commentary argued that chronic traumatic encephalopathy does not rise to the level of a verifiable disease and remains at the level of case report, citing arguments that traumatic brain injury does not cause neurodegeneration, that protein deposits in the brain poorly predict behavioural symptoms, and that p-tau is not necessarily toxic or self-propagating.
effect_or_estimate: Argumentative, no new data
boxing_specific: Partly (references the boxing 'dementia pugilistica' debate directly)
limitations: A single-author opinion piece, not primary evidence; contested by the neuropathology consensus (A5-083); included here for honest representation of the state of debate, not as an endorsement.
citation: Randolph (2018). Chronic traumatic encephalopathy is not a real disease. Arch Clin Neuropsychol.
ppbf_implication: Include in the PPBF evidence ledger to demonstrate that SHADOW represents scientific disagreement rather than a single narrative. Neither minimise nor alarm: the honest statement is that pathology is established, causal dose-response in living amateurs is not.
verified_title: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy is not a real disease.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Professional Fighters Brain Health Study — methods
claim: The Professional Fighters Brain Health Study is a longitudinal study of active professional fighters (boxers and mixed martial artists), retired professional fighters and matched controls, designed over 5 years with anticipated enrolment of more than 400 boxers and MMA athletes, using annual 3-tesla MRI, computerised cognitive assessment, speech analysis, mood and impulsivity surveys and blood sampling, with a composite fight exposure index developed as a summary measure of cumulative traumatic exposure.
population: Active and retired professional fighters plus controls
effect_or_estimate: Composite fight exposure index as predictor
limitations: Professional fighters only — not amateur, not youth, not community participants; volunteer cohort; the composite exposure index is study-specific and not a validated general tool.
citation: Bernick et al. (2013). Professional fighters brain health study: rationale and methods. Am J Epidemiol.
ppbf_implication: The strongest available longitudinal design in combat sports. PPBF should track its outputs rather than attempt its own neuro-imaging research. Note explicitly: findings apply to PROFESSIONALS.
verified_title: Professional fighters brain health study: rationale and methods.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Sparring volume and brain volumes — an unexpected direction
claim: In 94 active professional MMA fighters from the Professional Fighters Brain Health Study, adjusted multivariable regression found that a HIGHER number of weekly sparring rounds during typical training was significantly associated with LARGER left (beta=13.5 microlitres/round, 95% CI 2.26-24.8) and right (beta=14.9, 95% CI 3.64-26.2) caudate volumes, with no significant association with thalamus, putamen, hippocampus or amygdala volumes; more weekly sparring rounds was NOT significantly associated with smaller volumes.
study_design: Cross-sectional analysis within a longitudinal cohort
effect_or_estimate: Caudate: +13.5 and +14.9 microlitres per weekly sparring round; null for other regions
boxing_specific: Partly (MMA, not boxing; sparring is the exposure)
limitations: CROSS-SECTIONAL and CORRELATIONAL — cannot establish direction of causation; MMA sparring differs from boxing sparring; self-reported sparring rounds; larger caudate volume is not established as beneficial or harmful; survivorship bias is plausible (fighters who tolerate high sparring keep fighting); confounded by motor-skill training effects the authors themselves raise.
citation: Esagoff et al. (2023). Sparring and the Brain: The Associations between Sparring and Regional Brain Volumes in Professional Mixed Martial Arts Fighters. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: IMPORTANT ANTI-ALARMISM ENTRY: the simple assumption 'more sparring equals visible brain atrophy' was not supported in this cohort. PPBF should still minimise unnecessary head-impact exposure on precautionary grounds, but must not cite atrophy as an established consequence of sparring volume in this population.
verified_title: Sparring and the Brain: The Associations between Sparring and Regional Brain Volumes in Professional Mixed Martial Arts Fighters.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Sparring rounds correlate with a blood biomarker
claim: In the Professional Fighters Brain Health Study with plasma samples from 471 participants, baseline neurofilament light differed across groups with active boxers having the highest levels, higher baseline NF-L correlated with lower baseline MRI regional volumes and lower cognitive scores, and the number of sparring rounds completed by active fighters correlated with NF-L (95% CI 0.0116-0.4053, p=0.0381) but not with tau.
population: Active and retired professional fighters and controls
sample_size: 471 plasma samples; 126 with multiple yearly samples
effect_or_estimate: Sparring rounds correlated with NF-L (95% CI 0.0116-0.4053, p=0.0381); active boxers highest baseline NF-L
limitations: Correlational; the confidence interval nearly touches zero and the p-value is marginal; NF-L is a non-specific marker of axonal injury with many causes; professional population only; blood biomarkers are not clinically actionable for individual athletes at present.
citation: Bernick et al. (2018). Longitudinal Performance of Plasma Neurofilament Light and Tau in Professional Fighters: The Professional Fighters Brain Health Study. J Neurotrauma.
ppbf_implication: Provides the strongest single justification for treating COUNTED SPARRING ROUNDS as the key modifiable exposure variable in PPBF. Sparring rounds is a number a coach can log for free — and it is the exposure variable that correlated with a biological marker.
verified_title: Longitudinal Performance of Plasma Neurofilament Light and Tau in Professional Fighters: The Professional Fighters Brain Health Study.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Traumatic encephalopathy syndrome and longitudinal decline in fighters
claim: In a secondary analysis of 130 active and retired professional fighters older than 34 from the Professional Athletes Brain Health Study, 52 (40%) were adjudicated as traumatic encephalopathy syndrome positive under 2021 clinical criteria; TES-positive athletes were older with significantly lower education, and showed statistically significant between-group differences and interactions across all MRI volumetric measurements, with greater increases in lateral and inferior lateral ventricles and a decrease in the hippocampus.
effect_or_estimate: 40% TES+; significant volumetric divergence including ventricular enlargement and hippocampal decrease
limitations: TES-positive athletes were older and less educated, both established confounders for cognitive and volumetric outcomes; TES criteria are clinical and evolving; selected older professional cohort; observational.
citation: Conway Kleven et al. (2023). Longitudinal Changes in Regional Brain Volumes and Cognition of Professional Fighters With Traumatic Encephalopathy Syndrome. Neurology.
ppbf_implication: Establishes that measurable divergence exists in older professionals with clinical syndrome. Does NOT establish risk for amateur or youth participants. PPBF's amateur/community messaging must not import this finding.
verified_title: Longitudinal Changes in Regional Brain Volumes and Cognition of Professional Fighters With Traumatic Encephalopathy Syndrome.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Professional boxing exposure has fallen dramatically over a century
claim: A review of published studies and analysis of active professional boxer data found that since the 1930s the average duration of a professional boxer's career dropped from 19 years to 5 years and the mean number of career bouts fell from 336 to 13, despite no significant decline in participation rates from 1931 to 2002.
effect_or_estimate: Career length 19 y to 5 y; career bouts 336 to 13
limitations: The inference that CTBI incidence will therefore diminish is a projection, not an observed outcome; bout count omits sparring exposure, which may not have fallen proportionately; two-country data.
citation: Clausen et al. (2005). The risk of chronic traumatic brain injury in professional boxing: change in exposure variables over the past century. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Crucial context for honest guardian communication: the historical 'punch-drunk' literature reflects exposure levels (300+ bouts, 19-year careers) that no contemporary amateur or community participant approaches. Anchoring modern risk to that literature overstates it.
verified_title: The risk of chronic traumatic brain injury in professional boxing: change in exposure variables over the past century.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Neurodegenerative mortality in repetitive-head-impact sports — preliminary
claim: A systematic review with meta-analysis found six moderate- to high-quality retrospective studies including 41,699 athletes in contact sports (boxing, basketball, ice hockey, American football and soccer), of which three studies comprising 37,065 male professional soccer players could be meta-analysed, reporting no differences in risk of all-cause (p=0.138), cardiovascular (p=0.085) or cancer mortality.
sample_size: 6 studies, 41,699 athletes; 3 studies meta-analysed (37,065 soccer players)
effect_or_estimate: No difference in all-cause, cardiovascular or cancer mortality in the meta-analysable subset
boxing_specific: Partly (boxing included in the review but the meta-analysis was soccer)
transfer_status: Other-sport transfer for the pooled estimate
limitations: The pooled analysis is soccer players, NOT boxers — a critical distinction usually lost in citation; retrospective designs; described by the authors as preliminary findings; mortality is a blunt outcome that misses morbidity.
citation: Morales et al. (2021). Mortality Risk from Neurodegenerative Disease in Sports Associated with Repetitive Head Impacts: Preliminary Findings from a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Do NOT cite this as evidence about boxing mortality. It is included in the PPBF ledger specifically as an example of a finding that is routinely mis-transferred across sports.
verified_title: Mortality Risk from Neurodegenerative Disease in Sports Associated with Repetitive Head Impacts: Preliminary Findings from a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A review examined the consequences of repetitive subconcussive head impacts in sport, covering brain changes and associated measurement approaches.
effect_or_estimate: Mechanistic synthesis; no pooled estimate
limitations: Narrative review; the subconcussive literature uses heterogeneous exposure metrics and short-term outcome measures whose clinical meaning is unestablished.
citation: Di Virgilio et al. (2019). Understanding the Consequences of Repetitive Subconcussive Head Impacts in Sport: Brain Changes and Dampened Motor Control Are Seen After Boxing Practice. Front Hum Neurosci.
ppbf_implication: Background support for the precautionary principle in PPBF sparring policy: minimise unnecessary head contact even in the absence of diagnosed concussion, without claiming a quantified harm.
verified_title: Understanding the Consequences of Repetitive Subconcussive Head Impacts in Sport: Brain Changes and Dampened Motor Control Are Seen After Boxing Practice.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A review examined the use of biofluid markers to evaluate the consequences of sport-related subconcussive head impact exposure.
effect_or_estimate: Marker responses reviewed; no clinical decision threshold established
limitations: Biofluid markers are research tools with no established clinical decision threshold for individual athletes; assays and timing vary; not available or appropriate in a community gym.
citation: Lember et al. (2024). The Use of Biofluid Markers to Evaluate the Consequences of Sport-Related Subconcussive Head Impact Exposure: A Scoping Review. Sports Med Open.
ppbf_implication: Out of scope for PPBF operations. Recorded so the research backlog reflects that biomarker monitoring is not a currently deployable option.
verified_title: The Use of Biofluid Markers to Evaluate the Consequences of Sport-Related Subconcussive Head Impact Exposure: A Scoping Review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: The 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport (Amsterdam, October 2022) consensus statement, informed by 10 systematic reviews conducted over three and a half years, produced revised tools including the Concussion Recognition Tool 6 and Sport Concussion Assessment Tool 6 (and child versions) plus the new Sport Concussion Office Assessment Tool 6, and integrated a focus on para athletes, the athlete's perspective, concussion-specific medical ethics, athlete retirement and potential long-term effects including neurodegenerative disease.
sex: Male and female, including para athletes
study_design: International consensus statement informed by 10 systematic reviews
effect_or_estimate: Tools: CRT6, SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, Child SCOAT6
limitations: Consensus process reflects expert interpretation; the Concussion in Sport Group process has itself attracted criticism regarding scope and conflicts; the tools are screening and assessment aids for appropriately trained users, not diagnostic instruments for lay coaches.
citation: Patricios et al. (2023). Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport-Amsterdam, October 2022. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: AUTHORITY ANCHOR. PPBF adopts CRT6 as the RECOGNITION tool coaches may use to remove an athlete and escalate. SCAT6/SCOAT6 are for trained clinicians. SHADOW must never compute, score or interpret these instruments toward a clearance decision.
verified_title: Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport-Amsterdam, October 2022.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis registered on PROSPERO evaluated prevention strategies, unintended consequences and modifiable risk factors for sport-related concussion and head impacts, screening eight databases and including 192 of 220 eligible studies based on SIGN methodological quality ratings of high or acceptable.
effect_or_estimate: Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors evaluated across sports
limitations: Boxing-specific prevention evidence within this review is limited; the strongest prevention evidence in sport generally relates to rule changes and contact restriction, which are governing-body decisions rather than gym-level programming.
citation: Eliason et al. (2023). Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors for sport-related concussions and head impacts: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Supports PPBF prioritising EXPOSURE REDUCTION (contact policy, sparring rules) over equipment or strength interventions as the primary head-impact mitigation lever.
