verified_title: Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors for sport-related concussions and head impacts: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Headguards reduce lacerations, not concussion — position statement
claim: The Association of Ringside Physicians position statement concludes that headguards are highly effective in reducing facial lacerations in amateur boxers and appropriate where avoidance of laceration or auricular injury matters, but explicitly states that headguards should NOT be relied upon to reduce the risk of concussion or other traumatic brain injury, have not been shown to prevent these injuries in combat sports, and that although biomechanical studies suggest reduced linear and rotational cranial acceleration, changes in athlete behaviour toward more risk-taking when wearing headguards may offset any risk reduction.
effect_or_estimate: Effective for lacerations; NOT shown to prevent concussion; behavioural compensation flagged
limitations: Position statement rather than pooled data; the authors themselves call for further research; the behavioural-compensation mechanism is hypothesised rather than demonstrated in combat sports.
citation: deWeber et al. (2023). Headguard use in combat sports: position statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians. Phys Sportsmed.
ppbf_implication: PPBF POLICY-CRITICAL: headguards may be required for laceration protection in sparring, but must never be described to athletes, coaches or guardians as concussion protection. Write this into the sparring policy text verbatim in meaning.
verified_title: Headguard use in combat sports: position statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Headguard biomechanics — laboratory reduction in accelerations
claim: In a laboratory linear-impactor study using an instrumented Hybrid III head and neck system with a semirigid fist-and-glove interface at impact speeds of 4.1-8.3 m/s, peak contact forces were 1.9-5.9 kN; in 8.3 m/s fist-glove impacts mean peak resultant headform acceleration was approximately 130 g bare versus approximately 85 g in forehead impacts with an AIBA-approved headguard, and in 6.85 m/s bare impacts mean peak resultant angular accelerations of 5200-5600 rad/s2 were almost halved by the headguard.
effect_or_estimate: Bare ~130 g vs headguard ~85 g at 8.3 m/s; angular acceleration ~5200-5600 rad/s2 roughly halved
limitations: LABORATORY HEADFORM, NOT HUMANS — reduced headform acceleration has not translated into demonstrated concussion reduction in athletes (see A5-095); a rigid impactor differs from a live punch; single headguard model; no behavioural compensation is modelled in a laboratory.
citation: McIntosh et al. (2015). Boxing headguard performance in punch machine tests. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Textbook case of lab evidence not equalling field outcome. PPBF's evidence engine should carry both this and A5-095 linked, so SHADOW never surfaces the biomechanics finding alone as proof of protection.
verified_title: Boxing headguard performance in punch machine tests.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A Current Opinion article argued that the International Boxing Association's prohibition of headguards has generated controversy, demonstrated headguard effectiveness against cuts and lacerations, and stated there is insufficient evidence supporting headguard bans, while highlighting a gap in collaboration and communication between the IBA and smaller representative bodies for future policy reform.
effect_or_estimate: Argues insufficient evidence for headguard bans
limitations: An opinion article, not a systematic review; policy differs by governing body and age category — headguard requirements for junior and youth categories differ from elite senior rules in many jurisdictions.
citation: Le et al. (2025). The Case for Protective Headguards in Amateur Boxing and Implications for International Policy on Headguard Bans. Sports Med Open.
ppbf_implication: PPBF must store headguard policy as a per-jurisdiction, per-age-category RULE FIELD sourced from the applicable governing body, not as a global setting. Never present one nation's or one body's rule as universal.
verified_title: The Case for Protective Headguards in Amateur Boxing and Implications for International Policy on Headguard Bans.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Neck strength and concussion risk — inconclusive systematic review
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis identified five eligible articles and, across five planes of motion (flexion, extension, right and left flexion, and total), found NO statistically significant differences in neck strength between concussed and non-concussed athletes; some studies reported a positive trend toward concussion risk reduction with greater neck strength, and the authors concluded the evidence remains inconclusive and that further large randomised controlled trials are needed before neck strength can be recommended as a preventive strategy.
effect_or_estimate: No statistically significant differences across five planes of motion
transfer_status: Other-sport transfer (no boxing-specific concussion outcome data)
limitations: Only 5 eligible studies; heterogeneous neck-strength measurement methods; no boxing data; absence of evidence given small numbers is not evidence of absence.
citation: Postula et al. (2026). Evaluation of Neck Strength and Concussion Risk: A Systematic Review. Curr Sports Med Rep.
ppbf_implication: DEFINITIVE PPBF POSITION on the popular neck-strength claim: the concussion-prevention benefit is NOT established. Neck training may be programmed for other reasons, but PPBF must not market or log it as concussion prevention.
verified_title: Evaluation of Neck Strength and Concussion Risk: A Systematic Review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Neck strength — the most-cited supportive study
claim: In a study collecting preseason anthropometric measurements from 6704 high school athletes in boys' and girls' soccer, basketball and lacrosse across 51 high schools in 25 states, smaller mean neck circumference, smaller mean neck-to-head circumference ratio and weaker mean overall neck strength were significantly associated with concussion incidence.
study_design: Prospective observational pilot with tool validation
effect_or_estimate: Smaller neck circumference, smaller neck:head ratio and weaker neck strength associated with concussion
transfer_status: Other-sport transfer (soccer, basketball, lacrosse — NOT boxing)
limitations: CORRELATION NOT CAUSATION — observational; described by the authors as a pilot study; no boxing or combat-sport athletes; neck strength is confounded with body size, sport, sex and playing experience; strengthening the neck was not tested as an intervention.
citation: Collins et al. (2014). Neck strength: a protective factor reducing risk for concussion in high school sports. J Prim Prev.
ppbf_implication: This is the study most often cited to justify neck training for concussion prevention. PPBF must represent it accurately: an observational association in non-combat high school sports, not an intervention trial, and contradicted by the pooled analysis in A5-098.
verified_title: Neck strength: a protective factor reducing risk for concussion in high school sports.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Neck strengthening interventions — no injury-outcome evidence
claim: A systematic review searching four databases and screening 2462 articles found only THREE papers eligible for inclusion on neck strengthening and injury outcomes in adult collision-sport athletes; all reported only male participants (two rugby union, one American football), two found significant isometric neck strength improvement following intervention, and NONE reported any impact of neck strengthening exercises on cervical spine injuries, leading the authors to conclude there is currently a lack of evidence supporting neck strengthening interventions for reducing impact injury risk.
effect_or_estimate: 2 of 3 improved isometric neck strength; ZERO reported an injury-outcome effect
limitations: Only three eligible studies from 2462 screened — an extremely thin base; male only; no combat-sport data; adults only.
citation: Daly et al. (2021). A Systematic Review of Strength and Conditioning Protocols for Improving Neck Strength and Reducing Concussion Incidence and Impact Injury Risk in Collision Sports; Is There Evidence?. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol.
ppbf_implication: Second independent confirmation that neck training's INJURY-PREVENTION claim is unsupported. Neck training CAN increase neck strength; that is the only defensible claim PPBF may make.
verified_title: A Systematic Review of Strength and Conditioning Protocols for Improving Neck Strength and Reducing Concussion Incidence and Impact Injury Risk in Collision Sports; Is There Evidence?

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Neck training consensus — expert practice despite thin evidence
claim: A two-part systematic review and expert Delphi consensus study searched four databases to September 2024 on neck training interventions in sport, applying PRISMA, a modified Downs and Black quality assessment and GRADE, and then established expert consensus on best practices for implementing neck training aimed at reducing head acceleration events in collision, combat and motor sport.
population: Collision, combat and motor sport athletes
study_design: Systematic review plus expert Delphi consensus
effect_or_estimate: Consensus implementation guidance; GRADE-assessed underlying evidence
limitations: Delphi consensus reflects expert opinion where trial evidence is insufficient; the target outcome is head acceleration events, not concussion incidence; GRADE assessment of the underlying literature indicates limited certainty.
citation: Fownes-Walpole et al. (2025). Combining evidence and practice to optimise neck training aimed at reducing head acceleration events in sport: a systematic review and Delphi-consensus study. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: The most defensible position PPBF can take: if neck training is included, follow published consensus implementation practice, target head ACCELERATION as the hypothesised mechanism, and state that concussion reduction is unproven.
verified_title: Combining evidence and practice to optimise neck training aimed at reducing head acceleration events in sport: a systematic review and Delphi-consensus study.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Neck strength and head acceleration in soccer heading
claim: A systematic review of five cross-sectional studies found that higher neck strength is associated with lower head acceleration during purposeful heading in soccer (p<0.05, r<-0.5), and concluded that further research is needed to determine the most effective method of strengthening the neck musculature.
effect_or_estimate: Higher neck strength associated with lower head acceleration (p<0.05, r<-0.5)
transfer_status: Other-sport transfer (soccer heading, an ANTICIPATED self-initiated impact)
limitations: Cross-sectional only; soccer heading is a self-initiated, anticipated impact with neck pre-activation, which is mechanically very different from an unanticipated punch — this limits transfer to boxing severely.
citation: Peek et al. (2019). Higher neck strength is associated with lower head acceleration during purposeful heading in soccer: A systematic review. J Sci Med Sport.
ppbf_implication: The mechanism (stronger neck, lower head acceleration) has support ONLY in anticipated impacts. A boxer is often struck unanticipated. Flag this transfer limitation explicitly wherever PPBF discusses neck training.
verified_title: Higher neck strength is associated with lower head acceleration during purposeful heading in soccer: A systematic review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Neck strength and head impacts in football — opposite direction
claim: In 49 high school and collegiate American football players with preseason cervical testing and season-long Head Impact Telemetry System data, linemen with stronger lateral flexors and greater composite cervical strength had about 1.75 times INCREASED odds of sustaining moderate rather than mild linear head impacts compared with weaker linemen.
population: High school and collegiate American football players
effect_or_estimate: Stronger linemen: ~1.75x increased odds of moderate vs mild impacts
limitations: Observational; helmet-based sensors have known accuracy limitations; a plausible behavioural explanation is that stronger players engage more aggressively; football linemen contact is unlike boxing.
citation: Schmidt et al. (2014). The influence of cervical muscle characteristics on head impact biomechanics in football. Am J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Included deliberately: a finding in the OPPOSITE direction to the popular claim. PPBF's evidence ledger must retain disconfirming results so SHADOW's synthesis is not one-sided.
verified_title: The influence of cervical muscle characteristics on head impact biomechanics in football.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Cervical strength and head impacts in youth ice hockey — null
claim: In 37 youth ice hockey players (mean age 15.0 y) wearing accelerometer-instrumented helmets across a full season with preseason isometric cervical strength measured for multiple muscle groups and categorised into tertiles, NO differences were observed in linear or rotational head acceleration across strength groups for anterior neck flexors, anterolateral neck flexors, cervical rotators or posterolateral extensors.
effect_or_estimate: Null across all measured muscle groups (all p>0.05 for linear; rotational p=0.060-0.579)
limitations: Small n=37; helmet sensor limitations; youth population with maturational variation in strength; single season.
citation: Mihalik et al. (2011). Does cervical muscle strength in youth ice hockey players affect head impact biomechanics?. Clin J Sport Med.
ppbf_implication: Third independent null/contrary result in the neck-strength question, and in a YOUTH population directly relevant to PPBF's age range.
verified_title: Does cervical muscle strength in youth ice hockey players affect head impact biomechanics?

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Neck strength not protective for head impact exposure in a combat-training population
claim: In a prospective observational study of 28 civilian law enforcement cadets (9 female) undergoing occupational combat training with isometric neck strength measured by handheld dynamometer and head acceleration events over 5 g recorded by instrumented mouthguards, principal component analysis and adjusted regression demonstrated NO significant effect of neck characteristics on head acceleration events per exposure, median peak linear acceleration or median peak rotational velocity when controlling for sex.
population: Law enforcement cadets in combat training
study_design: Prospective observational study with instrumented mouthguards
effect_or_estimate: No significant effect of neck strength or girth on HAE quantity or magnitude
limitations: Small n=28; a training rather than competitive context; single cohort; mouthguard sensor limitations apply.
citation: Smith et al. (2025). Neck Strength Is Not a Protective Factor for Lower Repetitive Head Impact Exposure in Law Enforcement Cadets. Mil Med.
ppbf_implication: The closest population to PPBF's beginner boxing lane (novices in supervised combat training, mixed sex) and the result is NULL. Strongest single reason PPBF should not sell neck training as head-impact mitigation.
verified_title: Neck Strength Is Not a Protective Factor for Lower Repetitive Head Impact Exposure in Law Enforcement Cadets.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Neck strength review — performance and injury
claim: A review of neck muscular strength, training, performance and sport injury risk found differences in neck strength between playing positions, sexes and ages, that neck strength training programmes were generally effective for both untrained and trained participants using dynamic or isometric actions with various resistance devices, with a wide range of reported strength increases and the smallest gains from lower-intensity or lower-frequency programmes, limited evidence associating greater isometric strength or dynamic training with better head stabilisation during low-level force application, and a retrospective analysis of professional rugby union players indicating isometric training reduced match-related cervical spine injuries.
effect_or_estimate: Neck training reliably increases neck strength; head-stabilisation evidence limited to low-level force
limitations: Narrative review; the cervical-spine injury finding is from a RETROSPECTIVE analysis in rugby, not a trial; head stabilisation evidence applies to LOW-LEVEL force application, not punch-magnitude impacts.
citation: Hrysomallis (2016). Neck Muscular Strength, Training, Performance and Sport Injury Risk: A Review. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Defensible PPBF claim set: neck training increases neck strength (well supported); may aid head stabilisation at low force (limited); concussion prevention (NOT supported). Encode these three claims separately with different confidence levels.
verified_title: Neck Muscular Strength, Training, Performance and Sport Injury Risk: A Review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Maturity offset estimation — the original equations
claim: Sex-specific multiple regression equations predicting years from peak height velocity from height, sitting height, leg length and chronological age were developed in 152 Canadian children aged 8-16 and cross-validated in Canadian and Flemish samples, with coefficients of determination of 0.92 (boys) and 0.91 (girls) and standard errors of estimate of 0.49 and 0.50 years.
effect_or_estimate: R2 0.92 (boys) / 0.91 (girls); SEE 0.49 / 0.50 years
limitations: Developed in non-athlete Canadian/Flemish samples decades ago; accuracy degrades away from the time of peak height velocity and in early/late maturers; requires a sitting-height measurement many gyms do not take accurately.
citation: Mirwald et al. (2002). An assessment of maturity from anthropometric measurements. Med Sci Sports Exerc.
ppbf_implication: PPBF may estimate maturity offset non-invasively, but must display the estimation error and never treat a predicted age at PHV as a fact. Store as an estimate with uncertainty, per the SHADOW confidence model.
verified_title: An assessment of maturity from anthropometric measurements.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A validation of modified maturity offset prediction equations in independent longitudinal samples (193 boys aged 8-18, 198 girls aged 8-16) from the Wroclaw Growth Study found that predicted ages at peak height velocity approximated observed ages only in AVERAGE-maturing boys NEAR the time of peak height velocity, with a corresponding narrow window in girls, and noted that validation studies of the original equations had indicated major limitations.
effect_or_estimate: Accurate only for average maturers near PHV
limitations: The equations are systematically biased for early and late maturers — precisely the athletes for whom maturity information matters most; non-athlete samples.
citation: Kozieł et al. (2018). Modified Maturity Offset Prediction Equations: Validation in Independent Longitudinal Samples of Boys and Girls. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: HARD CONSTRAINT: PPBF must NOT use predicted maturity offset to group, match or restrict individual youth athletes, because the method is least accurate for the outliers. Use it only as a squad-level descriptive context, with the limitation surfaced.
verified_title: Modified Maturity Offset Prediction Equations: Validation in Independent Longitudinal Samples of Boys and Girls.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Biological maturation assessment in youth athletes
claim: A review of methods for assessing maturity status (skeletal age, secondary sex characteristics) and estimating timing (age at peak height velocity, age at menarche) plus two non-invasive anthropometric methods noted that the latter need further validation with athletes, and described how selection and exclusion in many sports follows a maturity-related gradient largely during puberty and the growth spurt.
effect_or_estimate: Maturity-related selection gradient described; anthropometric methods need athlete validation
limitations: Skeletal age requires radiographic imaging, which is inappropriate for routine screening; secondary sex characteristic assessment raises safeguarding concerns and should not be performed by coaches.
citation: Malina et al. (2015). Biological maturation of youth athletes: assessment and implications. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: SAFEGUARDING BOUNDARY: PPBF must NOT collect pubertal-stage or secondary-sex-characteristic data. Restrict to height, sitting height and weight, collected by trained staff under a documented youth-measurement protocol with guardian consent.
verified_title: Biological maturation of youth athletes: assessment and implications.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Growth, maturation and injury in youth athletes
claim: A scoping review of 30 eligible studies found that injury incidence and burden generally increased with maturity status, that growth-related injuries peaked during the adolescent growth spurt, that more rapid growth in stature and of the lower limbs was associated with greater injury incidence and burden, and that while maturity TIMING did not show a clear or consistent association with injury it may contribute to risk and burden through variation in maturity status.
effect_or_estimate: Injury burden rises with maturity status; growth-related injuries peak at the growth spurt; rapid growth associated with higher burden
transfer_status: Other-sport transfer to youth (no boxing-specific data located)
limitations: The authors note significant heterogeneity across samples and in how growth, maturation and injury were operationalised and measured; elite-pathway athletes only; predominantly male; no boxing data.
citation: Parry et al. (2024). Associations between growth, maturation and injury in youth athletes engaged in elite pathways: a scoping review. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: PPBF should track growth RATE (change in stature over time) as a low-cost monitoring variable and reduce high-impact loading during rapid growth phases — as a coach-reviewed adjustment, not an automated restriction.
verified_title: Associations between growth, maturation and injury in youth athletes engaged in elite pathways: a scoping review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A review of maturity-associated considerations for training load, injury risk and physical performance in youth soccer described how maturity-related changes in anthropometric and physical fitness characteristics are diverse among individuals particularly around peak height velocity, that players are at increased risk of overuse or growth-related injury during this time, and that implementing training interventions is consequently challenging.
effect_or_estimate: Descriptive; individual variability emphasised
limitations: Youth soccer, not boxing; the practical estimation tools inherit the accuracy limits of maturity-offset prediction (A5-108); male-focused.
citation: Towlson et al. (2020). Maturity-associated considerations for training load, injury risk, and physical performance in youth soccer: One size does not fit all. J Sport Health Sci.
ppbf_implication: Supports PPBF's principle of individualising youth load around growth rather than chronological age — with the explicit caveat that maturity estimation is imprecise.
verified_title: Maturity-associated considerations for training load, injury risk, and physical performance in youth soccer: One size does not fit all.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: The National Strength and Conditioning Association position statement on long-term athletic development argues that children and adolescents should engage in appropriately prescribed exercise programmes promoting physical development to prevent injury and enhance lifelong fitness behaviours, and that a structured, logical and evidence-based approach to developing athleticism is needed irrespective of whether the child participates in organised sport.
effect_or_estimate: Principles and recommendations
limitations: Position statements reflect expert consensus rather than pooled trial data; many long-term athletic development models remain largely untested longitudinally.
citation: Lloyd et al. (2016). National Strength and Conditioning Association Position Statement on Long-Term Athletic Development. J Strength Cond Res.
ppbf_implication: Provides the professional-body anchor for PPBF's youth development pathway. Cite for PRINCIPLES (broad athletic development, appropriate prescription) not for specific volumes.
verified_title: National Strength and Conditioning Association Position Statement on Long-Term Athletic Development.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Youth resistance training is safe when appropriately supervised
claim: The National Strength and Conditioning Association's updated position statement on youth resistance training, and a separate American Academy of Pediatrics clinical report on resistance training for children and adolescents, support appropriately designed and competently supervised resistance training for young people.
effect_or_estimate: Supported with supervision and appropriate design
limitations: Safety conclusions are conditional on competent supervision and appropriate progression — conditions a volunteer-staffed community gym must actively meet, not assume.
citation: Faigenbaum et al. (2009). Youth resistance training: updated position statement paper from the national strength and conditioning association. J Strength Cond Res.
ppbf_implication: Removes the 'weights stunt growth' myth from PPBF doctrine. BUT the supervision condition is a real operational requirement: PPBF must document coach qualification for youth resistance sessions.
verified_title: Youth resistance training: updated position statement paper from the national strength and conditioning association.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Early sport specialisation and overuse risk
claim: A clinical review defined sports specialisation as year-round training exceeding 8 months per year, choosing a single main sport and/or quitting other sports, and reported that specialised training in young athletes carries risks of injury and burnout with the degree of specialisation positively correlated with increased serious overuse injury risk; risk factors identified included year-round single-sport training, more competition, decreased age-appropriate play and individual sports requiring early technical skill development.
effect_or_estimate: Degree of specialisation positively correlated with serious overuse injury risk
limitations: Level 4 non-systematic review; the underlying evidence is largely cross-sectional and correlational; a separate review notes there is a limited number of comprehensive long-term outcome studies linking early specialisation to injury or burnout.
citation: Myer et al. (2015). Sport Specialization, Part I: Does Early Sports Specialization Increase Negative Outcomes and Reduce the Opportunity for Success in Young Athletes?. Sports Health.
ppbf_implication: Boxing is an individual sport requiring early technical skill — one of the listed risk factors. PPBF should actively encourage multi-sport participation in its youth lane and log other-sport participation as a load context field.
verified_title: Sport Specialization, Part I: Does Early Sports Specialization Increase Negative Outcomes and Reduce the Opportunity for Success in Young Athletes?

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A review of early sport specialisation noted there is no universally agreed terminology or definition for early sport specialisation, that there is a limited number of comprehensive long-term outcome studies identifying a potential link between early specialisation and musculoskeletal injury or burnout, and that methodologically sound prospective research is needed.
effect_or_estimate: Definitional inconsistency; limited long-term outcome evidence
limitations: Highlights that the early-specialisation literature suffers from definitional inconsistency, making pooled conclusions unreliable.
citation: Agel et al. (2021). Early Sport Specialization. J Bone Joint Surg Am.
ppbf_implication: Balances A5-114. PPBF's position should be 'encourage varied movement' framed as a development principle, not 'specialisation causes injury' framed as established fact.
verified_title: Early Sport Specialization.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Overuse injury, overtraining and burnout in young athletes
claim: An American Academy of Pediatrics clinical report described how imbalances of training load and recovery can produce overuse injuries from repetitive stress without sufficient recovery, that extended periods of training load exceeding recovery can produce systemic consequences including overtraining syndrome with decreased performance, increased injury and illness risk and endocrine, neurologic, cardiovascular and psychological derangement, and that burnout — physical or mental exhaustion with a reduced sense of accomplishment leading to devaluation of sport — is a primary reason for attrition in youth sports.
effect_or_estimate: Descriptive clinical framework
limitations: Clinical report reflecting professional consensus; no quantified load thresholds are supplied because none are validated for youth.
citation: Brenner et al. (2024). Overuse Injuries, Overtraining, and Burnout in Young Athletes. Pediatrics.
ppbf_implication: Authoritative basis for PPBF logging BURNOUT/attrition signals (engagement, enjoyment, attendance drop) alongside physical load in the youth lane. Attrition is a program outcome PPBF's grant reporting already needs.
verified_title: Overuse Injuries, Overtraining, and Burnout in Young Athletes.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Training load and injury in middle-school athletes
claim: A study examined the relationship between training load and injury among middle-school-aged athletes.
effect_or_estimate: Load-injury association examined in a young cohort
limitations: Observational; small and specific population; load measurement in young athletes is less validated than in adults.
citation: Albrecht et al. (2020). Training Load and Injury Among Middle School-Aged Athletes. J Athl Train.
ppbf_implication: One of very few load-injury datasets in the youngest athlete band PPBF serves. Cite to justify collecting load data in youth while acknowledging the evidence base is thin.
verified_title: Training Load and Injury Among Middle School-Aged Athletes.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Menstrual cycle and performance — trivial and low-quality evidence
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis using multilevel Bayesian models pooled pairwise effect sizes comparing exercise performance in the early follicular phase against all other menstrual cycle phases in eumenorrheic women, with the authors noting that data are conflicting and that no consensus exists on whether exercise performance is affected by cycle phase.
effect_or_estimate: Conflicting data; no consensus on cycle-phase effect
limitations: The underlying study quality is the central problem — see A5-119; small samples; poor cycle-phase verification in most primary studies; no boxing data.
citation: McNulty et al. (2020). The Effects of Menstrual Cycle Phase on Exercise Performance in Eumenorrheic Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: PPBF must NOT build cycle-phase-based training prescriptions. The evidence does not support them. Log cycle information only if the athlete chooses to, under strict privacy tiering, and use it for athlete-led self-management.
verified_title: The Effects of Menstrual Cycle Phase on Exercise Performance in Eumenorrheic Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Menstrual cycle research methodology is weak
claim: A review of menstrual cycle verification methods in recent exercise-science literature (2008-2018) found that only 44% of the selected studies measured actual concentrations of oestrogen and progesterone, that the likely inclusion of participants with anovulatory or luteal-phase-deficient cycles combined with small participant numbers has affected results, and recommended a combination of three verification methods for future research.
effect_or_estimate: Only 44% of studies measured hormone concentrations
limitations: Documents a methodological problem rather than resolving the underlying physiological question.
citation: Janse DE Jonge et al. (2019). Methodological Recommendations for Menstrual Cycle Research in Sports and Exercise. Med Sci Sports Exerc.
ppbf_implication: THE key citation for PPBF's honest statement that menstrual cycle evidence quality is LOW. Any SHADOW output touching cycle phase must carry this caveat.
verified_title: Methodological Recommendations for Menstrual Cycle Research in Sports and Exercise.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Menstrual cycle disorders and symptoms are prevalent
claim: A systematic review examined the prevalence of menstrual cycle disorders and cycle-related symptoms — including amenorrhoea, anovulation, dysmenorrhoea, heavy menstrual bleeding, luteal phase deficiency, oligomenorrhoea and premenstrual syndrome — among female athletes not using hormonal contraceptives, and evaluated the assessment methods used to identify them.
population: Female athletes not using hormonal contraceptives
effect_or_estimate: Prevalence of a range of MC disorders and symptoms
limitations: Definitions of each disorder varied across studies; self-reported symptoms; no combat-sport-specific data; excludes hormonal contraceptive users, a large group.
citation: Taim et al. (2023). The Prevalence of Menstrual Cycle Disorders and Menstrual Cycle-Related Symptoms in Female Athletes: A Systematic Literature Review. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Distinguishes SYMPTOM BURDEN (real and prevalent, worth an athlete-initiated conversation) from PERFORMANCE PHASE EFFECTS (unsupported). PPBF should support the former and avoid claiming the latter. Amenorrhoea is a medical matter for a clinician.
verified_title: The Prevalence of Menstrual Cycle Disorders and Menstrual Cycle-Related Symptoms in Female Athletes: A Systematic Literature Review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of oral contraceptive effects on exercise performance compared performance in OCP users against naturally menstruating women (phase-matched two ways) and compared OCP consumption against withdrawal phases.
population: Women using and not using oral contraceptives
effect_or_estimate: Between- and within-group comparisons performed
limitations: OCP formulations vary widely and are frequently not reported; study quality assessed but heterogeneous; no combat-sport data.
citation: Elliott-Sale et al. (2020). The Effects of Oral Contraceptives on Exercise Performance in Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: PPBF must not make contraceptive-status-based training recommendations. Contraceptive use is sensitive health data requiring the highest privacy tier and is not needed for coaching decisions.
verified_title: The Effects of Oral Contraceptives on Exercise Performance in Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of the effect of hormonal contraceptive use on skeletal muscle hypertrophy, power and strength adaptations to resistance exercise training identified only 8 eligible articles (54 effects, 325 participants) from 4669 screened.
effect_or_estimate: Very small eligible evidence base
limitations: Only 8 studies from 4669 screened — an extremely thin base; heterogeneous contraceptive formulations; no combat-sport data.
citation: Nolan et al. (2023). The Effect of Hormonal Contraceptive Use on Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy, Power and Strength Adaptations to Resistance Exercise Training: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-analysis. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Reinforces that PPBF should program resistance training for female boxers on the same principles as male boxers, because no evidence supports differentiating by contraceptive status.
verified_title: The Effect of Hormonal Contraceptive Use on Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy, Power and Strength Adaptations to Resistance Exercise Training: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-analysis.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: The 2023 International Olympic Committee consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport updated the 2018 statement following more than 170 original research publications, described emerging data on low carbohydrate availability and the interplay between mental health and REDs, presented updated Health and Performance Conceptual Models and a novel Physiological Model, and outlined guidelines for safe and effective body composition assessment to help prevent REDs.
effect_or_estimate: Conceptual and physiological models; body composition assessment guidance
boxing_specific: No (all sports; highly relevant to weight-category sports)
transfer_status: Cross-sport consensus, high relevance to boxing
limitations: Consensus level; energy availability is difficult to measure accurately in the field, which the consensus itself acknowledges; diagnosis requires clinical assessment.
citation: Mountjoy et al. (2023). 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: CRITICAL for a weight-category sport with youth participants. PPBF must have a RED-S awareness and referral pathway. SHADOW may surface risk-context flags (rapid weight change, missed sessions, reported fatigue) and route to a clinician. It must NEVER diagnose REDs or issue nutrition prescriptions.
verified_title: 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs).

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A critical review challenged the REDs construct, noting that the IOC 2023 consensus itself concludes energy availability is impossible to measure accurately enough in the field, that consequently the only apparent way to diagnose an athlete with REDs is by symptom presentation and risk factors, that the symptoms are rather generic and the causes likely multifactorial, and that it is very difficult to isolate the effects of low energy availability from other potential causes of the same symptoms.
effect_or_estimate: Argues the diagnostic construct is not field-measurable
limitations: A critique rather than new data; does not dispute that low energy availability causes harm, only the diagnostic construct and its application.
citation: Jeukendrup et al. (2024). Does Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Syndrome Exist?. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Reinforces the operational rule: PPBF flags RISK CONTEXT and refers. It does not diagnose. The diagnostic uncertainty is exactly why the decision belongs to a clinician.
verified_title: Does Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Syndrome Exist?

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Women are under-represented in exercise science
claim: An analysis of 972 original research articles from three journals in 1991 and 2021 found that although the average percentage of women per article as participants increased from 21.9% to 36.3%, in 2021 studies with smaller datasets (under roughly 3000 participants) still included fewer women (35.6%), and that greater representation of women as editors and authors was associated with more women participants.
effect_or_estimate: Women participants 21.9% (1991) to 36.3% (2021); 35.6% in smaller studies
limitations: Three journals only; gender/sex terminology conflation is acknowledged in this literature; does not itself quantify the consequence for recommendation validity.
citation: James et al. (2023). Underrepresentation of women in exercise science and physiology research is associated with authorship gender. J Appl Physiol (1985).
ppbf_implication: PPBF must attach a female-evidence-quality flag to any recommendation derived from predominantly male samples. This is implementable: a boolean plus a note on each evidence-ledger row — this registry does it in the 'sex' column.
verified_title: Underrepresentation of women in exercise science and physiology research is associated with authorship gender.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: An audit-based review of 11 resistance-training consensus statements and position stands encompassing 104,251,363 participants found that youth guidelines comprised 69% male participants, and identified 287 studies that included both sexes.
population: Participants in studies informing RT guidelines
effect_or_estimate: Youth resistance-training guidelines 69% male
transfer_status: Methodological — applies across strength and conditioning
limitations: An audit of representation, not of whether recommendations are actually invalid for women; participant totals are dominated by very large epidemiological datasets.
citation: Pandit et al. (2023). Data Informing Governing Body Resistance-Training Guidelines Exhibit Sex Bias: An Audit-Based Review. Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: Directly relevant: PPBF's youth resistance-training guidance inherits a 69%-male evidence base. State this in the framework rather than presenting guidelines as sex-neutral.
verified_title: Data Informing Governing Body Resistance-Training Guidelines Exhibit Sex Bias: An Audit-Based Review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: An analysis using National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data evaluated whether typical recruitment and participant characterisation practices in sport and exercise science — under-representing cisgender females, small sample sizes and misgendering — cause incorrect statistical decisions, using sample sizes common in the field (mean N=187, median N=20).
effect_or_estimate: Effects of imbalance, small n and misgendering on statistical decisions
limitations: A simulation using a general health survey rather than sport performance data; findings depend on the modelled effect structure.
citation: Navalta et al. (2023). Implications for cisgender female underrepresentation, small sample sizes, and misgendering in sport and exercise science research. PLoS One.
ppbf_implication: Supports PPBF collecting sex data carefully and separately from gender identity, with clear purpose limitation and privacy tiering, and not over-interpreting small-sample local findings.
verified_title: Implications for cisgender female underrepresentation, small sample sizes, and misgendering in sport and exercise science research.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Weight cycling in youth combat sports is prevalent
claim: A systematic review of rapid weight loss in youth Olympic combat sports found RWL is highly prevalent in children and adolescent combat athletes, ranging from 25% to 94% depending on the combat sport, age and level of competition, that these athletes regularly prompt RWL by increasing exercise frequency and intensity, decreasing fluid and food intake, training in impermeable suits and using sauna frequently, and that the magnitude of RWL ranged from approximately 1% to 6.3 ± 3.7% body mass.
effect_or_estimate: RWL prevalence 25-94%; magnitude ~1% to 6.3 ± 3.7% body mass
limitations: Prevalence varies enormously by sport and level; self-reported questionnaire data; retrospective recall; the health consequences in youth are not quantified by this review.
citation: Lakicevic et al. (2022). Patterns of weight cycling in youth Olympic combat sports: a systematic review. J Eat Disord.
ppbf_implication: SAFETY-CRITICAL for PPBF: youth weight cutting is common and the listed methods (impermeable suits, sauna, fluid restriction) are dangerous. PPBF must have an explicit NO YOUTH WEIGHT CUTTING policy. SHADOW must flag rapid body-mass change and route to a clinician and safeguarding lead — never advise a cut.
verified_title: Patterns of weight cycling in youth Olympic combat sports: a systematic review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Rapid weight change and self-reported injury in combat sports
claim: A 14-month study across 24 combat sports events collecting weight-management questionnaires one day post-competition and injury questionnaires seven days post-competition obtained 172 responses from 155 athletes (37 female, 118 male), of whom 88 (51%) reported no injury and 84 (49%) reported injury; rapid weight loss 7 days before weigh-in averaged 4.9 ± 3.4% (female) and 6.1 ± 3.2% (male), and 24 hours before weigh-in averaged 2.6 ± 2.1% and 3.0 ± 1.9% respectively.
limitations: Self-reported injury with no clinical verification; 49% injury self-report rate suggests a very broad injury definition; response bias likely; adults only.
citation: Doherty et al. (2025). Is there a relationship between rapid weight changes and self-reported injury in combat sports athletes? A 14-month study of 24 combat sports events. J Sci Med Sport.
ppbf_implication: These percentages describe what ADULT competitors DO — they are NOT recommendations and must never be presented as targets. PPBF logs body mass trend as an observation; weight-making advice belongs to a registered dietitian and physician.
verified_title: Is there a relationship between rapid weight changes and self-reported injury in combat sports athletes? A 14-month study of 24 combat sports events.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Combat sports weight-cut nutrition position stand
claim: The International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand on nutrition and weight-cut strategies for mixed martial arts and other combat sports comprises 16 approved points, including that as match duration increases beyond 4 minutes the aerobic contribution can rise to over 70% while anaerobic alactic and glycolytic pathways support high-output bursts, and that during the off-camp/general preparation phase athletes should maintain a weight ranging 12% to 15% above the weight division requirement.
study_design: Position stand (International Society of Sports Nutrition)
effect_or_estimate: Aerobic contribution >70% beyond 4 min; off-camp weight 12-15% above division
limitations: The 12-15% off-camp figure is a professional-body recommendation for ADULT competitive athletes and is not derived from a randomised trial; MMA-centred; explicitly NOT applicable to youth; nutrition societies have a different evidence standard from medical consensus bodies.
citation: Ricci et al. (2025). International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrition and weight cut strategies for mixed martial arts and other combat sports. J Int Soc Sports Nutr.
ppbf_implication: PPBF may reference this for ADULT athletes only, and only through a qualified nutrition professional. It must be excluded entirely from youth-facing material. SHADOW must not surface any weight-cut figure to an athlete or guardian.
verified_title: International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrition and weight cut strategies for mixed martial arts and other combat sports.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Acute weight loss strategies in Olympic combat sports
claim: A review of acute weight loss strategies for combat sports and applications to Olympic success summarised the performance effects of weight-making practices, the physiological nature of body-mass losses, and provided practical recommendations in the form of a decision tree for achieving acute body-mass loss while minimising performance decrement.
effect_or_estimate: Decision-tree guidance; no single numeric prescription
limitations: Elite adult context with professional support staff; the review addresses minimising performance decrement, not health protection in unsupervised settings; not applicable to youth.
citation: Reale et al. (2016). Acute-Weight-Loss Strategies for Combat Sports and Applications to Olympic Success. Int J Sports Physiol Perform.
ppbf_implication: Reference for the adult competitive lane only, under professional supervision. PPBF's default for all youth and novice athletes is: compete at natural weight.
verified_title: Acute-Weight-Loss Strategies for Combat Sports and Applications to Olympic Success.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Hydration status in elite youth boxers during weight-stable phase
claim: In 16 national-champion male youth boxers (17 ± 1 y) measured on three occasions during the 30 days before competition, urine osmolality and urine specific gravity increased from day 3 to day 10 by 16% and 0.4% respectively despite athletes being in their weight-stability period and consuming fluid ad libitum, and hypohydration was universally prevalent among all athletes on both test days (USG 1.027 ± 0.003; UOSM 1035 ± 108 mOsmol/kg).
effect_or_estimate: USG 1.027 ± 0.003; UOSM 1035 ± 108 mOsmol/kg; hypohydration universally prevalent
limitations: Small n=16; male only; single national squad; urinary markers have known limitations as hydration indices; 'weight-stable phase' still occurred within a competition preparation period.
citation: Zubac et al. (2016). Fluid balance and hydration assessment during the weight-stable preparation phase in elite youth boxers. J Sports Sci.
ppbf_implication: Striking finding for PPBF's youth lane: chronic hypohydration was universal even WITHOUT deliberate weight cutting. Fluid availability and education are cheap, high-value interventions. Do not require athletes to hit a urine-colour target — see A5-133.
verified_title: Fluid balance and hydration assessment during the weight-stable preparation phase in elite youth boxers.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Urinary dehydration markers have day-to-day reliability limits in youth boxers
claim: Analysis of 69 daily urine samples from 23 elite adolescent amateur boxers (17.3 ± 1.9 y) during the weight-stable phase evaluated the reliability and diagnostic accuracy of non-invasive urinary dehydration markers in field-based settings, finding uniform increments in urine osmolality of 11.2 ± 12.8% (lightweight) and 19.9 ± 22.7% (heavyweight) over the study, despite stable body mass and ad libitum fluid intake.
effect_or_estimate: Osmolality increments 11.2 ± 12.8% and 19.9 ± 22.7%; very large variability
limitations: The standard deviations exceed or approach the means, indicating very poor day-to-day precision; small sample; single squad.
citation: Zubac et al. (2018). Reliability of Urinary Dehydration Markers in Elite Youth Boxers. Int J Sports Physiol Perform.
ppbf_implication: PPBF must NOT use a single urinary hydration reading to gate participation. The measurement is too noisy day to day. Use fluid-availability policy and education instead of a measurement gate.
verified_title: Reliability of Urinary Dehydration Markers in Elite Youth Boxers.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Body composition of elite combat sport athletes
claim: Assessment of 94 Olympic combat sport athletes (56 male, 38 female) by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry within 7-21 days of competition found that most athletes were heavier than their weight division and that sport had a significant effect on physique traits including lean mass, lean mass distribution, stature and BMI, with the study also investigating the appropriateness of athletes' self-selected weight classes against the NCAA minimum wrestling weight scheme.
effect_or_estimate: Most athletes heavier than their declared division; sport-specific physique differences
boxing_specific: Partly (boxing among four Olympic combat sports)
limitations: DXA is not available to community gyms; elite adults only; cross-sectional; the minimum-weight scheme referenced was developed for wrestling, not boxing.
citation: Reale et al. (2019). Body composition of elite Olympic combat sport athletes. Eur J Sport Sci.
ppbf_implication: Confirms most elite combat athletes compete below their off-season mass. Relevant context, but body composition assessment in youth carries eating-disorder risk — PPBF should follow the IOC body-composition guidance (A5-123) and restrict such assessment.
verified_title: Body composition of elite Olympic combat sport athletes.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A review of endurance exercise performance in masters athletes reported that peak endurance performance is maintained until approximately 35 years of age, followed by modest decreases until 50-60 years of age with progressively steeper declines thereafter, and identified a progressive reduction in maximal oxygen consumption as the primary mechanism, with lactate threshold reduction contributing while exercise economy is comparatively preserved.
sex: Predominantly male in the underlying data
effect_or_estimate: Plateau to ~35 y; modest decline to 50-60 y; steeper thereafter; VO2max the primary mechanism
limitations: Endurance athletes, not combat athletes; predominantly male data; cross-sectional age comparisons confound ageing with cohort and training-history effects.
citation: Tanaka et al. (2007). Endurance exercise performance in Masters athletes: age-associated changes and underlying physiological mechanisms. J Physiol.
ppbf_implication: PPBF's masters lane (World Boxing categorises boxers over 40 as Masters, regulated by national federations) should expect aerobic decline but not assume proportional decline in skill or technique. Log age band as a programming context.
verified_title: Endurance exercise performance in Masters athletes: age-associated changes and underlying physiological mechanisms.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Recovery from resistance exercise in older adults — evidence gap
claim: A scoping review of exercise-induced muscle damage and recovery from resistance exercise in adults aged 65 and over identified current knowledge gaps and noted that little is known about recovery from resistance exercise in older adults, which may have implications for exercise prescription.
effect_or_estimate: Documents an evidence gap
limitations: Age 65+ is older than most masters boxers; not athletes in most included studies; scoping review documents gaps rather than providing prescriptions.
citation: Hayes et al. (2023). Recovery from Resistance Exercise in Older Adults: A Systematic Scoping Review. Sports Med Open.
ppbf_implication: PPBF should allow longer between-session recovery for masters athletes as a precautionary default, and label the specific interval as an assumption requiring local observation.
verified_title: Recovery from Resistance Exercise in Older Adults: A Systematic Scoping Review.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Sport-specific test validation in combat sports is methodologically weak
claim: A systematic review of sport-specific performance assessment in Olympic combat sports including amateur boxing found 39 eligible studies, of which the majority (74%) had sample sizes under 30 subjects, nearly one third lacked sufficient description of participants (anthropometrics, age, expertise level), 72% did not sufficiently report participant inclusion/exclusion criteria, and in 62% the description or inclusion of familiarisation sessions was incomplete or absent.
effect_or_estimate: 74% n<30; ~33% insufficient participant description; 72% insufficient inclusion criteria; 62% incomplete familiarisation reporting
limitations: The review's finding IS the limitation: the combat-sport test-validation literature is methodologically weak across the board.
citation: Chaabene et al. (2018). Tests for the Assessment of Sport-Specific Performance in Olympic Combat Sports: A Systematic Review With Practical Recommendations. Front Physiol.
ppbf_implication: FOUNDATIONAL for the PPBF test battery: sport-specific combat tests are largely under-validated. PPBF should favour general tests with strong validation plus locally established reliability, and be explicit that boxing-specific normative data mostly does not exist.
verified_title: Tests for the Assessment of Sport-Specific Performance in Olympic Combat Sports: A Systematic Review With Practical Recommendations.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test — validated intermittent capacity test
claim: The Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test showed a test-retest coefficient of variation of 4.9%, peak heart rate similar to an exhaustive incremental treadmill test (187 ± 2 vs 189 ± 2 bpm) with higher peak blood lactate, an eightfold increase in muscle lactate and reductions in muscle creatine phosphate (51%) and glycogen (23%), and elite soccer players improved Yo-Yo performance by 25 ± 6% and VO2max by 7% during a precompetition period.
effect_or_estimate: Test-retest CV 4.9%; peak HR 187 ± 2 bpm; Yo-Yo improved 25 ± 6% vs VO2max 7%
limitations: Soccer players, not boxers; male only; the running-based movement pattern differs from boxing footwork; boxing-specific normative data does not exist for this test.
citation: Krustrup et al. (2003). The yo-yo intermittent recovery test: physiological response, reliability, and validity. Med Sci Sports Exerc.
ppbf_implication: Feasible, equipment-light PPBF field test for intermittent capacity (cones, tape, audio track). Note explicitly: NO boxing normative data — PPBF must build its own local reference distribution.
verified_title: The yo-yo intermittent recovery test: physiological response, reliability, and validity.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: 30-15 Intermittent Fitness Test — validated across populations
claim: The 30-15 Intermittent Fitness Test and its sport-specific variants have demonstrated reliability, usefulness and validity across multiple populations, including intraclass correlation coefficients above 0.94 and coefficients of variation of 1.6% for maximal speed in young elite ice hockey players, with validity established against the running version used as a cardiovascular fitness reference marker.
effect_or_estimate: ICC >0.94; CV 1.6% for maximal speed
limitations: Not validated in boxing; requires ~40 m of space and an audio track; no boxing normative data.
citation: Buchheit et al. (2011). Reliability, usefulness, and validity of the 30-15 Intermittent Ice Test in young elite ice hockey players. J Strength Cond Res.
ppbf_implication: Alternative intermittent-capacity test with change-of-direction demand closer to boxing footwork than a straight-line test. Same caveat: PPBF must build local norms.
verified_title: Reliability, usefulness, and validity of the 30-15 Intermittent Ice Test in young elite ice hockey players.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: IMTP and CMJ reliability and sensitivity
claim: Studies of the countermovement jump and isometric mid-thigh pull report high relative reliability (ICC 0.97 and above in an elite sample) but that most IMTP parameters showed marginal ability to detect chronic change (smallest worthwhile change less than the standard error of measurement) except peak vertical force parameters, which showed good usefulness (SWC greater than SEM).
sex: Male and female (sex-based analysis in one study)
sample_size: n=45 elite; n=20 young soccer players
effect_or_estimate: ICC 0.97+; most IMTP parameters SWC<SEM; peak force SWC>SEM
limitations: Requires a force plate; most derived parameters are NOT sensitive enough to detect real change even when reliable; not boxing-validated.
citation: Pojskić et al. (2025). Are counter movement jump and isometric mid-thigh pull tests reliable, valid, and sensitive measurement instruments when performed after maximal cardiopulmonary exercise testing? A sex-based analysis in elite athletes. Front Physiol.
ppbf_implication: Key distinction PPBF must implement: RELIABLE is not the same as SENSITIVE TO CHANGE. Only report metrics whose smallest worthwhile change exceeds their measurement error. Most force-plate derivatives fail this test.
verified_title: Are counter movement jump and isometric mid-thigh pull tests reliable, valid, and sensitive measurement instruments when performed after maximal cardiopulmonary exercise testing? A sex-based analysis in elite athletes.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Functional Movement Screen does not predict injury
claim: A systematic review with meta-analysis of 24 appraised studies investigating whether Functional Movement Screen composite scores predict subsequent injury, and a separate systematic review and meta-analysis reporting good reliability and validity alongside pooled odds ratios for a score of 14 or below, together indicate that the FMS composite score has poor predictive value for musculoskeletal injury.
effect_or_estimate: Composite score predictive value poor despite acceptable reliability
limitations: Predominantly male; heterogeneous injury definitions; screening tests generally perform poorly as individual-level predictors regardless of reliability.
citation: Moran et al. (2017). Do Functional Movement Screen (FMS) composite scores predict subsequent injury? A systematic review with meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: PPBF must NOT use FMS or similar composite movement screens as an injury-risk gate. Movement screening may inform coaching and exercise selection; it must not generate a risk score that restricts participation.
verified_title: Do Functional Movement Screen (FMS) composite scores predict subsequent injury? A systematic review with meta-analysis.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Y-Balance Test — reliability yes, injury prediction weak
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 57 studies assessing the Y-Balance Test Lower Quarter examined reliability, whether performance varies by sex, sport and competition level, and injury-risk identification validity based on asymmetry, individual reach direction or composite score.
effect_or_estimate: Reliability established; predictive validity examined across asymmetry, reach and composite
limitations: Predictive validity for injury is weak in the broader literature (see also A5-141 for the general problem with screening tests); heterogeneous populations; no boxing data.
citation: Plisky et al. (2021). Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Y-Balance Test Lower Quarter: Reliability, Discriminant Validity, and Predictive Validity. Int J Sports Phys Ther.
ppbf_implication: Same rule as FMS: PPBF may use balance/reach testing descriptively, never as an injury-prediction gate. This is a hard constraint on the injury-risk engine.
verified_title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Y-Balance Test Lower Quarter: Reliability, Discriminant Validity, and Predictive Validity.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Seated/supine medicine ball throw — upper-body power proxy
claim: The seated medicine ball throw has been examined as a measure of upper-body power, with validity and reliability studies conducted in older adults and a supine upper-body power test validated in physically active male and female adults using a medicine ball.
population: Older adults and physically active adults
effect_or_estimate: Acceptable reliability as an upper-body power proxy
transfer_status: General transfer; NOT validated in boxers
limitations: Validated primarily in older adults and general physically active adults, NOT in boxers or combat athletes; throw distance depends on technique and release angle; no boxing normative data.
citation: Strand et al. (2022). Validity and Reliability of the Seated Medicine Ball Throw as a Measure of Upper Body Power in Older Women. J Strength Cond Res.
ppbf_implication: Pragmatic, near-zero-cost PPBF upper-body power test (one medicine ball, a tape measure, a wall). Flag clearly: validated outside boxing, so PPBF must establish its own reliability and reference range before trending it.
verified_title: Validity and Reliability of the Seated Medicine Ball Throw as a Measure of Upper Body Power in Older Women.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Heart rate variability monitoring — practices and limits
claim: Reviews of heart rate variability monitoring in athletes describe its application to training adaptation and prescription, while a separate review of heart rate monitoring notes both applications and limitations of heart-rate-derived indices for monitoring training status.
effect_or_estimate: Application frameworks; substantial day-to-day variability noted
limitations: HRV shows large within-individual day-to-day variation requiring rolling averages and long baselines; measurement conditions (posture, time of day, breathing) strongly affect values; no boxing-specific HRV guidance located.
citation: Lundstrom et al. (2022). Practices and Applications of Heart Rate Variability Monitoring in Endurance Athletes. Int J Sports Med.
ppbf_implication: HRV is NOT recommended as a PPBF priority: it requires consistent daily measurement conditions that a community gym cannot enforce, and adds cost without clear benefit over sRPE plus a wellness questionnaire. Record as a future option.
verified_title: Practices and Applications of Heart Rate Variability Monitoring in Endurance Athletes.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Cognitive function and hydration in combat athletes
claim: A study examined the cognitive function and taekwondo-specific kick performance of taekwondo athletes at different hydration states.
effect_or_estimate: Cognitive and sport-specific performance compared across hydration states
limitations: Taekwondo, not boxing; small sample; laboratory hydration manipulation.
citation: Zheng et al. (2024). The Cognitive Function and Taekwondo-Specific Kick Performance of Taekwondo Athletes at Different Hydration Statuses. Int J Sports Physiol Perform.
ppbf_implication: Supports treating hydration as a performance and safety issue in combat sports generally. PPBF's response should be fluid access and education, not measurement-based gating (see A5-133).
verified_title: The Cognitive Function and Taekwondo-Specific Kick Performance of Taekwondo Athletes at Different Hydration Statuses.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: A study reported that the menstrual cycle alters training strain, monotony and technical training length in young athletes.
effect_or_estimate: Cycle-associated variation in strain, monotony and technical training length
limitations: Small observational study; cycle-phase verification methods in this literature are generally weak (see A5-119); does not establish that training should be altered by phase.
citation: Cristina-Souza et al. (2019). Menstrual cycle alters training strain, monotony, and technical training length in young. J Sports Sci.
ppbf_implication: Consistent with allowing athlete-led adjustment. Does NOT support PPBF prescribing training by cycle phase. Cycle data, if collected at all, is highest-privacy-tier and athlete-controlled.
verified_title: Menstrual cycle alters training strain, monotony, and technical training length in young.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
claim: World Boxing Competition Rules specify a rest period of one minute between rounds for all competitions, categorise Men and Women boxers aged 19 to 40 as Elite, 17 to 18 as U19, 15 to 16 as U17, with the U15 age category regulated by Confederations and/or National Federations in consultation with their Sports and Competition and Medical Committees, and categorise boxers over 40 as Masters, also regulated by Confederations/National Federations. At the World Boxing Championships bouts for both men and women comprise three rounds of three minutes with a one-minute break.
effect_or_estimate: 3x3 min with 1 min rest; age categories U15/U17/U19/Elite/Masters
limitations: World Boxing rules are one of several international frameworks; the IBA operates a separate framework, and national federations set their own rules for U15 and Masters. Rules change between editions — PPBF must re-verify against the current rulebook.
citation: World Boxing. World Boxing Competition Rules (in force November 2024); World Boxing Championships competition format page.
verification: governing-body rulebook page fetched via web search 2026-08-07 (worldboxing.org PDF; worldboxingliverpool.com competition-format page)
ppbf_implication: PPBF conditioning must be built around the actual format an athlete competes under. Store sanctioning body, age category and round format as athlete-record fields — do not hardcode 3x3.

claim: The USA Boxing National Rulebook sets bout durations by age division, with Elite and Youth competitions at three rounds of no more than three minutes each, Junior competitions at three rounds of no more than two minutes each, and Prep divisions at three rounds of specified shorter durations (Pee Wee and Bantam one-and-a-half minutes, Intermediate two minutes in the 2021-revision text), with local competitions permitted to contest shorter rounds; a separate USA Boxing competition-rules document specifies that novice competitions may consist of up to three rounds of up to two minutes with discretion by local organisers and coaches, and that a boxer's registration begins at age 8.
effect_or_estimate: Elite/Youth 3x3 min; Junior 3x2 min; Prep divisions shorter; novice up to 3x2 min
limitations: Round durations differ BETWEEN USA Boxing rulebook editions (the 2017, 2021/2022 and 2025 texts differ on Prep division durations and on Elite/Youth Women formats) and between USA Boxing and international bodies. PPBF must verify against the edition in force for the specific event.
citation: USA Boxing. USA Boxing National Rulebook (editions revised 12/31/2021 and effective 01/01/2025) and USA Boxing Official Rule Book Competition Rules.
verification: governing-body rulebook PDFs fetched via web search 2026-08-07 (usaboxing.webpoint.us 2022 rulebook; usamastersboxing.com 2025 rulebook; usaboxing.org rules-clarification page)

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Sparring is a regulated activity with medical prerequisites (England Boxing example)
claim: The England Boxing rule book states that sparring is only permitted where a boxer is registered and has medical clearance appropriately documented, that under no circumstances is sparring permitted for any boxer under the age of 10, that boxers taking part in sparring must have completed an Annual Medical, be declared Fit to Box by a Doctor and not be serving a medical suspension, that all sparring must be conducted under the supervision of a qualified instructor, and that if a boxer receives a knockout or a sparring session is stopped due to blows to the head then protective medical suspensions and the England Boxing Concussion Protocol (with separate annexes for under-18s and over-19s) must be applied.
effect_or_estimate: Sparring requires documented medical clearance; minimum age 10; concussion protocol mandatory after head-blow stoppage
transfer_status: Boxing-specific — jurisdictional rule (England, NOT the USA)
limitations: JURISDICTIONAL: these are England Boxing rules and do NOT apply to PPBF operations in the United States. Cited as an example of how a governing body operationalises documented sparring clearance — USA Boxing requirements must be verified separately in its own Medical Handbook.
citation: England Boxing. England Boxing Rule Book / Technical and Competition Rules (2023-24 and 2025 editions), sections on medicals, sparring and medical suspensions.
verification: governing-body rulebook PDF fetched via web search 2026-08-07 (englandboxing.org 2025 rule book; 2023-24 rule book; coach guidance note)
ppbf_implication: MODEL FOR PPBF'S DATA MODEL: sparring eligibility is a function of (registration status, medical clearance on file, no active suspension, supervision present, minimum age). Every one of those is an ADMINISTRATIVE fact SHADOW can surface. The clearance itself is a doctor's determination.

track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: Post-bout medical suspensions are commission-set minimums, not physiological recovery times
claim: Association of Boxing Commissions regulatory guidelines provide that a boxer losing by technical knockout resulting from head blows shall receive a medical suspension of a minimum of thirty days, a boxer losing by knockout shall receive a minimum of sixty days, that at the discretion of the physician longer suspension periods may be issued for either, that boxers shall receive a mandatory seven-day rest period after competing with day 1 commencing the first day following the event, that a physician may issue a medical suspension at any time believed to be in the best interest of boxer safety, and that in all cases the decision by the physician to issue or extend a suspension is final. State regulation (e.g. Virginia Administrative Code 18VAC120-40-342) codifies equivalent minimums.
population: Professional boxers under North American commissions
study_design: Regulatory guideline and state administrative code
effect_or_estimate: TKO from head blows: min 30 days; KO: min 60 days; mandatory 7-day post-event rest; physician decision final
limitations: These are REGULATORY MINIMUMS for professional boxing under North American commissions, not physiologically derived recovery periods, and they vary by jurisdiction. Amateur governing bodies set their own separate suspensions. A minimum suspension expiring is NOT a medical clearance.
citation: Association of Boxing Commissions. ABC Regulatory Guidelines and Rules; Virginia Administrative Code 18VAC120-40-342 (Bout termination, knockout, technical knockout, medical suspensions).

It must NEVER render that as cleared, eligible, or safe to spar. The physician's decision is final and is the only clearance.
