track: A5 Physical Preparation / Load / Recovery / Injury & Head Impact
topic: American Academy of Pediatrics / Canadian Paediatric Society position on youth boxing
claim: A joint American Academy of Pediatrics and Canadian Paediatric Society policy statement notes that although boxing provides benefits including exercise, self-discipline and self-confidence, the sport encourages and rewards deliberate blows to the head and face, that participants are at risk of head, face and neck injuries including chronic and even fatal neurologic injuries with concussion among the most common injuries, and that these organisations oppose boxing as a sport for children and adolescents and recommend that physicians vigorously oppose youth boxing and encourage alternative sports in which intentional head blows are not central.
effect_or_estimate: Opposition to youth boxing participation
limitations: A policy position reflecting a risk-benefit judgement by paediatric bodies, not a quantified risk estimate; published 2011 and predates the current concussion consensus and much head-impact-sensor evidence; it opposes competitive boxing involving intentional head blows, and does not address non-contact boxing-based training programmes.
citation: et al. (2011). Policy statement—Boxing participation by children and adolescents. Pediatrics.
ppbf_implication: PPBF MUST engage with this position honestly in guardian-facing material rather than omit it. It is the strongest argument for PPBF's NON-CONTACT youth lane (Module 044) and for keeping head contact out of the youth pathway. Do not present youth boxing as endorsed by paediatric bodies — it is not.
verified_title: Policy statement—Boxing participation by children and adolescents.

track: A6 Gym Craft
claim: In elite GB amateur boxers under 5-year medical surveillance, the hand was the most frequently injured body location overall, in training and in competition, for both new and recurrent injuries.
effect_or_estimate: Competition total injury rate reported as 828 per 1000 h; hand injury rate in competition 302 per 1000 h; hand significantly higher than other locations
limitations: Single national squad; medically diagnosed injuries only; denominators for elite squad hours may not generalise to club/youth settings; rates per 1000 h in competition are not comparable to per-session gym metrics
citation: Loosemore M et al. Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study. Br J Sports Med 2015
ppbf_implication: Hand/wrist protection is the highest-yield equipment-and-technique target in a boxing programme; justifies making wrapping a governed SOP rather than a style preference. Hand-injury events should be a first-class entity in pilot.coach_observations / progression_gaps.
verified_title: Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study of medically diagnosed injury incidence and outcome.

track: A6 Gym Craft
claim: In the same elite GB cohort followed 2005-2012, finger carpometacarpal (CMC) instability and MCP joint extensor hood/capsule sprain ('boxer's knuckle') were significantly more common than any other hand or wrist diagnosis.
effect_or_estimate: Hand/wrist injury rate in competition reported as 347 per 1000 h; estimated training rate <0.5 per 1000 h
limitations: Elite population; small squad; injury capture depends on team medical staffing not available in a club setting
citation: Loosemore M et al. Hand and Wrist Injuries in Elite Boxing: A Longitudinal Prospective Study (2005-2012) of the Great Britain Olympic Boxing Squad. Hand (N Y) 2016
ppbf_implication: Names the two specific structures a wrap and glove system should be judged against: CMC column stability and the MCP extensor hood. SHADOW's hand-complaint taxonomy should use these terms, flagged to a clinician - never diagnosed by the app.
verified_title: Hand and Wrist Injuries in Elite Boxing: A Longitudinal Prospective Study (2005-2012) of the Great Britain Olympic Boxing Squad.

track: A6 Gym Craft
claim: Carpometacarpal joint instability in elite boxers is severe enough to require surgical fusion in a referral series, most commonly of the index and middle CMC joints and more often in the trailing (rear) hand.
effect_or_estimate: 82% (31/38) returned to the same level of boxing at a median of 8 months post-surgery (range 3-27 months); trailing hand affected in 87.5%
limitations: Surgical referral series = selection bias toward severe cases; single surgeon; no control group; does not establish that any wrapping method prevents CMC injury
citation: Ng CY et al. Hand Carpometacarpal Joint Instability in Elite Boxers: Injury Characteristics, Surgical Technique, and Outcomes. J Hand Surg Am 2022
ppbf_implication: Rear-hand dominance of CMC injury is a concrete asymmetry SHADOW can surface (rear-hand power volume vs. lead) for coach review. Long return-to-boxing timelines justify conservative early flagging of persistent dorsal hand pain to medical.
verified_title: Hand Carpometacarpal Joint Instability in Elite Boxers: Injury Characteristics, Surgical Technique, and Outcomes.

track: A6 Gym Craft
claim: In a consecutive series of 100 boxing hand injuries, 39% involved the thumb region (attributed mainly to forced thumb abduction) and 35% involved the bases of metacarpals 2-5 including the wrist joint (attributed to forced wrist flexion).
effect_or_estimate: 39% thumb region; 35% metacarpal bases/wrist; 26% phalanges and remaining metacarpals
limitations: 1987 case series; no denominator, no exposure data, mechanisms inferred clinically rather than measured; equipment and rules have changed since
citation: Noble C. Hand injuries in boxing. Am J Sports Med 1987
ppbf_implication: Supplies the mechanical rationale for the two non-negotiable wrap checkpoints: the thumb must be tied back to the hand (anti-abduction) and the wrist must be secured against forced flexion. Mechanism is clinical inference, not a measured causal test.
verified_title: Hand injuries in boxing.

track: A6 Gym Craft
claim: Boxer's knuckle is disruption of the MCP extensor hood/sagittal band with extensor tendon subluxation; direct surgical repair in professional athletes has been reported to restore full range of motion and allow return to professional sport.
sample_size: 8 professional athletes, 11 MCP extensor mechanism repairs
effect_or_estimate: All athletes regained full range of motion and returned to professional sport
limitations: Small surgical series without controls; outcome definition is surgeon-reported; says nothing about prevention or about whether wrapping alters incidence
citation: Hame SL, Melone CP Jr. Boxer's knuckle in the professional athlete. Am J Sports Med 2000
ppbf_implication: Defines the structure that knuckle padding is nominally protecting. PPBF coaches should treat persistent dorsal MCP pain/swelling with a sense of extensor-hood subluxation as a medical referral trigger, not a 'tape it and continue' item.
verified_title: Boxer's knuckle in the professional athlete.

track: A6 Gym Craft
claim: Boxer's knuckle and traumatic carpal boss are described in the surgical literature as the two most disabling hand injuries specific to boxing, with distinct anatomy and predictable pathology.
effect_or_estimate: No pooled effect estimate; descriptive surgical review
limitations: Narrative review by treating surgeons; no incidence denominator; conclusions about 'most disabling' are clinical judgement, not measured
citation: Melone CP Jr et al. Disabling hand injuries in boxing: boxer's knuckle and traumatic carpal boss. Clin Sports Med 2009
ppbf_implication: Supports a two-item dorsal-hand symptom screen (dorsal MCP vs. dorsal carpal/CMC) in PPBF athlete journals, routed to medical rather than interpreted by SHADOW.
verified_title: Disabling hand injuries in boxing: boxer's knuckle and traumatic carpal boss.

track: A6 Gym Craft
claim: Non-union of scaphoid fractures in boxers is documented in the orthopaedic literature as a recognised therapeutic problem.

claim: Low energy availability risk is measurable in female combat-sport athletes during the pre-competition period and is associated with altered physiological function in that window.
population: Chinese female combat athletes (judo, freestyle wrestling, sanda)
study_design: Cross-sectional screening (LEAF-Q, EDE-Q) with a small prospective subgroup
sample_size: 84 screened; 11 judo athletes in the prospective subgroup
effect_or_estimate: Effect sizes not extractable from abstract; direction reported as adverse in the LEA group
boxing_specific: No — combat sport but not boxing
limitations: Very small prospective subgroup (n=11); single-country sample; questionnaire-based LEA classification; not generalisable to youth or to US community programmes
citation: Zhang Y, et al. The impact of low energy availability risk on pre-competition physiological function in Chinese female combat athletes. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2025.
ppbf_implication: Supports a pre-competition LEA screening trigger for female PPBF boxers, routed to a dietitian — not an in-app score.
verified_title: The impact of low energy availability risk on pre-competition physiological function in Chinese female combat athletes.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: The existence of REDs as a discrete syndrome is contested in the literature; at least one 2024 peer-reviewed critique explicitly questions whether the syndrome, as defined, exists.
effect_or_estimate: No pooled estimate; the disagreement is definitional and causal-inferential, not a dispute about the harm of severe energy deficiency
limitations: A critique is not evidence of absence of harm; the underlying harms of severe energy deficiency are separately well-documented
citation: Areta JL, et al. Does Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Syndrome Exist? Sports Med. 2024.
ppbf_implication: SHADOW should present REDs as the dominant consensus framework while flagging the live scientific debate; it must not present REDs risk output as diagnostic.
verified_title: Does Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Syndrome Exist?

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Carbohydrate intake should be judged by whether carbohydrate availability is adequate for the specific session; during sustained high-intensity events lasting about one hour, small carbohydrate amounts (including mouth rinsing alone) can enhance performance via central nervous system effects, while 30-60 g/h is an appropriate target for longer events and up to 90 g/h may benefit events over 2.5 h.
study_design: Authoritative narrative review underpinning IOC/IAAF guidance
effect_or_estimate: 30-60 g/h for longer events; up to 90 g/h for >2.5 h; mouth-rinse effect for ~1 h events
transfer_status: Endurance-sport transfer; a 3x3 min amateur bout or a 3x2 min youth bout is far shorter than the durations these intake rates were derived for
limitations: The 30-90 g/h intake targets do not apply to a boxing bout; only the ~1 h/mouth-rinse and daily-availability principles plausibly transfer
citation: Burke LM, Hawley JA, Wong SHS, Jeukendrup AE. Carbohydrates for training and competition. J Sports Sci. 2011.
ppbf_implication: PPBF fueling structures should target carbohydrate availability across the training day, not in-bout carbohydrate feeding.
verified_title: Carbohydrates for training and competition.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Endogenous glycogen stores are maximised by a high-carbohydrate diet of 8-12 g carbohydrate/kg/day, and are depleted most by high-volume exercise.
population: Healthy exercising adults, particularly highly trained individuals
effect_or_estimate: 8-12 g/kg/day for maximal glycogen storage
limitations: 8-12 g/kg/day is an upper-bound glycogen-loading figure derived largely from endurance contexts; it is not a routine intake for a boxer and is not appropriate as a default target
citation: Kerksick CM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: nutrient timing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017.
ppbf_implication: SHADOW may surface the range with its endurance-context caveat; it must never compute a per-athlete gram target.
verified_title: International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrient timing.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Deliberate periodised carbohydrate restriction ('train low') has not been shown to produce a consistent performance advantage over high carbohydrate availability in endurance-trained athletes.
effect_or_estimate: No consistent performance benefit reported
transfer_status: Endurance transfer; no boxing-specific train-low evidence identified
limitations: Endurance-only population; short intervention durations; heterogeneous 'train low' protocols; the 2023 IOC REDs consensus separately flags low carbohydrate availability as a REDs contributor
citation: Gejl KD, Nybo L. Performance effects of periodized carbohydrate restriction in endurance trained athletes - a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021.
ppbf_implication: PPBF should not adopt train-low protocols; combined with REDs risk in a weight-category sport the risk/benefit is unfavourable.
verified_title: Performance effects of periodized carbohydrate restriction in endurance trained athletes - a systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Carbohydrate mouth rinsing improves cycling time-trial performance in a pooled analysis, and a separate meta-analysis examined its effect on muscle strength and muscular endurance.
effect_or_estimate: Positive pooled effect for cycling time trial; strength/endurance effects examined separately with smaller and less consistent effects
boxing_specific: No — cycling and general resistance-exercise populations
transfer_status: Non-boxing transfer; no boxing-specific mouth-rinse trial identified
limitations: Effect is small and context-dependent; benefit is largest in a fasted or glycogen-depleted state; no combat-sport replication located
citation: Brietzke C, et al. Effects of Carbohydrate Mouth Rinse on Cycling Time Trial Performance. Sports Med. 2019; and Ataide-Silva T, et al. Crit Rev Food Sci Nutr. 2022.
ppbf_implication: A plausible, low-risk, zero-cost tool for a boxer who cannot tolerate food close to a bout; label as untested in boxing.
verified_title: Effects of Carbohydrate Mouth Rinse on Cycling Time Trial Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: A daily protein intake of 1.4-2.0 g/kg body weight/day is sufficient for most exercising individuals to build and maintain muscle mass; higher intakes of 2.3-3.1 g/kg/day may be needed to maximise retention of lean body mass in resistance-trained individuals during hypocaloric periods.
population: Healthy exercising individuals; resistance-trained individuals for the hypocaloric range
effect_or_estimate: 1.4-2.0 g/kg/d general; 2.3-3.1 g/kg/d during energy restriction in resistance-trained individuals
transfer_status: General-sport transfer; the hypocaloric range is directly relevant to a boxer in a longitudinal weight descent
limitations: Ranges derive largely from adult male resistance-training studies; upper range is not validated in youth or in adolescents still growing; intakes are population ranges, not individual prescriptions
citation: Jager R, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017.
ppbf_implication: SHADOW may display the population range with caveats; a per-athlete gram target during weight descent is a dietitian decision.
verified_title: International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: In a randomised trial of young men in a ~40% energy deficit combined with intense exercise, a higher protein intake (2.4 g/kg/d) produced greater lean mass gain and fat mass loss than a lower intake (1.2 g/kg/d) over four weeks.
effect_or_estimate: Higher-protein group showed greater lean mass gain and greater fat mass loss over 4 weeks
transfer_status: Non-boxing, male-only transfer; the energy deficit was severe and supervised
limitations: Male-only; four weeks; a ~40% deficit under full dietary control is not replicable in a community gym; no female or adolescent replication in this trial
citation: Longland TM, et al. Higher compared with lower dietary protein during an energy deficit combined with intense exercise promotes greater lean mass gain and fat mass loss. Am J Clin Nutr. 2016.
ppbf_implication: Supports 'protein first' as the framing principle for any supervised weight descent; the specific 2.4 g/kg figure must not be auto-applied.
verified_title: Higher compared with lower dietary protein during an energy deficit combined with intense exercise promotes greater lean mass gain and fat mass loss: a randomized trial.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Per-meal muscle protein synthesis shows a saturable dose relationship; approximately 20 g of high-quality protein maximally stimulated myofibrillar protein synthesis after leg resistance exercise in young men, while after whole-body resistance exercise 40 g produced a greater response than 20 g.
study_design: Two acute dose-response crossover trials plus a narrative review of distribution
effect_or_estimate: Saturation near 20 g after single-limb work; greater response at 40 g after whole-body work
limitations: Very small samples; acute muscle protein synthesis is a surrogate, not a performance or hypertrophy outcome; dose scales with the lean mass activated; not validated in youth or female athletes
citation: Moore DR, et al. Am J Clin Nutr. 2009; Macnaughton LS, et al. Physiol Rep. 2016; Murphy CH, et al. Nutrients 2020 (distribution review).
ppbf_implication: Justifies a 'protein at each main meal' STRUCTURE in PPBF education rather than a gram-per-meal prescription.
verified_title: Ingested protein dose response of muscle and albumin protein synthesis after resistance exercise in young men.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Whether spreading protein evenly across meals improves muscle-related outcomes is not settled; a 2020 review found the observational and randomised evidence supporting the distribution concept is inconsistent.
study_design: Narrative/systematic review of observational and RCT evidence
effect_or_estimate: No consistent benefit demonstrated for even distribution over total daily intake
limitations: Total daily protein intake appears to dominate; distribution effects, if present, are small; boxing-specific data absent
citation: Murphy CH, et al. Protein Distribution and Muscle-Related Outcomes: Does the Evidence Support the Concept? Nutrients. 2020.
ppbf_implication: PPBF should teach total daily protein adequacy first; even distribution is a reasonable habit, not an evidence-mandated rule.
verified_title: Protein Distribution and Muscle-Related Outcomes: Does the Evidence Support the Concept?

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: The case for high-fat/low-carbohydrate diets improving sports performance has been re-examined in the peer-reviewed literature and remains unresolved rather than settled in either direction.
study_design: Narrative review / opinion in a peer-reviewed journal
effect_or_estimate: No pooled estimate; the review frames the question as open
limitations: High-fat approaches reduce the capacity for high-intensity work in several reported contexts; no boxing-specific trial identified; the debate is largely endurance-framed
citation: Burke LM. Re-Examining High-Fat Diets for Sports Performance: Did We Call the 'Nail in the Coffin' Too Soon? Sports Med. 2015.
ppbf_implication: PPBF should not endorse a low-carbohydrate/high-fat approach for boxers; fat intake guidance should come from the ACSM/AND/DC joint position stand.
verified_title: Re-Examining High-Fat Diets for Sports Performance: Did We Call the 'Nail in the Coffin' Too Soon?

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: The goal of prehydrating is to begin activity euhydrated with normal plasma electrolytes; drinking during exercise should prevent excessive dehydration (defined in the position stand as greater than 2% body-weight loss from water deficit) and excessive electrolyte change. Sweat rate and sweat electrolyte content vary considerably between individuals, so fluid replacement should be individualised.
effect_or_estimate: >2% body-weight water deficit is the stated threshold for 'excessive' dehydration
limitations: 2007 position stand; the 2% figure is a threshold below which performance decrement is generally avoided, not a validated individual trigger; individual variability is explicitly large
citation: Sawka MN, et al. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007.
ppbf_implication: Supports a session pre/post body-weight change log in PPBF as an observation, not as an automated hydration verdict.
verified_title: American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Overhydration is a distinct and potentially fatal risk: exercise-associated hyponatraemia is addressed by a dedicated international consensus development conference, whose 3rd statement was published in 2015.
population: Exercising individuals; endurance and military populations most reported
effect_or_estimate: No single numeric threshold appropriate for app use; diagnosis is biochemical (serum sodium)
transfer_status: General transfer; relevant to boxers who 'water load' before a weigh-in
limitations: Most documented cases arise in prolonged endurance events; the boxing-specific risk from deliberate water loading before weigh-in is plausible but not quantified in the literature located
citation: Hew-Butler T, et al. Statement of the 3rd International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus Development Conference, Carlsbad, California, 2015. Br J Sports Med. 2015.
ppbf_implication: PPBF must state that 'drink more' is not universally safe advice and that water loading protocols are outside the app's scope entirely.
verified_title: Statement of the 3rd International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus Development Conference, Carlsbad, California, 2015.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Dehydration assessment requires distinguishing loss of hypo-osmotic body water (intracellular dehydration) from iso-osmotic loss (extracellular dehydration); single-measure field methods have meaningful diagnostic and biological variation.
effect_or_estimate: No single field method is presented as sufficient alone; method error is the review's central theme
limitations: Field hydration measures (urine specific gravity, urine colour, body-mass change) each carry error; combining measures is recommended over relying on one
citation: Cheuvront SN, Kenefick RW. Dehydration: physiology, assessment, and performance effects. Compr Physiol. 2014.
ppbf_implication: SHADOW must not convert a single hydration measure into a clearance or readiness verdict; it may log the measure with its uncertainty.
verified_title: Dehydration: physiology, assessment, and performance effects.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Sweating rate and sweat sodium concentration vary substantially within and between individuals, and unstandardised sweat-testing methods produce inconsistent or inaccurate results.
effect_or_estimate: Large intra- and inter-individual variability; no defensible population default value
limitations: Because variability is large and method-dependent, any single sweat sodium figure applied to an athlete is unreliable
citation: Baker LB. Sweating Rate and Sweat Sodium Concentration in Athletes: A Review of Methodology and Intra/Interindividual Variability. Sports Med. 2017.
ppbf_implication: PPBF must not publish a default electrolyte replacement number; TBD pending in-gym sweat-rate measurement if ever undertaken.
verified_title: Sweating Rate and Sweat Sodium Concentration in Athletes: A Review of Methodology and Intra/Interindividual Variability.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Iron deficiency is common in athlete populations, with reported deficiency in approximately 15-35% of female athlete cohorts and approximately 5-11% of male athlete cohorts; exercise-induced elevation of hepcidin is a proposed contributing mechanism.
population: Athletes, especially female and endurance athletes
effect_or_estimate: ~15-35% of female athlete cohorts; ~5-11% of male athlete cohorts
transfer_status: General athlete transfer; no boxing-specific prevalence located
limitations: Cohort prevalence ranges depend heavily on the ferritin cut-off used, which is not standardised; endurance-weighted evidence base; correlation between exercise and hepcidin does not establish causation of clinical deficiency
citation: Sim M, et al. Iron considerations for the athlete: a narrative review. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2019.
ppbf_implication: Iron status is a blood test ordered and interpreted by a physician; SHADOW may raise a referral flag, never a supplement recommendation.
verified_title: Iron considerations for the athlete: a narrative review.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: The interpretation of iron status in athletic females has been argued to require a shift from the older paradigm, indicating the ferritin thresholds and screening approach are not settled.
effect_or_estimate: No single agreed ferritin threshold; the paper's argument is that the conventional paradigm is inadequate
limitations: Threshold disagreement means any app-side numeric iron rule would encode a contested value
citation: Sim M, Dawson B, Landers G, Trinder D, Peeling P (author set per record). Iron status in athletic females, a shift in perspective on an old paradigm. J Sports Sci. 2021.
ppbf_implication: PPBF must not hard-code a ferritin cut-off; the value is TBD and owned by the athlete's physician.
verified_title: Iron status in athletic females, a shift in perspective on an old paradigm.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Iron deficiency and iron deficiency anaemia are documented in adolescent athletes of both sexes, including in sports that are not calorie-restricting.
population: Adolescent basketball and football players in Israel
study_design: Retrospective cross-sectional analysis of clinical records
effect_or_estimate: Prevalence stratified by ferritin thresholds (mild <=30, moderate <=20, severe <=10 ug/L)
limitations: Two sports-medicine centres in one country; retrospective clinical records; ball-sport population, not weight-category athletes
citation: Constantini N, et al. Iron Deficiency and Anemia in Male and Female Adolescent Athletes Who Engage in Ball Games. J Clin Med. 2023.
ppbf_implication: Supports including iron in PPBF's youth medical-referral prompts, not in any app-side calculation.
verified_title: Iron Deficiency and Anemia in Male and Female Adolescent Athletes Who Engage in Ball Games.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: In a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials in athletes, oral vitamin D supplementation raised serum 25(OH)D concentrations; the effect on physical performance was the separate question the review was designed to test.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
effect_or_estimate: Consistent increase in serum 25(OH)D; performance effects reported as far less consistent
limitations: Small number of trials; heterogeneous doses, baseline status, latitude and season; raising a biomarker is not the same as improving performance
citation: Farrokhyar F, et al. Effects of Vitamin D Supplementation on Serum 25-Hydroxyvitamin D Concentrations and Physical Performance in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Sports Med. 2017.
ppbf_implication: Vitamin D testing and dosing is a physician decision; SHADOW may not suggest a dose.
verified_title: Effects of Vitamin D Supplementation on Serum 25-Hydroxyvitamin D Concentrations and Physical Performance in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Vitamin D insufficiency prevalence in elite athletes has been estimated in a systematic review and meta-analysis that also examined differences between sexes and between adults and adolescents.
effect_or_estimate: Prevalence estimate with sex and age-group subgroup comparisons
limitations: Prevalence depends on the insufficiency cut-off used and on latitude and season, both explicitly identified as moderators
citation: Wilson-Barnes SL, et al. Prevalence and novel risk factors for vitamin D insufficiency in elite athletes: systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Nutr. 2022.
ppbf_implication: Punxsutawney's latitude and an indoor training environment are plausible risk modifiers; this is a physician-screening prompt, not an app rule.
verified_title: Prevalence and novel risk factors for vitamin D insufficiency in elite athletes: systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: The IOC supplements consensus notes that calcium intakes of 1500 mg/day and 1500-2000 IU vitamin D are recommended to optimise bone health specifically in athletes with low energy availability or menstrual dysfunction, and that skin exposure to sunlight normally accounts for about 90% of vitamin D supply.
population: Athletes with low energy availability or menstrual dysfunction
sex: Both, with female emphasis for the menstrual-dysfunction subgroup
effect_or_estimate: Calcium 1500 mg/day; vitamin D 1500-2000 IU/day in that specific clinical subgroup
limitations: These figures apply to a defined clinical subgroup under medical management, not to a general gym population, and must not be generalised
citation: Maughan RJ, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018.
ppbf_implication: These are clinician-managed values; SHADOW may cite them in coach education, never issue them to an athlete.
verified_title: IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: The IOC consensus identifies a small set of supplements with good evidence of direct performance benefit: caffeine, creatine (as creatine monohydrate), nitrate, sodium bicarbonate, and possibly beta-alanine; a complete nutritional assessment should precede any supplement decision.
effect_or_estimate: Five named agents with 'good evidence'; all other categories are framed as unsupported or risk-bearing
transfer_status: High-performance athlete transfer; explicitly not addressed to youth or community athletes
limitations: The consensus is written for high-performance adult athletes; it does not endorse supplement use in youth, and the assessment-first requirement is frequently ignored in practice
citation: Maughan RJ, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018 (also IJSNEM 2018).
doi_or_pmid: PMID 29540367 / DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027; parallel publication PMID 29589768 / DOI 10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0020
verification: pubmed:PMID 29540367 (full text via PMC5867441) and PMID 29589768 (metadata)
ppbf_implication: PPBF's default position is food-first and no supplements for minors; the five-agent list is coach-education content only.
verified_title: IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Caffeine improves exercise performance at doses of 3-6 mg/kg body mass; very high doses (about 9 mg/kg) are associated with a high incidence of side effects without additional benefit, and the most common timing is 60 minutes pre-exercise.
sex: Both, though the underlying study base is predominantly young men
study_design: Position stand (ISSN) plus umbrella review of 21 meta-analyses
effect_or_estimate: 3-6 mg/kg effective; minimum effective dose possibly as low as 2 mg/kg; >=9 mg/kg no added benefit and more side effects
transfer_status: General exercise transfer; sodium-bicarbonate and combat-specific work exists separately but caffeine trials in boxing were not located
limitations: Umbrella review graded most evidence as moderate with some low to very low quality; most included studies were in young men; caffeine is not on the WADA Prohibited List but is on the Monitoring Program; it affects sleep and anxiety
citation: Guest NS, et al. ISSN position stand: caffeine and exercise performance. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021; Grgic J, et al. Br J Sports Med. 2020 (umbrella review).
ppbf_implication: PPBF position: no caffeine supplementation guidance for minors; adult content is education only, with sleep and anxiety caveats.
verified_title: Wake up and smell the coffee: caffeine supplementation and exercise performance-an umbrella review of 21 published meta-analyses.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Creatine monohydrate increases intramuscular creatine and improves high-intensity exercise performance; a commonly cited protocol is a loading phase of 20 g/day for 5 days followed by 3-5 g/day maintenance, or approximately 0.1 g/kg body mass/day.
study_design: Position stand (ISSN) plus a follow-up ISSN review of common questions
effect_or_estimate: Loading 20 g/day x 5 days; maintenance 3-5 g/day or ~0.1 g/kg/day
transfer_status: General exercise transfer; no boxing-specific creatine trial located
limitations: Creatine causes intracellular water retention and an increase in body mass, which is a direct conflict for a weight-category athlete near a weigh-in; the ISSN position addresses safety in adults, not in a community youth programme
citation: Kreider RB, et al. ISSN position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017; Antonio J, et al. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021.
verification: pubmed:PMID 28615996 and PMID 33557850 (metadata + abstracts retrieved); dose protocol confirmed in IOC consensus full text PMC5867441
ppbf_implication: The mass-gain effect makes creatine a weight-making conflict; PPBF should route any adult interest to a dietitian and prohibit recommendation to minors.
verified_title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation in exercise, sport, and medicine.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Whether the physiological benefits and safety profile of creatine established in adults extend to children and adolescents is not established; the literature on paediatric creatine use is described as limited relative to the adult evidence base.
effect_or_estimate: No adequate paediatric efficacy or long-term safety dataset identified
transfer_status: N/A — the gap is the finding
limitations: Absence of demonstrated harm is not demonstration of safety; the paediatric literature is dominated by clinical rather than athletic applications
citation: Jagim AR, Kerksick CM. Creatine Supplementation in Children and Adolescents. Nutrients. 2021; and Creatine supplementation in the pediatric and adolescent athlete - a literature review. J Orthop. 2023.
ppbf_implication: PPBF position: SHADOW must never recommend creatine to a minor; any parent/athlete question routes to a physician and dietitian.
verified_title: Creatine Supplementation in Children and Adolescents.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Sodium bicarbonate at doses from 0.2 to 0.5 g/kg improves muscular endurance performance and performance in combat sports including boxing, judo, karate, taekwondo and wrestling; ergogenic effects are most established for high-intensity tasks lasting between 30 seconds and 12 minutes, and 0.2 g/kg appears to be the minimum effective single dose.
sex: Both (the position stand states effects in men and women)
study_design: Position stand (ISSN) plus a combat-sport-specific systematic review and meta-analysis
effect_or_estimate: 0.2-0.5 g/kg; minimum effective single dose 0.2 g/kg; effects established for 30 s to 12 min tasks
boxing_specific: Partially — boxing is named in the ISSN position stand; the combat meta-analysis is judo-weighted
transfer_status: Combat-sport evidence exists but the pooled combat analysis is small and judo-dominated; direct boxing trials are sparse
limitations: Gastrointestinal distress at ergogenic doses is explicitly flagged by the IOC consensus and can impair rather than improve performance; the combat-sport meta-analysis is based on only eight studies with surrogate outcomes (blood lactate, RPE, Wingate power, Special Judo Fitness Test)
citation: Grgic J, et al. ISSN position stand: sodium bicarbonate and exercise performance. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021; de Oliveira LF, et al. Curr Nutr Rep. 2022.
ppbf_implication: Not appropriate for PPBF youth or novice lanes; the GI-distress risk near a bout is a real harm pathway.
verified_title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: sodium bicarbonate and exercise performance.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Four weeks of beta-alanine supplementation at 4-6 g daily significantly increases muscle carnosine and has been shown to improve exercise performance, with more pronounced effects in open end-point tasks lasting 1 to 4 minutes; the only reported side effect is paraesthesia, attenuable with divided lower doses of about 1.6 g or a sustained-release formula.
effect_or_estimate: 4-6 g/day for at least 2-4 weeks; effects strongest for 1-4 min tasks; divided 1.6 g doses reduce paraesthesia
boxing_specific: No — the 1-4 min task window overlaps a boxing round but no boxing-specific trial was located
transfer_status: General exercise transfer with a plausible task-duration match to boxing rounds
limitations: 2015 position stand; the IOC consensus lists beta-alanine only as 'possibly' evidence-supported; strength and long-duration endurance effects are explicitly stated as needing more research
citation: Trexler ET, et al. International society of sports nutrition position stand: Beta-Alanine. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2015.
ppbf_implication: Task-duration match makes beta-alanine a plausible boxing hypothesis; it remains untested in boxing and out of scope for PPBF youth lanes.
verified_title: International society of sports nutrition position stand: Beta-Alanine.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: In a meta-analysis of 123 studies and 1705 participants, inorganic nitrate ingestion produced a small but statistically significant improvement in exercise performance (SMD 0.101; 95% CI 0.051 to 0.151; I-squared 0%), with nitrate salt supplements not as effective as beetroot juice.
study_design: Systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression
transfer_status: General transfer; no boxing-specific nitrate trial located
limitations: The pooled effect is small; oral antibacterial mouthwash use abolishes the nitrate-nitrite conversion pathway; most trials are in endurance contexts
citation: Gao C, et al. Factors that Moderate the Effect of Nitrate Ingestion on Exercise Performance in Adults: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analyses and Meta-Regressions. Adv Nutr. 2022.
ppbf_implication: A food-first route (leafy greens, beetroot) is low-cost and food-access-compatible; the expected effect is small and unproven in boxing.
verified_title: Factors that Moderate the Effect of Nitrate Ingestion on Exercise Performance in Adults: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analyses and Meta-Regressions.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Undeclared doping substances are highly prevalent in commercial sports nutrition supplements: of 66 high-risk products purchased from Dutch web shops, 25 (38%) contained undeclared doping substances including the stimulants oxilofrine, BMPEA and NBDMPEA.
study_design: Laboratory analysis by an ISO 17025 accredited screen (LGC)
sample_size: 66 products from 21 brands across 17 web shops
effect_or_estimate: 38% (25/66) contained undeclared doping substances
transfer_status: N/A — applies to any athlete purchasing supplements
limitations: Deliberately targeted high-risk product categories, so 38% is not the market-wide contamination rate; single-country web-shop sample; contamination prevalence varies enormously by product category
citation: Duiven E, et al. Undeclared Doping Substances are Highly Prevalent in Commercial Sports Nutrition Supplements. J Sports Sci Med. 2021.
ppbf_implication: PPBF should treat any non-certified supplement as a live anti-doping and health risk and say so plainly to athletes and parents.
verified_title: Undeclared Doping Substances are Highly Prevalent in Commercial Sports Nutrition Supplements.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: A review of 23 qualifying studies found substances prohibited by WADA, including prohormones and stimulants, present in most of the dietary supplements analysed across that literature.
study_design: Review of analytical studies (446 identified, 23 met inclusion)
effect_or_estimate: Prohibited substances present in most analysed supplements across the included studies
limitations: Included studies used varied analytical methods and targeted varied product categories; a synthesis of contamination studies is not a market prevalence estimate
citation: Martinez-Sanz JM, et al. Intended or Unintended Doping? A Review of the Presence of Doping Substances in Dietary Supplements Used in Sports. Nutrients. 2017.
ppbf_implication: Reinforces PPBF's food-first default and its no-supplement position for minors.
verified_title: Intended or Unintended Doping? A Review of the Presence of Doping Substances in Dietary Supplements Used in Sports.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: The World Anti-Doping Code applies strict liability: an athlete is responsible for any prohibited substance found in their sample regardless of how it got there or whether there was intent to cheat, with the burden on the athlete to establish how the substance entered their system if seeking a reduced sanction.
population: All athletes subject to the WADA Code
effect_or_estimate: No numeric threshold; the principle is categorical
transfer_status: Applies to any PPBF athlete competing under a WADA Code signatory
limitations: Jurisdictional scope matters: not every PPBF athlete is subject to the Code at every level of competition, and professional boxing commissions operate their own testing regimes
citation: World Anti-Doping Agency. Strict Liability in Anti-Doping (Questions & Answers).
verification: web_search: WADA strict liability Q&A page retrieved 2026-08-07
ppbf_implication: PPBF athlete and parent education must state strict liability explicitly before any supplement conversation.
independent_verification_detail: governing body, statute, regulator or repo document — URL + retrieval date in verification column

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: USADA recognises NSF Certified for Sport as the third-party certification programme best suited to reduce supplement risk, while stating that using a certified product significantly reduces but does not eliminate the chance of testing positive; certification includes a manufacturing audit and label evaluation, not just finished-product testing.
population: Athletes subject to US anti-doping jurisdiction
effect_or_estimate: Risk reduction, not elimination; no numeric residual-risk figure is given
transfer_status: Applies to any PPBF athlete who chooses to use supplements
limitations: Certification is a risk-reduction step, not a safety guarantee; USADA explicitly advises verifying the lot number rather than trusting a printed logo; dietary supplements are regulated post-market in the US
citation: US Anti-Doping Agency. Supplement Risk and NSF Certified for Sport; Third-Party Testing Guidance; Athlete Advisory: Always Verify Third-Party Certified Logos.
verification: web_search: USADA supplement risk / third-party testing pages retrieved 2026-08-07
ppbf_implication: If an adult PPBF athlete uses a supplement, third-party certification plus lot verification is the minimum standard PPBF should state.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: A 2025 systematic review of doping in combat sports reported that anabolic agents, diuretics, hormone modulators and NSAIDs are commonly detected, particularly among athletes in heavier weight categories and those engaging in rapid weight loss.
sample_size: 6 of 21 identified articles met inclusion criteria
effect_or_estimate: Qualitative pattern only; the review included only six studies
transfer_status: Combat-sport evidence directly relevant to boxing
limitations: Only six included studies; the association between rapid weight loss and diuretic detection is correlational and does not establish that weight cutting causes doping; detection rates reflect testing programmes, not true prevalence
citation: Doping in combat sports: a systematic review. Phys Sportsmed. 2025.
ppbf_implication: The diuretic-plus-weight-cut pattern is a specific PPBF education point: the fastest weight-making shortcuts are also anti-doping violations.
verified_title: Doping in combat sports: a systematic review.

claim: USA Boxing operates a daily weigh-in model: all boxers must weigh in on the day they box, with zero tolerance for any overweight and a daily weigh-in duration of one hour or until completed.
population: Amateur boxers under USA Boxing sanction
effect_or_estimate: Same-day (daily) weigh-in; zero tolerance for overweight
limitations: Rulebook provisions change by edition; local/regional (LBC) competitions may set weigh-in process at the Official in Charge's discretion; PPBF must read the current edition rather than rely on this summary
citation: USA Boxing National Rule Book (editions revised 1 January 2024 and 1 January 2025).

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Professional boxing typically uses a day-before weigh-in, and this differs by jurisdiction: the British Boxing Board of Control requires weigh-in not less than 24 and not more than 36 hours before a tournament, while Pennsylvania regulation requires professional weigh-in no more than 24 hours (30 hours under extenuating circumstances) before the contracted contest time and allows an overweight boxer no more than 3 pounds of loss in a 3-hour reweigh window.

claim: The WBC weight management programme adds pre-bout weight checks at 30, 14 and 7 days before a title bout, at which the boxer must not exceed the division limit by more than 10%, 5% and 3% respectively, plus a same-day arena check at which the boxer must not exceed the official weigh-in weight by more than 10%.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Rapid weight loss is highly prevalent in child and adolescent combat athletes, reported at 25% to 94% depending on sport, age and competition level, with a magnitude ranging from about 1% to 6.3 (SD 3.7) percent of body mass; the review's authors conclude RWL needs stringent regulation and ideally should be banned in this population.
sample_size: Not extracted (multiple studies across combat sports)
effect_or_estimate: Prevalence 25-94%; magnitude ~1% to 6.3 +/- 3.7% body mass
transfer_status: Combat-sport youth evidence, directly applicable to PPBF's youth lane
limitations: Wide prevalence range reflects heterogeneous self-report instruments; self-reported RWL is subject to recall and social-desirability bias; the recommendation to ban is the authors' conclusion, not a governing-body rule
citation: Berkovich BE, et al. Patterns of weight cycling in youth Olympic combat sports: a systematic review. J Eat Disord. 2022.
ppbf_implication: This is the primary published support for PPBF adopting a categorical prohibition on youth weight cutting.
verified_title: Patterns of weight cycling in youth Olympic combat sports: a systematic review.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: In a systematic review of 16 studies (4432 participants: 156 female, 4276 male) across boxing, judo, MMA, taekwondo and wrestling, the largest changes in body mass occurred in mixed martial arts cohorts, with rapid weight loss of 7.4 (SD 1.1) kg (about 10%) and rapid weight gain of 7.4 (SD 2.8) kg (11.7 +/- 4.7%); recovery duration permitted ranged from 3 to 32 hours.
effect_or_estimate: MMA extremes: RWL 7.4 +/- 1.1 kg (~10%); RWG 7.4 +/- 2.8 kg (11.7 +/- 4.7%); recovery window 3-32 h
boxing_specific: Partially — boxing is one of five sports included
transfer_status: Combat-sport evidence directly relevant; the MMA extremes are not boxing values
limitations: Only 3 of 16 studies reported RWL directly (14 reported RWG); female representation is 3.5% of the sample; the review explicitly flags a lack of data; the extremes are MMA-specific and must not be presented as boxing figures
citation: Barley OR, Chapman DW, Abbiss CR. The Magnitude of Rapid Weight Loss and Rapid Weight Gain in Combat Sport Athletes Preparing for Competition: A Systematic Review. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019.
ppbf_implication: Magnitude scales with the recovery window the ruleset permits; the same-day amateur weigh-in structurally limits the incentive.
verified_title: The Magnitude of Rapid Weight Loss and Rapid Weight Gain in Combat Sport Athletes Preparing for Competition: A Systematic Review.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: In official California State Athletic Commission data on 399 male professional boxers (2015-2018), 389 (97.5%) gained weight between official weigh-in and competition, with a mean gain of 4.4 (SD 2.2) kg, corresponding to 7.2 (SD 3.5) percent of body mass; 82 athletes (20.6%) gained 10% or more, and international-promotion competitors gained more than regional competitors (8.0 +/- 3.0% vs 6.6 +/- 3.7%).
population: Male professional boxers licensed in California
study_design: Retrospective analysis of official commission weight records
effect_or_estimate: 97.5% gained weight; mean 4.4 +/- 2.2 kg (7.2 +/- 3.5%); 20.6% gained >=10%; international 8.0 +/- 3.0% vs regional 6.6 +/- 3.7% (p<0.001)
transfer_status: N/A — direct boxing evidence, but professional (day-before weigh-in) not amateur
limitations: Single-state commission records; male only; measures weight regain, which is an indirect indicator of the preceding weight cut, not a direct measure of it
citation: Rapid weight gain following weight cutting in male professional boxers. Phys Sportsmed. 2021 (California State Athletic Commission data 2015-2018).
ppbf_implication: This is the strongest boxing-specific quantification available and should anchor PPBF's professional-lane risk education.
verified_title: Rapid weight gain following weight cutting in male professional boxers.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: In 17 male elite amateur boxers, a body-mass loss of 5.6 (SD 1.7) percent achieved by fluid and food restriction plus induced sweat loss produced measurable decreases in total body water (6.0 +/- 0.9%), extracellular water (12.4 +/- 7.6%), total haemoglobin mass (5.3 +/- 3.8%) and blood volume (7.6%).
effect_or_estimate: 5.6 +/- 1.7% body-mass loss; total body water -6.0 +/- 0.9%; extracellular water -12.4 +/- 7.6%; total haemoglobin mass -5.3 +/- 3.8%; blood volume -7.6%
limitations: Very small sample (n=17), male only, young adult; CO-rebreathing and bioimpedance estimates carry their own error; a reduction in total haemoglobin mass has implications for oxygen carriage that this study did not link to bout outcome
citation: Reljic D, et al. Rapid weight loss and the body fluid balance and hemoglobin mass of elite amateur boxers. J Athl Train. 2013.
ppbf_implication: Demonstrates that a boxer's weight cut is a measurable haematological and fluid-compartment event, not merely a scale number.
verified_title: Rapid weight loss and the body fluid balance and hemoglobin mass of elite amateur boxers.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: A meta-analysis of weight cutting in combat athletes found exercise performance was unchanged between pre-rapid-weight-loss and post-rapid-weight-gain (g = 0.22; 95% CI -0.18 to 0.62), but small reductions immediately post-RWL in maximal strength (g = -0.29; 95% CI -0.54 to -0.03) and repeated high-intensity-effort performance (g = -0.37; 95% CI -0.59 to -0.16).
effect_or_estimate: Pre-RWL vs post-RWG g=0.22 (95% CI -0.18 to 0.62, non-significant); post-RWL maximal strength g=-0.29; repeated high-intensity effort g=-0.37
transfer_status: Combat-sport evidence; laboratory performance tests, not bout performance
limitations: Laboratory tests are surrogates for competitive boxing performance; the recovery window varied from 3 to 36 hours, so the null pre-to-post-RWG result cannot be applied to a same-day amateur weigh-in with a short recovery window; absence of a detected decrement is not evidence of safety
citation: Effects of Weight Cutting on Exercise Performance in Combat Athletes: A Meta-Analysis. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2022.
ppbf_implication: Critical for PPBF messaging: 'performance largely recovers' is a professional-lane, long-recovery-window finding and must not be extended to same-day amateur weigh-ins or to health outcomes.
verified_title: Effects of Weight Cutting on Exercise Performance in Combat Athletes: A Meta-Analysis.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Two boxing studies found rapid weight loss and post-weigh-in weight regain were not associated with competitive success: in 100 elite Australian boxers (30 women, 70 men) regain did not differ between winners and losers, and in 83 elite European youth male boxers boxing experience rather than RWL predicted medal winning.
population: Elite amateur boxers (Australian national championships; European youth championships)
sex: Both (Australian sample); male only (European youth sample)
effect_or_estimate: Australia: pre-bout mass above weigh-in by 2.12 +/- 1.62% (men) and 1.49 +/- 1.65% (women); no difference between winners and losers. Europe: boxing experience OR 1.33 (95% CI 1.06-1.66) for competitive success; only 25% were in the RWL group
limitations: Observational; absence of an association in these samples does not prove weight cutting confers no advantage in other contexts; the European study was male-only and single-championship; competitive success is a coarse binary outcome
citation: Reale R, et al. Weight Regain: No Link to Success in a Real-Life Multiday Boxing Tournament. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2016; Rapid Weight Loss Is Not Associated With Competitive Success in Elite Youth Olympic-Style Boxers in Europe. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018.
ppbf_implication: This is the strongest counter-argument PPBF coaches can give athletes: in boxing specifically, the cut has not been shown to buy wins.
verified_title: Weight Regain: No Link to Success in a Real-Life Multiday Boxing Tournament.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: In the same European youth boxing study, more than 45% of the 83 boxers self-reported using several weight-cutting methods simultaneously that are known to be serious health hazards, and 33% reported muscle weakness as a consequence of rapid weight loss.
population: Elite youth male boxers from 12 European countries
effect_or_estimate: >45% used multiple hazardous methods simultaneously; 33% reported muscle weakness
limitations: Self-report; male only; elite youth sample not representative of a community club; symptom reporting is subjective
citation: Rapid Weight Loss Is Not Associated With Competitive Success in Elite Youth Olympic-Style Boxers in Europe. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018.
ppbf_implication: Combined-method cutting in minors is documented in boxing; PPBF's prohibition and its escalation triggers must name the specific methods.
verified_title: Rapid Weight Loss Is Not Associated With Competitive Success in Elite Youth Olympic-Style Boxers in Europe.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Three previously healthy collegiate wrestlers died during November-December 1997 while engaged in intentional rapid weight loss; all three restricted food and fluid and maximised sweat losses by exercising vigorously in hot environments while wearing vapour-impermeable suits under warm-up suits, producing dehydration and hyperthermia.
effect_or_estimate: 3 deaths in a 33-day period; the fatal method combination is explicitly described
transfer_status: Other-combat-sport transfer; the method combination is identical to that reported in boxing
limitations: Case series, not a rate; the underlying incidence of death from rapid weight loss is not established; wrestling's rules and weigh-in structure differ from boxing's
citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Hyperthermia and dehydration-related deaths associated with intentional rapid weight loss in three collegiate wrestlers - North Carolina, Wisconsin, and Michigan, November-December 1997. MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep. 1998 (also reported in JAMA).
ppbf_implication: These deaths are the historical basis for the NCAA weight-management programme and are the core of PPBF's prohibited-practices list.
verified_title: Hyperthermia and dehydration-related deaths associated with intentional rapid weight loss in three collegiate wrestlers--North Carolina, Wisconsin, and Michigan, November-December 1997.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: In 12 male wrestlers, high-intensity sport-specific training combined with rapid weight loss produced significant increases in kidney function markers compared with identical training without rapid weight loss: blood urea nitrogen (p=0.002), uric acid (p<0.001) and serum creatinine (p=0.006).
effect_or_estimate: BUN p=0.002; uric acid p<0.001; serum creatinine p=0.006; Cystatin-C slightly elevated after both phases
limitations: Very small sample (n=12); male only; biochemical markers are surrogates and their elevation does not equal clinical acute kidney injury; short-term study with no follow-up
citation: Rapid weight loss can increase the risk of acute kidney injury in wrestlers. BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med. 2023.
ppbf_implication: Renal strain is a documented harm pathway; any PPBF athlete presenting with symptoms after a cut is a physician referral, not a coach judgement.
verified_title: Rapid weight loss can increase the risk of acute kidney injury in wrestlers.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: Rapid weight loss in elite judo athletes affected balance and reaction time as well as strength; a separate study found 5% rapid weight loss over 48 hours significantly worsened urine specific gravity and affected judo-specific performance measures.
sex: Both (38 athletes, mixed) and male only (n=18 study)
effect_or_estimate: Balance and reaction time decrements post weigh-in; USG significantly higher after 5% loss
limitations: Judo is not boxing; small samples; the boxing-specific consequence for a sport where head-impact avoidance depends on reaction time and balance is inferred, not measured
citation: Effects of Rapid Weight Loss on Balance and Reaction Time in Elite Judo Athletes. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018; Effect of Rapid Weight Loss on Hydration Status and Performance in Elite Judo Athletes. Biology. 2022.
ppbf_implication: Degraded balance and reaction time in a sport where the athlete is being punched in the head is the single most important PPBF safety argument; label it as judo-transfer, not boxing-proven.
verified_title: Effects of Rapid Weight Loss on Balance and Reaction Time in Elite Judo Athletes.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: The evidence on whether rapid weight loss impairs physical performance is not uniform: one study reported that rapid weight loss of up to five percent of body mass in less than seven days did not affect physical performance, and an updated systematic review found no clear consistent negative effect across performance parameters.
study_design: Primary study plus updated systematic review
effect_or_estimate: No significant performance decrement detected at <=5% loss over <7 days in the cited work
limitations: These null findings concern PHYSICAL PERFORMANCE measured in a laboratory, not health, not cognition, not head-impact tolerance, and not youth; a null result in an underpowered study is weak evidence of no effect; performance neutrality is not a safety endorsement
citation: Rapid Weight Loss of Up to Five Percent of the Body Mass in Less Than 7 Days Does Not Affect Physical Performance. Front Physiol. 2022; Effects of Different Rapid Weight Loss Strategies and Percentages on Performance-Related Parameters in Combat Sports: An Updated Systematic Review. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2023.
ppbf_implication: SHADOW must present both sides: performance-neutrality findings exist and are frequently used to justify cutting; they do not address health, youth, or same-day weigh-in contexts.
verified_title: Rapid Weight Loss of Up to Five Percent of the Body Mass in Less Than 7 Days Does Not Affect Physical Performance in Official Olympic Combat Athletes With Weight Classes: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis.

track: T7-Performance Nutrition
claim: The NCAA wrestling weight management programme requires a urine specific gravity of 1.020 or lower before body-composition assessment, sets a minimum competitive weight based on 5% body fat for men (with a separate women's packet using a 12% floor), and limits descent to a maximum of 1.5% of body weight per week.
effect_or_estimate: USG <=1.020; 5% body fat floor (men) / 12% (women); maximum 1.5% body weight loss per week
transfer_status: Other-combat-sport regulatory transfer; boxing has no equivalent programme
limitations: The NCAA's own packet states the 1.020 threshold is partly evidence-based and partly arbitrary; state high-school federations use 1.025 instead, showing the threshold is not settled; body-fat floors are derived from prediction equations with their own error
citation: NCAA Wrestling Weight Management Program Packets (men's and women's, 2023-24 through 2025-26 editions).
verification: web_search: NCAA men's and women's Weight Management Program packet text retrieved 2026-08-07; UIL/CIF/MPSSAA 1.025 variants also retrieved
ppbf_implication: This is the best-developed regulatory model PPBF could adapt; its numbers are wrestling's and would require PPBF validation before adoption.
