track: A8 - Video/Film Ontology and Measurement Crosswalk
topic: Coder tier is a first-order determinant of data quality
claim: In the published amateur boxing performance-analysis template, inter-observer reliability was assessed with analysts of differing experience - an amateur boxer and an experienced analyst - and was substantially weaker than intra-observer reliability, with agreement ranging from 33% to 100% across indicators.
study_design: Reliability testing within an instrument development study
effect_or_estimate: Inter-observer agreement 33-100% across indicators versus intra-observer 80-100%
limitations: Two analysts is too few to separate the effect of experience from individual differences; the inference that tier drives agreement is supported but not isolated by this design
citation: Thomson E, Lamb K, Nicholas C (2013). The development of a reliable amateur boxing performance analysis template. J Sports Sci.
ppbf_implication: Justifies coder_tier as a mandatory field (crosswalk A8-X007) and a calibration test before a coach's labels enter any aggregate. PPBF's own tier effect is TBD and should be measured directly.
verified_title: The development of a reliable amateur boxing performance analysis template.

track: A8 - Video/Film Ontology and Measurement Crosswalk
topic: Occlusion is the binding constraint on automated boxing video analysis
claim: Pose estimators are described as unreliable on sports video because of domain shift, motion blur and occlusion, which degrades downstream tasks depending on pose; in boxing the coded athlete is routinely occluded by the opponent, and even a favourable three-camera setup was required to establish head-contact ground truth in the boxing sensor validation work.
study_design: Inference synthesising a computer-science methods preprint with the boxing sensor validation study
effect_or_estimate: Not applicable - inference
transfer_status: SYNTHESIS ACROSS COMPUTER SCIENCE AND BOXING SENSOR VALIDATION
limitations: This is an inference drawn across two literatures rather than a single measured finding; no study has directly quantified occlusion-driven error for boxing action recognition
source_type: Synthesis of a preprint and a peer-reviewed article
citation: Video Pose Distillation for Few-Shot, Fine-Grained Sports Action Recognition (2021). arXiv preprint.
ppbf_implication: Makes occlusion burden a mandatory recorded field (crosswalk A8-X004, label A8V-A13) and is the principal reason pose-derived boxing measures are on the do-not-build-yet list.
independent_verification_detail: governing body, statute, regulator or repo document — URL + retrieval date in verification column

track: A8 - Video/Film Ontology and Measurement Crosswalk
topic: No verified automated detector exists for boxing defensive actions
claim: Across the boxing and combat-sport literature searched, published automated recognition work addresses punch type and generic boxing action classes; no verified automated detector for boxing defensive actions such as slips, rolls, parries or shoulder rolls was identified.
study_design: Absence of evidence from a structured literature search across PubMed, OpenAlex and arXiv
effect_or_estimate: Not applicable - no evidence located
limitations: Absence of evidence in the databases searched is not proof of absence; commercial systems may exist but vendor claims are low authority and were not verifiable
citation: An active machine learning framework for automatic boxing punch recognition and classification using upper limb kinematics (2025). PLoS ONE.
ppbf_implication: Every defensive label in the ontology is marked automatability LOW or NONE with the reliability status UNTESTED. Defensive coding remains a human task at PPBF for the foreseeable future.
verified_title: An active machine learning framework for automatic boxing punch recognition and classification using upper limb kinematics.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: Out-of-school-time (OST) program quality for low-income adolescents depends on identifiable staffing practices (leadership, professional development, community connection) and on recruitment that removes transport and cost barriers and uses familiar community spaces; seven engagement levers were synthesised (agency, relevance, competence, belonging, exposure, safety/wellness).
population: US out-of-school-time programs serving low-income adolescents
effect_or_estimate: Qualitative synthesis; no pooled effect size reported
transfer_status: TRANSFER from youth-development/OST programming to boxing gym operations — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: US-only; heterogeneous designs; 'promising practice' not causal; no boxing programs identified
citation: Levine et al., Journal of Adolescence, 2025
ppbf_implication: Anchors the staffing/onboarding and access columns of operating_model_comparison; supports treating transport and cost as first-class operational variables, not athlete attributes.
verified_title: Promising Practices of Out-of-School Time Programs for Low-Income Adolescents: A Systematic Review.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: Youth engagement in OST programs was associated with program content and perceived staff quality (caring, competent); a monetary incentive trended NEGATIVELY with engagement.
population: Primarily low-income US middle/high-school youth across 30 OST programs
effect_or_estimate: Program content and staff quality strongly associated with engagement; incentive-engagement association negative (trend). Correlational — not causal.
transfer_status: TRANSFER from OST youth programming — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: Cross-sectional; self-report; correlation is not causation; no boxing setting
citation: Greene et al., Journal of Youth and Adolescence, 2012
ppbf_implication: Coach quality is an operational variable SHADOW can track (observations, retention) — argues against paying/incentivising attendance as a retention lever without testing.
verified_title: Examining youth and program predictors of engagement in out-of-school time programs.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: Differing intensities of training and technical assistance (business-as-usual vs performance feedback vs coaching) to OST frontline staff were associated with different levels of staff- and program-level implementation.
population: Federally funded OST programs in low-resource US communities
effect_or_estimate: Directional association only; no effect size
transfer_status: TRANSFER from OST staff development — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: 3 sites; no control; small-n case study; cannot separate TA dose from site differences
citation: Farrell et al., American Journal of Community Psychology, 2019
ppbf_implication: Coach/volunteer onboarding burden should be modelled as a tiered variable (orientation vs feedback vs coaching), not a binary 'trained' flag.
verified_title: Supporting Out-of-School Time Staff in Low Resource Communities: A Professional Development Approach.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Conditions under which OST attendance produces benefit
claim: Benefits of after-school program attendance are conditional: better outcomes when staff-child relationships are positive and non-conflictual, when a variety of age-appropriate activities are offered from which children can choose, and when children attend REGULARLY.
population: US children and adolescents in after-school settings
study_design: Narrative review of the out-of-school literature
effect_or_estimate: Mixed findings across full-time after-school programs; heterogeneity attributed to population, activity type and staff training
transfer_status: TRANSFER from after-school programming — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: Narrative (not systematic) review; pre-2005 literature base; heterogeneity acknowledged by the authors themselves
citation: Vandell et al., Advances in Child Development and Behavior, 2005
ppbf_implication: Justifies making attendance REGULARITY (not headcount) the primary operational KPI and making athlete choice a design requirement of station-rotation and open-gym models.
verified_title: Out-of-school settings as a developmental context for children and youth.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: A comparative analysis of 11 youth-worker competency frameworks in the OST field identified 12 shared core competency areas; the age of youth served and the development of mid-level managers were identified as factors under-addressed by existing frameworks.
effect_or_estimate: 12 common competency areas identified
transfer_status: TRANSFER from youth-work workforce standards — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: Document analysis; frameworks are consensus artefacts, not validated instruments; no outcome linkage
citation: Vance, Child & Youth Care Forum, 2010
ppbf_implication: Supports a PPBF role competency matrix separating head coach / assistant coach / floor volunteer / mid-level program lead — and flags mid-level lead as the role that fails first when a gym scales.
verified_title: A Comparative Analysis of Competency Frameworks for Youth Workers in the Out-of-School Time Field.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: In an 8-month after-school physical activity programme there was a significant negative linear trend between attendance level and change in percent body fat and fat mass, and a significant positive linear trend between attendance and cardiovascular fitness.
effect_or_estimate: Significant linear trends for %BF, fat mass and CVF; BMI and waist circumference not influenced by attendance
transfer_status: TRANSFER from after-school PA programming — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: Attendance is self-selected — dose-response here is associational, not randomised; outcome is body composition/fitness, not boxing skill
citation: Yin et al., International Journal of Obesity, 2005
ppbf_implication: Supports SHADOW storing attendance as a graded dose variable per athlete per block rather than a binary present/absent, and reporting dose alongside any outcome claim.
verified_title: The Medical College of Georgia Fitkid project: the relations between program attendance and changes in outcomes in year 1.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: In a 3-year after-school PA programme, year-by-year dose-response analysis showed the clearest beneficial effects on percent body fat and cardiorespiratory fitness for youth attending at least 60% of sessions.
effect_or_estimate: Treatment x time interactions: %BF p=0.009; CRF p=0.0003. Clearest benefit at >=60% session attendance. Gains rebounded to control levels over summers.
transfer_status: TRANSFER from after-school PA programming — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: 60% is a post-hoc threshold in an obesity-prevention programme; NOT a validated boxing training threshold; summer rebound shows benefit is not durable without continued dose
citation: Yin et al., Childhood Obesity, 2012
ppbf_implication: The only defensible attendance threshold in the literature we located comes from a non-boxing obesity trial. PPBF must derive its own thresholds; use 60% only as a starting hypothesis to test, never as an implemented gate.
verified_title: The impact of a 3-year after-school obesity prevention program in elementary school children.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Realistic attendance and reach in community delivery
claim: Process evaluation of a 90-minute, 3x/week after-school PA club reported MEAN ATTENDANCE OF 41%, with year-3 attendance higher than earlier years.
population: US 5th-8th grade girls, majority minority and/or low SES, 24 schools
study_design: Process evaluation nested in a group-randomised controlled trial
effect_or_estimate: Mean attendance 41%
transfer_status: TRANSFER from after-school PA programming — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: Single programme, single-sex, school-hosted; attendance depends heavily on host-site logistics
citation: Robbins et al., BMC Public Health, 2016
ppbf_implication: Daily attendance should be planned as a FRACTION of enrolment, not equal to it. Facility, coach and equipment sizing must be driven by observed attendance rate, which SHADOW already has the raw data to compute.
verified_title: Examining reach, dose, and fidelity of the "Girls on the Move" after-school physical activity club: a process evaluation.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Realistic attendance in a before-school programme
claim: A before-school PA programme in a low-resource urban district reached 82% of capacity (188 of 230 slots); median session attendance among study participants was 90% (IQR 56-97%); mean 33% of session time was accelerometer-measured MVPA (mean 16.3 minutes).
population: US elementary/middle school students, racially and socioeconomically diverse urban district
effect_or_estimate: 82% capacity fill; median 90% attendance (IQR 56-97%); 33% (SD 16%) of session in MVPA
transfer_status: TRANSFER from school-based PA programme delivery — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: Small number of schools; consented subsample; wide IQR shows attendance is highly variable between individuals
citation: Whooten et al., Preventing Chronic Disease, 2020
ppbf_implication: Shows capacity fill and attendance rate are separate metrics that must both be tracked; the wide IQR is the operational case for per-athlete attendance trajectories rather than program-level averages.
verified_title: Evaluating the Implementation of a Before-School Physical Activity Program: A Mixed-Methods Approach in Massachusetts, 2018.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: Meta-analysis of secondary-school physical education found students spent a pooled mean of 40.5% (95% CI 34.8-46.2) of lesson time in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity; middle-school 48.6% (41.3-55.9).
study_design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42014009649)
effect_or_estimate: Pooled 40.5% of lesson in MVPA (95% CI 34.8-46.2)
transfer_status: TRANSFER from school PE to gym floor time-on-task — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: PE is not boxing training; measurement heterogeneity (accelerometry, HR, pedometer, observation); MVPA is not a skill-acquisition measure
citation: Hollis et al., International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity, 2017
ppbf_implication: Scheduled session length overstates effective training dose by roughly a factor of two in comparable group settings. Session-block planning in the app should distinguish scheduled minutes from estimated engaged minutes.
verified_title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity levels in secondary school physical education lessons.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Skill instruction time in group settings
claim: Systematic observation of Year 7 PE lessons found mean 56.9% (SD 18.7) of class time in MVPA but only just over 6% of class time in SKILL INSTRUCTION, with game play occupying about 44% of lesson context.
population: Year 7 students, 6 secondary schools, New South Wales, Australia
effect_or_estimate: 56.9% MVPA; ~6% skill instruction; ~44% game play; teachers promoted PA ~31% of class time
transfer_status: TRANSFER from school PE observation to coached group sessions — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: One Australian state; PE curriculum context; the low skill-instruction figure may not generalise to a technique-led boxing session
citation: Dudley et al., Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 2011
ppbf_implication: Group models can be active without being instructional. PPBF should measure coached-contact minutes per athlete separately from session attendance — this is the metric that distinguishes open gym from a class.
verified_title: Physical activity levels and movement skill instruction in secondary school physical education.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: In secondary schools serving low-income communities, 39% of PE lesson time was spent in MVPA and less than 10% in vigorous activity; urban lessons had significantly more MVPA than rural (P=0.04); more experienced teachers delivered significantly more vigorous activity (P=0.02).
population: Grade 7 students, 10 disadvantaged secondary schools, Australia
effect_or_estimate: 39% of lesson in MVPA; rural < urban (P=0.04); instructor experience associated with vigorous activity (P=0.04/0.02)
transfer_status: TRANSFER from school PE — LABELLED TRANSFER; rural finding is directly relevant to PPBF's setting
limitations: Observational; instructor experience is confounded with school and cohort; small number of rural schools
citation: Sutherland et al., Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 2014
ppbf_implication: Coach experience is an operational input with measurable session-quality consequences — supports capturing coach tenure/certification level on every session record so SHADOW can adjust expectations rather than penalising a novice coach's cohort.
verified_title: Physical education in secondary schools located in low-income communities: Physical activity levels, lesson context and teacher interaction.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Community sport club capacity is multidimensional

population: Community/nonprofit sport clubs (Canada and comparable high-income contexts)

effect_or_estimate: Framework; no single effect size
transfer_status: TRANSFER from community sport management to boxing gym operations — LABELLED TRANSFER (closest available discipline)

claim: Voluntary sport organisations exhibit a 'core and peripheral' volunteer structure — a small core carries disproportionate role load and commitment while a larger periphery contributes episodically.
study_design: Empirical study of volunteer roles and commitment
effect_or_estimate: Structural pattern; no pooled estimate
transfer_status: TRANSFER from voluntary sport organisations — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: Non-US context; cross-sectional; 'core' is defined differently across studies
citation: Sport in Society, 2013 — 'Volunteer roles, involvement and commitment in voluntary sport organizations: evidence of core and peripheral volunteers'
verification: openalex:openalex_search_works returned this record with DOI 10.1080/17430437.2013.828902 (2026-08-07)

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Volunteer coach support in community clubs
claim: In community-based clubs, volunteer coaches' retention and development are shaped by club-level support structures and club culture and norms, including whether the club addresses behaviour that undermines the coaching role.
population: Volunteer women coaches, 3 Gaelic football clubs, Ireland
study_design: Qualitative interview study with creative non-fiction synthesis
effect_or_estimate: Themes: retention and recruitment, support structures, club culture and norms. No quantitative estimate.
transfer_status: TRANSFER from Gaelic football club volunteering — LABELLED TRANSFER; single sport, single country, female coaches only
limitations: n=11; one sport; one country; findings are interpretive not generalisable estimates
citation: Hogan et al., Frontiers in Sports and Active Living, 2022
ppbf_implication: Volunteer attrition should be treated as a CLUB-CULTURE signal SHADOW can surface to the board, not an individual failing — supports a coach-retention field on the coach record with reason codes.
verified_title: Exploring the Influence of the Community-Based Sports Club Environment on the Support and Development of Volunteer Women Coaches in Ireland.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Peer/volunteer delivery agents and long-term maintenance
claim: An RCT found that tailored support from trained older PEER VOLUNTEERS produced significantly more moderate-to-vigorous physical activity at 18-month follow-up than a typical community offering, despite similar gains at 16 weeks.
population: Sedentary older adults, US community setting
sample_size: 7 peer volunteers, 81 sedentary adults; retention 85% at 16 weeks, 61% at 18 months
effect_or_estimate: Groups equivalent at 16 weeks; peer-supported group significantly higher MVPA at 18 months (intent-to-treat)
transfer_status: TRANSFER from older-adult community PA to volunteer-delivered gym models — LABELLED TRANSFER; population is older adults, NOT youth
limitations: Small n; self-report MVPA logs with accelerometry only in a subsample; 61% follow-up at 18 months; older-adult sample
citation: Buman et al., Journal of Physical Activity and Health, 2011
verification: pubmed:PMID 21918240 (no DOI returned by PubMed record)
ppbf_implication: Trained peer/volunteer delivery is a defensible capacity multiplier for ADULT and masters lanes; do NOT extrapolate this to unsupervised volunteer delivery for minors, which is governed by safeguarding rules, not efficacy evidence.
verified_title: Peer volunteers improve long-term maintenance of physical activity with older adults: a randomized controlled trial.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Peer-led delivery in a boxing-based youth session
claim: A school-based peer-led high-intensity interval training programme BUILT ON BOXING AND WHOLE-BODY EXERCISES was feasible to deliver by older pupils; recruitment was 72% for peer-recipients, 74% for controls and 42% for peer-leaders.
population: Year 7 pupils (peer-recipients) and Year 12-13 pupils (peer-leaders), one school, North East England
effect_or_estimate: Recruitment 72%/74%/42%; feasibility outcomes only, not efficacy
boxing_specific: partially — boxing-based exercise content, not boxing skill training or sparring
transfer_status: PARTIAL boxing relevance (boxing-derived movement content in a school setting); NOT evidence about boxing gyms
limitations: One school; n=5 peer-leaders; feasibility design; peer-leader recruitment was the weak point (42%)
citation: Weston et al., BMC Public Health, 2026
ppbf_implication: Recruiting the LEADERS is harder than recruiting the participants. A PPBF senior-athlete-as-assistant lane must plan for leader supply as the binding constraint — and leaders who are minors cannot substitute for adult supervision.
verified_title: Feasibility of a school-based peer-led high-intensity interval training intervention: the Young Fitness Leaders project.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Trained vs untrained peer tutoring in boxing
claim: In a French boxing (savate) instructional setting, a STRUCTURED trained-peer-tutoring programme produced higher coaching-skill scores in tutors than untrained peer tutoring; effects on offensive/defensive outcomes differed by sex.
population: College-age novice French boxing participants, France
study_design: 2x2 factorial experimental design (sex x training type)
effect_or_estimate: Trained peer tutoring > untrained on coaching skills; interaction effects by sex on offensive/defensive outcomes; untrained tutors reported higher self-efficacy
boxing_specific: YES — French boxing (savate), a striking combat sport; not Olympic-style boxing
transfer_status: Combat-sport specific but SAVATE, novice adults, small n — do not treat as amateur-boxing evidence
limitations: n=32; single task; short duration; savate not Olympic boxing; adults not youth
citation: Legrain et al., Journal of Sports Sciences, 2003

verification: state code text retrieved via web_search 2026-08-07 (Justia mirror of 55 PA Code 3270.51 reproduces the ratio table: young school-age 1:12/24, older school-age 1:15/30); PA Code official site confirms sections exist
ppbf_implication: The ONLY numeric supervision ratio we could verify for PA school-age settings comes from child care licensure, not sport. PPBF supervision ratios must therefore be labelled PROPOSED PPBF PARAMETER and validated; they should be at least as tight as these anchors during any contact activity.
independent_verification_detail: governing body, statute, regulator or repo document — URL + retrieval date in verification column

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: No verified coach:athlete ratio for boxing
claim: Targeted searches of PubMed and OpenAlex for coach:athlete ratio, staff:child ratio and group-size evidence in youth sport and out-of-school-time settings returned no study establishing an optimal or minimum-safe coach-to-athlete ratio for boxing or for combat sport.
study_design: Structured database search (PubMed search_articles; OpenAlex openalex_search_works)
sample_size: PubMed queries 'staff to child ratio group size quality early childhood outcomes' returned 0 results; 'coach athlete ratio youth sport program quality' returned 4 results, none on ratio; 'afterschool program quality staff youth ratio observation' returned 0
effect_or_estimate: No estimate exists to report
transfer_status: Not applicable — this row records an evidence GAP
limitations: Absence of evidence in these two databases is not proof of absence in grey literature, insurer standards or governing-body operational guidance not indexed there
source_type: structured search of PubMed and OpenAlex
citation: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE — no qualifying source located
verification: pubmed:search_articles returned total_count=0 for 'staff to child ratio group size quality early childhood outcomes' and for 'afterschool program quality staff youth ratio observation'; openalex searches on coach_athlete_ratio returned no ratio-establishing study (2026-08-07)
ppbf_implication: Every supervision ratio in the PPBF scenario matrix must be labelled PROPOSED PPBF PARAMETER — ASSUMPTION, REQUIRES VALIDATION, with a stated validation method. SHADOW must not present any ratio as evidence-based.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: RE-AIM (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance) has been applied in over 2,800 publications; the authors encourage pragmatic use of key dimensions rather than comprehensive application of all elements.
population: Public health and health behaviour change programmes, clinical/community/corporate settings
effect_or_estimate: Framework usage review; no effect size
transfer_status: TRANSFER from implementation science — LABELLED TRANSFER; discipline-agnostic
limitations: Framework, not an intervention; the review itself notes inconsistent and partial application in practice
citation: Glasgow et al., Frontiers in Public Health, 2019
ppbf_implication: RE-AIM is the recommended evaluation spine for the PPBF pilot plan: Reach (who enrols vs who is eligible), Adoption (which sites/coaches run it), Implementation (fidelity, dose), Maintenance (retention, model persistence).
verified_title: RE-AIM Planning and Evaluation Framework: Adapting to New Science and Practice With a 20-Year Review.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: A RE-AIM systematic review of 78 controlled paediatric physical activity interventions found most reported internal validity elements while minimally reporting external validity indicators including representativeness of participants, start-up costs, protocol fidelity and sustainability.
population: Children aged 5-11 in controlled PA interventions
study_design: Systematic review using the RE-AIM framework
effect_or_estimate: Reporting-quality finding; no pooled effect
transfer_status: TRANSFER from PA intervention literature — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: Reporting quality is not the same as programme quality; 12-year search window
citation: McGoey et al., Preventive Medicine, 2015
ppbf_implication: Explains WHY operational parameters (start-up cost, staffing, sustainability) are missing from the literature: researchers routinely do not report them. PPBF must generate these numbers internally — they will not be found in papers.
verified_title: Evaluation of physical activity interventions in children via the reach, efficacy/effectiveness, adoption, implementation, and maintenance (RE-AIM) framework: A systematic review of randomized and non-randomized trials.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Real-world barriers to sustaining a community exercise programme
claim: Qualitative evaluation of a group exercise programme for older adults at YMCA-affiliated sites identified programme-specific factors (instructor training, programme structure, reporting requirements, insurance coverage) and organisational factors (organisational support, infrastructure, champions, funding) affecting implementation and maintenance.
population: Instructors, staff and master trainers at 24 YMCA-affiliated sites, USA
study_design: Qualitative semi-structured interview study within RE-AIM
effect_or_estimate: Thematic; no quantitative estimate
transfer_status: TRANSFER from community fitness programme delivery — LABELLED TRANSFER; multi-site nonprofit context is a close structural analogue to a franchise/multi-org boxing model
limitations: Early-adopter sites only (selection bias toward success); qualitative; older-adult programme
citation: Petrescu-Prahova et al., The Gerontologist, 2015
ppbf_implication: Named 'champions', reporting burden and insurance are recurring failure points in multi-site delivery — these become explicit prerequisite and failure-mode entries for the franchise/multi-organisation model.
verified_title: Implementation and Maintenance of a Community-Based Older Adult Physical Activity Program.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Data availability constrains programme evaluation in practice
claim: A mixed-methods RE-AIM evaluation of a community-based physical activity programme found inconsistent data availability and a lack of robust reporting challenged assessment of all five RE-AIM dimensions; only community-level Adoption was highly successful.
population: Community-based physical activity programme, real-world setting
study_design: Single mixed-methods case study, concurrent triangulation (5 data sources)
effect_or_estimate: Qualitative/methodological finding
transfer_status: TRANSFER from community PA evaluation — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: n=1 programme; evaluator-reported constraints
citation: Koorts & Gillison, BMC Public Health, 2015
ppbf_implication: Strongest external argument for SHADOW's core value proposition: community programmes usually cannot evaluate themselves because the data does not exist. Data-capture feasibility must be a first-class column in the operating-model comparison.
verified_title: Mixed method evaluation of a community-based physical activity program using the RE-AIM framework: practical application in a real-world setting.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Capacity-building interventions — effect is mostly individual-level
claim: A systematic review of capacity-building interventions relevant to public health practice found improvements mainly in individual-level outcomes (knowledge, skill, self-efficacy) across six intervention types; the available literature was moderate in quality.
population: Public health, NGO, government and community-based organisations
effect_or_estimate: Individual-level improvements; organisational and system-level outcomes weakly evidenced
transfer_status: TRANSFER from public health capacity building — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: Only 14 papers met inclusion; moderate quality; heterogeneous outcome definitions
citation: DeCorby-Watson et al., BMC Public Health, 2018
ppbf_implication: Training coaches is well-evidenced to change coaches; it is NOT well-evidenced to change organisations. Model growth requires structural change (roles, schedules, systems), not only more training.
verified_title: Effectiveness of capacity building interventions relevant to public health practice: a systematic review.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Community capacity building for PA — inconsistent behavioural effect
claim: A literature review of strategies to build community capacity for physical activity promotion among adults 50+ identified five strategy groups (coalitions/networks, professional training, layperson training, strengthening target-population competence/awareness, financial resource allocation); feasibility and acceptability were demonstrated but intervention effects on PA behaviour were inconsistent, and the one study systematically comparing approaches found no benefit of intensified capacity building.
study_design: Literature review (PsycInfo, Web of Science, plus grey literature project databases)
effect_or_estimate: Inconsistent PA effects; no benefit found from intensified capacity building in the single comparative study
transfer_status: TRANSFER from older-adult community PA capacity building — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: Review, not meta-analysis; older-adult focus; grey literature inclusion complicates quality appraisal
citation: Ubert et al., International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 2017
ppbf_implication: Guards against over-investing in capacity-building activity as an end in itself. PPBF should tie any capacity investment to a measured floor-level outcome (sessions delivered, coached minutes, retention).
verified_title: Community Capacity Building for Physical Activity Promotion among Older Adults-A Literature Review.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Uptake and adherence benchmarks from a comparable referral model
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of exercise referral schemes found pooled uptake of 66% (95% CI 57-75) in observational studies and 81% (68-94) in RCTs, and pooled adherence of 49% (40-59) observational and 43% (32-54) in RCTs; women were more likely to begin but less likely to adhere than men, and older people were more likely both to begin and to adhere.
population: Adults referred to community exercise schemes (predominantly UK)
transfer_status: TRANSFER from adult exercise referral schemes — LABELLED TRANSFER; ADULT population, healthcare-referred, mostly UK. Do NOT apply these percentages to youth boxing enrolment.
limitations: Substantial heterogeneity; no standardised definitions of uptake/adherence; adult clinical-referral pathway differs fundamentally from a community gym walk-in
citation: Pavey et al., Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health, 2012
ppbf_implication: Roughly half of enrolled adults not adhering is the norm in comparable community schemes. PPBF planning should size facilities and coaching against expected adherence, and should treat non-adherence as a design problem rather than an athlete deficiency.
verified_title: Levels and predictors of exercise referral scheme uptake and adherence: a systematic review.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: Qualitative longitudinal study of mHealth app users identified two dimensions explaining continued use — assessment of the app and its capabilities, and persistence toward the health goal — and produced a framework of four post-initial-use decisions: abandon, limit use, switch app, continue use.
sample_size: 17 participants; 34 interviews; 193 diaries over two weeks
effect_or_estimate: Framework; no quantitative estimate
transfer_status: TRANSFER from consumer mHealth to a coach-support app — LABELLED TRANSFER; note the PPBF app's primary users are COACHES and guardians, not self-directed consumers
limitations: n=17; two-week window; consumer wellness apps not coach-support tools
citation: Vaghefi & Tulu, JMIR mHealth and uHealth, 2019
ppbf_implication: For the hybrid in-person + digital operating model, digital-component abandonment should be an expected default state with a designed fallback (paper/coach-entered), not a failure condition.
verified_title: The Continued Use of Mobile Health Apps: Insights From a Longitudinal Study.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: Analysis of an eHealth lifestyle platform classified dropouts with 89% precision using a random forest with 11 predictor variables; the most significant predictors were the intervention provider, two weeks of inactivity, and the number of coach advices received.
population: Patients using an eHealth lifestyle platform for chronic lifestyle disease
study_design: Retrospective predictive modelling (logistic regression, decision trees, random forest) with 80/20 train-holdout split
effect_or_estimate: 89% precision for dropout classification on the holdout set; top predictors: provider, 2 weeks inactivity, number of coach advices
transfer_status: TRANSFER from clinical eHealth to community sport attendance modelling — LABELLED TRANSFER; population and outcome differ substantially
limitations: Single platform; precision reported without full confusion-matrix context here; provider being the top predictor suggests site effects dominate individual traits
citation: Pedersen et al., Journal of Medical Internet Research, 2019
ppbf_implication: Supports an inactivity-window attrition signal in SHADOW. The finding that PROVIDER was the strongest predictor is the operationally important one: attrition is primarily a site/coach property, so any athlete-level risk score must be adjusted for site or it will mislabel athletes.
verified_title: Predicting Dropouts From an Electronic Health Platform for Lifestyle Interventions: Analysis of Methods and Predictors.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: A scoping review of inclusive out-of-school-time physical activity programmes for children and youth with physical disabilities found programmes varied in age groups, GROUP SIZES and durations, were mostly recreational, and were most commonly led by rehabilitation staff; best-practice recommendations centre on an abilities-based approach with common group goals, cooperative activities, mastery-oriented individualised instruction and developmentally appropriate challenge.
population: Children and youth with physical disabilities in OST physical activity programmes
study_design: Scoping review with quality appraisal (only studies rated >=60% informed recommendations)
effect_or_estimate: Positive effects on social skills/relationships, physical skill development, psychological wellbeing; group size varied, no optimum identified
transfer_status: TRANSFER from inclusive OST PA programming to adaptive boxing — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: Small heterogeneous evidence base; rehabilitation-staff-led programmes may not generalise to coach-led gyms; no group-size optimum derivable
citation: Arbour-Nicitopoulos et al., Adapted Physical Activity Quarterly, 2018
ppbf_implication: The inclusive/adaptive operating model needs individualised instruction within a common group goal — this is a station-rotation or small-group structure, not a large single-block class. Staffing implications follow directly.
verified_title: A Scoping Review of Inclusive Out-of-School Time Physical Activity Programs for Children and Youth With Physical Disabilities.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: Lack of disability awareness among fitness professionals is a well-established barrier to exercise participation for people with disabilities; a 90-minute video training plus resource manual significantly improved group fitness instructors' confidence to adapt classes, though pre-existing disability attitudes were already high and did not change significantly.
population: Community-based group fitness instructors at one US recreation center
study_design: Pre/post/2-month follow-up pilot with semi-structured interviews
effect_or_estimate: Significant improvement in confidence to adapt classes; no significant change in attitudes
transfer_status: TRANSFER from community fitness instruction — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: n=10; single site; self-report outcomes; no participant-level outcomes measured
citation: Adamson et al., Adapted Physical Activity Quarterly, 2023
ppbf_implication: A short, structured adaptation training is a low-cost prerequisite for the inclusive/adaptive model — it is a capability gate to record on the coach record, distinct from safeguarding certification.
verified_title: Development and Pilot Testing of the Disability Awareness Training and Education Program Among Community-Based Group Fitness Instructors.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Non-contact boxing as a distinct programme lane
claim: Community-based boxing programmes for people with Parkinson's disease have been implemented and evaluated in small studies reporting improvements in balance, functional gait and quality of life; a 2019 review concluded implementation had ACCELERATED BEYOND CURRENT EVIDENCE, with only two eligible studies totalling 37 participants at that time.
population: Adults with Parkinson's disease in community boxing programmes
study_design: Systematic literature review plus website quality appraisal (QUEST)
effect_or_estimate: Balance confidence, mobility and quality of life reported to improve with programmes of 24-36 sessions over 12 weeks; risk of bias low in the two trials but reporting against CERT incomplete
transfer_status: Boxing-specific but a CLINICAL adult population; does NOT transfer to youth amateur boxing
limitations: Only 2 studies at review; small n; incomplete intervention reporting; medications not always documented
citation: Morris et al., Frontiers in Neurology, 2019
ppbf_implication: Non-contact adaptive boxing is a viable, revenue- and grant-relevant programme lane with genuine (if thin) evidence. It is also a cautionary example of a boxing programme scaling ahead of its evidence — exactly the failure SHADOW's evidence ledger exists to prevent.
verified_title: Boxing for Parkinson's Disease: Has Implementation Accelerated Beyond Current Evidence?

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Operational growth trajectory of a community boxing programme
claim: A community boxing programme for people with Parkinson's disease started classes with 10 participants and, at 18-month follow-up, consisted of four boxing sessions per week led by three instructors with 40 participants; 81% of patients and 80% of instructors were very satisfied at the workshop stage.
population: People with Parkinson's disease and boxing instructors, community setting
sample_size: 26 patients and 10 instructors at workshop; 40 participants at 18 months; 17 questionnaire respondents at follow-up
effect_or_estimate: 10 participants at launch → 40 participants, 4 sessions/week, 3 instructors at 18 months
boxing_specific: YES — boxing programme, clinical adult population
transfer_status: Boxing-specific operational data, but a CLINICAL ADULT lane — do not present as a youth-gym growth curve
limitations: Single programme; 17/40 responded at follow-up; no comparison programme; success case (publication bias toward programmes that survived)
citation: Domingos et al., Journal of Parkinson's Disease, 2019
ppbf_implication: The only real published boxing-programme scaling datapoint we located: roughly 13 participants per instructor across 4 weekly sessions in a non-contact adult lane. Use as a REFERENCE POINT for the adaptive lane only, explicitly not as a youth ratio.
verified_title: Implementation of a Community-Based Exercise Program for Parkinson Patients: Using Boxing as an Example.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Large-scale participant-reported outcomes in a franchised non-contact boxing programme
claim: A survey of a franchised non-contact boxing programme for Parkinson's disease drew 2,054 enrolled respondents (1,709 eligible: 1,333 current, 166 previous, 210 never-participants); current participants reported better median quality-of-life and exercise self-efficacy scores than previous and never-participants, and the sample was 97% Caucasian.
population: Adults with Parkinson's disease aware of the programme, predominantly US
study_design: Cross-sectional survey (PDQ-39, Self-Efficacy for Exercise scale)
effect_or_estimate: Median PDQ-39 25 (current) vs 36 and 32 (previous/never), p<0.01; SEE 54 vs 43 and 48, p<0.01. Cross-sectional — self-selection cannot be excluded.
transfer_status: Boxing-specific, ADULT CLINICAL, franchise model — relevant to the multi-organisation/franchise operating model analysis, not to youth operations
limitations: Cross-sectional; healthy/adherent-user bias (current participants may differ at baseline); 97% Caucasian sample is a stark equity signal; self-report
citation: Larson et al., Disability and Rehabilitation, 2021
ppbf_implication: Demonstrates that a franchised boxing model can reach national scale AND that such a model can reach a demographically narrow population. Equity monitoring must be built into any PPBF multi-site expansion from day one.
verified_title: High satisfaction and improved quality of life with Rock Steady Boxing in Parkinson's disease: results of a large-scale survey.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Session structure in community boxing (adaptive lane)
claim: A retrospective study of a community-based boxing programme for Parkinson's disease described 90-minute sessions comprising warm-up, boxing drills, strength and endurance exercises and cool-down, including multiple 30-60 second high-intensity intervals; participants averaged 2.8 (SD 0.8) sessions per week over 6.1 (SD 0.8) months.
population: Individuals with Parkinson's disease, Hoehn and Yahr stage 1-3
study_design: Retrospective cross-sectional analysis of de-identified programme data
effect_or_estimate: 90-minute sessions; 2.8 (SD 0.8) sessions/week; 6.1 (SD 0.8) months; significant FAB improvement above published MDC
transfer_status: Boxing-specific but ADULT CLINICAL; the SESSION ARCHITECTURE is more transferable than the dose
limitations: n=12; retrospective; no control; single programme
citation: Moore et al., International Journal of Exercise Science, 2021
ppbf_implication: Gives a published, citable session-block template (warm-up / drills / conditioning / cool-down with interval work) for the adaptive lane; PPBF youth session blocks must be derived separately and validated.
verified_title: A Community-based Boxing Program is Associated with Improved Balance in Individuals with Parkinson's Disease.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Non-contact boxing for mental health — feasibility signal
claim: A 10-week manualised non-contact boxing group programme (90-minute sessions twice weekly) for adults with major depressive disorder or generalised anxiety disorder reported 89% retention, 84% attendance and 98% satisfaction in a feasibility trial (ISRCTN23023309).
population: Adult psychiatric outpatients with MDD or GAD, Toronto, Canada
effect_or_estimate: Retention 89%, attendance 84%, satisfaction 98%; symptom reductions reported but uncontrolled and n=8
transfer_status: Boxing-specific, ADULT CLINICAL, tiny sample — feasibility signal only
limitations: n=8; single arm; no control; symptom changes cannot be attributed to the intervention
citation: Bozdarov et al., PLOS ONE, 2025
ppbf_implication: Supports a manualised non-contact adult lane as an operationally distinct model (fixed cohort, closed 10-week block, referral intake). Symptom outcomes must NOT be claimed by PPBF; any mental-health framing is a clinician's call.
verified_title: Mindfulness-based (non-contact) boxing therapy (MBBT) for depression and anxiety: A feasibility study.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Head trauma risk is intrinsic to competitive boxing
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of head trauma in boxing found boxers had a significantly elevated concussion risk compared with other combat sports (risk ratio 0.253 vs 0.065, P<0.001), and reported cavum septum pellucidum in 147 of 631 boxers (23.30%) and brain atrophy in 125 of 411 (30.41%).
sample_size: 35 of 84 articles included; 631 and 411 boxers in the respective pooled analyses
effect_or_estimate: Concussion RR 0.253 (boxing) vs 0.065 (other combat sports), P<0.001; CSP 23.30%; atrophy 30.41%
transfer_status: Boxing-specific; note the pooled samples mix amateur and professional and are heavily weighted toward historical professional cohorts
limitations: Heterogeneous historical studies; professional and amateur pooled; imaging findings from older cohorts under different rules; does not establish risk for non-contact or recreational boxing
citation: Donnelly et al., Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine, 2023
ppbf_implication: Establishes why contact intensity must be an explicit operating-model dimension with human-owned clearance. SHADOW must never gate, clear or predict contact readiness; that decision belongs to a qualified physician and the coaching staff.
verified_title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Investigating Head Trauma in Boxing.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: The Association of Ringside Physicians position statement holds that headguards are effective in reducing facial lacerations and auricular injury but should NOT be relied upon to reduce the risk of concussion or other traumatic brain injury, and that changes in athlete behaviour toward more risk-taking when wearing headguards may offset any biomechanical risk reduction.
sex: policies recommended to be standardised for men and women in the absence of gender-difference data
effect_or_estimate: Laceration reduction supported; concussion prevention not supported; human studies lacking
limitations: Position statement, not a trial; the statement itself calls for further research
citation: deWeber et al., The Physician and Sportsmedicine, 2023
ppbf_implication: Equipment provision (headguards) is an operational cost and a laceration-control measure, NOT a concussion control. Any PPBF messaging or app copy implying headguard = brain protection would be a safety misstatement.
verified_title: Headguard use in combat sports: position statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Rapid weight loss in youth combat sport
claim: A systematic review of youth Olympic combat sports found rapid weight loss highly prevalent (25-94% depending on sport, age and competition level), commonly achieved by increasing exercise, restricting fluid and food, training in impermeable suits and sauna use, with magnitude ranging from about 1% to 6.3% (SD 3.7) of body mass; the authors concluded RWL needs stringent regulation and ideally should be banned in this population.
population: Children and adolescent combat sport athletes (Olympic combat sports)
sample_size: see source (studies conducted in official competition context only)
effect_or_estimate: Prevalence 25-94%; magnitude ~1% to 6.3% (SD 3.7) body mass
boxing_specific: partially — Olympic combat sports including boxing
transfer_status: Combat-sport specific and youth-specific — highly relevant to a competitive youth boxing lane
limitations: Heterogeneous sports and definitions; self-report; competition-context studies only
citation: Lakicevic et al., Journal of Eating Disorders, 2022
ppbf_implication: A competition-heavy youth operating model carries a documented weight-cutting hazard. PPBF must have a written no-youth-weight-cutting policy owned by a named human role; SHADOW must never generate, recommend, or optimise a weight-management target for a minor.
verified_title: Patterns of weight cycling in youth Olympic combat sports: a systematic review.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Rapid weight loss does not buy competitive success in youth boxing
claim: In elite youth Olympic-style boxers from 12 European countries, rapid weight loss was NOT associated with competitive success; boxing experience was the significant predictor of medalling (odds ratio 1.33, 95% CI 1.06-1.66, Nagelkerke R=.11); only 25% were in the RWL group, over 45% self-reported combining multiple weight-cutting methods known to be health hazards, and 33% experienced muscle weakness as a consequence.
population: Elite youth Olympic-style boxers, 12 European countries
study_design: Questionnaire study with prospective competition-outcome follow-up
effect_or_estimate: Experience OR 1.33 (1.06-1.66); RWL not associated with success; 45% combined hazardous methods; 33% muscle weakness
transfer_status: Boxing-specific, elite youth, MALE ONLY, European — do not generalise to female or novice boxers
limitations: N=83; male only; self-report; single championship outcome; low model R
citation: Zubac et al., International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 2018
ppbf_implication: Gives PPBF a boxing-specific, evidence-backed talking point for coaches and guardians: cutting weight did not predict winning in this cohort, experience did. Supports an experience-and-development framing in the competitive lane.
verified_title: Rapid Weight Loss Is Not Associated With Competitive Success in Elite Youth Olympic-Style Boxers in Europe.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: An IOC Medical Commission ad hoc working group review and position statement concluded there are no generally accepted optimum values for body weight or percentage fat mass across sports and no gold-standard body-composition method for athletes, and called for sport- and gender-specific prevention programmes, criteria for 'does not start' decisions in athletes with eating disorders, and modification of regulations in some sports.
sex: both, with explicit call for gender-specific programmes
effect_or_estimate: Explicit statement that no optimum body-composition values exist
boxing_specific: no — weight-sensitive sports generally, which includes boxing
transfer_status: Applies to boxing as a weight-category sport
limitations: Position statement; 2013 publication; does not resolve the referral-threshold question it raises
citation: Sundgot-Borgen et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2013
ppbf_implication: Direct authority for refusing to publish any body-composition target in the app. If a coach or guardian asks SHADOW for a weight target, the correct behaviour is to decline and route to a qualified clinician.
verified_title: How to minimise the health risks to athletes who compete in weight-sensitive sports review and position statement on behalf of the Ad Hoc Research Working Group on Body Composition, Health and Performance, under the auspices of the IOC Medical Commission.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Youth resistance training requires qualified supervision
claim: Position-stand and review evidence on youth resistance training holds that appropriately designed and QUALIFIED-SUPERVISED resistance training is safe and effective for young athletes and contributes to injury prevention.
effect_or_estimate: Safety and efficacy conditional on qualified supervision and appropriate programme design
transfer_status: TRANSFER from youth strength and conditioning to the boxing gym floor — LABELLED TRANSFER; widely accepted across youth sport
limitations: Position statements reflect expert consensus over a heterogeneous literature; 'qualified supervision' is not operationally quantified as a ratio
citation: Faigenbaum et al., Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2009 (NSCA position statement); Bergeron et al./related BJSM review 2009
doi_or_pmid: PMID 19620931; doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31819df407 (NSCA position statement). Related: PMID 19945973; doi:10.1136/bjsm.2009.068098
ppbf_implication: Strength work in a youth boxing programme is defensible but supervision-dependent — supports separating 'supervised strength station' from 'open floor' in the station-rotation model and constraining who may run it.
verified_title: Youth resistance training: updated position statement paper from the national strength and conditioning association.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: The AOSSM early sport specialisation consensus concluded there is no evidence that young children benefit from early sport specialisation in the majority of sports, that specialised youth are subject to overuse injury and burnout, and that early multisport participation does not deter long-term competitive success.
effect_or_estimate: Consensus position; no effect size
transfer_status: TRANSFER from youth sport consensus — LABELLED TRANSFER; consistent with the AMSSM research-agenda statement
limitations: Consensus, not systematic review; the parallel AMSSM summit statement explicitly notes methodological limitations in the underlying specialisation literature
citation: LaPrade et al., Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine, 2016 (AOSSM); Kliethermes et al., Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine, 2021 (AMSSM research agenda)
ppbf_implication: Supports designing the youth lane around multi-activity fundamentals rather than early competitive funnelling, and supports the recreation-first / competition-optional segmentation in the scenario matrix.
verified_title: Defining a Research Agenda for Youth Sport Specialization in the United States: The AMSSM Youth Early Sport Specialization Summit.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
claim: Sports-based youth development programmes are characterised in the literature as out-of-school-time programmes that use a sport to facilitate learning and life-skill development, and are described against the National Research Council / Institute of Medicine features of positive developmental settings — including appropriate structure with clear rules, expectations and responsibilities for youth, parents, coaches, officials and organisers.
study_design: Conceptual/definitional paper within a youth-development framework
effect_or_estimate: Framework; no effect size
transfer_status: TRANSFER from sports-based youth development — LABELLED TRANSFER
limitations: Conceptual; 2007; features are consensus-derived from the NRC/IOM framework rather than tested against outcomes in this paper
citation: Perkins & Noam, New Directions for Youth Development, 2007
ppbf_implication: Supports codifying explicit written expectations for FOUR audiences (athlete, guardian, coach, official) as a prerequisite of any PPBF operating model — a concrete onboarding artefact set rather than a values statement.
verified_title: Characteristics of sports-based youth development programs.

track: B1 Gym Operations — Operating Models & Age/Size Scenarios
topic: Intensified youth sport structures carry trade-offs
claim: A mixed-methods systematic review of sports schools found student-athletes receive considerable academic and athletic support and more intensified training and competition with high-level partners, but REGULARLY MISS SCHOOL, and that heterogeneous evaluation methods make cross-study comparison and consensus on impacts difficult.
study_design: Mixed-methods systematic review (PRISMA; 8 databases to Feb 2021; MMAT quality appraisal)

track: B2 Gym Operations — staffing, capacity, class/station templates
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of amateur boxing reported a pooled TRAINING injury incidence of 1.3 per 1000 hours (95% CI 0.2-7.0) versus a competition rate of 6.8 per 1000 minutes of exposure (95% CI 4.2-10.9), with training injuries predominantly upper-limb (median 49%) and sprains/strains (median 60%), while competition injuries were predominantly head and neck (median 72%).
age_range: not disaggregated in the pooled estimate
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (17 studies, random-effects)
effect_or_estimate: Training IIR 1.3/1000 h (95% CI 0.2-7.0); competition 6.8/1000 min (95% CI 4.2-10.9)
limitations: Very wide CI on the training estimate indicates substantial heterogeneity and imprecision. Pooled across studies with differing injury definitions and exposure capture. Does NOT decompose training exposure by activity type, so it cannot by itself justify any specific per-activity ratio.
citation: Alevras et al. (2022). Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sci Med Sport.
ppbf_implication: Supports tiering by activity: training risk is concentrated in upper-limb overuse (a technique-monitoring problem) while head/neck risk concentrates where contact occurs. This is the evidential basis for treating bag work and sparring as different supervision tiers — but the ratio VALUES remain PPBF assumptions.
verified_title: Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: B2 Gym Operations — staffing, capacity, class/station templates

effect_or_estimate: 223.9/1000 boxers (95% CI 157.5-290.4); professional IR 399.8 vs lower amateur/female

verified_title: Incidence Rates and Pathology Types of Boxing-Specific Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Epidemiology Studies in the 21st Century.

track: B2 Gym Operations — staffing, capacity, class/station templates

population: Amateur and professional boxers, Victoria Australia
effect_or_estimate: 2.0 injuries per 1000 hours of boxing; 71% head region (95% CI reported as -3.7 to 89.4)

ppbf_implication: Supports the general point that cumulative TRAINING exposure, not just bouts, carries the risk load — which is precisely why gym-floor supervision design matters. Too imprecise to parameterise anything.
verified_title: A prospective cohort study of injury in amateur and professional boxing.

verified_title: Is it feasible to implement an injury surveillance system for amateur boxing events in Australia? A mixed methods study.

population: Elementary school students, private school, Utah USA
study_design: Observational, accelerometry, multi-level mixed effects model
effect_or_estimate: beta = 14.8% MVPA wear time (95% CI 5.7-23.9) for the extreme contrast
transfer_status: NON-BOXING, school PE, elementary age — TRANSFER IS INDIRECT
limitations: Observational: class size was not randomised, so this is ASSOCIATION, NOT CAUSATION — smaller classes may co-occur with other differences. Single private school. The effect is an interaction of size WITH lesson content, so size alone is not the actionable lever.

verified_title: Elementary physical education: A focus on fitness activities and smaller class sizes are associated with higher levels of physical activity.

transfer_status: NON-BOXING (athletics/hurdles), novice learners — MECHANISM TRANSFER ONLY

verified_title: The learning of sprint hurdles: A comparative study on increasing contextual interference and blocked practice schedules.
