ppbf_implication: PPBF EAP should be written as a chain, with a named owner per link and a time target per link, so a drill can be scored link-by-link.
verified_title: Part 7: Systems of Care: 2020 American Heart Association Guidelines for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Emergency Cardiovascular Care.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: The leading causes of sudden death in organised sport extend beyond cardiac arrest to head and neck injury, exertional heat stroke, exertional sickling, asthma, and environmental hazards; an EAP should cover all of them.
effect_or_estimate: Condition list and management recommendations (qualitative)
transfer_status: General athletic transfer; heat and sickling are less boxing-typical but not absent (weight-making, hot gyms)
limitations: Position statement; US context; some conditions (lightning) irrelevant to an indoor boxing gym
citation: Casa DJ, et al. NATA Position Statement: Preventing Sudden Death in Sports. J Athl Train. 2012.
ppbf_implication: The PPBF incident matrix must be multi-hazard, not cardiac-only. Drives the event_category taxonomy in incident_near_miss_and_escalation_matrix.csv.
verified_title: National athletic trainers' association position statement: preventing sudden death in sports.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Exertional heat illness is preventable and recognisable, and exertional heat stroke remains a leading cause of sudden death in sport; recognition and immediate cooling protocols belong in the venue EAP.
effect_or_estimate: Recommendation set (qualitative)
transfer_status: Transfer from outdoor/field sport; boxing-relevant via unventilated gyms, sweat suits and weight-making practices
limitations: No boxing-gym-specific thresholds; wet-bulb globe temperature policies are written for outdoor sport
citation: Casa DJ, et al. NATA Position Statement: Exertional Heat Illnesses. J Athl Train. 2015.
ppbf_implication: Add heat/humidity to the daily facility check and an explicit prohibition on plastic/rubber sweat suits in the SOP. Environmental thresholds for an indoor boxing gym are TBD.
verified_title: National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Exertional Heat Illnesses.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Any athlete with suspected sport-related concussion must be immediately removed from play and not return the same day; the Concussion Recognition Tool 6 (CRT6) is the non-clinician recognition instrument, and diagnosis and clearance are healthcare-professional decisions.
study_design: International consensus statement informed by 10 commissioned systematic reviews
effect_or_estimate: Consensus recommendation; CRT6/SCAT6/SCOAT6 tool set
boxing_specific: no (combat sport included in scope of sport-related concussion generally)
transfer_status: Cross-sport consensus applied to boxing; boxing differs in that head contact is intentional and repetitive
limitations: Consensus, not trial evidence; the CISG process has attracted criticism regarding industry involvement and long-term-risk framing; boxing-specific data are thin
citation: Patricios JS, et al. Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport - Amsterdam, October 2022. Br J Sports Med. 2023.
ppbf_implication: SOP-12 concussion escalation. SHADOW may present the CRT6 red-flag checklist, timestamp removal, and notify the guardian and the designated medical contact. SHADOW must never diagnose, never clear, and never compute a return-to-play date.
verified_title: Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport-Amsterdam, October 2022.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: CRT6 is the published recognition tool designed for use by non-medically-trained individuals to identify a suspected concussion and trigger removal.
effect_or_estimate: Tool (red flags, observable signs, symptom and memory prompts)
transfer_status: Cross-sport tool used in a boxing gym context
limitations: A recognition tool, not a diagnostic tool; sensitivity/specificity in community boxing settings not established
citation: Echemendia RJ, et al. The Concussion Recognition Tool 6 (CRT6). Br J Sports Med. 2023.
verification: pubmed:PMID 37316201 — search_articles(query='Concussion Recognition Tool 6 CRT6') returned it; get_article_metadata confirmed Echemendia RJ, Br J Sports Med 2023, doi 10.1136/bjsports-2023-107021
ppbf_implication: Attach CRT6 as a printed ringside card and as a read-only in-app checklist. SHADOW renders it; a coach completes it; a clinician interprets it.
verified_title: The Concussion Recognition Tool 6 (CRT6).

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Adolescent athletes who continued to play after a concussion took markedly longer to recover than those removed immediately.
population: Adolescent athletes with diagnosed sport-related concussion
effect_or_estimate: Recovery 44.4 (SD 36.0) days for those who played on vs 22.0 (SD 18.7) days for those removed (p=.003); 8.80x more likely to have protracted (>=21 d) recovery
transfer_status: Other-sport adolescent transfer to youth boxing
limitations: Small sample; not randomised — athletes who play on may have had different injury severity or reporting behaviour; single-centre
citation: Elbin RJ, et al. Removal From Play After Concussion and Recovery Time. Pediatrics. 2016.
ppbf_implication: Gives PPBF a concrete reason to write 'when in doubt, sit them out' into the SOP as a non-negotiable coach action. Confounded by indication — state as association, not proof.
verified_title: Removal From Play After Concussion and Recovery Time.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: In a large multi-site collegiate cohort, immediate removal from activity after sport-related concussion was associated with less time lost and shorter symptom duration than delayed removal.
population: US collegiate and service academy athletes
effect_or_estimate: 63.6% were delayed-removal; immediate removal associated with less time missed and shorter symptom duration after adjustment (R2 change .022-.046, p<=.001)
limitations: Observational; removal timing is not randomised; effect sizes modest in variance-explained terms
citation: Asken BM, et al. Immediate Removal From Activity After Sport-Related Concussion Is Associated With Shorter Clinical Recovery. Am J Sports Med. 2018.
ppbf_implication: Supports logging removal TIMESTAMP as a first-class field: time of suspected event, time of removal, delta. SHADOW may compute and display the delta for after-action review only.
verified_title: Immediate Removal From Activity After Sport-Related Concussion Is Associated With Shorter Clinical Recovery and Less Severe Symptoms in Collegiate Student-Athletes.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Pooled across studies, athletes who delayed reporting or continued playing recovered several days later than those who reported or were removed immediately.
effect_or_estimate: SMD 0.36 days (95% CI 0.066-0.662), p=0.017; immediate reporters recovered 5.4 days (95% CI -10.14 to -0.75) sooner
limitations: Small number of studies; heterogeneous definitions of 'delayed'; the raw-score CI is wide and crosses close to zero
citation: Barnhart M, et al. The Influence of Timing of Reporting and Clinic Presentation on Concussion Recovery Outcomes. Sports Med. 2021.
ppbf_implication: Reporting culture is the intervention target. PPBF should measure self-report latency as a programme KPI and never penalise an athlete for reporting.
verified_title: The Influence of Timing of Reporting and Clinic Presentation on Concussion Recovery Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: For children (5-12) and adolescents (13-18), strict rest is not recommended; early return to light physical activity and reduced screen time support recovery, and subacute assessment requires a multimodal tool.
study_design: Consensus recommendations derived from systematic reviews
effect_or_estimate: Qualitative recommendations; SCAT diagnostic discrimination best within first 72 hours
transfer_status: Cross-sport paediatric consensus applied to youth boxing
limitations: Consensus; limited paediatric trial evidence; nothing boxing-specific
citation: Davis GA, et al. Pediatric Sport-Related Concussion: Recommendations From the Amsterdam Consensus Statement 2023. Pediatrics. 2024.
ppbf_implication: PPBF must not encode a rest-until-symptom-free rule. Any graduated return content in the app is educational only and is executed under a clinician's written plan.
verified_title: Pediatric Sport-Related Concussion: Recommendations From the Amsterdam Consensus Statement 2023.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Boxing carries an elevated concussion risk relative to other combat sports, and studies of boxers report high proportions with cavum septum pellucidum, brain atrophy and cognitive abnormality; headguard benefit is contested.
sex: not disaggregated in the pooled figures
sample_size: 35 included articles; 631 boxers for cavum analysis, 411 for atrophy
effect_or_estimate: Concussion risk ratio 0.253 in boxing vs 0.065 in other combat sports (p<0.001); cavum septum pellucidum 147/631 (23.30%); brain atrophy 125/411 (30.41%)
limitations: Heavily weighted to older professional-boxer cohorts and to eras with different medical oversight; selection bias in imaging cohorts; the neurodegenerative proportions are NOT applicable to a youth non-contact PPBF programme
citation: Donnelly K, et al. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Investigating Head Trauma in Boxing. Clin J Sport Med. 2023.
ppbf_implication: Justifies conservative sparring-authorisation SOP and cumulative head-contact logging. Do NOT present these prevalence figures to parents as PPBF risk — they describe professional-era cohorts.
verified_title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Investigating Head Trauma in Boxing.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Instrumented mouthguards can quantify head impact exposure in boxing sparring; in beginner boxing courses most measured impacts were of low magnitude, with a right-skewed distribution and rare higher-magnitude events.
population: US Military Academy cadets in a compulsory introductory boxing course; separately, amateur boxers and MMA athletes
sex: male (n=22) in the cadet study; 23 athletes of whom 4 women in the boxing/MMA study
study_design: Instrumented mouthguard observational studies with video verification
effect_or_estimate: Cadets: mean peak linear acceleration 16.5 (SD 7.1) g, max 70.8 g; 640/809 (79.1%) between 10 and 20 g; mean peak angular acceleration 1.52 (SD 0.96) krad/s2
transfer_status: Boxing-specific but novice adult male military population — not youth, not female-representative
limitations: Very small samples; sensor artefact possible despite video verification; no dose-response to clinical outcome established; no safe threshold exists
citation: Fetchko K, et al. Mil Med. 2023. | Jansen AE, et al. Orthop J Sports Med. 2021.
ppbf_implication: Head-impact instrumentation is a plausible future PPBF research instrument, NOT a clearance device. No g-force threshold may be used to gate participation — none is validated.
verified_title: Characterizing Head Impact Exposure in Men and Women During Boxing and Mixed Martial Arts.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Amateur boxing injury rates are far higher in competition than in training, and the injured region differs: head and neck dominate in competition, upper limb in training.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohorts
effect_or_estimate: Competition 54.7 injuries/1000 athlete-exposures (95% CI 33.8-88.4) and 6.8/1000 min (4.2-10.9); training 1.3/1000 h (0.2-7.0). Competition head/neck median 72% (range 46-100%); training upper limb median 49% (40-53%)
limitations: Very wide confidence intervals, especially for training; inconsistent injury definitions and exposure denominators across studies
citation: Alevras AJ, et al. Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sci Med Sport. 2022.
ppbf_implication: Training-phase SOP should weight hand/wrist protection and technique; competition-day SOP should weight head/neck response. Distinct checklists, not one generic one.
verified_title: Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
topic: Hand and wrist injury dominance in training
claim: In an elite amateur squad tracked prospectively, the hand was the most injured location overall and in both training and competition, and more injuries occurred in training than competition.
effect_or_estimate: Total competition injury rate 828/1000 h; competition hand injury rate 302/1000 h; concussion incidence comparatively low
transfer_status: Boxing-specific but ELITE — do not apply these rates to novices or youth
limitations: Single national squad; medically-diagnosed injury definition inflates rates relative to time-loss definitions; elite training volumes
citation: Loosemore M, et al. Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study. Br J Sports Med. 2015.
ppbf_implication: Hand-wrap technique check and glove-condition check earn a place on the DAILY session checklist, not the monthly one. Supports an equipment-retirement criterion for compressed glove padding.
verified_title: Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study of medically diagnosed injury incidence and outcome.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Dentofacial injury is common across combat sports, supporting a mandatory mouthguard rule for any contact activity.
population: Combat sports practitioners across 14 disciplines including boxing
effect_or_estimate: Pooled dental injury prevalence 25.2% (12.3-40.8%); dentofacial 30.3% (18.1-44.1%); I2 = 100%
limitations: I2 = 100% — extreme heterogeneity means the pooled figure should not be read as a single population risk; retrospective self-report common in included studies
citation: Polmann H, et al. Prevalence of dentofacial injuries among combat sports practitioners: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Dent Traumatol. 2019 (epub); 2020 issue.
ppbf_implication: Mouthguard = mandatory equipment gate for any contact drill. Encode as a hard pre-contact checklist item; SHADOW may block a contact-session draft from being ISSUED until the item is ticked by a coach, but a coach makes the contact decision.
verified_title: Prevalence of dentofacial injuries among combat sports practitioners: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Prospective injury and illness data across Olympic combat sports are too heterogeneous in severity classification and exposure measurement to allow direct cross-sport comparison, which limits prevention-programme design.
population: Elite Olympic combat sport athletes (boxing, judo, taekwondo, wrestling)
study_design: Systematic review of prospective studies (>12 weeks)
sample_size: 9 studies, most at moderate risk of bias
effect_or_estimate: Boxing: head/face 45.8%, wrist 12.0%, lower back 7.8% of injuries (level 1/2b evidence)
transfer_status: Boxing rows are boxing-specific; the methodological conclusion is cross-sport
limitations: Moderate risk of bias in 6/9 studies; elite-only; no consensus injury definition
citation: Bromley SJ, et al. A systematic review of prospective epidemiological research into injury and illness in Olympic combat sport. Br J Sports Med. 2018.
ppbf_implication: PPBF should adopt ONE explicit injury definition and ONE exposure denominator (athlete-exposures and athlete-hours) from day one, so its own data are poolable. This is a data-model decision, not a coaching one.
verified_title: A systematic review of prospective epidemiological research into injury and illness in Olympic combat sport.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
topic: Skin infection burden in grappling contact sport
claim: Skin and soft-tissue infection is the dominant infectious-outbreak category in close-contact sport, with MRSA and tinea the leading pathogens.
effect_or_estimate: MRSA 7/21 (33%), tinea 6/21 (29%); skin and soft tissue was the site in 15/21 (71%); 12/21 (57%) involved high school or collegiate competitors
boxing_specific: no — predominantly wrestling, judo, American football
transfer_status: TRANSFER FROM GRAPPLING/COLLISION SPORT. Boxing has far less sustained skin-to-skin contact than wrestling; the shared-equipment and shared-surface routes transfer better than the skin-to-skin route
limitations: Publication bias toward investigated outbreaks; denominators absent; predates current MRSA epidemiology
citation: Collins CJ, O'Connell B. Infectious disease outbreaks in competitive sports, 2005-2010. J Athl Train. 2012.
ppbf_implication: Hygiene SOP is justified, but PPBF must state the transfer caveat in writing so nobody claims wrestling incidence rates apply to boxing.
verified_title: Infectious disease outbreaks in competitive sports, 2005-2010.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: In NCAA men's wrestling surveillance, skin infections were identified overwhelmingly during practice rather than competition, most caused time loss of 24 hours or more, and infections clustered heavily in a minority of team-seasons.
sample_size: 112 skin infections in 87 athletes across 78,720 athlete-exposures; 35 team-seasons
effect_or_estimate: Overall rate 14.23/10,000 AEs (95% CI 11.59-16.86); 22.3% recurrent; 65.2% of infections attributable to 5 team-seasons; 89.3% identified during practice; 74.1% caused >=24 h time loss; viral rate 1.72x bacterial
transfer_status: WRESTLING-DERIVED. Male-only. Applies to PPBF chiefly as evidence that clustering is environmental/organisational, not random
limitations: Male wrestling only; athletic-trainer-reported so undercounts unpresented cases; no boxing equivalent identified
citation: Herzog MM, et al. Epidemiology of Skin Infections in Men's Wrestling: NCAA Surveillance Data 2009-10 to 2013-14. J Athl Train. 2017.
ppbf_implication: Clustering in a minority of team-seasons is the actionable finding: outbreaks are a facility/practice-culture signal. PPBF should track infections per athlete-exposure and flag clustering for a human hygiene review.
verified_title: Epidemiology of Skin Infections in Men's Wrestling: Analysis of 2009-2010 Through 2013-2014 National Collegiate Athletic Association Surveillance Data.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Tinea gladiatorum, predominantly caused by Trichophyton tonsurans, spreads primarily by direct skin-to-skin contact in contact-sport athletes, with reported prevalence varying enormously across settings.
study_design: Systematic review of incidence studies plus narrative review
effect_or_estimate: Reported prevalence ranged from 2.4% to 100% across studies
transfer_status: WRESTLING-DERIVED; boxing exposure is lower but non-zero (clinch, shared gloves, shared bags, shared mats)
limitations: The 2.4-100% range is a statement of heterogeneity, not a usable risk estimate; case definitions and diagnostic methods vary widely
citation: Zalewski A, et al. Tinea Gladiatorum: Epidemiology, Clinical Aspects, and Management. J Clin Med. 2022. | Adams BB. Tinea corporis gladiatorum. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2002.
ppbf_implication: Skin-check protocol in the checklists document. Recognition is a coach/staff task; DIAGNOSIS and exclusion-from-participation are health decisions for a qualified clinician.
verified_title: Tinea corporis gladiatorum.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Evidence on environmental (mat) reservoirs for dermatophytes is mixed: one Iranian study cultured T. tonsurans from a third of surveyed mats, while another found no positive mat cultures and concluded person-to-person spread predominated.
population: Wrestlers and combat athletes in Iran
age_range: 10-19 most frequent group in one study
study_design: Two cross-sectional clinico-epidemiological studies with environmental sampling
sample_size: 270 wrestlers / 240 mat touch preparations (2011); 4240 athletes screened, 631 suspected (2020)
effect_or_estimate: 2011: 19.2% of wrestlers infected; 8/24 mats (33.3%) heavily contaminated with T. tonsurans. 2020: 6.5% (278/4240) confirmed; no positive dermatophyte culture obtained from mats
transfer_status: Wrestling/combat-sport transfer; mat contamination is directly relevant to a boxing gym floor
limitations: Two studies, same region, conflicting environmental results; culture sensitivity from surfaces is poor and a negative culture does not prove absence; neither study tested a cleaning intervention
citation: Aghamirian MR, Ghiasian SA. Mycoses. 2011. | Kermani F, et al. Mycoses. 2020.
ppbf_implication: Mat cleaning is justified on precaution and on general disinfection principles, but PPBF must NOT claim mat cleaning prevents a specified fraction of infections. Frequency is a PROPOSED PPBF PARAMETER, not an evidence-derived number.
verified_title: A clinico-epidemiological study on tinea gladiatorum in Iranian wrestlers and mat contamination by dermatophytes.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Prophylactic oral valacyclovir substantially reduced herpes gladiatorum outbreaks at a 28-day high-school wrestling camp over a 10-year observational period.
population: High-school wrestlers at a summer camp, Minnesota
sex: not stated (wrestling camp, presumed predominantly male)
study_design: Observational cohort over 10 seasons (comparison group = non-users)
effect_or_estimate: 84.7% decrease in probability of an outbreak among prophylaxis users; 36 outbreaks total
transfer_status: WRESTLING-DERIVED and setting-specific (residential camp, extreme skin-to-skin exposure). Transfer to boxing is weak
limitations: Not randomised — users self-selected; unmeasured confounding; camp setting not comparable to a community gym; a MEDICATION decision, entirely outside PPBF and SHADOW authority
citation: Anderson BJ, McGuire DP, et al. Prophylactic Valacyclovir to Prevent Outbreaks of Primary Herpes Gladiatorum at a 28-Day Wrestling Camp: A 10-Year Review. Clin J Sport Med. 2016.
ppbf_implication: Recorded for completeness of the evidence base ONLY. PPBF and SHADOW must never recommend, suggest, or route toward prophylactic medication. Any antiviral question goes to the athlete's clinician.
verified_title: Prophylactic Valacyclovir to Prevent Outbreaks of Primary Herpes Gladiatorum at a 28-Day Wrestling Camp: A 10-Year Review.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Weekly oral fluconazole reduced tinea gladiatorum incidence versus placebo in a randomised trial in wrestlers, and a long observational programme reported a large drop in incidence.
study_design: Double-blind placebo-controlled trial (2000); prospective 10-year longitudinal study (2009)
sample_size: RCT: not stated in abstract; longitudinal: 373 participants
effect_or_estimate: RCT: infection in 6% (fluconazole) vs 22% (placebo) vs 18% (not enrolled), p<0.05. Longitudinal: incidence fell from 67.4% to 3.5% over 10 years
transfer_status: WRESTLING-DERIVED. Not transferable to boxing as a practice recommendation
limitations: The 67.4%-to-3.5% figure is uncontrolled before-after over a decade with concurrent hygiene changes — not attributable to the drug alone; systemic antifungal prophylaxis in minors raises safety and stewardship questions
source_type: Randomised controlled trial and prospective cohort
citation: Kohl TD, et al. Pediatr Infect Dis J. 2000. | Brickman K, et al. Clin J Sport Med. 2009.
ppbf_implication: Evidence-base completeness only. OUT OF SCOPE for PPBF and prohibited for SHADOW: no medication recommendations, especially for minors.
verified_title: Fluconazole for the prevention and treatment of tinea gladiatorum.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: A survey of Pennsylvania high-school wrestling programmes found schools using more preventive practices reported MORE ringworm infections, and coaches were frequently involved in making the diagnosis.
effect_or_estimate: 84.7% of responding schools had >=1 diagnosed case; 33% of affected teams had a wrestler miss a match; more preventive practices associated with MORE infections (p<0.05); 60% of coaches involved in diagnosis
transfer_status: Wrestling-derived; the surveillance-bias lesson is general
limitations: Almost certainly reverse causation and detection bias — programmes with outbreaks adopt more practices and look harder. Do NOT read as evidence that prevention causes infection
citation: Kohl TD, et al. Tinea gladiatorum: Pennsylvania's experience. Clin J Sport Med. 2002.
ppbf_implication: Two lessons: (1) infection counts rise when you start looking, so PPBF must not interpret an early rise in recorded skin findings as a hygiene failure; (2) COACHES DIAGNOSING is a documented and undesirable practice — PPBF SOP explicitly forbids it.
verified_title: Tinea gladiatorum: Pennsylvania's experience.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Community-associated MRSA skin and soft-tissue infection occurs in contact-sport teams, is transmitted person-to-person and via shared equipment, and carries meaningful morbidity.
population: Collegiate American football players; athletic populations generally
study_design: Multi-programme retrospective analysis plus narrative reviews
effect_or_estimate: 33/491 (6.7%) diagnosed with MRSA; abscess 70%, cellulitis 16%; 90% underwent surgical drainage; 27% received IV antibiotics; extremity infections 30 vs truncal 7; occurred predominantly in the first third of the season (p<0.001)
transfer_status: COLLISION-SPORT TRANSFER. Abrasion + shared equipment routes are plausible in boxing; the turf-abrasion route is not
limitations: Single-sport, male, three programmes; the widely-cited 'up to 70% hospitalised' figure derives from selected outbreak reports, not a representative denominator
citation: Bowers AL, et al. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2008. | Rihn JA, et al. Am J Sports Med. 2005. | Redziniak DE, et al. Int J Sports Med. 2009.
ppbf_implication: Justifies: no sharing of personal protective equipment, cover-all-wounds rule, immediate reporting of any draining lesion, and prompt referral. Referral, not treatment.
verified_title: Community-acquired methicillin-resistant staphylococcus aureus: an emerging problem in the athletic population.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: NFHS and NCAA guidance specify minimum treatment durations before return to contact for common infectious skin lesions (e.g. 72 hours of topical antifungal for tinea corporis; 120 hours of oral antiviral for recurrent herpes gladiatorum; 72 hours after incision and drainage for MRSA abscess with no further drainage), while acknowledging the underlying evidence is limited.
population: US high school and collegiate contact-sport athletes, wrestling-centred
study_design: Governing-body position statement and medical release form; underlying evidence base explicitly acknowledged as incomplete by the issuing body
effect_or_estimate: Tinea corporis: >=72 h topical antifungal. Tinea capitis: 14 days oral. Primary HSV: 10-14 days oral antiviral. Recurrent HSV: >=120 h oral antiviral. MRSA abscess: I&D plus >=72 h treatment with no further drainage. Scabies/head lice: 24 h after topical treatment. Conjunctivitis: 24 h treatment and no discharge
transfer_status: WRESTLING RULEBOOK TRANSFER. Boxing bodies do not publish an equivalent skin-lesion table; applying these to boxing is a conservative organisational choice, not a boxing rule
limitations: NFHS itself states no definitive data allow prediction of when a lesion stops shedding transmissible organisms. Peer-reviewed commentary notes HSV DNA can be detected by PCR after 5 days of antiviral therapy, with unknown relation to infectivity. These are administrative return thresholds, not biological clearance
source_type: Governing-body position statement plus peer-reviewed commentary
citation: NFHS Sports Medicine Advisory Committee. Sports-Related Skin Infections Position Statement and Guidelines (2022 revision) and NFHS Medical Release Form for Participation with Skin Lesion(s). | Pujalte GGA, et al. More Than Skin Deep: Dermatologic Conditions in Athletes. Sports Health. 2022.
doi_or_pmid: PMID 35034516; doi 10.1177/19417381211065026 (commentary); NFHS statement has no DOI
verification: governing-body page fetched via web_search 2026-08-07 (assets.nfhs.org NFHS SMAC position statement, and NFHS medical release form mirrored at ohsaa.org and nchsaa.org); commentary verified pubmed:PMID 35034516
ppbf_implication: PPBF may ADOPT these thresholds as its house exclusion standard by governance decision, and SHADOW may display the adopted table and compute an earliest-eligible-return DATE for coach reference. SHADOW must never decide that a lesion is or is not infectious, and return requires written clinician clearance.
verified_title: More Than Skin Deep: Dermatologic Conditions in Athletes.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Daily pre-practice and pre-competition skin checks are the recommended prevention practice in wrestling; the recognition step is performed by staff, the diagnosis and clearance by a health-care professional.
effect_or_estimate: Practice recommendation; no controlled effect estimate located
transfer_status: WRESTLING PRACTICE STANDARD. In boxing the exposure is lower, so daily whole-body checks may be disproportionate; a visible-skin check is the proportionate analogue
limitations: No trial evidence that skin-check frequency reduces infection incidence; the practice is also a privacy and safeguarding-sensitive activity with minors
citation: National Federation of State High School Associations. Prevention Key to Reducing Skin Infections in High School Wrestling (NFHS article).
doi_or_pmid: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE — no DOI/PMID; governing-body web article
ppbf_implication: PPBF adopts a VISIBLE-SKIN check (face, neck, hands, forearms) at check-in, performed in an open area, never a private body inspection of a minor. Safeguarding constraint overrides hygiene convenience.
independent_verification_detail: governing body, statute, regulator or repo document — URL + retrieval date in verification column

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
claim: Hepatitis B transmission has been documented within contact-sport clubs, and hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for contact and collision sport athletes and for adolescent athletes.
population: Contact-sport athletes; Olympic wrestlers (Turkey); a wrestling club (Japan)
study_design: Narrative review with recommendations; cross-sectional serology study; molecular case-series
effect_or_estimate: 9/70 (13%) with occult HBV infection by PCR; 8/70 (11%) with HBV DNA detectable in sweat; correlation between blood and sweat HBV DNA r=0.52, p<0.01. Japan: identical full-length HBV sequences (subgenotype C2) in 3 club members, consistent with horizontal transmission
transfer_status: WRESTLING-DERIVED; boxing involves bleeding facial injury, so the blood-exposure route is directly relevant
limitations: Small samples; the sweat-transmission pathway is inferred, not demonstrated experimentally; single-country serology may not generalise; vaccination policy is a public-health decision, not a gym decision
citation: Kordi R, Wallace WA. Br J Sports Med. 2004. | Bereket-Yucel S. Br J Sports Med. 2007. | Takata Y, et al. Am J Case Rep. 2020.
ppbf_implication: Universal precautions and a stop-for-blood rule belong in the SOP: any bleeding stops the drill, wound is covered before return, blood-contaminated surfaces and clothing are handled with gloves and disinfected. PPBF does not advise on vaccination — it signposts to the athlete's clinician or public health.
verified_title: Blood borne infections in sport: risks of transmission, methods of prevention, and recommendations for hepatitis B vaccination.

track: B3 Gym Operations SOP / Facility / Hygiene
topic: Equipment contamination — what disinfection did and did not do
claim: Hand-contact surfaces of exercise equipment were frequently contaminated with rhinovirus, and in a one-week trial, twice-daily disinfection did not reduce the prevalence of viral isolation.
population: Two fitness centres in a US military community
study_design: Observational culture study plus before-after disinfection intervention
effect_or_estimate: Viruses (generally rhinovirus) on 63/100 (63%) surfaces; weight equipment 73% vs aerobic 51% (p=0.026); viral positivity 48% before cleaning vs 86% after (no reduction); no pathogenic bacteria cultured
transfer_status: General fitness facility; boxing gyms share the fomite structure (bags, gloves, ropes, handles)
limitations: Single week, two facilities, 2006 methods; culture positivity is not the same as transmissible dose; disinfection protocol, product and contact time were not characterised, so this is NOT evidence that correct disinfection fails
citation: Goldhammer KA, et al. Prospective study of bacterial and viral contamination of exercise equipment. Clin J Sport Med. 2006.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of dropout in youth soccer reported an annual weighted mean dropout rate of 23.9%, with meta-regression indicating rates stable from ages 10-19 and higher rates for girls (26.8%) than boys (21.4%).
population: Youth soccer players from five countries
competitive_level: Organised club youth soccer, mixed levels
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis with mixed-effects meta-regression; 12 studies identified, results based on 10 included articles
effect_or_estimate: 23.9% annual weighted mean dropout; girls 26.8%, boys 21.4%
transfer_status: TRANSFER FROM OTHER SPORT - soccer to boxing is unvalidated
limitations: Sport-specific to soccer; dropout definitions vary across the included studies; registration-based rather than attendance-based in most sources; no combat-sport data
citation: Percept Mot Skills, 2015. A systematic review and meta-analysis of dropout rates in youth soccer.
ppbf_implication: Supplies the ONLY defensible external order-of-magnitude reference for annual youth-sport attrition, but must be labelled as soccer. PPBF must not adopt 23.9% as a boxing target or benchmark; it is a comparator with an explicit population label (KPI B4-K034).
verified_title: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS OF DROPOUT RATES IN YOUTH SOCCER.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: Sex difference in youth sport dropout
claim: In the same youth soccer meta-analysis, annual dropout was higher for girls than boys, which supports mandatory sex-stratified reporting of retention rather than a single blended rate.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis with meta-regression
effect_or_estimate: Girls 26.8% vs boys 21.4% annual dropout
limitations: Soccer-specific; does not establish a mechanism; may not generalise to a sport with different sex-participation dynamics
citation: Percept Mot Skills, 2015. A systematic review and meta-analysis of dropout rates in youth soccer.
ppbf_implication: Sex-stratified retention (KPI B4-K084) is mandatory, not optional; an unstratified retention figure can conceal a real gap.
verified_title: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS OF DROPOUT RATES IN YOUTH SOCCER.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: Survival analysis is feasible on club registration data
claim: A retrospective cohort of Australian youth swimmers used Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with Cox regression on registration data and reported a median sustained participation of 4 years (95% CI 3.93-4.06), with 15.9% still participating at 10 years, and identified age group as associated with dropout.
population: New South Wales registered youth swimmers
study_design: Retrospective cohort using registration and competition data; Kaplan-Meier plus Cox proportional hazards
effect_or_estimate: Median sustained participation 4 years (95% CI 3.93-4.06); 15.9% participating at 10 years; hazard ratio for dropout markedly higher for 10-year-olds vs 15-year-olds
transfer_status: TRANSFER FROM OTHER SPORT - method transfers, the numbers do not
limitations: Swimming-specific; registration-based exposure (not attendance); retrospective; a national registry has far more complete follow-up than a single gym will have
citation: Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2020. Sink or Swim? A survival analysis of sport dropout in Australian youth swimmers.
ppbf_implication: Direct methodological precedent for the retention analysis plan: KM plus Cox on club registration/attendance data is an established approach in youth sport. PPBF should adopt the method and generate its own numbers, not import the swimming figures.
verified_title: Sink or Swim? A survival analysis of sport dropout in Australian youth swimmers.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: Dropout hazard varies by age and performance level
claim: A survival analysis of French swimmers (n=160,861 under age 21) using Kaplan-Meier curves reported dropout peaks at 13.16 years for girls and 17.50 years for boys, and a large gradient by performance level - at age 13 the top 10% of female swimmers had a dropout rate of 8.7% versus 78.1% for the bottom 10%.
competitive_level: Registered competitive swimming across performance levels
study_design: Registry cohort with chi-squared tests and Kaplan-Meier survival curves
effect_or_estimate: Dropout peak at 13.16 y (girls) and 17.50 y (boys); age 13 dropout 8.7% top decile vs 78.1% bottom decile (female)
limitations: Swimming-specific; performance-level stratification reflects a selection system that a community boxing gym does not operate; registry data cannot distinguish quitting from switching sports
citation: Front Sports Act Living, 2025. A survival analysis of dropout among French swimmers.
ppbf_implication: Supports stratifying PPBF retention curves by age band and by ability/lane, and warns that a program which visibly sorts athletes by performance may accelerate dropout among the lowest-performing - directly relevant to how PPBF designs its development lanes.
verified_title: A survival analysis of dropout among French swimmers.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: Dropout risk factors are multi-level, not individual
claim: A registry study of 1,898 male handball players completing U20 eligibility in Hungary (2013-2023) using logistic regression and survival analysis found youth-to-senior dropout associated with structural and organisational factors including competition reform exposure, homegrown status, late-adolescent club mobility and team competitive strength - not only individual-level factors.
study_design: Longitudinal registry cohort; multivariable logistic regression and survival analysis
effect_or_estimate: Associations reported for birth cohort, competition reform exposure, homegrown status, club mobility and team strength; specific coefficients not extracted here
transfer_status: TRANSFER FROM OTHER SPORT and from an elite population
limitations: Elite male handball; a youth-to-senior transition is a different construct from community-gym retention; observational, so associations are not causal
citation: Front Sports Act Living, 2026. The achievement-dropout paradox: structural and performance predictors of youth-to-senior transition attrition in elite handball.
ppbf_implication: Justifies including organisational and structural covariates (lane changes, coach changes, schedule changes, fee changes) in the PPBF dropout hazard model, not only athlete characteristics.
verified_title: The achievement-dropout paradox: structural and performance predictors of youth-to-senior transition attrition in elite handball.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 prospective cohort studies in amateur boxing reported pooled competition injury incidence of 54.7 per 1000 athlete-exposures (95% CI 33.8-88.4) and 6.8 per 1000 minutes of exposure (95% CI 4.2-10.9), and training injury incidence of 1.3 per 1000 hours (95% CI 0.2-7.0), with head and neck the most commonly injured region in competition (median 72%, range 46-100%).
sex: not disaggregated in the abstract; amateur boxing cohorts are predominantly male
age_range: Not specified in the abstract; predominantly adult amateur
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies; random-effects models
effect_or_estimate: Competition 54.7/1000 athlete-exposures (95% CI 33.8-88.4) and 6.8/1000 min (95% CI 4.2-10.9); training 1.3/1000 h (95% CI 0.2-7.0)
limitations: Very wide confidence intervals, especially for training; heterogeneous injury definitions and denominators across studies; competition populations, not community youth non-contact programs; the training estimate spans an order of magnitude
citation: J Sci Med Sport, 2022. Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
ppbf_implication: Establishes that athlete-exposures, exposure-minutes and exposure-hours are all in legitimate use as boxing injury denominators - and that they are not interchangeable. PPBF must fix ONE denominator per safety KPI and state it (KPIs B4-K040 to B4-K043). The wide CIs mean no external rate can serve as a PPBF safety target.
verified_title: Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
claim: A second systematic review and meta-analysis of 21st-century boxing epidemiology calculated injury incidence rates per 1000 boxers, per 1000 competition exposures, per 1000 minutes of competition and per 1000 minutes of training, with subgroup meta-analyses by boxing type - illustrating that a single 'boxing injury rate' does not exist independent of its denominator.
study_design: PRISMA systematic review with single-arm random-effects meta-analyses; Level of evidence 3
sample_size: Studies published January 2000 - November 2021 (count not extracted)
effect_or_estimate: Multiple incidence rates reported across four different denominators; sample-size weighted means with 95% CIs
limitations: Level 3 evidence; heterogeneity across boxing types; no youth community-program subgroup
citation: Orthop J Sports Med, 2023. Incidence Rates and Pathology Types of Boxing-Specific Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Epidemiology Studies in the 21st Century.
ppbf_implication: Reinforces that PPBF's dashboard must display the exposure denominator next to every safety rate, and must never compare a PPBF rate to an external rate computed on a different denominator.
verified_title: Incidence Rates and Pathology Types of Boxing-Specific Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Epidemiology Studies in the 21st Century.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: Elite boxing surveillance - training vs competition burden
claim: A 5-year prospective surveillance study of the Great Britain amateur boxing squad (66 boxers, 2005-2009) found hand injuries were the most common by location overall, more injuries occurred during training than during competition, and reported a total competition injury rate of 828 per 1000 hours.
population: Great Britain elite amateur boxing squad
study_design: Longitudinal prospective injury surveillance, medically diagnosed injuries
effect_or_estimate: Total competition injury rate 828 per 1000 hours; more total injuries in training than competition; hand the most-injured location
limitations: Single elite squad; small n; medically diagnosed definition (a national squad has medical staff a community gym does not, which inflates capture relative to a community setting); the per-1000-hour competition rate is not comparable to per-athlete-exposure rates
citation: Br J Sports Med, 2015. Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study of medically diagnosed injury incidence and outcome.
ppbf_implication: Training exposure, not just competition, must be captured in PPBF's safety denominators - most injury volume in this elite cohort occurred in training. Ascertainment differences between a medically staffed squad and a community gym mean PPBF's rate will not be comparable to this figure.
verified_title: Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study of medically diagnosed injury incidence and outcome.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: Boxing injury rate in a community-scale prospective cohort
claim: A one-year prospective cohort of 33 amateur and 14 professional boxers in Victoria, Australia measured training and competition exposure and recorded 21 injuries, of which most were to the head region (71%), with concussion the most common single injury (33%), and calculated an overall rate of 2.0 injuries per 1000 hours of boxing.
population: Registered amateur and professional boxers, Victoria, Australia
study_design: Prospective cohort with one-year follow-up and measured exposure
effect_or_estimate: 2.0 injuries per 1000 hours of boxing; 71% head region (the reported CI in the abstract spans an implausible negative lower bound, indicating an unreliable interval); 33% concussion
limitations: Very small sample (21 injuries total); volunteer participants; adult registered boxers, not youth; the reported confidence interval for the head-region proportion is not usable as printed; 2004-2005 data predates several rule changes
citation: Br J Sports Med, 2006. A prospective cohort study of injury in amateur and professional boxing.
ppbf_implication: Illustrates that small-cohort boxing injury estimates are extremely imprecise. PPBF must set a minimum-exposure floor before publishing any injury rate (KPI B4-K043 sets 10 incidents and 5000 athlete-sessions) and report raw counts below it.
verified_title: A prospective cohort study of injury in amateur and professional boxing.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
claim: The International Olympic Committee consensus statement on methods for recording and reporting epidemiological data on injury and illness in sport (2020), including the STROBE Extension for Sport Injury and Illness Surveillance, provides the standard for injury definitions, exposure denominators and reporting, developed by an expert working group through an open survey and a three-day consensus meeting.
population: All sports injury and illness surveillance
study_design: Expert consensus statement with reporting-checklist extension
effect_or_estimate: Methodological recommendations; no effect estimate
transfer_status: METHODOLOGICAL STANDARD - applies across sports including boxing
limitations: Consensus rather than trial evidence; written primarily for research surveillance rather than community-club operational reporting, so PPBF will need to adapt rather than adopt wholesale
citation: Br J Sports Med, 2020. International Olympic Committee consensus statement: methods for recording and reporting of epidemiological data on injury and illness in sport 2020 (including STROBE Extension for Sport Injury and Illness Surveillance).
verification: pubmed:PMID 32071062 (abstract retrieved); companion publication PMID 32118084 in Orthop J Sports Med also verified
ppbf_implication: PPBF should adopt IOC-consistent injury definitions and exposure denominators so its safety data is interpretable and comparable. This is the authoritative source for KPI B4-K040 to B4-K043 denominator design.
verified_title: International Olympic Committee consensus statement: methods for recording and reporting of epidemiological data on injury and illness in sport 2020 (including STROBE Extension for Sport Injury and Illness Surveillance (STROBE-SIIS)).

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: Head guards and head-blow stoppages in amateur competition
claim: A cross-sectional observational study of AIBA competitions, comparing World Series Boxing (no head guards) with head-guarded AIBA competitions and comparing the 2009/2011 world championships (head guards) with 2013 (no head guards), found the number of stoppages due to head blows was significantly decreased without head guards, alongside a notable increase in cuts.
population: Elite amateur boxers in AIBA competition
study_design: Cross-sectional observational study with prospective data collection by ringside physicians
sample_size: Not extracted; measured as stoppages per 10,000 rounds and per 1000 hours
effect_or_estimate: Significant decrease in head-blow stoppages without head guards; increase in cuts
transfer_status: BOXING-SPECIFIC but ELITE COMPETITION - does not transfer to gym sparring or youth
limitations: Observational and confounded by concurrent rule and population changes; stoppage counts are a proxy for brain injury, not a direct measure; elite adult competition only; head guards remain mandatory in many youth and national contexts
citation: Clin J Sport Med, 2017. Use of Head Guards in AIBA Boxing Tournaments - A Cross-Sectional Observational Study.
ppbf_implication: Stoppage counts are shaped by rules and equipment, not only by athlete or coach behaviour. This is a core reason KPI B4-K045 must be framed as a vigilance indicator and never benchmarked downward. PPBF must follow its own sanctioning body's current head-guard rule; nothing here authorises a local deviation.
verified_title: Use of Head Guards in AIBA Boxing Tournaments-A Cross-Sectional Observational Study.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: Rule changes alter verdict rates over time
claim: A review of 29,357 Olympic boxing bouts from 1952 to 2011 found that rule changes altered the rates of health-relevant verdicts - for example an increase in the RSC-Injury rate (0.72% to 2.42%) following the standing-count rule, and changes in RSC-Injury and RSC-Head rates following subsequent rule modifications.
sex: predominantly male over most of the period
study_design: Retrospective analysis of competition records across 59 years
effect_or_estimate: RSC-Injury rate rose from 0.72% to 2.42% after the standing-count rule; further changes in RSC-Head and RSC-Injury rates after later rule changes
limitations: Web-sourced retrospective records; ecological analysis with no individual-level data; confounded by concurrent changes in officiating, scoring and population; verdict recording practice itself changed over the period
citation: Br J Sports Med, 2013. Amateur boxing in the last 59 years. Impact of rules changes on the type of verdicts recorded and implications on boxers' health.
ppbf_implication: Bout verdict rates are a property of the rule environment, not a measure of coaching quality or athlete development. This is direct evidence against any win-rate or verdict-based performance metric (KPIs B4-K061, B4-K113).
verified_title: Amateur boxing in the last 59 years. Impact of rules changes on the type of verdicts recorded and implications on boxers' health.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: Acute symptom response to boxing head impacts is unresolved
claim: An exploratory observational cohort of seven competitive boxers used instrumented mouthguards and the SCAT5 symptom scale before, immediately after and 48 hours after sparring, and found no group-level difference in symptom scores pre- to post-sparring; the authors describe the acute dose-response relationship between head impact exposure and concussion as unresolved.
study_design: Exploratory observational cohort with instrumented mouthguards and repeated symptom measurement
effect_or_estimate: No group-level pre-post symptom difference; authors recommend individual-specific and cumulative approaches
limitations: Seven participants; exploratory qualitative analysis of impact metrics; no control condition; self-reported symptoms are under-reported in competitive settings; a null result at n=7 is uninformative about a true effect
citation: J Sci Med Sport, 2026. Exploring the link between acute symptom changes and repetitive head impacts in boxing sparring.
ppbf_implication: There is NO validated head-impact or symptom threshold PPBF could implement. KPI B4-K046 reports symptom-flag rates descriptively and routes every flag to a qualified human; SHADOW must never compute a safe-exposure threshold. TBD - PPBF cannot resolve this and must not attempt to.
verified_title: Exploring the link between acute symptom changes and repetitive head impacts in boxing sparring.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: Head impact exposure measurement in novice boxing
claim: Instrumented mouthguards worn by 22 male US Military Academy cadets during a compulsory introductory boxing course captured 809 video-verified impacts across 205 analysed player-bouts, averaging 3.9 impacts per player-bout.
population: US Military Academy cadets in an introductory boxing course
study_design: Observational instrumented-mouthguard study with video verification; preliminary dataset
effect_or_estimate: Mean 3.9 video-verified impacts per player-bout
transfer_status: BOXING-SPECIFIC but young-adult male military cadets, not youth community athletes
limitations: Preliminary dataset; all male; young-adult military population under compulsory participation; impact counts are not injury outcomes; sensor data quality in boxing is a documented problem
citation: Mil Med, 2023. Measurement of Head Kinematics Using Instrumented Mouthguards During Introductory Boxing Courses in U.S. Military Academy Cadets.
ppbf_implication: Head-impact exposure is measurable in principle, but instrumenting youth athletes raises consent, cost and data-governance questions PPBF has not resolved. PPBF's practical exposure proxy remains logged sparring rounds and contact minutes (KPIs B4-K041, B4-K042).
verified_title: Measurement of Head Kinematics Using Instrumented Mouthguards During Introductory Boxing Courses in U.S. Military Academy Cadets.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: Acute cognitive effects across a boxing tournament
claim: A prospective controlled study of 82 collegiate amateur boxers in a 7-day single-elimination tournament, with 30 matched non-boxing controls, administered a computerised battery before the tournament and within two hours of each bout, testing simple and choice reaction time, working memory and learning across 142 tested bouts.
population: Collegiate amateur boxers with matched non-boxing controls
study_design: Prospective controlled study with repeated computerised cognitive testing
effect_or_estimate: Effect direction and magnitude not extracted from the abstract text available; design and measures verified
limitations: Participants had no history of recent concussion or prior brain injury, so results do not generalise to athletes with injury history; 2004 study using a computerised battery of that era; acute testing only, no long-term follow-up; tournament format concentrates exposure atypically
citation: Neurology, 2004. A prospective controlled study of cognitive function during an amateur boxing tournament.
verification: pubmed:PMID 15136671 (abstract retrieved; effect estimates not reproduced because the abstract text available was truncated before the results)
ppbf_implication: Repeated same-period bout exposure is a recognised research concern in amateur boxing. PPBF should record bout density per athlete as a monitored exposure variable, with any competition-scheduling decision made by a qualified coach and physician under the sanctioning body's rules - never by SHADOW.
verified_title: A prospective controlled study of cognitive function during an amateur boxing tournament.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: Boxing as a mental-health intervention - evidence is preliminary and non-contact
claim: A scoping review following PRISMA-ScR identified 16 documents using NON-CONTACT boxing exercise as an intervention, reporting reductions in symptoms of anxiety, depression, PTSD and negative symptoms of schizophrenia, and concluded that the evidence is preliminary.
population: Mixed clinical and general populations in the included documents
study_design: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of academic and grey literature
effect_or_estimate: Reported symptom reductions across several conditions; the authors characterise the evidence as preliminary
transfer_status: BOXING-SPECIFIC but NON-CONTACT and largely adult clinical populations
limitations: Scoping review, so no pooled effect estimate and no formal risk-of-bias synthesis; includes grey literature; the interventions are non-contact boxing-style exercise, which is a different exposure from competitive boxing training; mostly adult, not youth
citation: Am J Lifestyle Med, 2022. Boxing as an Intervention in Mental Health: A Scoping Review.
ppbf_implication: PPBF may honestly describe non-contact boxing-style exercise as having preliminary mental-health evidence in adult populations. It must NOT claim mental-health outcomes for its youth contact program, and must not present this as validation of PPBF's own effect (KPI B4-K085).
verified_title: Boxing as an Intervention in Mental Health: A Scoping Review.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: England Boxing - protective medical suspensions and age-graded participation
claim: The England Boxing rule book applies protective medical suspensions where a boxer receives a knockout or where a sparring session is stopped because a boxer received blows to the head, requires return via the England Boxing Concussion Protocol with separate annexes for under-18s and over-19s, prohibits a boxer serving a medical suspension from boxing, and sets age-graded participation rules including that a child under 10 may join a club and take classes but may not box competitively, take a skills bout, or spar, with round durations and weight-difference limits specified by age category.
population: Amateur boxers registered with England Boxing
effect_or_estimate: Rules, not estimates: medical suspension following KO or head-blow sparring stoppage; concussion protocol by age band; under-10 sparring and competition prohibition; 2 kg weight-difference limit in the youngest categories
transfer_status: JURISDICTION-SPECIFIC - England Boxing rules do not apply in the United States
limitations: Applies only within England Boxing's jurisdiction; rulebook editions change annually, so the specific edition must be cited; PPBF operates under USA Boxing rules and must not apply England Boxing provisions as if they were its own
citation: England Boxing Technical and Competition Rules (2025 and 2026 editions) and England Boxing Rule Book (2019, 2022/23, 2023/24 editions), sections on medical suspensions, concussion protocol annexes B1/B2, and age categories.
verification: web_search retrieved England Boxing rulebook PDFs on englandboxing.org (2019, 2022/23, 2023/24, 2025 and 2026 editions), 2026-08-07; provisions on medical suspension after KO or head-blow sparring stoppage, concussion protocol annexes, under-10 restrictions and 2 kg weight limits confirmed in the retrieved text
ppbf_implication: Confirms that (i) sparring incidents, not only bouts, trigger protective suspensions in at least one major jurisdiction, and (ii) age-graded contact restriction is a rulebook matter. PPBF must encode its OWN sanctioning body's current rules, and KPI B4-K047 must be parameterised by jurisdiction rather than hard-coded.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: USA Boxing - post-KO restriction affidavit, age divisions and bout-experience requirements
claim: USA Boxing rules require the ringside doctor to complete and sign a Restriction Affidavit after a bout resulting in knockout or technical knockout, recommending prescribed rest days or protective restrictive measures, with the data recorded in the USA Boxing database; the rulebook sets age divisions (for example Junior 15-16, Youth 17-18, Elite 19-40), sets minimum bout counts for entry to certain advancing competitions, and prohibits exhibition bouts.
population: Amateur boxers registered with USA Boxing
age_range: Age-banded divisions from Junior through Elite and Masters
effect_or_estimate: Rules, not estimates: mandatory Restriction Affidavit after KO/TKO with prescribed rest days set by the ringside doctor; division age bands; bout-count minimums for certain advancing competitions; exhibition bouts prohibited
limitations: Rulebook editions are revised annually (editions dated January 2024 and January 2025 were both retrieved); PPBF must work from the current edition, and local boxing committees and state commissions may add requirements
citation: USA Boxing National Rule Book (editions effective January 1, 2024 and January 1, 2025), sections on Restriction Affidavits after KO/TKO, age divisions, competition entry requirements, and the prohibition on exhibition bouts.
verification: web_search retrieved USA Boxing National Rule Book PDFs (2022, January 2024 and January 2025 editions) and the USA Boxing rules-clarification page listing passbook decision codes RSC, RSC-I and ABD, 2026-08-07; the Restriction Affidavit, age-division and bout-minimum provisions were confirmed in the retrieved text
ppbf_implication: The rest period after a KO/TKO is set by the ringside physician on a per-case affidavit, not by a fixed formula. SHADOW must therefore store and enforce the physician's recorded restriction (KPI B4-K047) and must never compute, shorten or infer one. Verdict codes for KPI B4-K061 should follow the USA Boxing passbook vocabulary.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: Concussion management is governed by consensus protocol, not by program metrics
claim: The consensus statement on concussion in sport from the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport (Amsterdam 2022) provides the international consensus framework for sport-related concussion, with a documented methodology and companion paediatric recommendations.
study_design: International expert consensus statement with a published methodology paper and paediatric companion
effect_or_estimate: Consensus recommendations; not an effect estimate
transfer_status: CROSS-SPORT CONSENSUS applying to boxing among other sports
limitations: Consensus rather than trial evidence; requires qualified clinical personnel to apply; boxing-specific application still runs through the sanctioning body's own protocol
citation: Br J Sports Med, 2023. Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport - Amsterdam, October 2022. Companion papers: Amsterdam 2022 process methodology summary; Pediatric Sport-Related Concussion: Recommendations From the Amsterdam Consensus Statement 2023.
doi_or_pmid: PMID 37316210 (main statement); PMID 37316208 (methodology); PMID 38044802 (paediatric recommendations in Pediatrics)
verification: pubmed:PMID 37316210, PMID 37316208 and PMID 38044802 (searched and metadata retrieved)
ppbf_implication: Concussion recognition, management and return decisions belong to qualified humans under this consensus and the sanctioning body's protocol. SHADOW is explicitly prohibited from concussion assessment, clearance or return-to-play decisions across KPIs B4-K045, B4-K046 and B4-K047.
verified_title: Amsterdam 2022 process: A summary of the methodology for the Amsterdam International Consensus on Concussion in Sport.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: Injury definition materially changes measured burden
claim: A cohort of preprofessional ballet (n=85) and contemporary (n=60) dancers completing weekly health-problem questionnaires under three injury definitions - time loss, medical attention, and any complaint - was designed specifically to describe how the choice of definition changes estimated injury prevalence, incidence and severity.
study_design: Prospective cohort with weekly self-report (modified OSTRC health-problem questionnaire) plus physiotherapist injury reports
effect_or_estimate: Injury burden estimates differ by definition; percent agreement between registration methods was assessed
transfer_status: METHODOLOGICAL - the finding is about measurement, and transfers across sports
limitations: Dance population, predominantly female; the specific magnitudes are dance-specific and are not transferable, only the methodological point is
citation: J Orthop Sports Phys Ther, 2018. The Influence of Injury Definition on Injury Burden in Preprofessional Ballet and Contemporary Dancers.
ppbf_implication: PPBF must FIX and PUBLISH its injury definition before computing any safety rate (KPI B4-K043), and must break the trend series if the definition ever changes. Comparing a PPBF rate to any external rate computed under a different definition is invalid.
verified_title: The Influence of Injury Definition on Injury Burden in Preprofessional Ballet and Contemporary Dancers.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
claim: An analysis using two oncology phase II trials as worked examples plus simulation showed that informative censoring biases the Kaplan-Meier estimate, with the magnitude of bias depending primarily on the proportion of patients informatively censored and secondarily on the hazard ratio between censored and continuing patients.
study_design: Methodological paper with worked trial examples and simulation study
effect_or_estimate: Bias magnitude driven mainly by the proportion informatively censored, secondarily by the hazard ratio between groups
transfer_status: METHODOLOGICAL - applies to any survival analysis including sport retention
limitations: Oncology context; the principle transfers but the specific magnitudes do not
citation: J Clin Oncol, 2014. Impact of informative censoring on the Kaplan-Meier estimate of progression-free survival in phase II clinical trials.

track: B4 Gym Operations - Success Definition, KPIs, Retention
topic: Cluster structure must be accounted for in program analysis
claim: Methodological literature on cluster randomised and multicentre designs establishes that observations grouped within clusters (classes, coaches, sites) are correlated, that the intraclass correlation coefficient governs the design effect, and that designs with small numbers of clusters require specific analytic treatment.
study_design: Statistical methodology papers on cluster design and analysis
effect_or_estimate: Design effect determined by cluster size and the intraclass correlation; small-cluster designs require adjusted methods
limitations: Written for trial design; PPBF's setting is observational, so the relevance is to standard-error estimation rather than to randomisation
citation: Stat Methods Med Res, 2011. Efficient design of cluster randomized and multicentre trials with unknown intraclass correlation. Supporting: Stat Med, 2020. Design and analysis of three-arm parallel cluster randomized trials with small numbers of clusters.
verification: pubmed:PMID 21937473 and PMID 33258219 (searched and metadata retrieved)
ppbf_implication: Athletes are clustered within coaches and classes. The dropout model must use a random effect or standard errors clustered on coach or class; ignoring clustering understates uncertainty and would make coach-level differences look more real than they are - a direct input to the prohibition on coach ranking (KPI B4-K115).
verified_title: Efficient design of cluster randomized and multicentre trials with unknown intraclass correlation.
